communities.name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the bands, the sessions
communities.parent_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band
communities.narrative: Nearly every sample is a musician's memory of Jelly Roll Morton, told by about eighty interviewees from the Tulane and Rutgers collections, with a few from the Smithsonian and Hamilton. The stories run from his Gulf Coast boyhood and Storyville and Chicago days (1900s-1920s) through the Red Hot Peppers recording sessions of the late 1920s to his New York years and his last tours and recordings around 1938-39. Tellers describe him as a flashy dresser, a braggart who claimed to have invented jazz, a lecturer, and a man who could be both unkind and generous. They also recall the practical side of working for him: who played on which record date, how loose or how carefully written his arrangements were, one-nighters in broken-down cars, and short, poorly paid tours. Opinions differ on his standing: some defend him as the inventor of jazz and a gifted composer, while Danny Barker says he had no following among Black audiences. Several tellers had no idea who he was at first. The only clear outlier is Machito's account of how "Tanga" came about, which does not involve Morton.

Recording sessions: personnel, arrangements and who played on which sides

communities.name: Fats Waller: appetites, bottles and big-hearted fun
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Almost every sample is a musician's memory of Fats Waller, mostly from 1920s Harlem and the 1930s, with the last recollections placed in 1943. The tellers are sidemen, bandleaders, a manager, friends and younger players, and they largely agree on one picture: Waller as a generous, larger-than-life entertainer. The stories centre on his enormous appetite (25 hamburgers on the bus to Atlantic City, three chickens and three steaks at one sitting), his drinking (gin on a tray, bottles for every bandsman, whisky from a pail) and his gestures of kindness, such as filling the Howard Theater with neighborhood kids and candy or buying a coat for his barber's family. The venues recur: the Lincoln and Lafayette theatres, Connie's Inn and the Apollo, where he played organ and fronted his big band. The accounts differ in focus. Some are about his musicianship and band leadership, others about his managers and recording work, and the last are about his death on a train in 1943. A few samples have nothing to do with Waller, among them tap dancer Walter Beatty, the Cafe Society boogie-woogie pianists and Fats Domino's producer, so the cluster has some stray edges.

communities.name: Drafted: musicians in the wartime armed services
communities.parent_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years
communities.narrative: Musicians recall being called up, dodging, or being rejected for the draft in the Second World War, mostly between 1941 and 1946. Some were inducted into Army, Navy, Marine, or Air Force units, where they often ended up in service bands, chorales, or USO shows. Kenny Clarke gives the fullest account: Camp Upton, segregated training, a chaplain who kept him off D-Day, racial violence at a camp, the 13th Special Service chorale, and demobilisation at Fort Dix. Others tell shorter stories of avoiding service. Charlie Barnet was inducted seven times and never taken, and Basie and Lester Young are variously said to have been drafted or to have got out. The draft also broke up bands, and Lester Young and Jo Jones leaving Basie is told by Basie, Jo Jones, and Freddie Green. Segregation runs through the Black musicians' accounts, and Slam Stewart remarks on the irony of fighting for a country that denied them rights. A few samples drift to wartime civilian work or overseas touring, and one is a 1960s Cuban draft, so the cluster is dominated by draft and service but is not perfectly pure.
threads: Called up, inducted, or rejected: the draft and how musicians avoided it

communities.name: Reading the crowd: who the audience was
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: Musicians from very different eras and scenes talk about the audiences they played for and how those crowds shaped what they did. The stories run from 1920s New Orleans dances and the Jean Goldkette band, through 1940s big-band crowds and 1950s Dixieland clubs and R&B circuits, to Brisbane in the early 1960s, Beijing in 1997 and a Zoom jam session in 2020. The tellers agree that an audience is something you have to learn to read. Its makeup depends on the venue, its age and its expectations. A mismatch, such as a swing arrangement played to a traditional-jazz crowd, shows up quickly. Differences lie in the kind of audience described: packed rooms demanding authentic Dixieland, young working-class listeners, attentive chamber-style listeners, a mostly senior online group, and a Beijing crowd that rejected Chinese instruments in jazz. Cosimo Matassa adds a recording-side view, where a record has to stand alone because buyers lack the club atmosphere. The cluster is small and the common thread is broad, so it holds together as a theme rather than as one shared event.
threads: Misreading and learning to read an audience
Crowds that packed the room or demanded a style (Dixieland, R&B circuit)

communities.name: Brother Richard Spikes, barber and inventor
communities.parent_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
communities.narrative: Almost every story here comes from one interview, with Benjamin "Reb" Spikes, who talks about his brother Richard Spikes, a barber who spent his nights inventing. The inventions run from the early 1900s to Richard's death in 1965. They include a railroad block signal that reportedly paid about $400,000 from backers in Bisbee, with Hiram Johnson's support and Earl Warren as his lawyer. Others are an automotive gearshift, a rotating barber chair, a metal milk-bottle cap, a tank sampler sold to Shell, and a hydraulic bootblack chair taken to New York in 1938-40 until the war stopped production. Wartime patents appear too: a guided torpedo the government took and a dive-bomber machine gun. A few passages cover brother Johnny's smaller inventions, such as a writing guide for the blind. Patricia Willard, the interviewer, reads from the patent list at one point. One outlier comes from Lee Paige, who designed a "New Look" men's suit in the late 1940s. It is a different kind of inventiveness and has nothing to do with the Spikes family. The story is not about music, but it does show how a musician's family made a living and how Black entrepreneurs got patents and commercial backing.

communities.name: Leaving Cuba: defection, exile and the green card
communities.parent_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Most of the stories here are told by Cuban jazz musicians, chiefly Paquito D'Rivera and Ignacio Berroa, about leaving Cuba and what it cost them. They are set mainly around 1980: the Peruvian Embassy crisis and the Mariel boatlift pushed D'Rivera to defect from a European tour by walking out of the Madrid airport. Berroa escaped by boat, and Luis Conte was sent out alone as a boy in 1967 after Castro's military decree. The tellers agree that the state controlled what, when and with whom musicians played, that jazz and the Beatles were treated as hostile, and that families were effectively held hostage against defection. They differ in what they stress. D'Rivera gives a detailed, repeated account of the escape and how officials and bandmates reacted, and explains why Chucho Valdés stayed. Berroa dwells on his father's break with the revolution and on why people flee Cuba rather than the reverse. After arrival, the stories turn to the paperwork of staying, such as the US consul's interview, the wait for a green card, and the call home on tricked Madrid payphones. Hide Tanaka's green card story, about a Japanese bassist who overstayed his visa, and a Mississippi prison-escape story from Matthew Maxey are looser fits that share only the theme of fleeing or getting papers.
threads: D'Rivera's 1980 defection at the Madrid airport
Mariel boatlift and Peruvian Embassy crisis escapes

communities.name: Heading north: first trips to Chicago
communities.parent_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene
communities.narrative: Many musicians, mostly Black and mostly from New Orleans, Mississippi and Tennessee, tell how they first got to Chicago as boys or teenagers, between about 1903 and the late 1920s. They often ran away or slipped off, riding freight trains, coal tenders and railroad passes. Alberta Hunter, Zutty Singleton, Eddie Barefield and Russell Moore tell these as adventures with hardship in them: hunger, jail, homesickness, sleeping in odd places, and sending home for fare. Milt Hinton, Andrew Blakeney and Danny Barker tell it from the family side, as part of the Great Migration. They describe Chicago as the country's crossroads, with railroad, stockyard, porter and hotel jobs for Black families. The cluster also picks up a few weaker neighbours: travel in the other direction, to New Orleans or elsewhere, and interview openings. The tellers agree on how Chicago drew migrants. They differ on whether the trip was a family move or an escape, and on how much music figured in it.

communities.name: Monk Montgomery's fight for jazz in Las Vegas
communities.parent_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work
communities.narrative: In the early 1970s Monk Montgomery, the bassist, takes a call from Red Norvo about a three-week Las Vegas job. The word "Vegas" angers him, and he agrees only because Norvo says he is stuck. He plays the Tropicana lounge, where the entertainment director wanted jazz. That run ends around 1972 with the Red Norvo Trio, while the Blue Room books Basie, Sarah Vaughan and Armstrong. Unable to find a real jazz outlet, Monk turns from performing to hustling. He refuses showroom jobs as tokenism, pitches a Hilton director's four-wall idea (the director then dies), and writes an M-G-M proposal for a jazz theater with Sunday spectaculars. An M-G-M executive refuses to discuss it, which is his biggest disappointment. After he talks to Billboard and the trades, he gets threatening phone calls. A month with The Drifters at the Sahara is one of his worst musical experiences, though it gets him back to Las Vegas. Nearly all the central samples come from one Rutgers interview with Monk. The few outsiders, such as Doug Carn defending Vegas and Chitlin Circuit players, only touch on the topic. The shared story is a single musician's, not a story different musicians tell in common.
threads: Norvo's call and the Tropicana lounge jazz job

communities.name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader
communities.parent_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader
communities.narrative: Nearly every segment here is a musician's account of Benny Goodman, told by players, producers and critics who auditioned for him, toured with him, turned him down or watched him work. The stories span roughly 1930 to 1975, running from the Ben Pollack band and Chicago and New York in the early 1930s, through the swing-era big band, the small groups and the 1949 bebop band, to the 1962 State Department tour of the Soviet Union and his late-career bands of the 1970s and 80s. Tellers largely agree on his character: a demanding perfectionist with a famous glare, careful about time, dress and written parts, moody and eccentric, tight with pay and contracts, yet capable of generosity, such as the fugue he joined Benson in or the introduction he gave Zottola. They differ on how they judged him. Some enjoyed working for him, Buddy Tate for one, while others, like Marian McPartland, felt he disliked their playing. Others chose not to join his band, among them Art Hodes, Juan Tizol and Ted Bunn. The tellers are mostly sidemen, drummers and bassists, plus a few critics and managers, and they set Goodman against Artie Shaw, Teddy Wilson, Gene Krupa and John Hammond. A handful of samples, such as Kirkeby's agency stories and Roland Hanna on Mingus, only touch Goodman in passing, but the cluster as a whole is his leadership and the experience of being in or near his bands.
threads: Auditions, offers and joining the band
Goodman's perfectionism, glare and moods

communities.name: Working under the great conductors
communities.parent_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press
communities.narrative: Jazz and studio musicians recall their encounters with classical conductors and soloists, mostly in the 1940s through the 1960s. Rudy Mazzari, a New Orleans Symphony bassist and librarian, supplies the most detail. He describes Heifetz insisting on louder basses in Indianapolis, Stokowski walking off during a Mardi Gras ball, Freccia struggling to explain himself in English, Hilsberg, and Milstein coming in wrong at rehearsal. Others tell shorter stories about Bernstein (his pulse, his City Center Symphony, the Met), Fritz Reiner inviting Muggsy Spanier to a Philharmonic rehearsal after hearing him at Nick's, and Toscanini and Stokowski premiering the Shostakovich Seventh. The tellers share an interest in how a conductor's beat, temperament and rehearsal manner treated players. They differ in setting, from symphony halls and opera pits to Condon's and recording dates. The pack is only loosely a single story, since a few samples are about admired individual musicians or jazz-in-the-orchestra disputes rather than conductors.

communities.name: Sportin' Life: John W. Bubbles in Porgy and Bess
communities.parent_name: Band singers and accompanying vocalists
communities.narrative: This cluster is dominated by John W. Bubbles's first-person account of being cast as Sportin' Life in George Gershwin's Porgy and Bess, set around its 1935 premiere in New York. Gershwin picked him after watching his vaudeville act repeatedly, working through his manager, and then coached him privately at home on "It Ain't Necessarily So" and the "boat to New York" song because Bubbles and his partner Buck Washington could not read music. Bubbles tells the rehearsal and opening-night stories in vivid scene-by-scene detail: conductor Alexander Smallens threatening to throw him out for missing a downbeat while Gershwin called him a "black Toscanini", missing his entrance and leaping down four flights of stairs, and coming in late on the happy dust scene with Bess. He also describes the production team, where Gershwin left staging to others and the only conflict was DuBose Heyward wanting the lyrics heard against Gershwin wanting the music. Chuck Green adds a second-hand note praising Bubbles's Sportin' Life as a favorite of Gershwin. One sample, Joe Wilder clashing with a conductor and winning the principal trumpet chair through blind auditions under Jonel Perlea, shares only the jazz-musician-in-classical-music thread and does not belong to the Porgy and Bess story.
threads: Gershwin choosing Bubbles after watching his act
Private coaching because he and Buck could not read music

communities.name: Nat King Cole before stardom: the Los Angeles years
communities.parent_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds remember Nat King Cole in the years before and just as he became a star, mostly in Los Angeles and Hollywood between about 1937 and the late 1940s. Bassist John Simmons tells the most detailed version: taking the bass job in Cole's band at the Ubangi Club in 1937, befriending Nat and his wife Nadine, watching Nat begin to sing, and later seeing him protect his voice in 1947. Others recall hearing the trio before it was famous (JJ Johnson at the Three Sixes, Slam Stewart and Budd Johnson at Hollywood parties and sessions, Harry Edison at an early date at Glen Wallichs' studio). Several stress the lean early years and the surprise that Cole became a vocalist: Red Callender recalls shared ham hocks and beans and the trio with Wesley Prince and Oscar Moore, and Ernie Fields says Cole told him he too had once claimed he could not sing. Leon Rene, who recorded the trio, and Chuck Mancuso, who argues Cole deserved his record sales, give the business and popular-success angle. A few segments (Wilbur Ware in Chicago in 1953, Cole's brother Eddie in Chicago) stretch the story beyond Los Angeles, but the shared subject remains personal memories of Cole and his trio.

communities.name: Hoboing freight trains across the Depression Southwest
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Young Black musicians recall riding freight trains and hoboing during the Depression, roughly 1929 to 1936, mostly across Texas, Oklahoma and toward California. Buck Clayton describes riding inside, under and on top of freight cars on the way to Los Angeles in 1929. John Simmons tells a run of connected stories from 1935: being put off a train near Amarillo, walking through a dust storm, being chased out of Dalhart by a railroad detective and posse, and riding a fruit train to Los Angeles. Howard McGhee is thrown off the train near Amarillo while heading for California. Jay McShann and Buster Smith tell similar tramping stories from Tennessee, Kentucky and Ohio, with broke musicians dodging railway agents and sharing hobo fires and meals. The tellers agree that travel was cheap, dangerous and improvised, and that Black travelers faced hostility in certain towns. They differ mainly in destination, with California for some and home or the next job for others. Milt Hinton's visit to a Texas house he stayed in during 1936, with the Joe Louis fight on the radio, is a looser fit that shares the place and period but not the hoboing.

communities.name: Making a living in New York jazz, 1958-70
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: These stories are set in New York City from the late 1950s to about 1970, and they share one loose thread: how jazz people kept things going when the commercial side of jazz was shaky. The largest block is Dan Morgenstern's account of his own working life: the New York Post, early liner notes for Prestige at $35 a piece, the fall and rescue of Metronome, his unpaid editing of Bob Thiele's Jazz magazine (paid in liner notes), and freelance translating. Around that sit musicians' accounts of building their own structures: the 1964 October Revolution in Jazz organised by Cecil Taylor and Bill Dixon, the Jazz Composers Orchestra and its record distribution, Tom McIntosh's co-op New York Jazz Sextet, the Collective Black Artists in 1969 with $2 dues and concerts in Ornette Coleman's loft, and 1970s loft jazz. Orrin Keepnews's remark on Cannonball keeping control of his work, compared with Wes Montgomery and Monk at their labels, fits the theme only loosely. The tellers agree that money and venues were scarce and that musicians and writers had to organise themselves, but they come from different worlds (a critic and editor, avant-garde players, a producer-composer), so the shared subject is a general one rather than a single event.
threads: Morgenstern at Metronome, the New York Post and liner-note work

communities.name: Ben Webster: gentle, drunken, beloved tenor man
communities.parent_name: Bandstand fights, knives and tempers
communities.narrative: Nearly every sample is a musician's portrait of tenor saxophonist Ben Webster, told by sidemen, bandleaders and friends from Kansas City and Chicago in the 1930s through 52nd Street and the Ellington years in the 1940s, then Washington, New York and finally Copenhagen and Europe in the 1960s. The tellers agree on a double character. Sober, he was sweet, generous, funny, a champion storyteller and a great ballad player who could make you cry. Drunk, he was volatile and fierce, and the stories give incidents: a razor at the Three Deuces, a rifle at a Harlem window that landed him in Bellevue, a hotel window in Philadelphia, a fight Mingus ran from, and a tooth knocked out of Billie Holiday's dog. They differ on how bad it was. Some, like Maxwell and Eddie Alley, remember a gentle friend, and Maxwell even remembers a teetotaler. Others, like Collins, Simmons and Frishberg, remember danger. Cliff Leeman adds a distinct strand of cowboy gear, horseback riding and a dog in Rock Creek Park in 1947-48. Smaller strands cover his rivalry with Don Byas, his path from Horace Henderson's band to Fletcher Henderson and Duke Ellington, and his late friendships in Europe.

communities.name: Playing the White House for presidents
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians recall being booked to play for sitting presidents and their guests, from Truman's 1949 inaugural ball and the Roosevelt-era dances, through Kennedy's intern concerts, Johnson's inauguration and state dinners, Nixon's 1969 Duke Ellington 70th birthday party, and the Ford, Carter, Reagan and Clinton years. The stories are set mostly in Washington, D.C. and at the White House, with a notable detour to the 1988 Reagan-Gorbachev summit in Moscow, where Dave Brubeck, who supplies about a quarter of the segments, played for dissidents and generals. Tellers range from big-band sidemen such as Cliff Leeman and Russell Moore, who worked inaugural balls and society dates with Lester Lanin, to bandleaders and stars such as Brubeck, Percy Heath, Dorothy Donegan, Clark Terry and Milt Hinton. They agree that the invitation was the high point of a career, and they dwell on logistics: how the gig came about, who else was on the bill, protocol and receiving lines, outfits, and photographs or tapes of the night. They differ in tone, from pride and anecdote to Mingus's and Baker's wary remarks on the politics behind the invitations, and Heath's pointed song about Watergate.
threads: Ellington's 70th birthday party at the Nixon White House
Inaugural balls and society dates from Truman to Carter
Brubeck at the Kennedy and Johnson White House and the 1988 Moscow summit
Clinton-era White House jazz and the Newport anniversary
Politics behind the invitations, from Rockefeller to Watergate
Getting booked, outfits, photographs and who shared the bill

communities.name: Tracking down musicians: addresses and relatives
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: This cluster is mostly interviewer-driven talk about locating other musicians rather than a story the players tell. In the clearest segments, interviewers ask for addresses, phone numbers, wives and relatives of fellow musicians. Examples are Walter Blue's wife and relatives, Alvin Pernell or Alton Purnell on Dolphin Street, Joe Rena's address, and the Celestin band members' addresses. The Tulane interviews supply most of these, and the musicians in them are mainly New Orleans players, many of whom had moved to California. Most of the search talk takes place during the interview itself, so no period can be assigned. Tellers respond by naming neighbors, churches, streets, sisters-in-law and other contacts who might lead to the person. A looser group of segments strays from this into brief identifications of people or asides. These include Phil Wilson's daughter being named for Marian McPartland, a Brubeck aside about a wealthy supporter that Gioia says will be edited out, Princess Belle's surname, and Jack Jenny's wife Bonnie Lake. The shared subject is real in the first half and thin in the rest, so the cluster is only partly coherent.
threads: Asking for addresses and phone numbers
Finding a musician's wife or relatives
Neighborhood and church landmarks as leads
New Orleans musicians who moved to California
Side remarks identifying wives, friends and supporters

communities.name: Early New Orleans bands and the players who worked them
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: This small cluster gathers life-and-career recollections of New Orleans musicians and associates, set mostly between about 1908 and 1940. The tellers, drawn largely from the Tulane archive with a few from Rutgers, move through family backgrounds, first instruments, first jobs and the bands they worked in, such as Papa Celestin's, Sam Morgan's, Papa Jack Laine's Reliance Band, the Halfway House Orchestra and King Oliver's. They name rival pianists and trumpeters, venues like the Gypsy Tea Room, Club Desire and Canal and Rampart Street dives, and they place Louis Armstrong, Bolden, Oliver and Jelly Roll Morton as reference points. Some segments are long fused blocks, such as short biographical interviews or a family history of the Brunies brothers, and several drift into side subjects like race relations, black radio, a print shop job or why a player stayed in New Orleans. The tellers share a milieu rather than one event, so the cluster reads as a loose set of local band-and-biography stories rather than a single shared story.
threads: Family backgrounds, first horns and first jobs
Working in Celestin, Morgan, Laine and Oliver bands
Honky-tonk and dive venues on Decatur, Canal and Rampart
Louis Armstrong, Bolden and Morton as yardsticks
Rivalries among local pianists and trumpeters
New Orleans race relations, radio and nightlife

communities.name: Bebop-era bands and the Max Roach–Clifford Brown circle
communities.parent_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band
communities.narrative: These segments are musicians' recollections of the small groups and bandstands of the late 1940s through the 1950s, with a loose center of gravity in the Max Roach Quintet, Clifford Brown, Sonny Rollins and the Philadelphia players around them. Several tellers describe how a working group came together: Dave Brubeck's octet forming in Milhaud's class, the Milt Jackson Quartet growing into the Modern Jazz Quartet, and Jerome Richardson's quartet. Others recall joining Max Roach's band after Clifford Brown's death, including Barry Harris and Charles Lloyd on Booker Little's grief. Minton's Playhouse, Birdland and 52nd Street recur as places where players met and sat in. Toshiko Akiyoshi's USO-era encounters with Pettiford's group and Oscar Peterson, and Philly Joe Jones's naming story, add the view from younger players, outsiders and sidemen. The tellers share a period and a circle of names, but not one event. Some stories are about forming a band, others about a person's temperament, and a few drift off topic, such as Chuck Green's tap dancers and Norman Brownlee's visit from Charlie Spivak.
threads: How small groups formed: Brubeck's octet, the Milt Jackson Quartet becoming the MJQ
Joining Max Roach's band after Clifford Brown's death
Minton's, Birdland and 52nd Street as meeting places
Portraits of Philly Joe Jones, Clifford Brown and Max Roach
Toshiko Akiyoshi and the USO-era musicians
Auditions and sideman gigs with Rollins, Mongo and Richardson

communities.name: Learning to play Latin and Brazilian music on the job
communities.parent_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: Jazz musicians from many generations recall being thrown into Latin and Brazilian music and having to learn it quickly, often by getting it wrong in public first. The clearest version is Doc Cheatham's, set in New York in the 1940s: Mario Bauza fired him on the first night, and Machito later fired him again, because he could not lock in with the rhythm. He learned the beat in a conjunto, was rehired, and eventually toured with Machito and played in Marcelino Guerra's band. Later players tell the same story with other bandleaders: Kenny Barron learned the Latin repertoire and first played bossa nova with Dizzy Gillespie, David Finck learned Latin and samba bass lines in Paquito D'Rivera's band, and Vince Lateano learned regional grooves from Poncho Sanchez in Cal Tjader's group. Younger tellers describe deliberate study of instruments and feels, such as Jason Marsalis on bata and Casa Samba, Chris Parker on Latin rhythms after the Bolero session, and Arturo O'Farrill on conga and timbale patterns. Around these sit several looser items: Big Nick Nicholas and Billy Taylor on Latin bands and dance clubs in 1940s New York, Joe Wilder fronting a fake Spanish band, and recording sessions with Latin percussionists. The tellers agree that Latin music was a separate discipline that had to be learned, but they differ on whether the lesson came from a bandleader, a percussionist or records.
threads: Fired for not hearing the clave: Doc Cheatham with Bauza, Machito and Guerra
Learning Latin and bossa nova in Dizzy Gillespie's and other bandleaders' bands
Studying percussion and rhythms deliberately: conga, timbales, bata, samba
Latin bands and dance clubs in 1940s-60s New York
Brazilian music and bossa nova reaching American players
Latin jazz recording sessions and pioneers such as Tjader and Puente

venues: That Was the Week That Was

communities.name: Bossa nova arrives: Jobim, Getz and Brazil
communities.parent_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds describe encountering Brazilian music, above all the bossa nova wave of the early 1960s, and what it meant to them. The core story is the arrival of the music through Joao Gilberto and Antonio Carlos Jobim's records and through Stan Getz and Charlie Byrd, who brought it to American audiences. Jon Hendricks gives the most detailed account. In 1962 he wrote English lyrics for Desafinado after other lyricists declined, wrote One Note Samba, met Jobim, and took part in a State Department-sponsored Brazilian concert in New York. Others, such as Gil Evans, Kenny Burrell, Bob Rosengarden and Big Nick Nicholas, talk about the music's harmony, its role for the guitar, and how its feel differs from Latin rhythm. Gus Johnson recalls touring Brazil with Ella Fitzgerald and the World's Greatest Jazz Band and learning the beat. Later voices from the 1970s to the 1990s, including Tom Lellis, Slide Hampton and Kenny Barron, tell of discovering Brazilian music through friends, hearing Brazilian communities in Paris, or forming a group with Trio da Paz. The tellers agree it is sophisticated, romantic and close to jazz. They differ in whether they met it as a 1962 craze or as a lasting influence. A few samples, such as Horace Henderson's on Getz in DownBeat, only touch the subject.
threads: Hendricks writing English lyrics for Desafinado and One Note Samba
Getz, Byrd and Jobim bringing bossa nova to the US in 1962
Brazilian rhythm versus Latin feel and the role of the guitar
Touring Brazil and learning the bossa nova beat
Later encounters with Brazilian musicians and Trio da Paz

communities.name: Playing with Miles Davis: sidemen's recollections
communities.parent_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell stories about working with, meeting or watching Miles Davis, from his St. Louis and Juilliard beginnings in the early 1940s through the electric band of the early 1970s and the late-1980s sidemen. Elvin Jones recalls Miles recovering in Detroit in 1955. Lee Konitz recalls the 1948-50 nonet and its Royal Roost weeks. Jimmy Cobb tells of Kind of Blue and of leaving the band for Tony Williams. Ron Carter calls the 1960s quintet a laboratory, and Dave Liebman describes On the Corner, the lack of rehearsals and the 1974 Carnegie Hall concert. JJ Johnson and Clark Terry tell friends' stories of Miles's generosity, his addiction years and his sitting in on dates. The tellers agree that Miles gave little direction and led by example and by shifting the music's direction. They differ in period and in what they stress: recording sessions, band mechanics, personal anecdotes or disputes about the biographies. A few samples only mention Miles in passing (Phil Woods on Gil Evans, Art Farmer on a 1995 session, Cobb on his trio), so the common thread is a person rather than one event.
threads: Joining the band: how sidemen got the Miles job
Recording sessions: Kind of Blue, the nonet, Walkin', On the Corner
Band mechanics: no rehearsals, little direction, the quintet as laboratory
Friends' anecdotes: addiction years, generosity, sitting in
Going electric and the early 1970s band
Leaving Miles and who replaced whom

communities.name: Remembering Cannonball Adderley: the man, the band, the sound
communities.parent_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers musicians' and producers' recollections of alto saxophonist Cannonball Adderley, and of his brother Nat and their quintet. Nearly all the tellers are younger players, critics or record people (many are Monk Rowe's Fillius Jazz Archive interviewees) who heard him live, met him, or learned from his records between the 1950s and 1980s. Many describe him as a person: joyful, warm, humble, intelligent, hospitable, with a huge appetite, a former teacher who talked to and educated his audiences. Others speak about his playing, citing his tone, his command of the alto, his fluency by ear and his ballads, often by naming records such as Country Preacher, Mercy Mercy Mercy, Big Man, the Village Vanguard album and the Nancy Wilson date. Some are first-hand accounts of playing, recording or touring with him (Yusef Lateef, Ernie Watts, Phil Woods, Kidd Jordan), and the tellers largely agree on his generosity and musicianship. A few segments drift off Cannonball to other subjects, such as George Avakian's Columbia productions and Russell Procope's refusal to recreate the Kirby band, but they are the exception.
threads: Cannonball as a warm, funny, generous person
Hearing him live and meeting him
His alto tone, ear and influence on younger saxophonists
Records discussed: Country Preacher, Mercy Mercy Mercy, Big Man, Nancy Wilson
Playing, recording and touring with the Adderley quintet
Nat Adderley and the Adderleys' early years and business

communities.name: Working with Bill Evans: hiring, recording, remembering
communities.parent_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band
communities.narrative: Nearly every sample is a musician or producer talking about Bill Evans, who is tagged in 19 of the 45 segments and whose trio in 8. The stories run from the mid-1950s New York club scene to his death around 1980. Early on, George Russell meets him on the Staten Island ferry, Sam Most hears him as the intermission pianist at The Composer, and Orrin Keepnews finds him through Mundell Lowe's demo and records his first trio album. Keepnews also tells of the poor sales, the cover quotes from Miles Davis and others, and the 1961 Village Vanguard recordings made days before Scott LaFaro's death. Gunther Schuller recalls hiring Evans for Atlantic, his solo on All About Rosie, playing Wagner piano scores together, and helping him with money for drugs. Sidemen and collaborators such as Ron Carter, Lee Konitz, Toots Thielemans, Marty Morell and Joe LaBarbera describe recording dates, auditioning for the trio, and his lack of ego and his commitment. Late-life accounts, including David Baker on the Living Time date, deal with his decline. The tellers broadly agree on his musical gift and integrity. They differ on the rumored personal troubles: Carter says he never saw any, while Schuller describes the drug problem directly.
threads: Discovering and first recording Evans in the 1950s
Keepnews on sales, cover quotes and the 1961 Vanguard sessions
Schuller, Wagner and Evans at Atlantic
Sidemen recording with Evans and auditioning for the trio
Evans's character, drugs and late-life decline
Comping and harmonic influence on other pianists

communities.name: Joining Dizzy Gillespie's band
communities.parent_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: Musicians from several generations tell how they came to play with Dizzy Gillespie and what the band was like from inside. The stories run from his first 52nd Street group and the 1944 Eckstine band, through the late-1940s big band with its Afro-Cuban repertoire, to the 1950-51 sextet, the 1956-60 State Department-era big band and small groups, and Kenny Barron's and Ignacio Berroa's hires in 1962 and 1981. Recurring beats are how the call came (a recommendation from Ike Quebec, Mario Bauza, James Moody or Quincy Jones, or an audition), who was in the personnel, and the learning that followed. Players describe memorizing the book, reading Gillespie's conducting cues and hand signals, and the arrangers behind the sound, including Gil Fuller, Gerald Wilson and Melba Liston. They agree that the band was a school and an honor, though some, such as Benny Golson, found it humbling. They differ on the era, from the uneven ensembles of the Birdland Dream Band to the touring salary life of the quintet. A smaller group of samples, about Billy Eckstine's band, the Plantation, Don Redman's booked dates and the Famous Door, sits on the edge, as the tellers are mostly sidemen, arrangers and sitters-in.
threads: How the call came: recommendations, auditions and being hired unheard
Personnel lists of the 1946-50 big band and later sextets and quintets
Learning on the job: memorizing the book, conducting cues, hand signals, arrangers
Afro-Cuban influence and Latin recruits such as Candido and Berroa
Melba Liston as trombonist, arranger and musical director
Eckstine and other precursor bands of the mid-1940s that fed Dizzy's band

communities.name: Bud Powell: genius, breakdown and being looked after
communities.parent_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell stories about pianist Bud Powell, set mostly between 1942 and 1956 in Harlem, Philadelphia, Birdland and later Paris. The earliest accounts come from Cootie Williams's band, where Charlie Holmes remembers a seventeen-year-old who refused to play the theme as written, repaid a five-dollar loan with seven, and was called a genius even by a white bandleader. The most repeated episode is the Philadelphia beating by police and his hospitalisation (told by Cootie Williams, Al Hall and Jackie McLean). Around it come tales of electroshock and psychiatric damage, and of friends and neighbours who looked after him: McLean escorting him around Harlem, Mary Lou Williams calming him, and Percy Heath getting him home from Birdland. Younger players (McLean, Toshiko Akiyoshi, Chick Corea) recall meeting him, sitting in with him, or praising his composing. Tellers agree he was brilliant, fragile and damaged, and differ mainly in which phase of his life they saw. Nearly every segment is a portrait of the same man.
threads: Young Bud in Cootie Williams's band, 1942
The Philadelphia police beating and hospitalisation
Psychiatric treatment, electroshock and its damage
Looking after Bud in Harlem and at Birdland
Younger musicians meeting and sitting in with him
Bud as composer and pianist compared with peers

communities.name: Dizzy Gillespie the man: humor, generosity, mentor
communities.parent_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and all three major collections describe Dizzy Gillespie as a person rather than only as a trumpeter. The dominant picture is of a clown whose zaniness hid deep seriousness: Ira Gitler recalls Teddy Hill's "Dizzy like a fox", Mingus says the clown image hides warm playing, and Mike Longo describes "three Dizzy Gillespies" (the screwball, the spiritual John Gillespie and the serious musician). Tellers agree he was generous, accessible and an unusually good bandleader and teacher; Junior Mance, David Baker, Slide Hampton and J.J. Johnson (who contrasts him with the less approachable Parker) credit him with giving them opportunities, advice and a musical education. A second strand fixes particular moments around him: hearing him sit in with Cab Calloway in 1939, the Calloway firing story, the Eckstine and big-band years, Mario Bauza and Machito introducing him to Afro-Cuban rhythm and Chano Pozo, and late-life appearances at the Blue Note shortly before his death in 1993. The stories run from the late 1930s to the early 1990s and are told by bebop peers, Latin musicians, younger protégés and club promoters such as Joe Segal. They differ mainly in vantage point, some personal and affectionate, others tied to specific bands or events, and a few drift to Parker, Pozo or the teller's own career.
threads: Clown on the surface, serious musician underneath
Dizzy as generous mentor, teacher and employer
Dizzy and Bird as a pair, and Dizzy compared with other leaders
Calloway band years and the paper-airplane firing
Bauza, Machito and Chano Pozo bringing Afro-Cuban rhythm to Dizzy
Late-life encounters, birthday tributes and the last Blue Note nights

communities.name: Bucking contests between advertising wagon bands
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Nearly every sample tells the same story: before dances and ball games, New Orleans bands advertised from horse-drawn wagons and later trucks, and when two or three rival bands met on a street corner they "bucked" or "cut" each other, playing in turn or at once to draw the crowd. The tellers place it mostly in the 1910s and 1920s, with a few reaching back to the 1900s, and they name the same contenders: Jack Carey, Kid Ory, Buddy Petit, Punch Miller, Chris Kelly, Kid Rena, Sam Morgan and Joe Oliver. Corners such as Roman Street, Gravier Street and Tremé recur, along with National Park and the Fair Grounds. Tellers agree on the format, with applause or hall attendance deciding the winner, and on tricks like tying wagons together or playing soft to pull a crowd. They differ on whether a winner was ever declared, and on who came out ahead, with uptown favoring Carey and downtown favoring Olympia. Players from many bands tell it, as do a few white musicians who recall contests with Black bands. A couple of samples drift to other contests: a police ball repertoire and an out-of-town contest against Celestin.
threads: Advertising wagons and trucks as the stage for band battles
How winners were judged: applause, crowds, hall attendance
Famous matchups: Ory vs Carey, Punch vs Kid Rena, Kelly vs Rene
Tricks and tactics: tying wagons together, playing soft, swing
Cross-color and out-of-town contests

communities.name: Playing with and around Thelonious Monk
communities.parent_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: Musicians of several generations tell stories about Thelonious Monk the man and the musician, mostly set in New York from the late 1940s through the 1960s, with the Five Spot, the Village Vanguard and the Village Gate as recurring rooms. The tellers include sidemen and peers such as Roy Haynes, Elvin Jones, Sam Jones, Putter Smith and Eddie Bert, younger players such as Chick Corea, George Benson, Cedar Walton and Charles Tolliver, singers such as Sheila Jordan and Abbey Lincoln, and Lorraine Gordon, who promoted him in the late 1940s. They agree that his music was hard to follow and deceptively simple: odd tempos, extra bars, no rehearsals, and tricks that threw bassists and drummers. Many first dismissed or misunderstood him (Ramsey Lewis, Chuck Israels, John Simmons) and later came to treat him as a mentor and an essential repertory. They differ in tone, since some tell affectionate anecdotes of his silence, humor, dancing and falling off a stage, while others stress his generosity, his regard for other players, and his rehearsals for the big-band arrangements. A few segments drift to neighbouring subjects, such as Bud Powell, Mary Lou Williams and the drummer Monk Hazel, who is not Thelonious Monk.
threads: Misunderstanding Monk at first, then learning his music
Joining his band: no rehearsals, odd tempos and extra bars
Monk offstage: silence, humor, dancing and eccentric anecdotes
Gigs at the Five Spot, Village Vanguard and Village Gate
Monk as mentor and essential repertory for younger players
Promoting and documenting Monk: Lorraine Gordon, the big band, the planned biography

communities.name: Minton's Playhouse, Monk and the birth of bebop
communities.parent_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: Musicians recall Minton's Playhouse in Harlem in the early 1940s as the place where bebop was worked out, with Thelonious Monk at its center. Tellers such as Tiny Grimes, Slam Stewart, Happy Caldwell and Eddie Barefield describe the house band, the open sitting-in and the cutting sessions. Dizzy Gillespie, Kenny Clarke and Bud Powell appear alongside Monk, and Grimes calls it where modern jazz started. Mary Lou Williams adds the view from her own circle: Monk and Powell rehearsing a big band in a basement, Powell idolising Monk, and her apartment as a place where the new players gathered to write and play. A few accounts reach into the later 1940s, when Chico Hamilton and John Simmons heard or worked with Monk at the Royal Roost. Howard McGhee's account is about learning the new Minton's repertoire to keep up. The tellers agree that Minton's was the crucible. They differ on who deserves credit: Williams says Gillespie created real bebop and Monk worked for him. Most samples share this subject, but the loosest ones (Hamilton, McGhee, Simmons) are only tangentially about it.
threads: Minton's house band and open jam sessions
Monk's style and his rehearsal big band
Mary Lou Williams's circle: Bud Powell and her apartment
Cutting sessions and learning the new chords
Monk and Dizzy at the Royal Roost in the late 1940s

communities.name: Cutting the first bebop records in New York
communities.parent_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the recording dates of the mid-1940s and early 1950s where bebop was first put on record, mostly in New York. The strongest strand is the 1944-47 sessions around Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker and Coleman Hawkins. Budd Johnson describes Hawkins organizing the 1944 date with Dizzy, Clyde Hart and Howard McGhee, and the Savoy dates are recalled through their personnel and sponsor Herman Lubinsky. Sidemen such as Trummy Young, John Collins and Jimmy Maxwell tell it from the working side: they were hired for these small-group dates without belonging to the bands, and Collins says he was the first-call guitarist in New York. Buddy DeFranco recalls his Metronome All-Stars solo as his first recorded bebop, and JJ Johnson is vague about the chronology of the Hawkins and Parker records. Jackie McLean's 1951 Dig session with Miles Davis is a later outlier in the same record-date frame. The tellers often cannot recall personnel or dates exactly, and a few segments drift into New York as the center of the scene or into other bands such as Whiteman and Prado.
threads: Hawkins's 1944 date and the first bop records
Savoy dates, personnel and sponsor Lubinsky
Sidemen hired for Dizzy and Parker small-group sessions
Metronome All-Stars and first recorded bebop solos
Fuzzy memories of personnel and chronology
Miles Davis and Jackie McLean at the Dig session

communities.name: Black big bands on the 1940s theater and ballroom circuit
communities.parent_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows
communities.narrative: These stories are set mostly in the late 1930s through the 1940s. Musicians recall big bands and package shows playing the Black theater and club circuit: the Apollo, the Cotton Club, the Zanzibar and Savoy in New York and Harlem, the Paradise in Detroit, and the Palace, Dew Drop Inn and Dewdrop in the South. Some tell it as players inside the bands. Joe Thomas and Big Nick Nicholas describe Claude Hopkins's band, Roy Haynes and Gene Ramey describe Luis Russell's, and Hank Jones describes Billy Eckstine's. Others tell it as young fans in the audience, such as Tex Stephens in a Southern town and Teddy Edwards in Detroit, who remember touring bands like Andy Kirk's, Erskine Hawkins's and Basie's passing through. The tellers agree that the theater stage-show circuit was the main place to hear and work with these bands. They differ on perspective and place, and on whether they are talking about a band's personnel and quality or about the venues and acts. The cluster is loose, and the connecting thread is bands and venues rather than one event.
threads: Claude Hopkins's band at the Cotton Club, Roseland and the Zanzibar
Luis Russell's band and the Moe Gale package shows
Fans hearing touring bands at Southern theaters and dance halls (Tex Stephens)
Big-band stage shows at the Apollo and Paradise theatres
Billy Eckstine's band and the Cotton Club anecdote
Vocal groups sharing the bill: Ink Spots and the Cats and the Fiddle

bands: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

communities.name: Older players on bebop: baffled, hostile, or won over
communities.parent_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy
communities.narrative: Across about a hundred interviews, musicians who came up in swing, Dixieland and big-band jazz recall their reaction to bebop when Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker arrived in the 1940s. The setting is mostly New York, with Minton's Playhouse, 52nd Street and the Royal Roost as the places where many first heard it. Many tellers were hostile or puzzled. They said bop had too many notes, no melody and no tune to whistle, that it could not be danced to, and that it would ruin young players. Others, such as Doc Cheatham, Maxine Sullivan and Horace Henderson, admired Parker and Dizzy but could not or would not play it, or came to like it later. A smaller group read bebop in social terms: Billy Taylor, John Simmons and Luther Henderson see it as Black musicians reclaiming their music, or building harmonies to shut out outsiders. Others judge its effect on the audience, saying it was rude to ignore listeners and that it cost jazz the teenage dance crowd. The tellers also disagree on whether bop was a continuation of jazz tradition or a break from it. A few later-generation voices add a 1980s view, with festivals celebrating Bird and one listener who found the records dull until he heard Barry Harris live. A handful of samples are tangential, such as a Metronome All-Star session and a teaching story, but the opinion-of-bebop thread dominates.
threads: Dismissing bop: too many notes, no melody, not danceable
Hearing Dizzy and Bird for the first time at Minton's and on 52nd Street
Staying with swing or Dixieland rather than learning bop
Bop as Black pride and as a barrier to outsiders
Bop's effect on audiences, drummers and the big bands
Later conversions and retrospective appreciation

communities.name: First hearing bebop: Bird and Diz on record
communities.parent_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy
communities.narrative: Musicians from many places and generations tell of the moment they first heard bebop, usually through Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie. The setting is mostly the mid-1940s to early 1950s, though a few tellers place it later, in the 1960s or even the 1990s. Most first met the music on records: Parker's solos with Jay McShann, the Dial sides, "Things to Come", "One Bass Hit" and "Salt Peanuts". Others heard it live, on a troopship or Army furlough, in a barbershop, or in a city such as Paris, Chicago, Detroit or Indianapolis. Tellers often describe being puzzled or finding it foreign at first, then converted, and many say the encounter made them boppers. They learned the new vocabulary by slowing down records, analyzing them by ear, or copying Dizzy's heads. Swing players such as Frank Foster, Nat Hentoff and Pete Jolly describe the shift from Hodges, Carter or Basie to Parker, and some, like Roswell Rudd and Marian McPartland, came to bebop late or hesitantly. The group runs from saxophonists and pianists to vocalists, vibraphonists and a young bassist.
threads: Hearing Parker's records for the first time
Puzzled, then converted from swing
Learning bebop language by ear and from records
Hearing bebop in Paris, on troopships and on furlough
Local scenes taking up the new music (Indianapolis, Chicago, Detroit)
Family and friends handing over the records

communities.name: Knowing Charlie Parker: encounters and portraits of Bird
communities.parent_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds tell what it was like to meet, hear, play with or simply be around Charlie Parker, mostly in the years from the late 1930s to the early 1950s. The stories are set in Kansas City, New York (52nd Street, Birdland, the Apollo), Chicago and on tour with the McShann, Hines and Eckstine bands. Tellers recall first meetings (a barbecue-place jam, a Harlem sidewalk, a friend's house), sitting in with him, being invited to join his band, and short scenes such as the parakeet that greeted him, rabbit-skinning, chess and a borrowed couch. They broadly agree that he was intelligent, generous and kind, and that his playing was astonishing even when he was in poor shape or dozing. They differ on his personality: some found him businesslike or distant, others nurturing, and a few describe him putting people down. Addiction, money and the lack of recognition at the time run through many accounts. A lone dissenter, the collector Al Rose, finds him unexceptional. The tellers range from sidemen who worked with him (Malachi, Grimes, McGhee, Buster Smith, Haynes) to younger players and writers who met him briefly (Slide Hampton, Phil Woods, Gunther Schuller). A few segments only mention him in passing or are about other subjects, such as Roosevelt's death or Giants football.
threads: First meetings with Bird and what he was like as a person
Playing and sitting in with Parker: gigs, jams, invitations to join his band
Kindness, generosity and mentoring of younger players
Addiction, collapse and unreliability on and off the bandstand
Parker in the McShann, Hines and Eckstine bands
Recording dates, Birdland and JATP, and his practicing and musical ideas

communities.name: Remembering Milt Hinton, the beloved "Judge"
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Most of these segments are tributes to the bassist Milt Hinton, told by younger bassists and by colleagues who worked beside him from the 1930s and 40s onward. The tellers recall how they met him, at Michael's Pub, at Bill Lee's house with the New York Bass Choir, or through a contractor, and what they admired. They praise his sound and his slap technique, his stories, and his kindness and generosity. They also recall his "Judge" nickname, his calming presence on the bandstand, and his long friendships. Some tellers speak of his later years, including a 1996 illness and recovery, and an Arbors jazz party tribute around 2000. Cozy Cole and Jimmy Jones place him in the 1939-42 and 1940s-70s periods, while David Finck, Howard Alden and Nicki Parrott remember him in the 1980s and after. A few samples drift away from Hinton, toward Nat Hentoff's writing, Jaco Pastorius's Word of Mouth session, and Joe Wilder's humility. These outliers are marginal, so the cluster is one subject with a few strays.
threads: Meeting Milt Hinton for the first time
His sound, slap technique and bass legacy
The 'Judge' nickname and long friendships
Kindness, humility and character
Tributes, parties and his later years
Strays: Hentoff, Jaco's Word of Mouth, Joe Wilder

communities.name: John Hammond discovers and promotes Basie and others
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers stories about John Hammond, the producer and talent scout, and how his ear, money and connections moved musicians into the New York spotlight. The core is the mid-1930s Count Basie story. Hammond hears the band on Kansas City radio, writes letters, arrives at the black hotel in Kansas City in 1936, and helps bring Basie east. Basie men such as Jo Jones, Freddie Green, Buddy Tate and Joe Turner tell it, and so does Basie himself, who credits Hammond with being responsible for the band. Hammond is also credited with the Roseland opening, the Black Cat and Famous Door jobs, the Camel Caravan exposure and the Willard Alexander booking deal. Around this core are parallel scouting tales: Ernie Fields being tracked down in Tulsa and auditioned in Wichita in 1939, Hammond financing a raid on Nat Towles' Omaha band, and Teddy Wilson being found through the radio. The scope stretches to later Columbia signings (George Benson and Denny Zeitlin in the 1960s) and to Hammond's Black Cat jam nights and Spirituals to Swing. The tellers agree Hammond was generous and decisive, and differ mainly on which band he was backing and how big his role was. The setting is mostly New York and Kansas City, 1935 to 1942, told largely in the Rutgers interviews.
threads: Hammond comes to Kansas City and brings Basie to New York
Ernie Fields's 1939 audition and Hammond's tracking him down
Hammond's money and role behind Basie, Goodman and others
Black Cat and Village jam sessions, Roseland opening and the Freddie Green party
Later Columbia signings: Benson, Zeitlin and Hammond's legacy
Basie sidemen settling in New York: Woodside Hotel and hiring

bands: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

communities.name: What the early bands played: tunes and repertoire
communities.parent_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days
communities.narrative: Across about ninety interviews, mostly from the Tulane archive with a good share from Rutgers, musicians are asked what tunes their bands actually played and they answer by naming them. The tunes are the ragtime and early jazz standards of roughly 1900 to the 1940s: Tiger Rag (with its shouted "hold that tiger" and arguments over who played or sang it first), Maple Leaf Rag and other Joplin rags from the Red Back Book, High Society, Panama, St. Louis Blues, plus waltzes, quadrilles, blues and popular songs. Several tellers say how repertoire was gathered. Bands played by head, shared or bought sheet music from St. Louis publishers, and drew on the Red Book rags, and the readers and the fakers pull that in different directions. Others describe particular bands' lists, such as Jack Carey's, Papa Celestin's, Papa Jack Laine's, Bolden's and the Villa Venice band's. Later revivalists such as Nick Polites in Melbourne describe repertoire taken from Bunk Johnson and George Lewis records. The tellers agree that New Orleans repertoire mixed ragtime, blues, marches and dance numbers, but they differ on which rags were really played, how hard they were to read, and who introduced which tune.
threads: Tiger Rag: who played it first and the words sung to it
Joplin rags and the Red Back Book: hard to read, rarely played
Repertoire of a specific band: Carey, Celestin, Laine, Bolden
Playing by head versus sheet music, and sharing or buying books
Waltzes, quadrilles, blues and pop songs in dance and show sets
Revival-era repertoire taken from Bunk Johnson and George Lewis records

communities.name: Playing the blues for the tape recorder
communities.parent_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues
communities.narrative: These are moments when the interview stops being talk and turns into performance: the interviewee, or a host or companion, is asked to sing or play, usually blues, on the spot for the interviewer's recorder. Lemon Nash is the clearest case. He is asked what blues were played at Spano's or Kaiser's, names the honky-tonks and cabarets where he sang, and then plays and sings songs such as one about days of the week and one about three women in his life. Others do the same on a smaller scale. George Guesnon sings his own "Going Home Blues" as a favor for a Swedish band. Buddy Burns prepares to play a barrelhouse piano man. Johnny Lala and his hosts play tunes for visitors, and Roy Carew restarts a piece at the piano. Several segments are really tape chatter or logistics: hesitation about playing, poor light, a paused recording, a garbled transcript, or a session that ends on trumpet and trombone. Almost all come from Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, from many different interviewees, and they carry no clear period. The shared thread is music made during the recording session, not a common story or era, so the cluster is loosely coherent at best.
threads: Lemon Nash singing and playing old blues on guitar
Asked to play or sing for the interviewers or visitors
Performing an original blues as a favor or greeting
Hesitation, logistics and paused recordings around playing
Trying to recall a barrelhouse pianist or a song's source

communities.name: Songs on the tape: informal music-making at interviews
communities.parent_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers moments when the interview turns into an impromptu performance, or the tape simply captures singing, piano playing and room noise rather than recollection. Interviewers (often the Tulane field worker Allen) set up the microphone, test the recorder, or play back records, and interviewees, relatives and bystanders sing or play: Ida Goodson and Sammy Lee at the piano in 1961 with a freight train passing, Carrie Boote singing Alabama Bound, Lionel singing at Punch Miller's session, performance tapes of The Panic Is On, and a bawdy piano song amid chatter. A few segments drift into adjacent memory, such as ringaround games and forgotten old songs, whist and card games, Dalton Richards reminiscing on Sunday mornings, or Frank Amacker recalling the Spikes Brothers' music store on Central Avenue and singing the blues again. The tellers do not share a period or a story. What they share is that the music itself, not talk about it, is the content, and most of it comes from the Tulane collection. It is a loose grouping of performance and recording-mechanics segments, not one shared tale.
threads: Singing and playing for the microphone at home sessions
Tape set-up, playback and room chatter
Performance tapes with applause and guitar solos
Old songs, ringaround games and half-remembered tunes
Side topics: card games, the Spikes Brothers music store

communities.name: Quiet generosity: musicians helping musicians
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians tell stories of private acts of kindness and giving, most often toward other musicians in need. Gene Krupa secretly saved part of Red Rodney's pay, John Hammond quietly paid Sandy Williams's dentist, Jerry Lewis paid hospital bills for Frank Socolow's burned son, Pannonica de Koenigswarter lifted Monk, Sonny Clark and Art Blakey out of poverty, and Duke Ellington sent money and flowers during an operation (though he would not lend for a house). Others describe their own giving: Helen Humes tipping staff and mailing $100 checks, Danny Barker working with youth for nothing, Alberta Hunter clothing a ragged girl, Mary Lou Williams feeding people, and Jamey Aebersold sending instruments to prisoners. The tellers largely agree that giving is its own reward, and several say it comes back to you. The set is loosely held together: it runs from the 1940s to 2013 and drifts into pride, refusal of charity (Bartok, Dr. Mayer), a fraught favor to Sidney Bechet, and wistful reflections on lost friendships and aging in jazz. A few samples sit only at the edge of the theme.
threads: Bandleaders and patrons quietly paying a colleague's bills
Personal generosity: tipping, gifts, working for nothing
Aebersold's philanthropy and the prison instrument program
Refusing charity or payment out of pride
Feeding and housing fellow musicians in hard times
Loneliness and missing the jazz fraternity in later life

communities.name: Touring package shows and revues, 1940s-50s
communities.parent_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters
communities.narrative: Musicians recall joining or running multi-act touring packages and revues in the late 1940s and 1950s: Eddie Durham's 1947 Cavalcade of Jazz with Jack Teagarden and Dinah Washington, and his 1953 theater package with Little Richard's band. Others tell of the 1951 and 1952 big shows with Nat King Cole, Sarah Vaughan and Stan Kenton, and of Pullman-car stadium tours. Several set the story in Las Vegas, where Horace Henderson, Eddie Palmieri and Theodore Bunn worked the Billy Williams Revue, Tito Rodriguez's doomed show and Louis Jordan's group. Others cover Honolulu, a Miami Cotton Club revue and a Boston variety tour. The tellers agree on the logistics: who booked and staged the show, what the stars were paid, who backed which act. They differ in outcome, from hits to shows ruined by absconding promoters, lawyers or confusion. The tellers are mostly sidemen, arrangers and bandleaders. A few segments, such as Stanley Kay's correction about his role with Buddy Rich, are only loosely related.
threads: Cavalcade of Jazz and Eddie Durham's package shows
Big star packages with Nat Cole, Sarah Vaughan and Dinah Washington
Las Vegas revues of the 1950s
Backing rock and roll and R&B acts on the road
Staging, booking and promoter trouble
Show-band engagements in Miami, Honolulu and Boston

communities.name: Jazz musicians crossing into rock bands
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians from the jazz world tell how they landed gigs, sat in or toured with rock and pop acts and with big-name bandleaders, mostly from the 1970s to the 2000s and often set in New York. The clearest strand is Donald Fagen's Rock and Soul Revue and Steely Dan, told by Joe Ascione, Catherine Russell and Bernard Purdie, who describe being heard at clubs such as Elaine's or Catch a Rising Star and then getting the call. Branford Marsalis and David Murray recount sitting in with the Grateful Dead, playing Dark Star or appearing at Madison Square Garden, and admire the band's musicianship. Bobby Militello tells of the 1981 audition for the Dave Brubeck Quartet after Maynard Ferguson, and Sam Kininger describes opening for and sitting in with Dave Matthews Band. The tellers agree that the entry was a phone call or a chance to sit in, not a formal audition. Some samples, such as Joel Dorn's record-label account and Tim Ries's medley, drift away from this subject.
threads: Getting the call for Donald Fagen's Rock and Soul Revue and Steely Dan
Sitting in with the Grateful Dead
Auditioning for the Dave Brubeck Quartet in 1981
Opening for and sitting in with Dave Matthews Band
Record-label and session work on the pop side

bands: Donald Fagen's Rock and Soul Revue

communities.name: Papa Celestin's band: splits, wartime break, Paddock comeback
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Musicians who worked with or around Oscar "Papa" Celestin tell the history of his band and its personnel across three decades. The earliest stories, set in the mid-1920s, concern the split of the Tuxedo bands, a dispute over a dollar and the Southern Yacht Club contract, with Ba Ba Ridgley and Bill Matthews giving the Ridgley side and others recalling how Don Albert and Celestin pulled players away. A second strand is the early 1940s, when Celestin gave up music, took a shipyard job, broke his leg, and then formed a wartime band with Ricard Alexis, Albert Walters and others. The longest strand is the late-1940s and 1950s comeback at the Paddock Lounge on Bourbon Street, where Celestin took the job from Ridgley, demanded $300 a week, and fell ill. After his death Eddie Pearson took the band over. Tellers (sidemen like Albert Jiles, Joseph Thomas, Jeanette Kimball and Sidney Brown) agree on the broad outline of who played when, but often say they cannot speak to years they were away, and they differ on details such as who led the band at which point. A few samples drift to other bandleaders (Sam Morgan, Eddie Johnson, Pete Lala's) and are only loosely connected.
threads: The Tuxedo band split and Ridgley's dispute with Celestin (1920s)
Celestin's shipyard years, broken leg and 1941 wartime band
The 1949 Paddock Lounge comeback on Bourbon Street
Who played in Celestin's band and who replaced whom
Celestin's illness, $300 demand, death and Eddie Pearson taking over
Other bandleaders' breakups and personnel raids (Don Albert, Sam Morgan)

communities.name: Benny Carter: gentleman bandleader and arranger
communities.parent_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people
communities.narrative: Musicians who worked with or admired Benny Carter describe him as a dignified, courteous gentleman and a master arranger and bandleader. The stories are set mostly from the 1930s and 1940s (Carter's orchestra, around 1939 to 1941), with later recollections from the 1980s and 1990s of playing, recording or appearing with him. Sidemen such as Vic Dickenson, Horace Henderson, Bobby Johnson Jr. and Eddie Sauter stress his patient, thorough rehearsals, his perfectionism and the discipline of his band. They compare him to Don Redman, and Horace Henderson and others note how he marked phrasing and shading in his charts. Quentin Jackson marvels at his skill on trombone, trumpet, piano and alto. Younger players such as JJ Johnson, Vince Lateano and Joe Wilder call him a role model and speak of his class and the writing on the 1990 album A Gentleman and His Music. The tellers agree on his character and craft and differ mainly in era and in whether they were band members or later admirers. A few samples, such as Winard Harper on Betty Carter, are about a different Carter and fit only loosely.
threads: Carter's patient, thorough rehearsals and perfectionism
Dignified gentleman: manner, smile and the nickname King
Arranger's craft: marking charts, comparison to Don Redman
Multi-instrumentalist: alto, trumpet, trombone, piano
Later admirers: role model, recording and playing with him in the 1990s

communities.name: Ella Fitzgerald and Chick Webb's band
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Most of these stories orbit Ella Fitzgerald's rise through Chick Webb's orchestra and what happened to the band after him. Tom Whaley, a theatre music director at the Lafayette and Apollo, claims he introduced her to Webb, and Teddy McRae says Webb picked her from the Apollo amateur show. McRae, who was Webb's straw boss, is the main teller. He recalls the front men (Bardu Ali, then Babe Wallace), Benny Carter declining to take over, and Moe Gale giving the band to him in 1939. Ram Ramirez and Eddie Barefield describe the band continuing as Ella Fitzgerald's orchestra after Webb died in 1940, and Barefield led it until 1942. Sets in Harlem and on the road, around the Savoy and Apollo, with stops in Chicago, Boston and Pittsburgh. A second strand has sidemen from later decades (Gus Johnson, Roy Haynes, John Lamb, James Moody) who worked behind Ella in the 1940s and 1950s, and Don Albert regrets turning her down in the 1930s. A few samples are off-subject: Eddie Dawson on Celestin and Emma Barrett, John Handy on big band offers, and Cliff Leeman's illness, which ends his job with Shaw.
threads: How Ella was discovered and brought to Chick Webb (Apollo amateur night, Whaley)
McRae and the band's leadership after Webb: front men, Benny Carter, Moe Gale
Ella Fitzgerald's orchestra under Barefield and Ramirez, 1940-42
Sidemen working behind Ella in the 1940s-50s (Gus Johnson, Roy Haynes, Moody, Lamb)
Missed chances and brushes with Ella in the 1930s (Don Albert, Maxine Sullivan)

communities.name: Playing society gigs with Luckey Roberts
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Most of the central stories are about Luckey (Lucky) Roberts, and about Ford Dabney, and the society orchestras they led in New York in the 1920s and early 1930s. Black bands were hired for private parties, teas, dances and regattas on the estates and yachts of millionaire families on Long Island, at Tuxedo Park and in Southampton, which is a different circuit from the downtown ballrooms. Jacques Butler joined Roberts's nine-piece band in 1931-32 as Depression work dried up. He says it demanded classics, the latest numbers and impeccable deportment. Mario Bauza says Roberts also played Latin material at these parties and treated him like a son. Danny Barker, Garvin Bushell, Quentin Jackson and Howard Scott agree that Roberts and Dabney had the best society jobs available to Black musicians. The tellers are mostly New York players, and the Roberts material is consistent. The rest of the cluster is looser. A few New Orleans musicians (Julius Handy, Babe Stovall, Henry Russ) describe private uptown parties, holiday country parties and Roof Garden crowds, and a Bob Wilber segment about Sidney Bechet at Nick's is unrelated. The pack's core is 12 segments, and the roughly 38 in total are more loosely related.
threads: Lucky Roberts's society orchestra and its standards of deportment
Estate, yacht and regatta engagements for millionaire families
Ford Dabney and Roberts as the top society pianists
Latin numbers and personal ties with Roberts (Bauza)
Private parties for wealthy families in New Orleans
Depression-era pay and the move to the city

communities.name: Interviewer quizzes players on half-remembered names
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: These segments are moments in interviews where the interviewer reads out lists of names, bands or acts from union magazines, old rosters or other interviews, and the musician tries to place them. The answers are mostly "I didn't know them", "I can't recall the last name" or a wrong guess. Examples include Tom Zimmerman at Tom Anderson's, Syke Collins and Alan in Chicago, the Fort Myers band, Katie Crippen's act, Blind Charlie and Zeb, whose surnames nobody remembers, and the Chicago violinists and pianists put to Doc Cheatham. Some tellers do pin a name down, such as Eblen Rau on the architect Jinx Dybal, Carrie Boote on pianist Walter Johnson, who died in India, and Benny Waters on Charlie Gaines. Emile Barnes explains that musicians were known by first names only, which is why surnames get lost. The period runs from about the 1910s to the 1960s, mostly in Chicago, New Orleans and Mobile, and the tellers come from the Tulane and Rutgers collections. The shared subject is the interview exercise of name identification and its failures. It is not a single event or place.
threads: Interviewer reads out names from lists and magazines
I never knew them: failed recognition
Musicians known only by first names
Guessing and correcting identities
Chicago players from the 1920s
Pinning down a name at last

communities.name: Who I sounded like: singers on influence and imitation
communities.parent_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists
communities.narrative: Musicians are asked who shaped their style and whether anyone sounds like them, and most of the tellers here are singers. They set the stories mainly in the 1930s to 1950s, with some reaching back to the blues records of the 1910s and 1920s. The same few names recur as the reference points: Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, Mildred Bailey, Peggy Lee, Ethel Waters and Sarah Vaughan. Maxine Sullivan says nobody pinned her style on anyone, and that Dinah Shore and Peggy Lee acknowledged her. Mildred Bailey warned her not to become a second Ella. Helen Humes and Sippie Wallace describe being compared to Billie, Mildred or Bessie Smith. Jackie Cain, Etta Jones and Nancy Wilson name idols and describe moving from an idol's influence to their own sound. A few instrumentalists tell it in their own terms: Kenny Davern on Armstrong's versus Parker's followers and on clones, Norris Turney on the altoists he admired, and Henry Johnson on guitar icons. The tellers agree that influence is unavoidable but that the aim is a personal sound. They differ on whether they were imitated or only compared.
threads: Naming the singers who shaped me (Billie, Ella, Mildred Bailey, Sarah Vaughan)
Being told I sound like someone else
Whether anyone imitated my style
Moving from an idol's influence to my own sound
Instrumentalists on influences and clones (Armstrong vs. Parker followers, guitar icons)

communities.name: Inside the Ellington band: Duke, Strayhorn, Hodges
communities.parent_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men
communities.narrative: Musicians across many collections tell stories about Duke Ellington's orchestra and the people around it, mostly set between the late 1920s and the 1960s in New York, Chicago and on the road. The recurring subjects are how players joined, subbed for or turned down the band (Cootie Williams after Bubber Miley, Johnny Hodges leaving Chick Webb, Charlie Holmes and Doc Cheatham declining, Lee Young and Cozy Cole sitting in), and Ellington's hands-off, never-firing style of leadership. Another strand concerns Billy Strayhorn's collaboration with Duke and Hodges, his work habits and his death. Smaller strands cover Ellington's recordings and writing (one-take sessions, A Drum Is a Woman, Come Sunday, the Sacred Concerts, backward titles) and outsiders recalling first hearing the band or being offered a job. Band members such as Williams, Brown, Greer and Whaley speak from inside the band, while Tate, Mingus, Briggs, Cole and Hampton speak as outsiders who admired it. The tellers agree on Duke's greatness and his loose control over his men, and differ mainly in whether they joined or declined. The cluster is broad because Ellington is the link rather than a single episode, and a few samples (Collier on Koko, Al Hall, Art Baron) barely touch the theme.
threads: Joining, subbing for and turning down Ellington's band
Duke's hands-off leadership and never firing anyone
Billy Strayhorn's collaboration and work habits
Johnny Hodges and other key sidemen
Ellington's recording, writing and Sacred Concerts
Outsiders hearing Ellington or being offered a job

communities.name: The blues queens: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey and the Smiths
communities.parent_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, New York, Chicago and the touring circuits talk about the classic women blues singers of the 1920s, above all Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, Ma Rainey and Clara Smith, with Ethel Waters, Ida Cox and Trixie Smith at the edges. Some tellers worked with them: Billie Pierce played piano on Bessie's show, Garvin Bushell toured with Mamie Smith's band, Herman Autrey met Ma Rainey in Texas, Ram Ramirez and Al Hall backed Bessie late in her career. Others only heard them on records or in theaters and offer comparisons of voice and style, so Mamie is a smooth vaudeville singer, Ma Rainey is less dynamic than the Smiths, and Bessie is a favorite almost everywhere. A recurring origin story is Perry Bradford getting Mamie Smith to record Crazy Blues in 1920, which set off the rush for blues singers named Smith. Tellers agree on Bessie's stature but differ on how impressed they were by Ma Rainey, and some say they never worked with the women, who ran their own shows and groups. The samples are mostly 1910s-30s recollections, with a few interviewer-driven asides.
threads: Playing for or touring with Bessie, Mamie and Ma Rainey
Comparing the singers' voices and styles
Perry Bradford and the Crazy Blues recording
Rival Smith shows and touring-show gossip
