Hearing the blues queens on records and in theaters
Accompanying blues singers in the studio

communities.name: What to charge: pricing arrangements and commissions
communities.parent_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work
communities.narrative: Arrangers, composers and players explain how they set a price for their writing and playing. Most are working arrangers and orchestrators (Michael Abene, Bill Holman, Tom Malone, Marty Sheller, John Fedchock, Jerry Hey, Dave Rivello), and they tell broadly the same story. Union scale is the usual benchmark: Local 802 orchestrator rates, or a per-bar formula. Beyond that, the price depends on the client and what the job will bear. Some keep a standard fee, some negotiate, and some, like Rivello, have no fixed fee and ask about the budget first. Exclusive commissions are priced higher than ordinary work. Several also describe taking jobs for love of the music, or working free or cheaply. Yanow warns that giving work away lowers respect, and Rufus Reid is unsure how to price composing at all. Most of the samples are modern, with no dated period. The odd one out is John Simmons, who recalls a 1944 court case and whether he asked over or under scale. The tellers differ mainly on how rigid their rates are and on whether they share rates with each other.
threads: Union scale as the pricing benchmark
Standard fee versus negotiating per client
Pricing exclusive commissions and compositions
Working for love or for free
Record companies and producers paying late
Knowing your worth and sharing rates with peers

communities.name: What the blues is, and why jazz rests on it
communities.parent_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it
communities.narrative: Across 71 interviews from all four archives, musicians stop to say what the blues is and why it matters. Most of the stories are reflective and have no fixed date or place. Where places come up, they are the Mississippi Delta, Chicago, Memphis and New York, with Africa as a distant root. The tellers largely agree that the blues is the foundation: the first form, the music of Black culture, the root of jazz, rock, R&B and country, and "the American gift to the world." Sippie Wallace, Jay Cee Johnson, Ray Blue and Theodore Bunn define it as feeling, soul, life experience or "spirit music" rather than a set of notes. Jazz players such as Jimmie Crawford, Harold Mabern, Leonard Phillips and Steve Turré say that anyone who cannot play the blues does not belong in jazz, and that technique or classical training cannot replace blues feeling. Others describe origins and styles: ring shouts and spirituals, Delta versus urban or regional blues, and British blues, which Red Holloway says writes about cars and bridges rather than life. Some stories are loosely attached, with a blues title or mention but another main subject, such as Slash, the Tin Roof Blues factory and bluegrass.
threads: Defining the blues: feeling, soul and life experience
Blues as the root of jazz, rock, R&B and country
Blues origins: spirituals, ring shouts, Africa and the Delta
Real versus sophisticated, urban versus country, and British blues
The blues as a test of a jazz musician, and a form to teach
Women, singers and blues voices such as Bessie Smith and Muddy Waters

communities.name: Where the blues came from, and Handy's claim
communities.parent_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, Memphis, Texas, Chicago and New York talk about the blues: where it came from, who first played or published it, and what it means to play it. Many of the tellers set the story between about 1890 and 1920. They say they heard blues from infancy or on plantations, among railroad work gangs, and in the tonks and dance halls. Several name Buddy Bolden, Blind Lemon Jefferson, Lead Belly and Baby Seals. W. C. Handy is the most frequent figure. Roy Carew, Jeff Riddick, Jasper Taylor and Nick La Rocca discuss his Memphis Blues, his publishers and royalties, and whether he really originated the blues, while Alphonse Picou claims to have composed the blues first. A second strand has later players (Harold Mabern, Red Holloway, Bob Cranshaw, Clay Jenkins, Branford Marsalis) describing how they learned or studied the blues, and why feeling and grounding matter more than technique. The theme is broad and not every sample fits it, such as the Carol Bash and Mary Lou Williams film interview and the band-history talk by William Ballariel. The tellers disagree mainly about who was first, and they differ on whether the blues was folk music, vulgar dance music or published songwriting.
threads: Hearing the blues first: plantations, railroad gangs and tonks
Handy, Memphis Blues and the question of who invented the blues
Roy Carew on early published blues and New Orleans composers
Blues pickers and singers: Blind Lemon, Lead Belly, Bolden's band
Later players learning and studying the blues
Playing blues in dance bands and clubs

communities.name: Setting the record straight on reputations
communities.parent_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press
communities.narrative: Musicians push back on how a colleague has been portrayed, whether by a writer, a critic or the rumor mill. The clearest and largest strand is Red Norvo on Mildred Bailey. He insists she was a perfectionist and honest to a fault but never vicious, that the "temperamental" label was used to blame her for bad results, and that a phrase in Dave Dexter's book made it seem she hated Billie Holiday when she meant it as the highest compliment. Elsewhere, Zutty Singleton talks about Jelly Roll Morton's bragging and bad reputation (he says Jelly could back it up). Gene Ramey says a writer misquoted Charlie Parker on Lester Young and the McShann band. Victor Moore disputes another account of Bix Beiderbecke's trip. Ken Poston says West Coast musicians were dismissed by critics and differed from their reputations. Art Farmer recalls Bill Evans writing a letter to defend Tony Scott. The samples span roughly the 1920s to the 1970s and come from all four collections. What holds them together is the recurring complaint that printed accounts and gossip distorted a person, rather than any one event or place. Outside the Norvo and Mildred Bailey material, the link is loose.
threads: Red Norvo defending Mildred Bailey as perfectionist, not malicious
The 'temperamental' label and rumors that stuck
Books and writers misquoting musicians (Dexter, Bird and Prez)
Jelly Roll Morton's bragging and reputation
Critics versus the real West Coast and bebop-era players
Colleagues defending each other (Bill Evans and Tony Scott)

communities.name: Trios, small groups and dream bands
communities.parent_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom
communities.narrative: This cluster is a loose gathering of musicians talking about the makeup of small ensembles, with the piano trio, and especially the Oscar Peterson Trio, as its clearest center. Sam Jones, Louis Hayes, Herb Ellis, Ray Brown and Marian McPartland describe the trio's difficult written unison parts, its heavily arranged music and its demands on the sidemen, set mostly in the 1950s and 1960s. Other tellers discuss the drumless or bassless trio (Ron Carter's Stryker trio, Jake Hanna on Benny Goodman trios), duos (Jim Hall with Bob Brookmeyer), and the trio as a conversational format (Hide Tanaka on Mance, Bill Charlap on his trio with the two Washingtons). A second strand moves away from trios altogether: interviewers ask musicians to name a dream band or the players they would still like to work with, and Bobby Gordon, Howard Alden, McPartland, John Abercrombie and Randy Sandke answer with lists of names. A few samples are only loosely related, such as Plas Johnson's L.A. quartet, Chico Freeman's best musical situations and Lorraine Gordon on Paul Motian at the Vanguard. The tellers share an interest in who plays with whom and in what format, but they do not tell one common story, and the periods run from the 1940s to the 2000s.
threads: Playing in the Oscar Peterson Trio and its arranged music
Trio formats: drumless, bassless and duo settings
Leading or joining a working trio or quartet
Dream bands and players they would still like to play with
Best musical situations and favorite groups

communities.name: Who shaped my playing: pianists and other influences
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Musicians answer the interviewer's standing question about influences, and the answer is mostly a list of pianists. Players from the 1920s to the 1970s name the records and live performers who formed their style: Fats Waller, Teddy Wilson, Earl Hines, Nat Cole, Art Tatum, George Shearing and Oscar Peterson for the swing-to-bebop generation, then Bud Powell, Bill Evans, McCoy Tyner, Herbie Hancock and Chick Corea for those who came up in the 1950s to 70s. Many tellers are pianists, such as Ramsey Lewis, Kenny Barron, Roger Kellaway, Denny Zeitlin and Allen Toussaint. Others are horn players, singers, guitarists or organists (Hubert Laws, Tom Lellis, Houston Person, Pete Levin) who say pianists or other instrumentalists shaped how they improvise. The tellers agree that a style is a blend of many models, and a few say they had no single influence or were trying to escape the great pianists. Where they differ is in the models they cite: boogie-woogie and swing records for the older players, modern jazz and the Miles Davis and Coltrane quartets for the younger ones, plus a few classical or Latin models. Some segments sit at the edges, such as Toussaint replacing Huey Smith on the road and George Wein's club ambitions, because influence talk leads into other topics.
threads: Swing and boogie-woogie piano models: Waller, Wilson, Hines, Yancey, Ammons
Shearing, Peterson, Tatum and Billy Taylor as the 1950s models
Bud Powell and bebop piano as a model
Bill Evans, Tyner, Hancock and Corea for the 1960s-70s generation
Non-pianists citing pianists or other instrumentalists as models
Having no single influence, or trying to escape the great pianists

communities.name: Sorting out dates and band chronologies
communities.parent_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene
communities.narrative: In this cluster, interviewers and musicians stop to work out when things happened and in what order. The tellers are New Orleans, Chicago and Kansas City players, plus a few later figures such as Toshiko Akiyoshi. They try to fix the year they moved to a city, the order of the bands they worked with, or the date of a photograph. Interviewers often press for years, or read back a letter or a list. The musicians usually answer with approximate dates and admit they are bad with them. Rudy Mazzari does this outright, Nick La Rocca corrects contract dates, and Eddie Dawson corrects the dates for dance halls with Manetta. Others reconstruct careers by band, such as Samuel Lovett moving between George Lee and Thamon Hayes in Kansas City and Chicago, or John Levy's Chicago groups. A few samples are plain band-and-venue rundowns, such as Lillie Delk Christian's brief Cotton Club job and Jimmy McPartland's Wolverines bookings, and they fit only loosely. The shared thread is the work of dating and sequencing a career, not one event or place, so the cluster is mixed.
threads: Interviewer and musician untangling the order of years
Admitting poor memory for dates and giving rough estimates
Correcting dates in letters, contracts and photographs
Career rundowns by bandleader: Thamon Hayes, George Lee, Earle Warren, Boyd Atkins
Lists of Chicago, Kansas City and New Orleans dance halls and clubs

communities.name: Putting Bix's piano pieces on paper
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: This is the story of Bix Beiderbecke the pianist and composer, and above all of how his piano pieces were committed to paper. It is set in the late 1920s and just after his death in 1931, in the world of the Paul Whiteman and Jean Goldkette orchestras. Most of it comes from arranger Bill Challis, who recalls notating Bix's five piano pieces for the publisher Jack Robbins. He describes how In a Mist took about six months and ended with Bix improvising an ending and a slow theme. He also describes how Candlelights, Flashes and In the Dark followed the same formula. He explains why the pieces sound alike, how he wrote Davenport Blues from a record after Bix died, and why he refused to notate For No Reason at All in C. He links Bix's harmony to Eastwood Lane's piano music, with its sixths, ninths and augmented chords. Other tellers (Mugsy Spanier, Victor Moore, Jim Cullum) add a wider picture of Bix drawn to the piano, the organ and the classics, and of his friendship with Hoagy Carmichael. Challis supplies the detailed, firsthand account. The others offer briefer impressions, and the shared theme is Bix's piano writing.
threads: Challis notating In a Mist for Jack Robbins
Candlelights, Flashes and In the Dark in the same formula
Why the piano pieces sound alike; Davenport Blues from a record
Refusing to notate For No Reason at All in C
Eastwood Lane and Bix's harmony
Bix at the piano and organ, and what he might have become

communities.name: Electric pianos and synthesizers: taking them up, giving them up
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Pianists and other keyboard players recall the arrival of the Fender Rhodes, Wurlitzer, clavinet, Moog and later the DX7 in jazz, mostly from the late 1960s through the 1980s. Some took them up out of practical need: club pianos were bad or rentals too costly, the drummer was too loud, or the band was moving toward fusion and rock-jazz (Zawinul's "Mercy, Mercy", Miles's pedals on the Rhodes, Lonnie Liston Smith's approach to its own colors). A large group tells a return-to-acoustic story. Hal Galper dumped his electric piano in the Hudson, Paul Smith quit studio work in 1972 after a month without touching a piano, Denny Zeitlin left a decade of synth rigs, and Ellis Marsalis sold his Rhodes and argued electric piano detaches the music from its tradition. Others, like Horace Henderson, Lou Donaldson and Horn Shirley, moved to organ for economic reasons. The tellers agree on the hassle of cables, equipment and mechanics, and differ on whether the instruments were new colors or a threat to the piano.
threads: Fender Rhodes and Wurlitzer sound and fusion-era adoption
Dumping or selling the electric keyboard to return to acoustic piano
Synthesizers and Moog rigs, studio work and the DX7
Bad club pianos, rental costs and hauling equipment
Switching to organ for economic reasons
Marsalis's argument that electric piano undermines the tradition

venues: New Orleans Center for Creative Arts

communities.name: Art Tatum: the man, the cards and the cutting nights
communities.parent_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and cities tell what it was like to hear, meet and be around Art Tatum. The stories are set mostly between the late 1920s and the mid-1950s, in Toledo, Cleveland, Chicago, New York and Los Angeles. Many are first-hearing tales: Eddie Barefield and Quentin Jackson at Toledo dances, Red Callender spellbound by "Tiger Rag" in Cleveland, and the stunned crowd at New York's Rhythm Club when he arrived with Adelaide Hall's group and Fats Waller gathered the pianists. Others describe working beside him, such as Milt Hinton and John Collins at Chicago's Three Deuces and Roy Eldridge jamming at Val's in the Alley. A large share concern Tatum as a person: his near-blindness (Eldridge doubts it was total), his pinochle playing and memory for cards, his heavy beer drinking, his dislike of being asked to play, and his death from uremia. Tellers agree on his overwhelming command of the piano and on the after-hours "wiping out" of other pianists; they differ on small facts such as how blind he was and when and where they first met him. The tellers are mostly pianists, bassists, trumpeters and sidemen, with a few writers and younger players such as Dan Morgenstern and Oscar Peterson's circle.
threads: First hearing Tatum in Toledo, Cleveland and at the Rhythm Club
Working beside him at the Three Deuces in Chicago
Cards, beer and near-blindness: Tatum the person
After-hours cutting sessions where he wiped out the pianists
Friendships, visits and meetings with younger pianists
Late years: recordings, concerts, illness and death

communities.name: Pianos: Steinways, bad club uprights, and electric keyboards
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Pianists and a few engineers, label people and dealers talk about the instrument itself: which pianos they play, which they dread, and how they get good ones. A strong strand is loyalty to the Steinway. Hank Jones became a Steinway player on the Jazz at the Philharmonic tours, Teddy Wilson prefers a nine-foot German Steinway, McCoy Tyner values the company's artist program, and Skitch Henderson tells of Steinway 199 and Horowitz. The opposite strand is the club piano. Richard Wyands, Toshiko Akiyoshi and George Handy describe out-of-tune pianos, broken pedals and spinets, Birdland's pianos included. In one story Billy Taylor persuades Morris Levy to buy Birdland a Steinway after Slim Gaillard wrecks the old one with a drink. Smaller strands cover the Fender Rhodes suitcase piano and the Yamaha electric piano, miking a grand in the studio, and the piano trade: selling player pianos at Werlein's, a piano bought on 125th Street in 1928 and a $150 piano painted black for Earl Hines. The tellers are mostly pianists from the 1920s to 2000s across all four collections. They agree that piano quality varies widely and shapes the playing, but they do not share a single event, so the unity is the topic, not one story.
threads: Why pianists prefer Steinways (Hank Jones, Teddy Wilson, Tyner)
Terrible club pianos and getting venues to buy better ones (Birdland)
Electric pianos: Fender Rhodes suitcase and Yamaha
Studio and concert pianos: miking, tuning, matching grands
Buying, selling and owning pianos (Werlein's, 125th Street, the $150 piano)

communities.name: Working for Lena Horne: bands, conductors and her act
communities.parent_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands
communities.narrative: The core of this cluster is musicians recalling work with Lena Horne, from her stint as a singer with Charlie Barnet's band around 1941 through her 1945-55 touring and recording years. Barnet and Horace Henderson tell how she was fetched from Harlem and a movie house when his singers went hoarse, sang at the Paramount and Valencia, and left after Dinah Shore objected to being outshone. Horace Henderson, Luther Henderson, Chico Hamilton and Gus Johnson then describe being hired as her pianist, arranger, drummer or trio member, and working under her husband and conductor Lennie Hayton at venues such as the Capitol Theatre, Chez Paris and the Waldorf. The tellers agree on Hayton as a mentor and on the pay and show-business discipline of backing a star singer. They differ in tone: Hamilton is warm about eight years with her, while Johnson found her unpredictable vocal style so stressful that his blood pressure rose and he quit. About a third of the samples drift to other accompanied singers (Pearl Bailey at the Village Vanguard, Liza Minnelli, Mattie Hite, Gladys Lundy, Patsy at the Dew Drop), so the Horne story is clear but not the whole cluster.
threads: Lena Horne joins and leaves the Charlie Barnet band, 1941
Horace Henderson assembling her small band and recording dates, 1945-49
Lennie Hayton as conductor, husband and mentor
Eight years behind her: Chico Hamilton and Gus Johnson on playing for a star singer
Other singers and their accompanists: Pearl Bailey at the Vanguard, Liza Minnelli, cabaret blues singers

communities.name: Hearing Tony Jackson, the great New Orleans pianist, in Chicago
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans and Chicago remember Tony Jackson, the Storyville-era pianist, singer and composer of "Pretty Baby." The stories are set mostly between 1900 and 1915, in the New Orleans district and then in Chicago, where Jackson was a featured star at the Elite No. 1 and No. 2 on State Street and at the Deluxe Cafe. Tellers such as Zutty Singleton, Glover Compton, Alberta Hunter and Billy McBride describe seeing or hearing him, and Singleton says he went to Chicago specifically to hear him after learning his fame at the "25" club in New Orleans. They agree Jackson was a remarkable pianist and composer, and several note that he played beautiful music that was not strictly jazz. Some tellers, such as Big Bill Thompson and Singleton, knew him only by reputation or by seeing him in passing. William Russell places him next to Jelly Roll Morton, and other segments place him among the other piano players who made the rounds of the houses and clubs. The tellers are mostly New Orleans-connected musicians, with most segments from the Tulane collection.
threads: Tony Jackson as pianist and composer of Pretty Baby
Zutty Singleton traveling to Chicago to hear him at the Deluxe Cafe
The Elite clubs on State Street and the Chicago cafe scene
New Orleans district piano players and Jackson's reputation at the 25 club
Jackson compared with Jelly Roll Morton and other early pianists

communities.name: Remembering the pianists: who played piano and how
communities.parent_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered
communities.narrative: Across hundreds of interviews, musicians talk about pianists: who the good ones were, how they played, and where they worked. Most of the stories are set between about 1900 and the 1950s, mainly in New Orleans (the Storyville district, Gravier Street houses, cabarets, fish fries and dance halls), Chicago, and the New York stride scene. Interviewees from the Tulane and Rutgers collections often answer an interviewer's prompt with a list of names, many of them obscure or never recorded, such as Steve Lewis, Burnell Santiago, Camilla Todd and Buddy Gurns. Others, notably Rutgers and Smithsonian interviewees, rank famous players against one another: Earl Hines, Art Tatum, Fats Waller, Teddy Wilson, Willie the Lion Smith and Teddy Weatherford. Tellers agree that pianists were central to dance bands and sporting houses, and that Hines, Waller and Tatum set the standards for style. They differ on who was best and on how reliable their memories of the early players are. The cluster is loose, though, and a few segments are about something else, such as piano rolls, a recording-session dispute and a ragtime festival.
threads: New Orleans district and sporting-house piano players
Ranking the greats: Hines, Tatum, Waller, Weatherford
Harlem stride pianists and the New York scene
Blues, ragtime and solo pianists who never recorded
Women pianists and pianists in dance bands
Looking for forgotten pianists the interviewer wants to find

communities.name: House rent parties and fish fries
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians recall playing, or growing up around, house rent parties: private gatherings where hosts charged a small admission and sold food and drink to raise the rent, with a hired pianist (often a stride or boogie-woogie player) working all night for small pay. The stories are set mostly in the 1920s and early 1930s, with an earlier Philadelphia memory from about 1909 and a few later recollections from the Depression years. Places named include Chicago, Philadelphia and New York. Tellers describe twenty-five-cent admissions, pigs feet, potato salad, fish fries and bathtub liquor. Pay is a dollar, fifty cents or tips plus food. Pianists such as Bill Fry, Rock, Fats Waller and James P. Johnson turn up as the figures who made the parties. Several tellers, among them Charles Thompson, Eddie Barefield and Freddie Green, say these parties were where they learned to play before they joined bands. Most of the cluster is one subject, but the last sample, Maxine Sullivan's movie-house contest in Rankin, belongs to a different story, and a few others touch piano rolls and speakeasy gigs only loosely.
threads: Rent parties as a way to raise rent, with food, liquor and small admission
Pianists hired to play all night for a dollar, tips and food
Learning to play at rent parties before joining bands
Fish fries, speakeasies and fish bars as piano gigs
Chicago stride and boogie-woogie piano scene

communities.name: Playing a recording back during the interview
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Most of these segments are moments when an interviewer, often Monk Rowe at Hamilton's Fillius Jazz Archive, stops to play a recording and asks the musician to listen and react. The recording may be the musician's own CD (Holly Hofmann, Howard Levy, Houston Person, Stefon Harris on Hutcherson's "Now"), a group's track (Swing 7 with Johnny Varro), a Time-Life reissue where the lead trumpeter is to be identified (John Best), a tune the guest chose (Rusty Dedrick's Hoagy Carmichael track), or an old record from the family (Charlie Bocage and A. J. Piron's 1923-24 sides). The talk centers on what the ear catches: a modulation the player does not recall, countermelodies on a second hearing, written versus open passages, an improvised line or a low register. A smaller strand is about memory of music and lyrics, such as Will Shade and Vic Dickenson forgetting words, or Sudhalter worrying she retains little of what she hears. A few segments do not belong, such as the praise of HBO's Treme and Herman Autrey on Una Mae Carlisle and Stuff Smith. It is a loose interview-practice thread across collections, not one shared story, and almost no segment has a datable period.
threads: Interviewer plays the musician's own CD or track and asks for reactions
Identifying players and parts on an old or reissued recording
Comparing an original record with a worn copy
Forgetting lyrics and not retaining music heard
Guest-chosen tunes and personal links to them
Stray asides, such as the Treme series and Stuff Smith

communities.name: Norman Granz and Jazz at the Philharmonic
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell the story of Norman Granz and his Jazz at the Philharmonic (JATP) concerts. It begins in 1940s Los Angeles, where Granz ran Sunday jam sessions at Normandie Hall and Billy Berg's for about nine dollars a man. Red Callender, Trummy Young and Harry Edison recall these sessions, which led to the first Philharmonic concert in 1944 with Nat Cole and Illinois Jacquet. From 1945-46 the JATP tours took stars such as Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins, Buck Clayton, Helen Humes, Flip Phillips and Buddy Rich across the United States, and later to Europe and Japan. The tellers agree that Granz paid unusually well, travelled first class, treated players fairly, and favoured jam-session and blues playing. They also agree that he put strangers together on stage and on record, often in one take, and later built Oscar Peterson and Ella Fitzgerald's careers around his organization. They differ on details: how the idea originated, how long the early tours ran, and whether he was open to newer ideas such as John Lewis's. Many of the tellers were sidemen who joined, toured with or merely met the JATP circle, so the story reads as a collective portrait of Granz as impresario.
threads: Granz's early Los Angeles jam sessions and the first JATP concert
Joining JATP and the first cross-country tours
Granz as employer: top pay, fairness and first-class travel
Granz's all-star jam-session philosophy and one-take recordings
JATP abroad in Europe and Japan with Oscar Peterson as leader
Granz's later management and recording of Ella Fitzgerald and others

communities.name: Jazz musicians meet the symphony orchestra
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: These segments gather stories of jazz players crossing into the concert hall: writing for, playing with, or conducting symphony orchestras and working with classical composers. The strongest strand is Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto, written for the Woody Herman band in 1945-46 and premiered at Carnegie Hall. Herman, Chubby Jackson and Billy Bauer tell it, and Herman returns to it for the Everest re-recordings and a hoped-for 1980 Stravinsky festival revival. Other tellers describe later orchestral encounters. Jane Ira Bloom premiered a symphonic piece at Carnegie Hall, Virginia Mayhew played in a Zappa work for the Berkeley Symphony, and Alan Raph played Villa-Lobos and The Rite of Spring. Wayne Shorter talks about orchestras learning to improvise in the Dudamel era. Al Hall and Jimmy Jones recall symphony dates for Erroll Garner in the 1950s and 60s. The tellers agree these dates were hard, risky and prestigious, but they span 1945 to 2012 and several unrelated occasions, so the cluster is a loose common thread rather than one story.
threads: Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto and the Herman band
Premieres and nerves at Carnegie Hall
Symphony dates with Erroll Garner
Commissioned orchestral works by jazz composers
Playing classical repertory as a jazz player
Orchestras learning to improvise

communities.name: Working the band circuit: D.C., Philadelphia and the Jersey shore
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians tell how they moved from one band job to the next in the Mid-Atlantic corridor between Washington, Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the New Jersey shore, mostly from the mid-1930s to the early 1950s. Leonard Phillips supplies most of the stories. He recounts his arrival in Washington in 1935, small club bands such as Johnny Ridgely's and Booker Coleman's, the 1942 walk-a-thon bands, and John Malachi's band at Crystal Caverns. He then covers summer 1941 at Long Branch and Asbury Park, and the 1950s house-band and R&B road work with Ivory Joe Hunter and Tiny Bradshaw. Happy Caldwell and Herman Autrey tell parallel wartime stories from Philadelphia and Atlantic City, about union agents, leaders such as Charlie Gaines and Bardu Ali, and clubs like Club Harlem and the Midway. A few outside voices, including Ram Ramirez, Arnett Cobb, Benny Golson and Doc Cheatham, add single Philadelphia or Atlantic City engagements that fit the geography but not the Phillips career narrative. The tellers agree that work depended on who was leading, who was drafted, and which seasonal room was open. The cluster is really one musician's career chronicle plus a looser regional scene.
threads: Leonard Phillips's Washington band jobs, 1935-44
John Malachi's band and young D.C. players
Summer 1941 hotel and club work at Long Branch and Asbury Park
Wartime Philadelphia and Atlantic City club bands
House bands and R&B tours: Howard Theatre, Ivory Joe Hunter, Tiny Bradshaw
Single engagements in Philadelphia and Atlantic City told by other musicians

communities.name: Steady gigs: club and restaurant residencies
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians describe the regular rooms where they worked once the big-band or touring years were behind them, or between larger jobs. The stories are mostly set from the mid-1950s to about 2000. They include Snub Mosley's trio dates at the Frolic and in the Catskills, Erskine Hawkins at the Copacabana and the World's Fair, a house rhythm section at the Roosevelt Grill, a trio at Windows on the World, and weekly restaurant gigs in the 1990s and 2000. West Coast players such as Jack Sheldon, Ernie Watts and Andrew Blakeney tell of Los Angeles clubs, movie-star bands and weekend jobs. Mary Lou Williams's account of leaving Cafe Society is the one sample that sits apart, since it concerns a 1946 residency and its end. The tellers agree that the work is steady, often in restaurants or resorts, and is often a step away from their earlier fame. The samples share a loose common thread of where and with whom they played, not one event, and the segmenter's categories (later career, band or employer, venue scene) confirm the blend.
threads: Catskills and resort-circuit trio work
New York restaurant and hotel house bands
Los Angeles clubs and movie-star bands
Weekly gigs in later career
Leaving a long residency (Cafe Society)

communities.name: The Dew Drop Inn and Rampart Street nightlife
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: The core of this cluster is New Orleans Black nightlife in the 1940s and 1950s, centered on Frank Painia's Dew Drop Inn and the clubs along Rampart and LaSalle Streets. George "Tex" Stephens, who wrote Painia's ad copy and walks through the clubs block by block, supplies the most detail. Tommy Ridgley, who was house band there in 1956-58, Milton Batiste and Lawrence Cotton add the musician's view. They describe the Dew Drop as a club, a hotel for visiting stars such as Ray Charles, James Brown and Little Richard, and a hiring hall where musicians left messages and found gigs. They also cover rival and neighboring clubs (Foster's, the Robin Hood, the Blue Eagle, the Keyhole), the "Mayor of Rampart Street," stranded bands, and the promoter circuit linking New Orleans, Lake Charles and Texas. Tellers agree on Painia's generosity and the Dew Drop's central role, and Stephens adds its later decline. The cluster also takes in a few loosely related segments, such as Tuts Washington's career summary and Tom Stagg on the Bunk Johnson Society, which share only the New Orleans music scene.
threads: The Dew Drop as club, hotel and hiring hall
Frank Painia's generosity and the club's decline
Backing visiting R&B stars as house band
Walking tour of Rampart Street clubs and its characters
Promoters and the Louisiana-Texas circuit
Stranded bands and touring acts

communities.name: Stage and show work in New York and London, 1960s-70s
communities.parent_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands
communities.narrative: This is a loose cluster of musicians describing work in theater, musicals and show-business engagements, mostly in New York and London between the 1960s and late 1970s. The strongest thread is the Hoofers tap-dance show told by Chuck Green: the Bert Wheeler Theater run, the move to the Mercury Theater, celebrity audiences, the renaming as The Hoofers, and his fill-in role in Curly McDimple. Annie Ross recalls London theater, including The Threepenny Opera, Kennedy's Children and the touring revue Wham! Bam! Thank You, Ma'am. Others describe pit and house-band work, such as Eddie Barefield's years in the Madison Square Garden circus and ice-show band and the Poconos summers, and Joe Wilder's return to Broadway shows after ABC. A few singers and players tell one-off stories about off-off-Broadway productions (Maxine Sullivan's My Old Friends, Ruth Brisbane's barn show), the Brel revue, Las Vegas, Monterey and commercial or record work. The tellers share a setting of working in shows and steady employment outside jazz clubs. They do not share a single event or subject, and a few samples, such as the 2021-22 SNL guest-band interview, fall outside the period and theme entirely.
threads: The Hoofers tap show: Bert Wheeler and Mercury Theaters
Annie Ross in London theater and touring revues
Madison Square Garden circus and ice-show house band
Broadway and off-off-Broadway musicals
Resort and commercial gigs: Poconos, Las Vegas, studio dates

communities.name: Landing a first job in New Orleans bands
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1920s through the 1960s describe arriving in or passing through New Orleans and getting work with a particular band or club. The earliest tellers, such as Lizzie Miles, Sadie Goodson, Frank Goudie and Clayton Duerr, recall first jobs at places like Bucktown, the Pelican and Beverly Gardens. They are set around 1919-26 and name bandleaders such as Papa Celestin and Manuel Manetta. Others describe joining or sitting in with working bands. Russell Moore got the trombone chair by sitting in with Celestin in 1939. Sal Gutierrez replaced a player in Willie Rosenblum's band. Don Albert's band took on a player who had only a few gigs with Sidney Desvigne. Later outsiders, including Bob Havens, Rudy Mazzari and Peter Ecklund, came to New Orleans in the late 1940s through the 1960s, drawn by the revival and the Dixieland scene. Havens, for example, went from Ralph Flanagan's band to George Girard's New Orleans Five on Bourbon Street. The tellers share the circumstance of getting a job or a band slot, but the eras, places and kinds of work differ, so the subject is loose.
threads: First cabaret and club jobs in 1920s New Orleans
Sitting in and getting the chair in a working band
Short stints and moving on from New Orleans
Outsiders drawn to New Orleans Dixieland in the 1950s-60s
Joining named bands like Celestin, Desvigne, Girard and Flanagan

communities.name: Fletcher Henderson: gentle leader, poor businessman
communities.parent_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people
communities.narrative: Musicians who played with or around Fletcher Henderson describe the man and his leadership, mostly in the 1920s to 1941 and mostly in New York. The tellers largely agree that he was quiet, kind, easygoing and well schooled, and strict only about the music. Many say he was a milquetoast about discipline: the band was late, undisciplined and rarely full on the stand, and he had no business sense or manager like Irving Mills. Several (Gil Evans, McPartland, Bushell, Cheatham, Joe Thomas) tell the same irony: Benny Goodman played Henderson's arrangements and got rich, John Hammond's Goodman connection took the band's momentum, and Henderson died poor. A few differ in tone. Howard Scott remembers the 1924-25 band as the top band, with nightly inspections, and others note his aloofness, and his brother Horace's mistreatment of him. Tellers are sidemen, arrangers and sitters-in, nearly all from the Rutgers interviews. The cluster is slightly diffuse at the edges, where individual segments drift to Hammond, Chick Webb or Trumbauer.
threads: Henderson's quiet, easygoing, educated character
A weak disciplinarian and poor businessman
Goodman got rich on his arrangements while he died poor
John Hammond and the loss of the band's momentum
Horace Henderson and family troubles
The 1920s band as the top band, and its stars

communities.name: Learning from Bix and Trumbauer records
communities.parent_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, Chicago, Berlin and the big bands recall learning jazz from phonograph records in the 1920s, above all the white "hot" records of Bix Beiderbecke, Frankie Trumbauer and Red Nichols, alongside Paul Whiteman, Jean Goldkette, Fletcher Henderson and the Wolverines. Leonard Phillips supplies the richest account: he and Lester Young learned Bix and Trumbauer solos such as Singin' the Blues, Mississippi Mud and In A Mist by ear, even working out three-part harmonies, and notes that records seldom named the players. Arthur Briggs tells the same story from Berlin, where a dealer set aside every new American release and the band bought records like hot cakes. Black and white players alike, among them Ridgley, Darensbourg, Waters, Dickenson, Carter and Thomas, name Trumbauer's C-melody solo and Nichols's small groups as admired models, and some stress the influence on their style without changing it. They differ on whether this was a distinct style from Henderson's big-band jazz and on how much race mattered, since Darensbourg says the records were assumed to be by white musicians. A few samples drift toward general record collections (Bauduc, Zanco) rather than this specific lineage.
threads: Lester Young and Phillips learning Bix and Trumbauer solos off records
Arthur Briggs buying American records in Berlin
Singin' the Blues and Trumbauer's C-melody sound
Red Nichols and Miff Mole admired by Black musicians
Records as the way bands copied Whiteman and Dixieland
Race and the assumption that Bix records were by white players

bands: Red Nichols and His Five Pennies

communities.name: Forming my first band: who played with me
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: In this cluster, musicians recall the first band they started or joined, and the story is mostly a roll call of who was in it. The tellers name the members and instruments (drums, trombone, banjo, bass), the band's name, how many pieces it had (often six), and how long it lasted, usually a year or two before it broke up or changed its name. Most of the stories are set in the 1910s and 1920s and are told largely by New Orleans players, including Peter LaCaze, Adolphe Alexander, Albert Burbank, Albert Artigues, Ray Bauduc, Red Clark and Eddie Marrero. A few later or outside examples appear, such as Professor Longhair's late-1930s group, Jimmy Cobb's late-1940s quartet, Hubert Laws's Afro-Classic Ensemble and Wild Bill Davison's Ohio Lucky Seven. A second strand comes from Cuba, where Machito and Candido Camero list the sextetos and septetos they played in, such as Agabama, Maria Teresa Vera's septeto, Apolo and Gloria Habanera, in 1926 to the early 1940s. The tellers agree that the first band was small, local and informal. They differ in scale and setting: Cuban stories trace a ladder of named ensembles and cabarets, while US stories mostly describe a single early group. Some summaries note transcription trouble, as when the speech recognition loops on one name.
threads: First bands of New Orleans players in the 1910s-20s
Six-piece spot bands and amateur groups with named members
Cuban sextetos and septetos: Machito and Candido Camero
First groups of later players: quartets and ensembles
Bolden-era and older bandleaders forming bands

communities.name: Worst gigs and train wrecks
communities.parent_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor
communities.narrative: Musicians asked about their "worst gig" or "most unusual gig" tell short, rueful stories of nights that went wrong. The majority come from a recurring interview question, most heavily in the Hamilton (Fillius) interviews, with a smaller number from Rutgers and the Smithsonian. They are set mostly between the 1940s and 2000, and range across New York, Los Angeles, New Jersey, Rochester and Australia, with trips to New Zealand, Japan and Scandinavia. Many are about the club-date and wedding circuit: wrong-fit bands, ad hoc groups, indifferent crowds, and a rented keyboard at an estate where nobody listened. Others are musical train wrecks, such as a rhythm section and horn on different forms, a tune that falls apart on a band's first night, or an unprepared sub without the scores. A third strand is mishaps with equipment and logistics: a pulled amp plug at the Apollo, a curtain taking a bass drum, music books left on a train. The tellers agree that these nights taught endurance, preparation or when to stop and start over, but they differ in tone, from comic to humiliating to mildly dismissive. A few samples (a first December at the Vanguard, Frank Alkyer's missed opportunities, the Boston Pops date) fit loosely or not at all.
threads: Worst gigs at weddings, parties and club dates
Tunes falling apart: train wrecks on the bandstand
Unprepared or underrehearsed: subbing and sight-reading disasters
Equipment, stage and travel mishaps (lost music, drums, amps)
Bizarre venues and hostile or absent audiences
Lessons learned from bad nights

communities.name: Practical jokes and pranks on the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor
communities.narrative: Musicians from nearly every era and collection tell stories of band-room humor: pranks played on colleagues, bandleaders and even a recording engineer. The classic tricks recur across tellers: limburger cheese or cayenne pepper in a mouthpiece, water in a baritone or tuba, taped piano keys, swapped valves, stink bombs, alarm clocks hidden in bags on the bus, balloons popped during a solo, and life-size dummies seated in the trombone section. They are set mostly between the 1920s and 1960s, in big bands (Ellington, Basie, Herman, Fletcher Henderson, Hampton) and small groups such as the Peterson trio, and reach back to Papa Jack Laine's New Orleans boy bands of the 1890s-1900s. Tellers agree that jokes were a way of relieving tension and needling one another, though Butler notes thin-skinned players sometimes quit over the teasing, and some, like Tizol, claim not to remember their own pranks. The outer edge of the cluster drifts into general humor and character anecdotes, such as comic routines in vaudeville acts, Joe Venuti legends, eating and drinking contests, and a few stories where the joke is thin or absent, so the core is a clear majority rather than the whole.
threads: Pranks on mouthpieces, horns and instruments
Stink bombs, alarm clocks and bus or stage gags
Band teasing, nicknames and needling the leader
Famous jokers and characters such as Bill Harris and Joe Venuti
Comedy acts and gags in performance
Contests, drinking and other horseplay on the road

communities.name: Hunting for lost band photographs
communities.parent_name: Hunting for old band photographs and scrapbooks
communities.narrative: Across dozens of interviews, mostly the Tulane/Hogan Jazz Archive sessions in which Bill Russell and other interviewers sit down with early New Orleans musicians, the shared story is the search for photographs of the old bands and players. Interviewers ask whether any pictures survive of figures such as Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit and Buddy Bolden, and the musicians answer that none exist, that someone else has them, that a picture was lent and never returned, or that a photographer snapped the band and never delivered the prints. Where pictures do turn up (the Excelsior and Pete Lala's band, the Peerless band, a Bunk Johnson band photo, scrapbooks, clippings, record covers), the sessions turn into identifying faces, dating the picture and arranging to borrow and copy it. Tellers differ in whether they are guarding a precious surviving print, regretting a lost one, or just flipping through a scrapbook, and a few mention photographers who vanished. The setting is mainly the 1910s to 1930s as seen from interviews in the 1950s and 60s, with a handful of later echoes from Rutgers and Smithsonian interviews, such as Sheila Jordan's loft photographs and Jimmy Cobb's Kind of Blue session photos. A few segments only loosely fit, for example the Coda article search, the Mahogany Hall wallpaper and the Miles Davis videotape, which are about locating or handling relics and documents rather than photos.
threads: Asking whether any pictures of Chris Kelly, Buddy Petit and Buddy Bolden survive
Lost or lent-out band photographs never returned
Identifying and dating faces in old band pictures
Scrapbooks and clippings looked through during the interview
Arranging to borrow and copy photographs
Photographers who took pictures and vanished

communities.name: The studio scene dries up: Los Angeles session work in decline
communities.parent_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life
communities.narrative: Musicians who worked the Los Angeles and New York studios tell how the staff and session scene that once supplied steady, well-paid work for orchestra players faded. Paul Smith remembers the 1950s as the best studio years, with the decline visible by the early 1960s. Others, such as Bill Watrous (1976 to 1990), Harry Edison and Abe Most, place the collapse in the 1970s to 1990s. The tellers broadly agree on the causes: synthesizers and machines replacing live players, changing tastes and self-contained groups, work moving to Canada and overseas for economic reasons, and contractors and the union (Local 47) controlling who got called. They differ on the union: Ralph Humphrey says it set useful scale but did too little for production-side work. Players such as Sonny Igoe and Abe Most describe adapting by teaching, leaving studio calls, or playing tribute bands. Bobby Shew adds a practical view of what a studio call involved, including doubles pay and the Universal contractor Sandy DeCrescent. The pool is small and mostly Hamilton interviews, and one sample (Chris Parker on Simmons drums in the film Hoosiers) is only loosely related.
threads: Golden years of 1950s studio orchestras and their decline by the 1960s
Synthesizers, machines and changing film-scoring tastes
Work leaving Los Angeles for Canada and overseas
Local 47, scale, residuals and the contractors who made the calls
Leaving studio work for teaching and tribute bands

communities.name: Claiborne Williams and the Donaldsonville society bands
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Musicians from the river parishes and New Orleans remember Professor Claiborne Williams's Donaldsonville orchestra and the polished, reading-based dance bands of the same world, such as John Robichaux's. The setting is mostly the 1900s to the 1920s: dances in Donaldsonville, Reserve and Gramercy, school and college functions at Holy Family, and trips into New Orleans, including the Pelican roof garden. Tellers agree that Williams was a violinist who taught every instrument. They describe a big band of 14 to 16 pieces that played stock arrangements and waltzes and was hired for dances. His son George and his trombonist brother played in it. Louis Nelson, Eddie Summers, John L. Jones and Roger Mitchell speak of the Williams band directly. Willie Foster and Doc Souchon place it beside Robichaux's house band at La Louisiane, which played from arrangements and hired some hot players. A few samples, such as Algiers dance bands and Reserve halls, only share the general subject of local dance bands. Most tellers are Tulane interviewees, and they stress the contrast between this sweet, classical society music and hot jazz.
threads: Claiborne Williams's orchestra: size, repertoire and family members
Violin-leading bandleaders playing stock arrangements and waltzes, not hot jazz
Williams and Robichaux bands compared
Dances and halls in Donaldsonville, Reserve and the river parishes
Other local dance bands such as those in Algiers

communities.name: Local bands before the big names
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the local and community bands of their home places: country brass bands, string bands, family ensembles, dance orchestras and a few classical or chamber groups. The settings are mostly rural and small-town Louisiana (Deer Range, Day Range, Oakville, Baton Rouge, Napoleonville, Thibodaux) in the 1890s to 1910s, with a few stories from elsewhere, including Boston, Homestead, Texas and Portland, Oregon. Tellers name the bands, their leaders and players, and where they played. Some stress when a type of band started, such as Ben Kelly saying the string band came after he took up music. Others describe the music they grew up hearing, such as Cosimo Matassa's family polkas and mazurkas. The strands share only the subject of local ensembles. They differ in genre, place and era, from a symphony orchestra at St. Catherine's Hall to a 1980s Western swing band. The tellers are mostly New Orleans-area Tulane interviewees, with some from Rutgers.
threads: Rural Louisiana brass and string bands
Family and community ensembles of childhood
Dance bands in northern cities such as Boston
Orchestras and chamber music, from the Tio orchestra to Xavier concerts
Comic and novelty duos at white dances
Later country and Western swing bands

communities.name: Why Detroit produced so many jazz musicians
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds, including Detroit natives, visiting players and one-time residents, reflect on Detroit as a jazz city, mostly in the 1930s through the 1950s. Kenny Burrell traces the talent to migration for auto work, family incomes that could buy instruments, and opportunity. Frank Foster contrasts Detroit's large Black neighborhoods and cultural energy with Cincinnati, and ties them to the later rise of Motown. Eddie Locke frames the city as an environment where people learn from one another. Billy Mitchell and Big Nick Nicholas recall the club life of the late 1930s and early 1940s, with its black and tan clubs and the Carlton Hotel district. Sheila Jordan finds the Club Sudan and its scat singers, and Ron Carter remembers Detroit's clubs on his first road gig in the 1950s. Hank Jones is the skeptic, with no explanation for the outpouring of talent and a suspicion that the "Detroit sound" was a writer's phrase. The tellers agree that Detroit was exceptionally rich in musicians, but they differ on whether that can be explained.
threads: Migration, auto jobs and money for instruments
Detroit's large Black neighborhoods and Motown
Black and tan clubs and show lounges of the 1940s
Musical families and mentoring
Skepticism about the 'Detroit sound'
First road gigs and visits to Detroit clubs

communities.name: Naming the saxophonists: brief portraits of reed players
communities.parent_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists
communities.narrative: Across 32 interviews, mostly from Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive with a few from Rutgers and Hamilton, musicians are asked about saxophonists they knew and answer in short, name-by-name sketches. The tellers list the sax and clarinet players who passed through a band (Desvigne's and Ridgley's men, the Owls, Fate Marable's boat, a California band), and add a line or two of character or fate. Examples are a gut-bucket altoist, a player who lost his mind, a man nicknamed Nose who later repaired saxophones, and a sideman who is still working in New York. The settings run from the 1920s to the 1970s and range across New Orleans, Mississippi, Texas and California. The one exception to the interwar pattern is a pair of 1970s-era recollections of John Klemmer, an early New Age saxophonist from Don Ellis's band. The samples share an instrument and a format, the quick roll-call of a player, but no single event or story, so this is a loose cluster rather than a shared narrative.
threads: Roll-calls of sax and clarinet players in a bandleader's band
Riverboat and territory-band reed men (Marable, Rabbitfoot, California)
Short character sketches: style, fate, later life
Players from Mississippi and Texas who came to New Orleans
John Klemmer and the Don Ellis band

communities.name: Getting hired into a big band, Calloway and others
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they landed jobs in, moved between, or left working big bands in the 1930s and 1940s. The strongest strand is Cab Calloway's orchestra. Eddie Barefield, Mario Bauza, Quentin Jackson and Budd Johnson each describe how the offer came: a tip from a friend like Chu Berry or Doc Cheatham, a substitution at the Cotton Club, or an audition at a theater such as the Adams in Newark or the Hippodrome. Calloway's band comes across as the best-paying and best-organized, though Budd Johnson also mentions getting a pink slip at the Capitol Theater. Around that core sit similar career-path accounts from other bands: Les Hite and Joe Liggins on the West Coast, Don Albert's band breaking up in Cincinnati, Herbert Leary's local swing band in New Orleans, and Benny Carter's 1938 band in Harlem. The tellers agree that a band job turned on personal recommendation, timing and who was leaving. They differ in scale, from touring New York orchestras to local bands that made only short trips. The cluster is small, and outside the Calloway accounts it mostly shares the form of a joining-and-leaving anecdote, not one event.
threads: Cab Calloway makes an offer: Cotton Club subs and theater auditions
Pay, uniforms and organization in Calloway's band
Notices, pink slips and leaving a band
Local and regional swing bands: Leary, Albert, Lopreston
West Coast and Harlem band hopping: Hite, Liggins, Benny Carter

communities.name: Working for Cab Calloway: discipline, pay and showmanship
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Musicians who played in or alongside Cab Calloway's orchestra, mostly in the late 1930s through the 1940s, tell what it was like to work for him. The strongest agreement is on his discipline and his generosity: he demanded punctuality, clean uniforms and no drinking or marijuana, and he fired offenders and any clique. He also paid on time, bought uniforms, travelled first class by Pullman, gave paid vacations and Christmas bonuses, and advanced money for instruments, families and babies. Jonah Jones, who joined at the Stanley Theater in Pittsburgh in 1941 and stayed eleven years, supplies the most detail, including the three rules Cab set him, rotating features, and Cab directing every solo with his stick. Milt Hinton, Danny Barker, Quentin Jackson and Cozy Cole echo the praise for his fairness and his gift as an entertainer. A few voices differ or add nuance. Teddy McRae felt the band was well drilled but lacked Chick Webb's spirit. Horace Henderson says Cab was no musician and picked up arrangements by ear. A couple of samples are only loosely related: a Pensacola sighting of a bandleader compared to Cab, and Walter Thomas bawling out Cab at the Cotton Club.
threads: Strict discipline: punctuality, uniforms, no drugs, firing cliques
Paying well: wages, advances, loans, paid vacations and Christmas money
Traveling first class: Pullman berths, theatres and dressing rooms
Cab as showman and entertainer who controlled the soloists
Jonah Jones joining and living in the band for eleven years
Comparisons with other leaders and outside views of Cab

communities.name: Forming a new band: lineups, names and first gigs
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how a specific group came together: who was recruited, where the band rehearsed, how it got its name and which gig or contract launched it. The strongest strand is the late-1950s and early-1960s small-group scene. Chico Hamilton and Ken Poston describe the pianoless Mulligan quartet and the cello quintet that followed (Fred Katz, Jim Hall, Buddy Collette) after John Graas died. Benny Golson, Curtis Fuller and Cedar Walton tell how the Jazztet formed around Art Farmer, with Curtis Fuller suggesting the name, Steve Allen financing rehearsals, and Walton joining for ten dollars more. Others join the pattern: Slide Hampton and Branford Marsalis on Art Blakey's band, Art Farmer on Horace Silver's group, JJ Johnson's quintet with Nat Adderley, and Allen Toussaint on putting the Meters together. The tellers agree that these bands formed through personal connections and luck of timing, often with cooperative aims. The wider samples drift into other subjects, including Dave Brubeck's trio, Hubert Laws on a Herbie Hancock session, a Hamilton College student band, and Nick Brignola taking up baritone, so only a loose majority share the theme.
threads: Hamilton, Mulligan and the pianoless quartet and cello quintet
Forming the Jazztet: Golson, Farmer, Fuller and the name
Joining Art Blakey's and Horace Silver's bands
Small-group sidemen finding gigs and raises
Putting the Meters together in New Orleans

bands: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

communities.name: Keeping records, papers and collections, and where they go
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: Across Tulane, Hamilton, Rutgers and Smithsonian interviews, musicians are asked what has become of their own records, papers, tapes and memorabilia, and what should happen to them. Most of the central samples are archival housekeeping. Horace Henderson says his sister keeps 78s and Fletcher Henderson's papers in Georgia. Woody Herman says a friend holds nearly all his recordings. Curtis Fuller and Jack DeJohnette describe personal archives of tapes and gold records. Cliff Leeman and Theodore Saunders talk about donating papers or music to the Smithsonian, Wyoming or the Institute of Jazz Studies. Others, such as George Avakian, Quinn Wilson and Cosimo Matassa, say they never kept papers, letters or session logs, so the difference is between keepers and non-keepers. The Tulane interviews add a second strand: Bill Russell's collecting project, callers sent to the Tulane archive, William Ballariel handing band music to the interviewer, and the interviewer asking to borrow a record to tape. The cluster is a loose common thread rather than one tightly shared story. Some samples are only incidental logistics (a Bix book shop, a bugle-call booklet), and the period is mostly unstated, with dates from the 1920s to 1998.
threads: Where their own 78s, tapes and papers are kept
Donating collections to archives such as the Institute of Jazz Studies and the Smithsonian
Never saving letters, photographs or session logs
Interviewers collecting, borrowing and receiving music and records
Plans to catalogue or open an archive

communities.name: Dizzy, Cab and the spitball knife fight
communities.parent_name: Bandstand fights, knives and tempers
communities.narrative: Most of this cluster retells one famous incident: in 1940-41, in Cab Calloway's orchestra, a spitball or paper wad landed on stage, Cab blamed Dizzy Gillespie, and the quarrel ended with a knife. Dizzy cut or scratched Cab's hand or leg, and Dizzy left or was fired. Bandmates and witnesses tell it from the inside: Milt Hinton, Danny Barker, Jonah Jones, Cozy Cole (of the Cab Jivers) and Mona Hinton. They disagree on the details. Some say Cab slapped Dizzy first. Some say Milt deflected the blade. Jonah Jones says he was the one throwing the paper wads. Cab's own book is said to blame Milt. Aftermath stories follow: Charlie Barnet refused to hire the man who cut Cab, Dizzy joined the Les Hite band, and years later in Nice Cab showed Dizzy the scar and the two were friends. A few outlying segments extend the knife motif to other times and people. Dizzy pulls a knife on Mingus after Massey Hall, Ben Webster draws one on Dizzy, and a Dizzy temper story is set in Amsterdam. Another outlier is about Willie Lewis's band fighting in Portugal.
threads: The spitball incident and Cab's blame
Dizzy draws a knife, leaves or is fired
Cab's hatred of trash on stage
Aftermath: Barnet refuses Dizzy; Cab shows the scar in Nice
Other Dizzy tempers and knives (Mingus, Ben Webster, Amsterdam)

communities.name: Charles Mingus's temper, fights and chaotic bands
communities.parent_name: Bandstand fights, knives and tempers
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections tell stories about working for Charles Mingus, and the stories centre on his volatile temper and the disorder around his bands. The main set piece is the 1962 Town Hall concert. Eddie Bert, Toshiko Akiyoshi, Clark Terry, Buddy Collette and Snooky Young describe unfinished music, copyists on stage, Mingus stopping every piece and threatening to quit, and Clark Terry rescuing the night with Ellington tunes. They agree that Mingus hit trombonist Jimmy Knepper before that concert. A second strand is the physical confrontations of the 1950s, from the Cleveland fight in which Mingus punched Jackie McLean and McLean knifed him, to the dispute with Juan Tizol in Ellington's band, where Tizol's account disagrees with the one Mingus gives in Beneath the Underdog. Others recall how they were hired, at jam sessions in Greenwich Village or at the Showplace, and how they were fired, since Mingus would dismiss the whole band, and sometimes himself. Further stories cover his tantrums over money, such as wrecking a piano at a club that hadn't paid him, and his demanding, hard-to-read music. Most of the tellers were sidemen or peers in the 1950s and 1960s, and a few late samples are only loosely related (a Buffalo arranger's band, Jacques Butler's rival bandleader, a Ron Carter bandstand argument), which suggests a broader theme of bandstand conflict.
threads: The 1962 Town Hall concert fiasco and Clark Terry's rescue
Mingus hitting people: Knepper, McLean, Tizol and Tony Scott
Getting hired and fired by Mingus
Mingus's tantrums over money and club owners
Difficult music and rehearsals in Mingus's big band and workshop
Bandstand fights in other bands

bands: Charles Mingus Town Hall big band

communities.name: Piron and Robichaux: New Orleans society bands
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Most of these stories are about the two leading society orchestras of New Orleans, A. J. Piron's and John Robichaux's, as musicians remembered them from the 1910s through the 1930s. Tellers describe Piron's polished, strictly reading band of about eight to twelve pieces. It played note-for-note arrangements for wealthy, mostly white audiences at Spanish Fort, the Gravier Street roof garden, teas, carnival balls, country clubs and on the Streckfus boat. Others locate themselves by the bands they passed through, such as Robichaux, Piron, Silver Leaf, Supreme, La Vida and Ridgley's. They recount who replaced whom, who played piano or drums, and how second bands covered for the leaders. Kid Ory, Edmond Hall, Cie Frazier, Hypolite Charles and Willie Hightower tell it from the sidelines or from inside the bands. Tellers agree that these were the better-class reading bands, set apart from the rougher dance-hall groups. They differ on lineups, dates and even which leader was the left-handed fiddler. A few samples drift to other hotel and roof-garden bands, such as the Jung Hotel in the 1930s or the Blue Room around 1950, which fit only loosely.
threads: Piron's polished reading band for society audiences
Robichaux and Piron as early influences and rivals
Career sequences: moving between Robichaux, Piron, Silver Leaf and other bands
Venues: Spanish Fort, Gravier Street roof garden, Streckfus boat, balls and teas
Reading bands versus rougher dance-hall bands
Band lineups, sidemen and replacements

communities.name: Riding the advertising wagon and truck
communities.parent_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1900s through the 1940s describe how New Orleans dance bands advertised their dances by riding through the streets on horse- or mule-drawn furniture wagons and later on trucks. Tellers such as Kid Ory, Fess Manetta, Papa Jack Laine, Eddie Dawson, Earl Foster, Edgar Mosley and Joseph Rene recall the practical details. Signs were hand-painted on the sides, and boys handed out bills. The band sat in a set order, with the trombone at the tailgate, the bass at the rear and the drummer against the cab. The band played short numbers only when the wagon stopped on corners. They agree that trucks replaced wagons around the 1920s. Their accounts differ on whether it was a full orchestra or a small group, and several mention rival bands meeting at corners and playing against each other. A few related stories cover playing on the sidewalk in front of the hall to draw a crowd, and Gretna and Moss Point dances advertised by wagon. A small number of outliers (an Arizona parade band, a 1950s prom band, a recording engineer's sock hops) do not belong to the subject.
threads: Wagons giving way to trucks
Where each player sat
Playing on corners and band battles
Signs, handbills and advertising a particular dance
Playing outside the hall to draw a crowd

communities.name: Learning tunes on the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Musicians from many regions and decades describe learning the standard repertoire, song forms and chord changes not in classrooms but on the job: at jam sessions, club residencies, sit-in nights and first gigs. Settings run from Memphis and Baltimore's North End Lounge to Detroit, Tulsa, Toledo, Boston's Wally's Cafe, New York's Onyx Club and Playboy Club, a Heidelberg club and cruise ships, mostly from the late 1940s through the 1960s with a few 1990s tellers. The typical beat is exposure and embarrassment followed by instruction. A young player cannot play the blues or a waltz, is tested or sat out by older players, and a bassist, bandleader or peer then calls out changes or explains the form. Tellers agree that playing nightly, often by ear, taught more than formal study (Lonnie Liston Smith found only classical theory at college; Kenny Burrell calls Detroit a university without walls). They differ in route: some learn from records and transcription, some from older sidemen, some from famous elders such as Garner or Donald Bailey. The cluster is loose, since a few samples are about blues origins or collecting records rather than learning tunes.
threads: Jam sessions and sit-ins as a second school
Older players testing and teaching the young
Learning standards and form by ear
Nightly club residencies versus classroom study
Transcribing records and learning from famous elders

communities.name: Remembering Lester Young: Pres, his language and his ways
communities.parent_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and collections tell stories about Lester "Pres" Young, mostly as a person rather than as a set of recordings. The core of the cluster is the 1930s and 1940s Count Basie years in Kansas City and New York, but the tellers also reach back to his Minneapolis childhood and the Young family band, and forward to his 1950s work with Jazz at the Philharmonic and Birdland tours. The recurring points are his wholly original talk, nicknames and slang ("Lady Day", "Sweets", "Holy Man", "the slave", "George Washington"). They also dwell on his gentleness, humor and quiet manner, and on small scenes such as the dice games on the Basie bus, the gin hidden on a tour bus, and his stepping between friends in a fight. Colleagues like Harry Edison, Jo Jones, Buster Smith and Hank Jones agree he was an independent original who copied nobody, and they describe his sound and his horn. Younger players and critics recall him as a teacher or reference point, as in Frank Foster's verdict that he played too many notes, or a first Lester record bought as a teenager. Some tellers, such as Leonard Phillips, correct the written record on his early years, and Mingus and others differ on how the Army years changed him. A few samples drift to Lee Young, the Young family or musicians in general, so the shared subject is strong but not perfect.
threads: Pres's private vocabulary, slang and nicknames
Life with Basie: bus dice games, roads and rooms
Early years: Young family band, Minneapolis and carnival life
His sound, horn and originality as a tenor stylist
Gentleness, humor and peacemaking in the 1950s and JATP tours
Setting the record straight: biography, reputation and influence

communities.name: What the band wore: uniforms, caps and dress codes
communities.parent_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians describe what their bands wore and why it mattered. Most of the stories are set in New Orleans from about 1900 to the 1930s, and they are told mainly by Tulane interviewees. The brass bands come up again and again: the Excelsior, Eureka, Tuxedo, Onward, Eagle, Golden Rule, Magnolia and Imperial. Tellers recall the colours and cuts of the outfits, such as blue braided coats, green Eagle Band outfits, fireman or military-style caps and scoop hats with plumes. They also say who wore them, and for which jobs: parades and funerals in uniform, tuxedos for dances, cafes and advertising. Some tellers claim firsts, like Sidney Desvigne's claim to have led the first uniformed big band in the city. Others stress pride in appearance, and the cap even helped Pops Foster with girls. The accounts differ on details, for instance which band had uniforms first and whether mismatched or secondhand outfits were acceptable. A few later voices carry the subject forward: Joe Wilder on the 1940s big bands, Milton Batiste's insistence on dress for Olympia, and a 2006 revival band's straw hats.
threads: Brass band uniforms and caps in early New Orleans
Tuxedos and suits required for night-spot and dance work
Colours, cuts and which band wore what
Borrowed, secondhand and mismatched outfits
Big band uniforms and pride in appearance
Later revival bands keeping up the dress tradition

communities.name: Playing in the old brass bands
communities.parent_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the street and funeral brass bands of early New Orleans and the surrounding Louisiana towns, mostly in the 1900s through the 1920s. The tellers list who played in the Onward, Tuxedo, Eureka, Excelsior and Allen's bands, often under leaders such as Manuel Perez, Chris Kelly and Kid Rena. They agree on the basic shape: about ten to twelve pieces, with cornets, trombones, altos, baritone, bass and drums, hired for parades, funerals and lodge marches. They differ on how the bands played. George Lewis says the old bands read their music, Jim Robinson says Buddy Petit's band played by head, and August Lanoix objects to saxophones in a brass band. A few accounts come from plantation and country bands around Thibodaux and Woodland. Others separate brass-band work from dance-band work, as when Cie Frazier says the Young Tuxedo was strictly a dance band. Nearly all the tellers are New Orleans players from the Hogan Jazz Archive, recalling their first regular band jobs and their older relatives' bands.
threads: Band lineups and personnel (Onward, Tuxedo, Eureka)
First brass-band jobs and learning the work
Size, instrumentation and reading versus playing by head
Parades and funerals as the band's work
Country and plantation brass bands (Thibodaux, Woodland)
Brass bands versus dance bands

communities.name: Brass bands of New Orleans: who played in them
communities.parent_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the New Orleans brass bands they heard, marched with or played in, naming the Eureka, Tuxedo, Young Tuxedo, Olympia, Excelsior, Onward and Celestin's bands, along with smaller pick-up and neighborhood bands such as those in Algiers. The settings run from about 1906 to the mid-1960s, mostly the 1920s to 1950s, and nearly all the tellers are in the Tulane collection. Most of the stories are band-roster talk: who played trombone, bass, snare or bass drum, who managed or led the band, and who invited whom to play. Some tellers are listeners who followed the bands as boys or visitors, such as Bob Watts, Edgar Mosley and Ken Colyer. Others were working street-parade players, such as Earl Foster, Sidney Brown and Noon Johnson. A few tellers add comments on discipline and ensemble playing, as when Ernie Cagnolatti says players once stepped off together on the first beat and Lars Edegran discusses why a band does not play together. The tellers share a subject but not a single event, so the pack reads as many brief recollections of different bands rather than one story.
threads: Eureka and Tuxedo band personnel and rosters
Hearing and following parade bands as a boy
Playing street parades in pick-up and neighborhood bands
Drummers and bass drum in the brass band
Discipline, instrumentation and marching in step
Algiers and early-1900s night parade bands

communities.name: Social clubs, benevolent societies and their decline
communities.parent_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians, mostly interviewed at Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, explain how New Orleans Black social clubs, pleasure clubs and benevolent or burial societies worked. They describe who could join (vouching or investigation, age limits of roughly 18 to 65), monthly dues and meetings, and the separate pleasure and death funds. They also cover the benefits: sick pay, funeral costs, fines for members who missed a funeral, and annual outings. Tellers agree on the basic split: societies gave sickness and burial benefit, while clubs were for pleasure and often had no death or sick benefits. They also describe the anniversary parades, the expensive outfits and the plainer white-shirt, black-pants parade dress. Several compare clubs with insurance companies and banks, and some recall a big club such as the San Jacinto with about 1,500 members. A recurring closing note, mostly from older men looking back from the 1950s to 1970s, is that the old societies are dwindling, selling off halls, losing money and failing to attract young members. The period runs from the early 1900s to about 1970.
threads: How clubs and societies were run: joining, dues, meetings
Death benefits, sick pay and funeral obligations
Pleasure clubs versus benevolent societies versus insurance companies
Anniversary parades, outfits and outings
Decline of old societies, lost halls and fading membership
Musicians' own memberships and the clubs they played for

communities.name: Parading in New Orleans: Mardi Gras, brass bands and social clubs
communities.parent_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall playing for, watching, or growing up around street parades in New Orleans, above all at Mardi Gras and for the city's carnival and benevolent social clubs. The setting is mostly the 1900s to 1950s, along Canal Street, Claiborne Avenue, Rampart Street and the neighborhoods. Brass bands such as the Eureka, Tuxedo and George Williams bands play for Odd Fellows and Masons drill teams, the Zulu and white carnival clubs (Lions, Eleonora), and funerals. Tellers agree that parades were grueling: long routes, stops at bars and homes, easier tunes saved for the walk back, and a typical pay of a few dollars per parade. They differ on whether they enjoyed it. Some, such as drummers and trumpeters, say they gave it up because of the walking, while brass-band regulars treat it as steady work. Some tellers focus on childhood memories of masking, Indians and carnival songs. Others recall the carnival balls and Rex orchestras, or later worries about violence and repertoire at second lines. A few outliers (Ken Colyer's band in Britain, Italian feast bands, a 1919 strike parade) widen the frame, and the cluster slides toward adjacent topics such as carnival ball engagements and band personnel.
threads: Mardi Gras day: playing, masking and watching as a child
Brass bands and club parades: Eureka, Tuxedo, Odd Fellows and Masons drill teams
The hardship and pay of parading: long routes, easier tunes, quitting
Carnival balls and krewe engagements (Rex, Zulu, Lions Club, Creole Fiesta)
Second lines, repertoire and street disorder in later decades

communities.name: Paying for the funeral band: societies, dues and cigar boxes
communities.parent_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line
