communities.narrative: Musicians from the early 1900s through the 1950s explain how New Orleans funeral brass bands got hired and paid. Benevolent and burial societies collected monthly or quarterly dues and hired the bands, often several, for members' burials. Where no society stood behind the dead man, neighbours passed a saucer or cigar box to raise the band's price. Pay is remembered as small, about three dollars a man in the 1890s and five or six dollars in the late 1950s. Bandleaders such as Allen and Carnish visited dying society members to line up the funeral job in advance, and some musicians joined societies to get that work. Tellers differ on detail: some say bands once played free, or only for musicians, while Jessie Charles separates donated jobs from paid parades. The union later took over arranging funeral bands. The tellers are mostly Tulane-archive New Orleans musicians, with a few outliers such as a plantation burial account and an Australian convention story that fit less well.
threads: Benevolent and burial societies, dues, and hiring the band
Passing the saucer or cigar box for a funeral band
What funeral jobs paid, and when bands played free
Bandleaders lining up funeral jobs through societies
The union and later changes in funeral band work

communities.name: Jazz funerals: dirges going, second line coming back
communities.parent_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers stories about New Orleans funerals and the brass bands that played them, mostly set between about 1900 and the 1960s. Musicians describe the same ritual shape: the band assembles at a society hall or corner, accompanies the body from church or undertaker to the cemetery with slow hymns and dirges on muffled snares, then "cuts the body loose" and strikes up lively numbers like "Didn't He Ramble" for the second line on the way back. Tellers such as Danny Barker, Herb Morand, Barney Bigard and William Ballariel recall the burial societies, grand marshals, horse-drawn hearses, and the all-night playing and drinking that followed at someone's house or a bar. Later musicians such as Michael White, Milton Batiste, Wendell Brunious and Clyde Kerr Jr. interpret the music as a celebration of a life and lament the tradition's erosion through tourists, kid bands and families wary of offense. A smaller set strays to wakes and funeral customs outside New Orleans (Miami, Tampa, Mississippi fife and drum) and to funerals of particular musicians such as George Lewis, Percy Humphrey and Ray Nance. Working players like Albert Jiles and Red Clark add the practical side: pickup bands, which bands got the work, and how many funerals a year they played.
threads: Anatomy of a jazz funeral: dirge out, hot music back, second line
Burial societies, grand marshals and who played the funerals
Wakes and all-night playing after the burial
Changing attitudes: tourists, revival bands and the tradition's erosion
Funerals of particular musicians (George Lewis, Percy Humphrey, Ray Nance)
Funeral customs outside New Orleans

communities.name: Playing the Newport Jazz Festival, 1954-65
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds recall playing, or being on the edges of, the Newport Jazz Festival in its first dozen years. Jo Jones and Cliff Leeman remember the first festival in 1954, held in the rain, with Eddie Condon conducting under an umbrella and Jones as house drummer backing Billie Holiday. Bud Freeman says George Wein hired him back after seeing him on TV, and he went on to play fourteen festivals. Jimmy Jones and Sheila Jordan describe the sets they played there. Other tellers describe Newport as a place of conflict. In 1960 Abbey Lincoln, Wilbur Ware and John Malachi recall the Roach and Mingus protest, the rebel counter-festival and a rowdy non-jazz crowd. In 1965 Carla Bley recalls the Jazz Composers Orchestra being booked into the Anti-Festival and getting a hostile audience. The cluster is dominated by Newport, but a few samples drift to other festivals such as Monterey and Boston Common, and to loosely related touring talk, so it is a clear majority rather than a uniform theme.
threads: The rainy first Newport festival in 1954
George Wein hiring and booking musicians
The 1960 protest and rebel counter-festival
Avant-garde bands at the 1965 Newport Anti-Festival
Singers and bandleaders recalling their Newport sets
Other festivals: Monterey and Boston Common

communities.name: Stepping out as a leader with your own band
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Musicians from many eras describe the moment they stopped being sidemen and started leading their own group. Count Basie says he simply wanted to try leading after a band in Little Rock (1935). Roy Eldridge formed a big band in 1943, Tiny Grimes led a quartet and sextet on 52nd Street and recorded for Blue Note (1944-45), and JJ Johnson chose his players by word of mouth for a first date in 1946-47. Big Nick Nicholas left Dizzy Gillespie around 1949 and learned the business side by taking small jobs. Later tellers include Junior Mance, who was offered a Verve album while with Dizzy, a leader who won a Village Vanguard week with Ron Carter, Kenny Barron and Lewis Nash in the early 1990s, and a woman who led a quartet and big band for years before being hired as a sideperson. Harry Fairconnetue's New Orleans weekend band and Don Alias's Stone Alliance fit more loosely. The tellers agree that leading means choosing personnel, finding work and handling business, though they differ on whether it was an ambition or a chance offer. The cluster is small and spans the 1930s to the 1990s, so the common thread is the step into leadership rather than any one scene.
threads: Why I wanted to lead: Basie, Eldridge and the first big bands
Choosing players for a first date as leader
Small groups on 52nd Street and Blue Note recordings
Leaving a star's band and learning the business
Record-label offers and club weeks as a leader
Weekend and cooperative bands alongside day jobs

communities.name: Choosing keys, flat keys and key changes
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection talk about keys as a practical and expressive problem on the bandstand. The largest strand is accompanying singers: finding the key that fits a vocalist's range, the confusion when a singer asks for a note and means something else, and the habit of transposing on the spot (Giacomo Gates, Lou Pallo, Michael Abene, Jack DeJohnette, Harold Mabern at Birdland). A second strand is why jazz leans on flat keys, which suit horns, and why odd or difficult keys trap players, as in Dave Pell's tale of Ray Brown's E-blues and Lester Young changing keys to unsettle horn players. A third strand covers modulation as an arranging device, from 1920s New Orleans and Chicago tunes that modulate to keep each chorus fresh, to 1930s three-minute records that forced abrupt key jumps, to chart modulations in the 1940s. Tellers also describe keys as feelings or colors (Jim Hall, Alan Broadbent, Sands). A few samples drift toward harmony and chord changes in general, such as passing tones, chord symbols and two-chord tunes, which is why the cluster is only loosely unified. Tellers are mostly working players, including guitarists, bassists, pianists and arrangers, and they largely agree on the practicalities. The main difference is that older players speak of habit and repertoire, while later ones talk about feel.
threads: Finding the right key for singers and transposing on the spot
Why jazz favors flat keys and what difficult keys do to players
Modulation and key changes as an arranging tool, from New Orleans to the three-minute record
Keys as feelings, colors and signals on the bandstand
Side drift into harmony, chord changes and chord symbols

communities.name: Working the New Orleans clubs c. 1950: George Lewis at El Morocco
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians recall steady club and bar jobs in New Orleans in the 1940s and early 1950s, with the George Lewis band's residency at El Morocco on Bourbon and Iberville (c. 1949-50) as the clearest shared episode. Joe Watkins, Bernard Steinau's 1950 journal entries and Sid Davilla describe the club, the lineup (Slow Drag Pavageau, Alton Purnell, Lawrence Marrero, Jim Robinson), and how manager Nick Gagliano found the band regular work. Watkins also tells how Reverend Kershaw and Dr. Ball then took the band to Cincinnati, Los Angeles and beyond. Other tellers describe different rooms and bands: Pete Herman's, the Harmony Inn, Happy Land and the Melody Inn, Speck's with Kid Thomas, and the Mardi Gras Lounge and Paddock. These stories share the setting of sit-in club jobs and personnel changes, but only some concern Lewis or El Morocco, so the cluster holds together loosely.
threads: George Lewis band's residency at El Morocco
Nick Gagliano managing and booking the band
From New Orleans to national tours (Cincinnati, Los Angeles)
Sit-in jobs at neighborhood bars and clubs (Harmony Inn, Happy Land, Melody Inn)
Band personnel shuffles and substituting for Lewis's men
Wartime and 1940s small bands (Kid Thomas at Speck's, Pete Herman's)

communities.name: Stopping the show: stage acts and showmanship
communities.parent_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows
communities.narrative: These stories are about performing for the stage rather than the dance floor: acts built to win an audience, and the showmanship that went with them. The most concentrated thread is John W. Bubbles telling of Buck and Bubbles in 1931. After the Ritz Brothers flopped at Loew's State, he vowed to quit unless they headlined, and the next morning they were on the marquee. He describes cutting a 14-minute act to nine minutes for the Ziegfeld Follies, dancing over the laughs, and stopping the show anyway, with Harry Richman quieting the house. He also describes doubling between the Lafayette uptown and the Follies downtown. Around that core sit band musicians, including Don Albert, Jimmie Crawford of the Lunceford band, Ernie Fields's Leon Wright, Sam Jones and New Orleans bandleader Johnny DeDroit. They recall the tricks that made a band a show: thrown and caught horns, promenading saxophones, glee-club arrangements, comedy dress acts and floor shows. The period is mostly the 1930s to 1950, and the tellers agree that visual routines and audience reaction mattered as much as the music. They differ in setting, since the vaudeville and Broadway headliner story is quite separate from the touring-band novelty acts. Because one interviewee supplies a quarter of the segments, the cluster leans heavily toward a single narrative.
threads: Buck and Bubbles headlining at Loew's State in 1931
Cutting the act to nine minutes in the Ziegfeld Follies
Doubling between the Lafayette in Harlem and downtown theaters
Band novelty routines: thrown horns, promenading sax sections, glee club
Comedy and dress acts within touring bands
Floor shows and backing variety acts

communities.name: Friends and colleagues: musicians on their bonds
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: In these short segments a musician talks about a particular person they know, usually a fellow musician, producer or collaborator, and what that person means to them. The dominant register is friendship and personal character: David Baker calls Ted Dunbar his brother and Muhal Richard Abrams a close friend, Candido Camero praises Bebo Valdes as the best person he has met in music, Bernie Kirsh remembers Chick Corea's generosity, and Buddy Tate and Jimmie Crawford recall friendships with Trumbauer and Sid Catlett. A second strand is professional admiration, with Ron Carter on Kenny Barron, Jack DeJohnette and Johnny Pate, and Herb Ellis on Joe Pass. A few are tributes read aloud by the interviewer, or first meetings. The period runs from the 1930s to the 1980s and later, across all four collections, and the tellers are jazz, session and popular musicians alike. The segments share the form of a short portrait of one named person rather than a single event, so the cluster is a loose genre of storytelling, not a tight subject.
threads: Lifelong friendship and brotherhood between musicians
Praise for a collaborator's playing and sound
Tributes and remembrances read or given after a death
First meetings and getting acquainted
Mentors and helpers who looked out for younger players
Long working partnerships with a bandleader or singer

communities.name: Rivalry, camaraderie and being easy to work with
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians across many interviews reflect on how players treat one another: whether jazz is a competition, whether the great ones are also good people, and what personality has to do with staying employed. The best-developed thread is Machito's account of 1950s Latin New York, where Tito Puente and Tito Rodriguez contended for top billing. Machito shrugs off the rivalry, comparing himself to a champion boxer, and says other bands' hits were good for the music. Elsewhere, Art Farmer, Candido Camero, J.C. Higginbotham and Allan Vaché describe jam-session competition as friendly, with drummers recommending each other for jobs. Sidemen such as Tom Malone, Jerome Richardson, Al Chez, David Torkanowsky and Ray Ricker add a working-musician's view: chops get you the first call, but being easy to hang with gets you called back. A few tellers contrast New Orleans players as modest and kind with commercial New York, or recall disappointing meetings with admired figures. The samples share a loose theme of musicians' character and competitiveness, but several (Levy, Drummond, Von Freeman, Ran Blake) drift to other reflections, so the cluster is only moderately unified.
threads: Machito on billing rivalry with Puente and Rodriguez
Friendly competition at jam sessions and cutting contests
Great musicians as fine people, and meeting heroes
Being easy to work with and getting called back
New Orleans modesty versus New York commercialism
Egos, hogging the spotlight and playing down to weaker players

communities.name: On the road with a working band
communities.parent_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters
communities.narrative: Musicians recall joining a leader's touring band and living the road: auditions, learning the book, one-nighters, and long bus or car travel. The largest strand is Woody Herman's orchestra, told by players who joined between the early 1950s and the mid-1960s (Coker, Beal, Zito, Temperley), with Nat Pierce recurring as a colleague. They agree that the work was constant and the travel rough. Beal describes a broken-down bus and a school bus to Newport, and Temperley found the bus travel too rigorous after eighteen months. Other tellers describe different leaders: Chico Hamilton's quintet, which worked 48 weeks a year and was Ron Carter's first tour in 1959, Herbie Mann's 1965-66 band, and Red Allen's pickup band in Mexico. Lou Donaldson and Snub Mosley instead describe starting their own tours and package shows. The common thread is the working life of a sideman on tour, but the leaders, eras and places vary, so it is a loose grouping rather than one story.
threads: Joining and auditioning for Woody Herman
Bus and car travel on one-nighters
Learning the book in a new band
Chico Hamilton's quintet and long club runs
Leaders putting together their own tours and package shows

communities.name: Disaster on the road: bus fires, crashes and lost gear
communities.parent_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters
communities.narrative: Musicians from big bands and small touring groups tell of things going wrong between gigs: buses that burned or lost their brakes, car and bus wrecks, a truck that overturned or caught fire, and instruments, uniforms and drums that were stolen or destroyed. The stories are mostly set from the 1920s to the mid-1950s, on southern, midwestern and eastern highways (Ohio, Iowa, Kentucky, Texas, West Virginia, Vermont, New Mexico). The recurring details are the practical losses: bass and drums burned, trunks of uniforms stolen, bands reaching the theater without their clothes or horns. A few tellers go further and recall deaths. The 1935 Earl Hines bus crash that killed Cecil Irwin is told by both Quinn Wilson and Theodore Saunders, and Arnett Cobb recounts the weekend before his own 1956 crash. Tellers agree that the road was dangerous and expensive. They differ in tone, with some stories played for near-comic escape and others told as grief. Tellers include sidemen and leaders from Black territory bands, swing orchestras and white dance bands alike. A couple of samples drift toward general touring anecdotes, such as a conned record machine and a snake thrown into a car.
threads: Bus fires and brake failures
The 1935 Earl Hines bus crash and the death of Cecil Irwin
Car and truck wrecks on tour
Stolen or burned instruments, drums and uniforms
Illness and pranks on the road

communities.name: Life on the road: buses, Pullmans and one-nighters
communities.parent_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans territory bands to the big swing orchestras and later bebop and jazz-rock players tell about the practical business of touring. The core is how the band travelled: Pullman cars and baggage cars on the Ellington, Calloway and Barefield theater tours, band buses and bought-and-repaired buses, cars on mud roads, and Greyhound or train for single trips. The setting is mostly the 1920s to 1950s, across Texas, Louisiana, the Deep South, Chicago and New York, with a few 1960s-70s voices. The tellers split on comfort. Swing-era players describe touring in style (private Pullmans, local bands meeting the train, avoiding Southern hotels), while Oliver-era and territory-band players stress breakdowns, pushing the bus, unpaid dates and running out of money. Later players such as Moody, Wess, Napoleon and Nancy Wilson describe the tedium and physical toll of road life, with bad meals, little sleep and endless travel days. A few samples only mention touring in passing, for example band-personnel stories and a ball-club trip, so the edges are loose.
threads: Pullman cars and baggage cars on swing-band theater tours
Band buses, breakdowns and mud roads in the territory bands
Touring in style versus hard travel with unpaid bands
The toll of the road: meals, sleep, boredom and long drives
Riding with the famous bands: Basie, Ellington, Calloway, Woody Herman
One-nighter circuits and booking across Texas, the South and the East

communities.name: Two Tuxedo bands: Celestin, Ridgley and the 1925 split
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Musicians who worked in or around the Tuxedo Band of 1920s New Orleans explain how it came to be two bands: Oscar "Papa" Celestin's and William "Ba Ba" Ridgley's. Ridgley, who managed and acted as business agent, describes the Tuxedo orchestra as his and the brass band as Celestin's, with the same men playing both and the two leaders passing funeral and dance work back and forth. Paul Barnes and Bill Matthews place the break around 1925 and link it to money (a "one-dollar split" is mentioned). Barnes says he and others persuaded Celestin to form his own band, with Jeanette Sullivan on piano. Eddie Marrero adds that John Marrero sided with Ridgley after the split while Simon Marrero played with Celestin. Harold Dejan and Fred Minor take up the practical question of how the two Tuxedo names were told apart. Most tellers are New Orleans sidemen who played the society jobs, brass band work and Tranchina's, and they mostly agree on the sequence. The outliers are a few segments about moving between bands, such as leaving Kid Rena for the Tuxedo band, and one about sorting out the order of a single musician's bands.
threads: The 1925 split between Ridgley and Celestin over money
Two Tuxedo bands, one pool of men: orchestra vs. brass band
Who went with whom: the Marreros and other sidemen choosing sides
Joining the Tuxedo Band from Kid Rena's and other bands for better pay
Celestin's comings and goings and the Fort Worth trip personnel

communities.name: Who was on the Detroit scene
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds name and place the players of Detroit's jazz community, mostly in the 1940s and 1950s with a few glances back to the 1930s and forward to the early 1960s. The recurring core is the cohort of Barry Harris, Tommy Flanagan, Kenny Burrell, Paul Chambers, Donald Byrd, Billy Mitchell and Hank and Thad Jones. Frank Foster (stationed or working in Detroit around 1949-50) and Curtis Fuller give the most detailed roll-calls, while outsiders such as Jon Hendricks, Sheila Jordan, Sammy Price and Quentin Jackson recall Detroit names they met. Several tellers describe what Detroit was like musically: show-style honking tenor bands, a forward drummers' beat, and the Showbar and jam-session circuit, and some describe the Detroit players arriving in New York around 1956. A few samples drift to neighbouring regional scenes such as Pittsburgh, Pontiac and Flint, or to the New Orleans-Detroit connection, and Hank Jones says he barely knew many of the names the interviewer put to him.
threads: Roll-calls of Detroit musicians in 1949-50
Barry Harris, Flanagan, Burrell and the Detroit cohort
Is there a Detroit sound: bands, beat and jam sessions
Detroit players arriving in New York in the 1950s
Neighbouring Michigan, Ohio and Pittsburgh scenes
1930s Detroit bands and soloists

communities.name: Ohio and Midwest bands and musicians before swing
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Musicians from the Rutgers, Smithsonian and Tulane interviews list the local players and bands of Ohio and the neighboring Midwest, mostly in the 1920s and 1930s. The clearest strand is Harry Edison's Columbus: he names Paul Tyler, Pete France, Earl Hood, John Hooks, Sy Oliver and Jimmy Crawford, and Zack White's band. He also places Columbus among the nearby dance towns of Cincinnati, Cleveland and Dayton. Quentin Jackson widens the map to Louisville-born players, to territory bands across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois, and to Buffalo as a hub that hosted Trent, Lunceford and Stuff Smith. Sam Wooding adds Detroit's twelve-piece bands around 1920. Frank Foster's later stories, from 1946-49, cover the personnel of the Wilberforce Collegians, and Curtis Fuller's 1950s memories of Cleveland and Buffalo players are the latest in the set. The samples agree that these were rich regional scenes, but they are mostly name-lists from different cities and eras, with no single event or plot.
threads: Columbus players and bands (Edison)
Ohio as a crossroads of dance towns
Territory bands and Louisville, Buffalo and Detroit
Wilberforce Collegians personnel
Cleveland and Buffalo players in the 1950s

communities.name: Reactions to Ken Burns's Jazz series
communities.parent_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press
communities.narrative: Musicians, critics and collectors interviewed around 2000-2001 react to Ken Burns's PBS documentary series Jazz. Nearly all the samples are about the series itself, and the tellers split on its value. Some, like Wycliffe Gordon, Carol Bash and Dick Hyman, defend or enjoy it for bringing jazz to a mass audience and for the publicity it gave the music. Many others criticise its omissions and balance. Hank Jones says it left out the Lafayette Theatre era. Burrill Crohn and Jackie McLean object to its reliance on consultants such as Stanley Crouch and Wynton Marsalis. Quincy Jones says the last two hours crammed in too many names and hurt Benny Carter. Several tell personal stories of being approached by Burns's office, refusing to take part (McLean on Coltrane, Quincy Jones), or having their own footage cut (Hyman's solo with Charlie Parker). Chico Hamilton dismisses the series as poor and says he does his own thing. Kenny Davern's wider complaint about Marsalis-era repertory and the decline of jazz sits at the edge of the cluster.
threads: Praise for bringing jazz to a mass audience
Omissions and imbalance, such as the Lafayette Theatre and Benny Carter
Marsalis and Crouch as consultants
Being asked to take part, refusing, or being cut
Wider complaints about the state of jazz and jazz history

communities.name: Chicago's South Side jazz scene, 1915-1945
communities.parent_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene
communities.narrative: This is a broad community of stories about Chicago as a destination and workplace for jazz musicians, mostly set between the late 1910s and the mid-1940s. New Orleans migrants such as Punch Miller, Bob Shoffner, Danny Barker, Ed Garland and Sam Dutrey recall arriving, finding work and joining or following King Oliver, Jimmie Noone and Freddie Keppard. Players from elsewhere, including Sammy Price, Milt Hinton, Happy Caldwell and Emmanuel Sayles, describe settling in, sitting in and meeting Earl Hines and others. The stories are anchored in the South Side entertainment district around State Street and 35th Street, and in venues such as the Dreamland, Royal Gardens, Sunset Cafe and Grand Terrace. Tellers mostly agree on the geography and the cast of bandleaders. They differ in what they stress: job-by-job band histories, portraits of individual players, or the social and economic setting, such as Prohibition, mixed audiences and the Great Migration. A few samples drift to later Chicago (Sun Ra in 1960, the 1949 trombone group, 1970s gigs) or to unrelated detail, so the shared subject is a place and era rather than a single event.
threads: Arriving in Chicago from New Orleans and the Great Migration
Working for King Oliver, Jimmie Noone and the Dreamland and Lincoln Gardens bands
Sitting in, jam sessions and meeting Earl Hines and Louis Armstrong
South Side clubs, State Street and the black entertainment district
Prohibition, audiences and how Chicago style changed
Later Chicago gigs in the 1940s to 1960s

communities.name: King Oliver's band goes west to San Francisco, 1921
communities.parent_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene
communities.narrative: The core of this story is King Oliver's 1921 trip from Chicago to California. Ed Garland, Lillian Hardin Armstrong, Minor "Ram" Hall and Joe Darensbourg all tell it. The band left Dreamland in Chicago around May 1921 and played a San Francisco dance hall, the Pergola Ballroom among others. They then moved on to Oakland, with Market Street and the Bay Area scene around them. Tellers list the personnel and agree on the broad outline. They differ on the details. Hall describes the dispute in which Oliver fired him and violinist Jimmy Palao, and the union then ruled in Hall's favour. Garland recalls the firings as abrupt, and he also describes a stranded big band at the Plantation. Armstrong adds that she returned to Chicago in early 1922. Local West Coast players such as Clem Raymond and Joe Darensbourg recall hearing or crossing paths with Oliver and Kid Ory, who was also active in California. Around this core are looser Oliver stories. Paul Barnes tells of leaving Celestin's band in 1927 after Oliver heard "My Josephine", and Lionel Reason tells of rejoining Oliver's ragged band in the mid-1930s. Don Ewell's Kid Ory item from the 1950s is the weakest fit. The tellers are mostly New Orleans and Chicago players from the Tulane and Rutgers collections.
threads: The 1921 Dreamland departure and San Francisco/Oakland engagements
Oliver's lineup and the firing of Minor Hall and Jimmy Palao
Local Bay Area and Los Angeles musicians meeting Oliver and Ory
Paul Barnes leaving Celestin to join Oliver after My Josephine
Later Oliver band decline in the 1930s

communities.name: Jazz meets the symphony: commissions and orchestral projects
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Later-career musicians describe taking jazz into the symphonic and classical world, either as soloists with orchestras and chamber groups or as composers and arrangers writing for them. Slam Stewart is the clearest voice. In the early 1970s he played concerto-style scores written for his bass with the Binghamton and Indianapolis symphonies, premiered Jack Martin's "A Symphonic Dream for Slam," and played classical works with jazz cadenzas alongside string quartets and a woodwind quintet. He also looked ahead to Berklee and Boston Pops dates and new scores for orchestras. Others, mostly working from the 1970s to the 2010s, tell the writing-side version: Frank Foster on the Jazzmobile Lake Placid Suite and hoped-for commissions such as a jazz mass and opera, Rufus Reid on a commissioned suite inspired by Elizabeth Catlett's sculpture, Dave Rivello on writing for strings and a high school studio orchestra, and Tom Malone on arranging pop hits for a symphony. The tellers share a sense of commissions, residencies and campus settings as the route into orchestral work. They differ in whether they are soloists being featured or composers being commissioned. Louis Nelson's segment on a Shreveport symphony and a pianist-teacher fits only loosely, so the cluster is a loose common thread rather than one tightly shared story.
threads: Slam Stewart playing bass with symphony orchestras
Jazz cadenzas with string quartets and woodwind quintet
Commissioned suites and works (Jazzmobile, Catlett-inspired suite)
Writing and arranging for strings and studio orchestras
Future plans: new scores, jazz mass and opera
Campus and conference settings for crossover projects

communities.name: Hearing the great swing bands: Henderson, Ellington, Lunceford
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds recall the big bands they heard, admired and argued over in the late 1920s and 1930s, with Fletcher Henderson's orchestra the constant reference point. Tellers such as Hayes Pillars, Quentin Jackson, Charlie Holmes and Ram Ramirez recall a first hearing of Henderson, often naming the whole personnel (Hawkins, Redman, Buster Bailey, Armstrong). Others rank the bands against one another: Jacques Butler calls Ellington versus Henderson a toss-up, Benny Waters rates Lunceford's showmanship above Basie's, and Gus Johnson prefers Ellington and Horace Henderson. The stories are set in New York, Chicago, Detroit and the touring circuit, at places like the Savoy, Roseland and the Chicago Armory. They agree that Henderson, Ellington and Lunceford set the standard and that arrangers such as Redman, Sampson and Wilcox shaped the sound. They differ on taste: Arthur Briggs found Henderson's recordings rough, while Kansas City players like Gene Ramey favored their own regional bands. The group also takes in McKinney's Cotton Pickers, John Kirby's sextet and lesser-known bands such as Alphonso Trent's. A few samples (Jack Teagarden on Texas bands, Hank Jones on Kirby, Nick La Rocca on early recording bands) drift toward a broader band-talk, so the shared subject is loose but real.
threads: First hearing Fletcher Henderson's band and naming its personnel
Ranking the best bands: Henderson vs Ellington vs Lunceford
Arrangers and the sound of the swing orchestra (Redman, Sampson, Wilcox)
John Kirby's sextet and McKinney's Cotton Pickers
Regional and overlooked bands (Trent, Gay Floyd, Speed Webb, Charlie Johnson)
Records, jukeboxes and the abundance of bands

communities.name: New Orleans jazz travels north: Chicago, New York and the Dixieland revival
communities.parent_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels
communities.narrative: Musicians from different generations tell how New Orleans jazz moved out of its home city and was received, imitated or reinterpreted elsewhere. The setting is mostly the 1910s to 1950s, in New Orleans, Chicago and New York. Older players such as Billy McBride, Al Rose and Benny Carter describe the spread itself. They credit New Orleans men moving to Chicago, the Original Dixieland Jazz Band's 1916 success, King Oliver's influence and records reaching New York. Carter is notably skeptical that New Orleans players really changed New York music, though he says they were respected there. A younger group, including Donn Andre, Bobby Gordon, Phil Mead and Bob Wilber, tells a related but different story. They learned the style from records or from the Eddie Condon and Jimmy Ryan's scene, and they argue over what to call it (Dixieland, classic jazz, Chicago style) and who the revivalists were. The tellers agree that the music moved north and east. They differ on whether the movement was an influence or a revival, and on whether the white Chicago and New York players kept it faithful. The samples share a loose geography and lineage more than one event, so the cluster is only moderately tight.
threads: How New Orleans players and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band spread jazz to Chicago and the North
Whether New Orleans music really changed New York in the 1920s, and which records New Yorkers heard
Chicago-style and Condon-circle players and their two-beat feel
Young revivalists in the 1940s-50s learning from records and New York clubs
Arguments over the term Dixieland versus classic or traditional jazz

communities.name: Remembering Bix Beiderbecke: the cornetist and his circle
communities.parent_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection talk about Bix Beiderbecke, the young cornetist of the 1920s who came up with the Wolverines and then played with Jean Goldkette and Paul Whiteman beside Frank Trumbauer. Some tell of hearing him live or sitting in with him, at Chicago hangouts like Wingy Manone's My Cellar, the Paradise Inn, a Cincinnati all-night spot, or a New York rehearsal where he taught Jimmy McPartland the Wolverines' arrangements. Others, such as Doc Cheatham, Chauncey Morehouse, Jacques Butler and Victor Moore, describe his tone, taste, modesty, quietness and habit of never playing a solo the same way twice. A good share of the stories concern his sources and influence: the Original Dixieland Jazz Band and New Orleans Rhythm Kings records the Chicago gang learned from, his debt to New Orleans players, the New Orleans cornetist Emmett Hardy, and imitators like Red Nichols. Collaborators such as Bill Challis and Armand Hug add arranging and piano detail, and younger players and critics reflect on his legend, his rumored private life, his grave and the Bix revival concerts. The tellers largely agree he was exceptional, but they differ on whether his playing sounded better in person, whether Red Nichols was comparable, and whether he deserves the myth. A few samples drift to neighbouring figures such as Bunny Berigan, Wild Bill Davison and Teschemacher, but Bix stays the common reference.
threads: Hearing and sitting in with Bix in Chicago and New York
Bix's tone, taste and quiet personality
Whiteman, Goldkette and Trumbauer years
Where Bix learned: ODJB, NORK records and Emmett Hardy
Challis and Hug on Bix's piano thinking and arrangements
Bix's legend, imitators and posthumous reputation

communities.name: Playing in the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis Orchestra, the New York big band formed in 1965-66 to play Thad's writing and best known for its Monday nights at the Village Vanguard. Its founders were New York studio players who wanted a band to blow in, and they rehearsed late on Monday nights at Jim and Andy's and later at A&R Studios. Founding members such as Snooky Young and Jimmy Owens, later joiners such as Jerry Dodgion, and subs such as Joe Temperley and Lew Tabackin tell how they came into the band, and Harold Danko tells how he came to play piano in the 1970s. Nearly all of them praise Thad as writer, soloist and conductor, and several call it the hardest or best band they ever played in. They differ on the details: Quentin Jackson dislikes touring, Jimmy Owens left after about three months because Mel Lewis would not let him take time off, and Woody Herman says the band fell apart outside New York. A few tellers come at it from the edges, through a guest guitar part on the album Consummation, Thad's Dick Cavett show band, or Mel Lewis's band after Thad left for Europe. The tellers are mostly horn and rhythm-section players, many interviewed for the Fillius Jazz Archive at Hamilton College.
threads: Founding the band for Thad's writing, with New York studio players and Monday rehearsals
Monday nights at the Village Vanguard
Joining or subbing for a chair in the band
Thad as writer, soloist and conductor
Mel Lewis's drumming and the band after Thad left
Recordings and the hard road life

communities.name: Playing for Count Basie: joining the band and the leader
communities.parent_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell about the Count Basie Orchestra from the inside or the audience: how they got the call, what the band was like, and what kind of leader Basie was. Joining stories run from Salva Sanders and Kenny Clarke in the 1930s, through Harry Edison, JJ Johnson, Gerald Wilson and Clark Terry in the 1940s, to Joe Wilder, Billy Mitchell, Curtis Fuller, Quentin Jackson, Butch Miles and John Heard in later decades. They are mostly set in Kansas City, New York (Birdland, the Strand), Chicago and on European tours. The tellers agree on Basie's economical piano, his loose, hands-off but disciplined leadership, his respect for soloists and the band's collective feel. They differ in emphasis: some stress the thrill of joining, others the discipline, the firings or the band's style taking priority over solos. A later strand, mainly from Frank Foster and Freddie Green's circle, covers the band after Basie's death and what its alumni carried into their own groups. The samples are mostly sidemen and arrangers, with some outside admirers such as Ramsey Lewis and Johnny Mandel. The cluster is large and anchored on one band and leader, but it mixes several kinds of story.
threads: Getting the call and auditioning for Basie
Basie as a leader: economy, discipline and respect for soloists
Band personnel, sections and the arrangers
Road stories: Birdland, Europe and the Strand
Outside admirers and the Kansas City roots of the sound
Lessons carried on after Basie, and the later band

communities.name: Piney Brown and the Subway jam sessions in Kansas City
communities.parent_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people
communities.narrative: Musicians from many bands remember Kansas City in the late 1920s and 1930s as a wide-open, around-the-clock town. Under the Pendergast regime, clubs and liquor stood open through Prohibition and the Depression, and the action centered on 18th and Vine. The recurring scene is the all-night jam session at the Subway, a club run by Piney Brown, a numbers man. Eddie Barefield, Vic Dickenson and Eddie Durham place themselves in these sessions. They name Joe Turner, Ben Webster, Basie and Jack Teagarden as fellow players, and say musicians phoned each other to come down. Brown is remembered as a patron who paid rent and got horns out of pawn for broke players. Tellers agree on the atmosphere and the patronage, and differ mainly in which club or street they name and which year they place it in. A few segments sit at the edges: a chauffeur who helped musicians in trouble, a 1938 shared room with jam sessions, and a much earlier Kansas City Bar story. Most tellers are Black swing-era players, and Rutgers interviews supply most of the segments.
threads: Kansas City's open, round-the-clock nightlife under Pendergast
All-night jam sessions at the Subway, 18th and Vine
Piney Brown as patron saint who paid rent and redeemed pawned horns
Jamming with Joe Turner, Ben Webster, Basie and Teagarden
Drummers tiring out in the long jams and being called to fill in
Bars and rooming houses that made up the wider Kansas City scene

communities.name: Kansas City nights: jam sessions and cutting contests
communities.parent_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds remember the Kansas City scene of the early-to-mid 1930s (roughly 1930-1937) as a place where music never stopped. Visitors and locals alike describe clubs and after-hours spots such as Pop Monroe's, the Subway, the Reno Club, the Cherry Blossom, the Lone Star and the Booker T. Hotel, where cheap bootleg or "needle" whiskey flowed and players jammed through the night and into breakfast sessions. Lester Young is the central figure: Vic Dickenson, Leonard Phillips, Theodore Saunders and Jerry Jerome all recall hearing or jamming with him, and several insist his style was already fully formed. A recurring episode is the cutting session, in which local tenors such as Budd Johnson, Ben Webster and Herschel Evans test and out-play one another and visiting stars, including Coleman Hawkins when Fletcher Henderson's men came through. The tellers include Kansas City natives like Mary Lou Williams and Jay McShann, territory-band sidemen, and outsiders such as the white drummer Cliff Leeman and Jerry Jerome, who were taken in by local players. They agree on the city's openness and its devotion to musicians, and differ mainly in which venues and players they foreground. A few samples drift off the subject, such as Lou Pallo on Les Paul in the 1980s.
threads: Jamming with Lester Young at Pop Monroe's and the Subway
Cutting sessions: tenor players testing each other and Hawkins
Clubs and after-hours spots: Reno Club, Cherry Blossom, Sunset Club
Basie, Pete Johnson and Joe Turner on 12th Street
Outsiders welcomed in: Leeman, Jerome and Lips Page
Hotel life, bootleg whiskey and the Booker T. Hotel

communities.name: Dancers, listeners and what audiences wanted
communities.parent_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1920s through the 1960s describe who their audiences were and how those audiences responded, usually contrasting people who danced with people who listened. Vic Dickenson recalls late-1920s fans who invited musicians home and listened as well as danced. Bill Challis separates attentive college crowds from ballroom dancers who only wanted fox trots. Teddy Edwards describes 1930s fans who saved for weeks to dress for a dance and stood listening because radio and records were all there was. Ruth Brown remembers Saturday-night crowds who unwound at the dance with artists close to the fans. Several bandleaders and sidemen (Buddy DeFranco, Sauter-Finegan, Slide Hampton, Eddie Bert on Kenton) tell of music that was too undanceable, too concert-minded or too bebop for dance crowds, which led to flopped dates or hostile floors. A few accounts, such as Dufour on how widely New Orleanians accepted jazz and Domber on informed jazz-party audiences, are more general reflections on reception. The samples share a loose subject, audience reception and dancing, but they range across eras, scenes and genres, so the cluster is only moderately cohesive.
threads: Fans who listened as well as danced
Undanceable music flopping with dance crowds
College listeners versus ballroom dancers
How devoted and enthusiastic audiences were in the swing era
General acceptance of jazz by the public and informed jazz-party audiences

communities.name: Radio and television work beyond the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands
communities.narrative: Musicians from many eras recall the jobs that put them in front of microphones and cameras rather than live audiences: network radio staff and freelance work, remote broadcasts from clubs and hotels, and later television variety shows, talk-show house bands and studio orchestras. The earliest tellers (Sam Wooding, Joe Darensbourg, Danny Barker, Lawrence Brown) set it in the 1920s and 30s, when only a few bands such as Duke, Cab and the Savoy had radio exposure and a nightly Cotton Club broadcast could go unpaid. The core is the 1950s to 70s, when New York and Los Angeles sidemen and arrangers (Milt Hinton, Bob Rosengarden, Johnny Mandel, Snooky Young, Bill Challis) talk about CBS and NBC staff calls, Your Show of Shows, the Steve Allen, Merv Griffin, Ed Sullivan and Cavett shows, and the Tonight Show band, and weigh the steady money and schedule against jazz gigs. Others tell it as leaders and stars, such as Nancy Wilson, Marian McPartland and Ramsey Lewis hosting or guesting on their own shows, or as engineers and writers like Rudy Van Gelder and Nat Hentoff who watched the media side. The tellers agree that broadcast work paid well and let them play elsewhere in the evenings, but differ on its musical worth, with some praising the guests and others calling the music stupid. The segments share a loose medium rather than one event, and a few strays (Sam Kininger on college radio, Alberta Hunter on watching television) only touch it.
threads: Tonight Show and talk-show house bands
Network radio and studio staff jobs, pay and freelancing
Radio remotes and early broadcasts from clubs and hotels
Variety shows and guest spots (Steve Allen, Ed Sullivan, Merv Griffin)
Musicians hosting or fronting their own radio and TV shows
Writing and arranging for television

communities.name: Advocacy and institution-building: giving back to jazz
communities.parent_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers musicians talking about the organizing work around the music rather than the playing. They describe founding or running groups: Collective Black Artists in New York (Jimmy Owens, Frank Foster, Slide Hampton), the Las Vegas Jazz Society and the Western Regional Federation for Jazz (Monk Montgomery), the South Florida Jazz and Swing society, and the all-women Diva Jazz Orchestra. Another strand is advocacy and mentoring, including teaching the business of music, school programs, and women's jazz festivals and mentoring for young women. A smaller strand covers funding and recognition: government subsidy, the NEA, cultural institutions, and Souchon's 1950s talk about which social classes accept jazz. Most stories are set from the 1960s to the 2000s, with some in the 1950s. The tellers broadly agree that jazz is poorly supported and that older musicians owe it to the next generation to share what they know. They differ on whether to organize by race, gender or region, and on whether funding should come from government or from sponsors and dues. The link between the samples is loose, so the cluster is a mix of related themes rather than one story.
threads: Collective Black Artists and teaching the business of music
Founding jazz societies and regional federations
Women in jazz: Diva, festivals and mentoring
Government funding, subsidy and the NEA
Giving back through education and school programs
Public acceptance and recognition of jazz

communities.name: Managing Nancy Wilson and the Cannonball album
communities.parent_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"
communities.narrative: Most of this cluster is manager John Levy's account of building Nancy Wilson's career in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Cannonball Adderley recommended her after Levy heard her at the Blue Morocco in Columbus. Levy groomed her, sent her on the road for about a year, got a demo to Capitol's Dave Cavanaugh and built demand before she recorded. Her Capitol deal led to the 1961-62 joint album with Cannonball, which Louis Hayes and others describe as lightly rehearsed, with the billing flipping to Nancy Wilson once it took off. Levy also tells how his other singers, Dakota Staton and Joe Williams, came to him through Capitol and Cannonball, and how Wes Montgomery arrived the same way. Sidemen and arrangers such as Roy McCurdy, Frank Tate and Jimmy Jones recall the album and later Capitol work from the musicians' side. The cluster is loosely held together. One or two samples, such as Red Tyler on Prince La La and Barbara George coming to AFO in New Orleans, only share the theme of a record company or manager signing artists. Levy dominates the cluster, and the accounts mostly agree, differing in whether they speak as manager or as players on the sessions.
threads: Hearing and signing Nancy Wilson
Grooming her before the Capitol debut
The Cannonball Adderley and Nancy Wilson album
Levy's other clients: Dakota Staton, Joe Williams, Wes Montgomery
Capitol sessions seen by sidemen and arrangers
Later split with her husband

communities.name: Favorite bands I played with
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections and eras are asked, usually near the end of an interview, which band or group they enjoyed most, and they answer by naming a favorite. The answers range across traditional New Orleans jazz (Alton Purnell on Bunk Johnson's and George Lewis's bands), Chicago and swing big bands (Quinn Wilson on Hines and Lefty Bates, J. C. Higginbotham on Luis Russell), mainstream and Dixieland groups (Ralph Sutton and Cliff Leeman on the Lawson-Haggart band, Bobby Gordon on The Orphan Newsboys) and later big bands (Scott Robinson on Illinois Jacquet and Mel Lewis). Tellers agree on the framing: the best band was the one that was fun, authentic or full of good musicians, and many contrast it with jobs that paid but meant less to them, such as Louis Jordan's show band. Most of the stories are set between the 1940s and 1970s, but the common thread is the interviewer's question rather than any one band, scene or place. A few samples, such as Ralph LaLama on learning from James Brown's rhythm sections, only loosely fit.
threads: Favorite band named in closing reflections
Authentic New Orleans bands of Bunk Johnson and George Lewis
Lawson-Haggart band as a mutual admiration society
Big bands enjoyed most (Hines, Luis Russell, Jacquet, Mel Lewis)
Paying jobs versus music they loved (Louis Jordan, Ink Spots)
Short stints with Condon, Spanier and Hackett

communities.name: How I got my name: nicknames and spellings
communities.parent_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names
communities.narrative: Across 183 interviews from Tulane, Rutgers, Hamilton and the Smithsonian, musicians are asked, or volunteer, how they or their colleagues got their names. The dominant story is the nickname origin tale, set mostly between the 1900s and the 1950s in New Orleans, Kansas City, New York and Chicago. Names arrive by accident or at someone else's hand: a stammering conductor turns Jones into Jonah, a bandleader adds Professor to Longhair, girls call a young trombonist Kid, a football tackle shortens Colezy to Cozy, and Basie deflects questions about how he became Count. Tellers often disagree or do not know the origin (Horace Henderson on Smack, the unexplained Gaiye), and some stories turn on promoters or club owners naming bands, such as Machito and his Afro-Cubans, Shawee, the Ink Spots and King Carter. A smaller strand concerns the spelling and legal form of real names, including passports, union checks and Creole spelling habits. Both sidemen and bandleaders tell it, often prompted by the interviewer, and it shades into musicians' slang and the habit of giving each other identities.
threads: How a musician got his nickname (Kid, Pops, Cozy, Hootie, Captain)
Count Basie's name and the band's nicknames (Sweets, Sampson, Chief)
Band and group names chosen by club owners or promoters (Shawee, Machito, Ink Spots, King Carter)
Professor Longhair and the title 'Professor'
Spelling, family and legal names (Rene/Rena, Callender, Juan Tizol, passport trouble)

communities.name: Milt Hinton replaces Al Morgan in Cab's band
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: The core of this cluster is a well-rehearsed story about how bassist Milt Hinton came to join Cab Calloway's orchestra in the mid-1930s. Al Morgan, Cab's bassist and Hinton's boyhood idol, quit the band to stay in California after being photographed for a film. Keg Johnson, already with Cab, recommended Hinton, who was playing the Three Deuces in Chicago with Zutty Singleton and Art Tatum. Calloway came into the club, asked Zutty to release him, and Hinton took the train to New York, calling his mother at 3 am. Hinton tells it himself several times, while Albert Morgan, Danny Barker and Walter P. Thomas confirm it from other angles. Around this core, the later and looser samples drift to related big-band lore: Calloway's early arrival in New York with Marion Hardy's Alabamians, Les Hite's band in California, and trumpet sections moving to Benny Carter. The Hinton-Morgan-Calloway sequence is a clear subject, but the periphery is only loosely related.
threads: Al Morgan leaves Cab for California and Hollywood
Keg Johnson recommends Hinton
Cab hears Hinton at the Three Deuces and asks Zutty Singleton for him
Hinton as a boy idolizing Morgan outside the Regal
Calloway's early path through Hardy's Alabamians
Les Hite and Benny Carter band personnel moves

communities.name: Ella Fitzgerald rises with the Chick Webb band
communities.parent_name: Band singers and accompanying vocalists
communities.narrative: These are stories about Ella Fitzgerald's discovery and rise in the mid-1930s. Most are set in Harlem and New York in 1934-38, around Chick Webb's orchestra. Tellers recall how she won the Harlem Opera House amateur contest and how Mario Bauza persuaded Webb to hire her despite her appearance. She briefly sang with Tiny Bradshaw, then stopped the show at the Apollo and Savoy. Teddy McRae supplies most of the detail. He describes how Jack Robbins and other publishers fed the band songs, how arrangers such as Van Alexander and Jimmy Mundy were hired, and how Ella's own nursery-rhyme idea became "A-Tisket, A-Tasket", her breakthrough hit. Goodman's borrowing of her for the Camel Caravan broadcasts and her early records recur as well. Maxine Sullivan adds the rivalry and repertoire question after "Loch Lomond". A few outliers stretch the period: Mike Wofford and Jim Hall recall accompanying Ella decades later (the 1960 Oscars show, the 1989-90 recordings), and Horace Henderson praises the singer Viola Jefferson, who outsang Ella with "A-Tisket A-Tasket" at the Chicago Savoy. Tellers agree on Ella's talent and on the song that made her, and mostly differ in vantage point (bandsman, fellow singer, later accompanist).
threads: Discovery at the Harlem Opera House amateur contest
Bauza persuades Chick Webb to hire her
Songs and arrangers for Ella in Webb's band
A-Tisket, A-Tasket becomes the hit
Borrowed for Goodman's Camel Caravan broadcasts
Later accompanists: Oscars show and 1980s recordings

communities.name: Joe Williams: the Basie blues singer remembered
communities.parent_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds talk about the singer Joe Williams, mostly as he was seen and heard with the Count Basie Orchestra from the mid-1950s on. Many first heard or met him with Basie at Birdland or in Chicago clubs such as Club DeLisa. Several credit him, along with the Ernie Wilkins and Frank Foster arrangements such as Every Day, with reviving the band's fortunes in the 1950s. The tellers agree that he was a natural, swinging, unflappable singer. They praise his phrasing, his storytelling and his lifting of the blues into an art form. Some knew him earlier, as a ballad singer with Lionel Hampton, in Gerald Wilson's band in St. Louis in 1946, or in Woody Herman-era baseball games. Arrangers, sidemen and young players describe writing for him, accompanying him and learning from him, such as the lesson that you must know a song's lyrics. Others tell personal anecdotes about golf in Las Vegas, his role as best man at a wedding, and his later small groups and guest spots with the Basie band. A few samples drift to neighbouring subjects, such as Tony Bennett or the Prez Conference.
threads: First hearing or meeting Joe Williams with the Basie band
Joe Williams and the 1950s Basie comeback, Every Day and the blues charts
Writing and playing for Williams: arrangers, fills and phrasing lessons
Earlier years: Hampton, Gerald Wilson in St. Louis, Club DeLisa and hard times
Later career: small groups, Las Vegas golf and guest spots with Basie
Admiration for his blues singing and technique

communities.name: Arranging around the track: building parts in the studio
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians and arrangers describe how arrangements get built in the recording studio, often around material that already exists. Alvin "Red" Tyler recalls New Orleans sessions where a singer's bare outline became a head arrangement on the spot. Larry Gold, Ron Carter on the CTI sessions, and Rob Mounsey describe writing strings and orchestration over nearly finished rhythm-and-vocal tracks. Jerry Hey says artists and producers sometimes sang him a phrase to write down. Other tellers describe arranging for particular records: Machito's key change for Miguelito Valdes, Eddie Palmieri's first La Perfecta album, Woody Herman's Steely Dan material, and Jimmy Heath's re-arranged big band record. Joel Dorn on layering backing voices fits loosely. The stories run from the 1930s-40s to the 1990s and 2000s, and the tellers are arrangers, sidemen and bandleaders from jazz, Latin, soul and studio pop. They agree that the arrangement is shaped by what the rhythm section or singer has already given them, but they are not telling one single episode.
threads: Head arrangements built on the spot from a singer's outline
Writing strings and horns over finished rhythm tracks
Producers and artists singing parts to the arranger
Arranging for a specific record or singer (Machito, Palmieri, Herman)
Layering backing vocals in the studio
Re-arranging older tunes for big band albums

communities.name: Did Stan Kenton's band swing?
communities.parent_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom
communities.narrative: Most of this cluster is musicians talking about Stan Kenton's orchestra and the long-running argument over whether it swung. Tellers who played in or around the band in the 1940s and 1950s, including Eddie Bert, Don Menza, Conte Candoli, Bill Holman and Jerry Coker, describe its brass-heavy, concert-orchestra sound. Many contrast it with Count Basie's or Woody Herman's lighter swing. Bauza, Menza, Soph and Bellson say it did not swing, or only did once Bill Holman wrote for it. Others stress its stars, its arrangers (Rugolo, Holman, Graettinger) and Kenton's role as organizer and front man. A few samples drift to other leaders such as Gerry Mulligan, Russ Morgan and Karolina Strassmayer's current band, and to Kenton's early days as a pianist modelled on Earl Hines. The tellers agree on Kenton's ambition and his unusual sound. They differ on whether that sound counts as jazz swing.
threads: Kenton versus Basie and Herman: what counts as swing
Joining and leaving the Kenton band, 1947-55
Kenton's concert-orchestra vision, brass and mellophones
Arrangers: Rugolo, Holman, Graettinger, Mulligan
Kenton the young pianist and Earl Hines

communities.name: Teddy Wilson's Billie Holiday studio sessions
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the Brunswick and Vocalion record dates that Teddy Wilson led for Billie Holiday in 1935-39, organised by John Hammond. Hammond drew an all-star pickup group from whichever band was in New York, so Basie, Goodman, Ellington and Calloway men all played together. Tellers include sidemen such as Jonah Jones, Cozy Cole, Freddie Green, Jo Jones and Milt Hinton, and Wilson himself. They agree on the casual, pick-up-the-best-players-in-town character of the dates, and they give personnel and dates such as January 1937 and Jan-Mar 1936. They differ in where they stand: some, like Freddie Green and Al Hall, remember a first or only date with Billie, and Hinton recalls recording on the side despite Cab Calloway's ban. A few samples drift to other session work, such as Mildred Bailey dates, Gus Johnson's 1946 New York dates and Teddy Wilson's sextet and V-Discs, but most stay on the Wilson-Holiday sessions.
threads: Hammond's all-star pickup sessions with whoever was in town
Personnel and dates of the Wilson-Holiday records
First or only recording date with Billie and Lester Young
Recording on the side despite band leaders' bans
Other studio work: Mildred Bailey, Ink Spots, V-Discs

communities.name: Working with Frank Sinatra: bands, books and Vegas
communities.parent_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands
communities.narrative: Most of these stories are about Frank Sinatra as an employer, bandleader-singer and presence in the room, told by the sidemen, arrangers and fellow performers who worked with him. They are set mainly between the late 1930s and the 1970s. Early tellers such as Jack Palmer, Wilbur Ware and Joe Bushkin recall him as a young singer with the Harry James and Tommy Dorsey bands. The bulk come from the 1950s and 60s, when Harry Edison, Red Norvo, John Collins, Cliff Leeman and Freddie Green describe touring, recording and backing him, and the Reprise-era charts of Johnny Mandel, Nelson Riddle and Quincy Jones. Las Vegas is the recurring setting: the Sands, Caesars Palace, Cal-Neva and Tahoe, with Basie's band and Norvo's small group playing behind him. Tellers agree on his perfectionism (41 takes of one song), his instinct as a musician, his dislike of rehearsal and his loyalty to players. They differ in emphasis between warm friendship and cautionary tales such as the Caesars Palace incident and his later politics. A few samples drift to other singers (Dinah Shore, Dana Valery, Sammy Davis Jr., Tony Bennett) or general Vegas and star-act routine, where Sinatra is only incidental.
threads: Sinatra's arrangers and charts: Riddle, Mandel, Jones, May
Backing him in Vegas and Tahoe: the Sands, Norvo's group, Basie's band
Studio perfectionism: retakes, tempos and live-band recording
Young Sinatra with the James and Dorsey bands
Personal portraits: friendship, generosity, temper and the Caesars Palace story
Other star singers and their bands (Ella, Bennett, Dinah Shore, Sammy Davis)

communities.name: Learning to tap dance before the music
communities.parent_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows
communities.narrative: In this small cluster, musicians recall learning to dance, especially tap and time steps, in the 1920s and 1930s, often before or alongside taking up their instruments. The tellers learned from relatives, such as Louie Bellson's sister Mary and Wilbur Ware's father. Others learned from touring shows and fellow acts, as Snooky Young did with the Brown Skinned Models and Red Norvo did with the Flaming Youth Revue. Professor Longhair, Illinois Jaquet and Tiny Grimes danced in amateur trios, at clubs and for tips on Bourbon Street, or played piano for dancers at the Hoofers Club. New Orleans dancers such as Naomi McGraw, Herbert Brown and Lu's partner Doug DeLille learned in the street. Drummers like Bellson say dancing helped their playing and their stage presence. Most tellers agree that dancing was a common route into entertainment and a skill bandsmen were expected to have. They differ mainly in setting, from New Orleans streets to Fort Worth, Chicago and New York stages. One sample, about a dancer-ukulele player starting out at the Kingfish, fits only loosely.
threads: Learning steps from family: sisters and fathers
Picking up tap from touring shows and revues
Street and club dancers in New Orleans
Amateur dance trios and the Hoofers Club
Dancing as a stepping stone to playing music

communities.name: Jazz guitar: rhythm chair, banjo and Charlie Christian
communities.parent_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about the guitar, and its cousins the banjo and mandolin, as a working rhythm instrument and as a lineage of players. The strongest strand, mostly told by later swing and mainstream players and by interviewers such as Rowe, centres on Freddie Green's unamplified, metronomic chunk in the Count Basie rhythm section. They discuss his technique (the right-hand fingernail, heavy strings, high action), why he never soloed, and the story of his sabotaged amp. Close behind are Charlie Christian and amplification: Eddie Durham's homemade amplified guitar, Christian as the great influence, and the Christian versus Django Reinhardt schools. Earlier New Orleans, Texas and Philadelphia musicians in the Tulane and Rutgers collections tell a different story, set mostly between the 1910s and 1930s. They recall the banjo-to-guitar shift, Johnny St. Cyr's instruments, the Marrero brothers, and blues fingerpickers. Many segments are only passing mentions of a player (Condon, Oscar Moore, Snoozer Quinn), so the cluster is held together by the instrument rather than by one event.
threads: Freddie Green's unamplified rhythm guitar in the Basie band
Charlie Christian, Eddie Durham and the arrival of the electric guitar
Banjo versus guitar in early New Orleans bands (St. Cyr, the Marrero brothers)
Guitar schools and influences: Christian, Django, Oscar Moore, chord stylists
Blues and fingerpicking guitarists in Philadelphia, Texas and New Orleans
Rhythm guitar in Condon, Pizzarelli and Dixieland settings

communities.name: Working with and around Billie Holiday
communities.parent_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her
communities.narrative: Almost every sample is a musician's memory of Billie Holiday, told by bandmates, accompanists, lovers and fellow singers. The stories run from her teenage years, with Danny Barker and J. C. Higginbotham seeing her around 1929-31, through her discovery by John Hammond and her time with Count Basie in 1937-38, to her 1940s club and recording years and her decline in the 1950s. Basie remembers her as straight on the job but fond of teasing him. John Simmons gives a long and harrowing account of living with her in 1942-44, including her heroin use and the violence between them. Others, such as Doc Cheatham, Horace Henderson, Slam Stewart and Chico Hamilton, describe how she handled a band, how she could frighten or charm people, and what accompanying her was like. Venues such as Cafe Society, Kelly's Stable, the Famous Door and Birdland recur, as do Lester Young, Mildred Bailey and Hammond. The tellers agree she was kind and professional despite her troubles, but they differ on her drinking, her drugs and the people around her. A few samples only mention her in passing, for example Charlie Barnet correcting Babs Gonzalez and Ingrid Sertso on Berendt's remark, so the cluster is a little loose at the edges.
threads: Meeting young Billie and John Hammond's discovery of her
Billie with the Basie band in 1937-38
Living and fighting with Billie: John Simmons's account
Heroin, drinking and her decline
Accompanying her in clubs and on record dates
Her voice, phrasing and character as other musicians judged them

communities.name: Band singers and working with vocalists
communities.parent_name: Band singers and accompanying vocalists
communities.narrative: Instrumentalists across eras talk about the singers they worked beside, chiefly the vocalists who fronted big bands and the women and men they accompanied. The set stretches from 1920s New Orleans bands, where members sang through megaphones, through the 1930s and 40s band-vocalist era (Ivie Anderson, Kay Davis and Joya Sherrill with Ellington; Midge Williams; Pha Terrell; Melvin Moore with Ernie Fields) to later arrangers and accompanists writing and playing for Sarah Vaughan, Peggy Lee, Ella Fitzgerald, Rosemary Clooney and Tony Bennett. Lawrence Brown supplies a long run of Ellington singer portraits, while sidemen such as Abe Most and Snooky Young reflect on how players felt about vocalists, resenting lost solo choruses or wishing they could sing themselves. Tellers agree that good jazz singers are rare and prized, and that accompanying a singer means listening and leaving space, but they differ on whether singers fit a band's jazz culture. The cluster is broad and loosely bound: many samples are single-singer portraits, and a few drift to gospel, a musician becoming a singer himself, or only mention a vocalist in passing.
threads: Ellington band singers: Ivie Anderson, Kay Davis, Joya Sherrill
Accompanying and writing for vocalists: Sarah Vaughan, Peggy Lee, Tony Bennett
Big-band girl and boy singers of the 1930s-40s
How instrumentalists felt about band vocalists
Early bands and singers before featured vocalists
Instrumentalists who became singers

communities.name: Working the clubs and bands of Detroit and other Black-circuit cities
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians recall landing a job in a particular city's club or band, with Detroit the strongest pull in the samples (about nine tagged mentions, plus Chicago, Cleveland, Baltimore and Washington, D.C.). The stories are set mostly between the 1920s and the late 1950s. In Detroit the tellers place themselves in the Plantation Club, the Graystone Ballroom, the Savoy and Club Harlem, and around McKinney's Cotton Pickers, where Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson are the names that come up. Russell Procope remembers earning $160 a week with McKinney's and going home homesick, Teddy Wilson recalls summers in Detroit hearing the big traveling bands, and Sammy Price and Big Nick Nicholas describe stays of a year or more. A second strand is the Washington, D.C. club scene of the early 1950s, told by Horn Shirley, who led trios and quintets at Abart's, the 7-T, Olivia's and the Bohemian Caverns. The tellers share an interest in naming rooms, bandleaders and pay. They differ in setting, since several stories are Detroit-centered and the rest happen in other cities. They also differ in era: some are 1920s-30s big-band stories and others are 1950s trio and quintet stories. Several tellers admit to fuzzy dates.
threads: Detroit clubs and ballrooms of the 1920s-40s
McKinney's Cotton Pickers and the big traveling bands
Horn Shirley's trios in Washington, D.C. lounges
Landing a first job in a new city and moving on
Hiring, pay and long hours on the bandstand

communities.name: Big band versus small group: freedom to solo
communities.parent_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection explain why they prefer small groups (solo, trio, quartet) to big bands, or what they gave up by working in one. The core complaint is solo space: in a big band the leader or arranger decides who plays, solos are short and unevenly shared, and the music sticks to the score. Vic Dickenson, Benny Waters, Big Nick Nicholas and Omer Simeon make this case, and Barney Bigard contrasts Armstrong's small band, where he could play as many bars as he wished, with Ellington's eight- or sixteen-bar solos and cliques. Buddy Tate and Buck Clayton recall getting few solos in the Basie band, and Tate says he would not make that sacrifice again. Pianists such as Pete Jolly, Richard Wyands and Randy Weston add that small settings let them stretch out and comp, and singers Maxine Sullivan and Annie Ross felt boxed in by big-band arrangements. A few voices push back or add nuance: some liked big bands or valued the discipline of a working ensemble, and Phil Woods wanted a real band rather than a single act. The stories run from the 1930s to the 1990s and are mostly told as general preferences rather than dated events. A handful of samples (Artie Shaw, Teddy McRae, the Doughboys versus Bob Wills) fit only loosely.
threads: Few choruses: leaders and arrangers control who solos
Great soloists leaving Basie and Ellington for freedom
Pianists and rhythm players who want room to stretch out and comp
Singers boxed in by big-band arrangements
Defending the working band: ensemble blend and discipline
Preferring solo, trio and quartet formats

communities.name: Working for Buddy Rich: taskmaster and bandleader
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians who played in or around Buddy Rich's big band (and a few other 1960s-80s road bands) describe what it was like to work for him. The stories run from about 1960 to the late 1980s. Most of the tellers were horn players, bassists and drummers who joined through recommendation or audition (Basin Street East, Birdland, the Riverboat) and who describe Rich as a military-style disciplinarian who yelled on stage, withheld pay and fired weak players. Many defend him: the toughness kept the band tight, he gave soloists space, he hired on playing rather than connections, and he could be funny and generous. Others, such as Magnusson, Davis and Bruce Johnstone, recall surviving his tirades and learning solid time. Several compare him with other leaders (Woody Herman, Maynard Ferguson, Harry James, Si Zentner), and a few tell of subbing for him when he was ill, including Louie Bellson in the 1960s and Dan D'Imperio in the late 1980s. A small minority of samples drift to other bandleaders (Buddy Johnson, Woody Herman alone) rather than Rich.
threads: Rich as taskmaster: yelling, discipline and tirades
Auditioning and getting hired for Rich's band
Defending Rich: humor, solo space, hiring on merit
Comparing Rich with Woody Herman, Maynard Ferguson and other bosses
Subbing for an ill or hospitalized Rich
Life on the road in the band

communities.name: The band as a family: getting along and staying together
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians from very different bands tell the same story: the best bands were run like families, and the music was good because the men got along. Tellers such as Erskine Hawkins, Freddie Green, Teddy Edwards, Lawrence Brown and Buster Smith describe 1930s and 1940s big bands (Hawkins's Birmingham men, Basie, Ellington, Ernie Fields) where sidemen looked after each other, chipped in for one another, stayed for years and felt no resentment toward the leader. Charlie De Vore and Sammy Penn make the same argument for small New Orleans-style groups, saying a band with bad feeling or arguments cannot play well. Marian McPartland and Chris Parker carry it into later decades: Jimmy McPartland's generosity toward her, and the mutual respect and football-team spirit of the 1970s studio band Stuff. They agree on loyalty, fairness and the absence of jealousy. They differ on scale and on regret: Brown mourns that the band changed, and Smith notes the one stingy member. The set is small and spread across collections, but the samples stay on this one theme, with the Marian McPartland segment only loosely related.
threads: The band as a happy family (big bands, 1930s-40s)
Fair leaders and no resentment among sidemen
Loyalty and no arguments in New Orleans bands
Chemistry and mutual respect in later groups (Stuff, McPartland)
Nostalgia for a brotherly band that later changed

communities.name: Leading a band: choosing, keeping and firing sidemen
communities.parent_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players
communities.narrative: Musicians from every era describe what it takes to run a band, from Kid Thomas Valentine and Johnny DeDroit in New Orleans to Elvin Jones, Gerald Wilson, Orrin Evans and Chris Parker. The recurring story is personnel: leaders vet players for reliability, humility and chemistry as much as for talent, and many say a steady lineup plays better because everyone knows their part. Kid Thomas kept his men for fifty years, and DeDroit's father told him never to break up a winning combination. Tellers also describe the unpleasant side, such as handling substitutes, replacing players diplomatically, and firing someone as a last resort. Others talk about the leader's other duties, including paying the band well, dealing with promoters and taxes, and learning bandstand management from leaders like Art Blakey and Horace Silver. Some, like Slam Stewart, prefer being a sideman to leading because of friction in the band. A few segments drift to co-led bands or arrangements built around a leader, but the shared subject is the craft and burden of bandleading. Tellers are mostly working leaders and sidemen, from New Orleans traditionalists to modern jazz bandleaders.
threads: Choosing sidemen for reliability and chemistry
Keeping a steady band together for years
Substitutes, replacing and firing players
What a leader owes: pay, business and bandstand skills
Learning to lead from Blakey, Silver and other leaders
Leader versus sideman, and co-led bands

communities.name: Drugs and drink in the jazz life
communities.parent_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and collections talk about drugs and alcohol as part of the jazz life, with the bebop era and Charlie Parker's example as the usual reference point. Most stories are set between the 1920s and 1960s, in New York, Chicago, New Orleans and Los Angeles, and in band and club settings. Tellers explain why it happened: itinerant life, late nights, performance pressure, wartime stress and frustration over racial and class contempt for the music. They agree that heroin ravaged a generation of peers. Many who abstained, such as Jim Hall, Luther Henderson, Barry Harris and Lou Donaldson, describe how they stayed clear, sometimes crediting church upbringing or fear. Others give first-hand accounts of addiction and recovery, among them Howard McGhee, Annie Ross and George Handy. Bandleaders such as Terry Gibbs, Woody Herman, Ellington and Basie describe house rules, discipline, or ending a band because of drugs. A few samples drift to drinking habits or unrelated topics, such as Buddhism study and a Jimmy Heath mention.
threads: Why musicians turned to drugs: bebop, Parker and the road
Staying clean: abstainers and their reasons
Personal addiction, detox and recovery
Bandleaders' rules on drinking and drugs
Heavy drinkers remembered, from New Orleans to bebop
Drugs in the district and Harlem, early scenes

communities.name: What I listen to these days
communities.parent_name: Listening to classical music, then and now
communities.narrative: Musicians and people around them are asked what they listen to now, and they answer in a casual, late-career register, mostly in interviews from the 1990s to about 2012. The most common answer is that they turn to classical music (Stravinsky, Bartok, Strauss, Elgar, Prokofiev, Ravel) rather than jazz, sometimes as a deliberate break from the music they play. Others stay with older big bands and favorites such as Ellington, Lunceford, Goodman, Armstrong and Coltrane.
