A smaller group follows newer artists, young drummers or current groups, and some listen to radio, Pandora, audiobooks or eclectic mixes. A few describe not listening at all, such as Sonny Rollins, who avoids recorded music to avoid being influenced, and several say they avoid their own records. The tellers agree that off-duty listening is wide and often non-jazz. They differ on whether they keep up with new music or stay with the old.
threads: Turning to classical music instead of jazz
Staying with Ellington, Armstrong and the big bands
Keeping up with younger artists and new groups
Not listening at all, or avoiding their own records
Radio, CDs, Pandora and how they listen
Spouses and non-players describing their own taste

communities.name: Jazz musicians on their classical listening: Stravinsky, Bartók and favorite composers
communities.parent_name: Listening to classical music, then and now
communities.narrative: Jazz musicians from many eras and all four archives talk about the classical music they love and how they came to it. The most common touchstones are Stravinsky (above all The Rite of Spring), Bartók, Ravel and Debussy, with Beethoven, Mozart, Shostakovich and Prokofiev also named. Older players, such as Bud Freeman, Victor Moore, Bill Challis and Armand Hug, recall Bix Beiderbecke listening to Debussy and the impressionists in the 1920s. Others describe a single moment of discovery: Charlie Parker playing the Rite for Howard McGhee in 1946, the Rite at Johnny Carisi's home for JJ Johnson, and Mose Allison's modern-classical listening at LSU. Younger and more academically trained musicians (Hubert Laws, Branford and Jason Marsalis, Harold Danko, Alan Broadbent) give favorite-composer lists and analytical comments on dissonance, structure and melody. The tellers agree that classical music, especially the early twentieth-century modernists, shaped their ears and writing. They differ on taste: Laws prefers the Russians and is cool on Mozart and Bartók, while Cedar Walton favors the moderns over Mozart. A few outliers (film composers, Gershwin, Brubeck, a record producer's taste in first albums) loosen the theme at the edges.
threads: Bix Beiderbecke and the 1920s players hearing Debussy and Ravel
Discovering The Rite of Spring through Parker, Carisi or college
Bartók, Stravinsky and modern composers as influence on writing
Favorite classical composers lists (Beethoven, Mozart, Shostakovich, Prokofiev)
Analyzing Stravinsky and Ravel from a jazz musician's view
Gershwin, film composers and the border of jazz and concert music

communities.name: Losing a father: death, burial and what he left
communities.parent_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren
communities.narrative: Musicians from many eras and regions recall the death of their fathers, and sometimes their parents or other close kin, as a fixed point in their life stories. The deaths range from about 1889 to the late 1970s. Many tellers pin down the date and age at death, such as 47, 49, 52, 57 or 63. Others describe the funeral or burial: the band playing at Ballariel's father's funeral, Norvo going home from vaudeville in Chicago, Sayles's father in Hope Cemetery, and O'Farrill burying his parents in Havana. A recurring tension is the road. Several musicians were on tour or away when a parent died, as with Gardner, Autrey, Humes and McPartland, while others, like Elvin Jones and Cobb, were at the bedside. Some tellers use the death to say who the father was, including a bandsman, a minister, a teacher or a barber. A few segments are off-center, such as the Kelly brothers on Chris Kelly's death and grave, and the Valdes father-and-son reunion. The cluster is mostly the New Orleans Tulane interviews plus later Rutgers and Smithsonian ones, and it is told across generations, with little disagreement among tellers.
threads: Dates, ages and causes of a father's death
Away on tour when a parent died
Funerals, burial and cemeteries
Remembering the father as a musician or teacher
Reconciliation, caring for a dying parent
Dating a relative's death to place him in history

communities.name: Deaths of relatives and associates, recalled in passing
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: The samples are short remembrances of someone's death, told by musicians and by relatives of musicians, mostly from Tulane and Rutgers interviews and set loosely between about 1939 and 1957. The dead are a father, a brother, an uncle who led a band, a club owner, a grandmother, a fellow trumpeter, an old friend and a respected trombonist who can no longer play. Tellers usually give an approximate date or age at death, a hometown (Hahnville, Raceland, Baltimore) and a line about whether the person played music. In several accounts the death has a practical effect: Joe Robichaux's uncle John dies while Joe is on a booking tour, Lee Young's father's death ends his band, and a club closes after its owner dies. Most of these are biographical asides rather than developed stories. They share the occasion of a death, not a single event or narrative, so the cluster is only loosely a community.
threads: Death of a father, brother or uncle
Death of a bandleader or club owner ending a band or venue
Approximate dates, ages and hometowns of the deceased
Whether the dead relative played music
Fellow musicians who have died or can no longer play

communities.name: Who was in the band: reconstructing Basie personnel
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Most of this cluster is musicians and interviewers working out who played in a band in a given year, with the Count Basie Orchestra at the center. The core is Freddie Green's interview with Stanley Dance, where Dance reads off line-ups and Green corrects or confirms them. They cover the 1939-42 departures (Herschel Evans replaced by Buddy Tate, Walter Page, the trombones), the 1944-45 band with Lucky Thompson and its nicknames, the 1946 band with Paul Gonsalves, the doubtful placement of Don Byas and Paul Bascomb, and the 1950-51 small group. Jo Jones does the same for the 1946 band, adding that he made only one record before leaving for Omaha. The settings run from about 1939 to 1952, with a few stragglers to 1969. Outside Basie, a handful of other musicians give personnel for other bands: Joanne Brackeen on Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, Jerry Coker on the Woody Herman sax section, and Cozy Cole on his own bands after 'Topsy'. These are short lists with little narrative, and they share only the personnel-roll format with the Basie material, so the cluster is a Basie core with a looser periphery.
threads: Stanley Dance reading Basie line-ups year by year
Sax and trombone turnover in the Basie band, 1939-46
Lucky Thompson, Paul Gonsalves and other short-stay players
Jo Jones on the 1946 band and leaving for Omaha
The 1950-51 Basie small group
Personnel lists for other bands (Blakey, Herman, Cozy Cole)

bands: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

communities.name: Roy Eldridge: the trumpeter everyone remembers
communities.parent_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds tell stories about trumpeter Roy Eldridge, "Little Jazz", as he was in the late 1920s and 1930s. Nearly every sample is a portrait of him: his range and stamina, his competitive habit of jumping onto bandstands and sitting in everywhere, and his reputation as a jam-session leader and giant of the trumpet, usually ranked just after Louis Armstrong. Tellers recall him in Pittsburgh, Cleveland, Chicago and New York. In New York they place him at the Three Deuces and the Savoy, where Dizzy Gillespie was the one player willing to jam with him, and Eddie Locke repeats a story of Dizzy outside Ryan's. Horace Henderson says he hired Roy in 1928 for his fast, correct playing, not for copying Coleman Hawkins' Stampede solo. Others dwell on odd details such as his embouchure change after tooth trouble and playing the trumpet lying on his back. The tellers agree on his energy and standing among musicians. They differ on the period and the setting, and some recall him in later decades, such as Locke in Toronto. The cluster's period is probably also inflated by a few stories set later in his life.
threads: Roy Eldridge's range, stamina and competitive energy
Jamming and cutting contests, with Dizzy Gillespie
Sitting in around Pittsburgh, Cleveland and Chicago
Joining Horace Henderson's band and his records with Krupa
Stage showmanship at the Three Deuces and the Savoy
Ranking him alongside Louis Armstrong

communities.name: Rehearsing the band: how much, how hard
communities.parent_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom
communities.narrative: Musicians across eras talk about rehearsing: how often a band met, who ran it, and whether it was worth doing at all. Swing-era leaders and sidemen (Don Albert's band rehearsing nearly daily on the road, Quinn Wilson on the self-policing Hines band, Redman's and Calloway's sections rehearsing themselves, Teddy McRae using idle theater weeks) describe rehearsals fitted into layoffs and travel. Early New Orleans players such as Punch Miller and Harold Dejan say bands rarely rehearsed or only twice a week, working by ear or from sheet music. Postwar and later voices contrast disciplined leaders (Wilbur de Paris, Horace Silver, Jon Hendricks, Roscoe Mitchell rehearsing nine to five) with spontaneous ones (Cannonball's band, Brubeck learning on the job) and with big bands that barely rehearse (Gap Mangione, Ronnie Zito's no-pressure union band, Vic Dickenson on boring rehearsals and Lester leaving Basie). The tellers agree rehearsal was a leader's tool for discipline and repertoire, but disagree on how much of it music really needs. A few samples drift toward big-band leading rather than rehearsal itself.
threads: Daily rehearsals and discipline in touring swing bands
Early New Orleans bands that rarely rehearsed or read music
Strict versus spontaneous leaders (de Paris, Silver, Cannonball, Brubeck)
Why rehearsals are boring: Dickenson, Lester and Basie
Modern big bands with little or no rehearsal

bands: Don Albert and his Ten Pals

communities.name: Rehearsing, memorising and head arrangements
communities.parent_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1920s through the 1980s describe how a band actually got its music into shape: rehearsing, memorising parts and, often, hardly rehearsing at all. In the big-band tellings, such as Don Albert's 150 numbered arrangements and Horace Henderson on Don Redman, rehearsals were thorough and attendance was expected. Arrangements were drilled until memorised, and leaders voiced chords on the spot. Marshall Allen describes the Arkestra's parts changing daily, so a missed rehearsal left you lost. Other tellers stress the opposite. Reb Spikes says make-up bands worked because everyone knew thirty standards. Charlie Holmes recalls Saratoga Club dances played mostly from head arrangements. Singers and small groups (Tommy Ridgley, Annie Ross, Monk Montgomery's quartet, Ruth Brisbane) describe informal run-throughs or a first session where the music simply clicked. The shared thread is the working method behind a band's sound, told by bandleaders, sidemen and singers across New Orleans, Harlem, Kansas City and later jazz scenes. The samples vary in era and ensemble size, so the subject is broad.
threads: Big-band rehearsals and memorising the book
Make-up bands and head arrangements without rehearsal
Leaders who taught parts and voiced chords by ear
Singers and small groups rehearsing informally
Parts that change daily and the cost of missing rehearsal

communities.name: The body's toll: injuries, illness and aging at the horn
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: In these stories, musicians talk about what playing and a life in music do to the body, and how they cope. The problems are physical: herniated discs and a bad back, arthritis, a nerve problem in the hand, trigger finger, double vision, vertigo, emphysema, a jaw problem that stopped one player for months, and numb arms and fingers from acoustic bass. Some are occupational, such as hauling every horn or a full drum set, or long jam sessions. Others come from the nightlife, as when Jacques Butler woke up unable to get a sound from his trumpet and was told he was worn out. Jackie McLean's teeth were pushed back by Mingus's blow. Many tellers are older players in the 1990s to 2010s who describe how age shapes what they can still do. Their responses differ: some treat soreness as a challenge and keep playing, some put the instrument down for a while, some switch instruments or give up touring, and some credit diet, vitamins and love of the horn. A few samples are only loosely related, such as Charlie Holmes on Blanchard building himself up at the Y, and Ben Sidran on the old age of Pepper Adams, Gil Evans and Johnny Griffin. The cluster spans all four collections and 51 interviews, so it is a broad, thinly spread theme rather than one event.
threads: Aching backs, hands and arthritis in older players
Mouth, teeth and jaw trouble that stops playing
Hauling horns and drum sets: the physical load of instruments
Burnout and exhaustion from late nights and long sessions
Illness, longevity and staying in shape
Coping: playing through, taking breaks, switching instruments

communities.name: Chu Berry's fatal crash on the road to Canada
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: The core of this cluster is the October-November 1941 car crash that killed saxophonist Chu Berry while Cab Calloway's band was traveling to Toronto and Montreal. Several members and sidemen of the band (Quentin Jackson, Cozy Cole, Jonah Jones, Teddy McRae) tell it. They agree on the main outline: Lamar Wright's car overturned near Youngstown, Ohio, after the driver braked into a skid and hit a bridge. The bus came upon the wreck, Chu was injured and delirious, and he died days later. Calloway waited until after the dance in Montreal to announce it and hired a replacement, and the tellers differ mainly in detail, such as the bus fire and the keepsakes Chu left. Around this core sit a few looser stories from other eras and collections in which a musician or arranger dies in a car or fire accident, such as Speed Webb's arranger who drove into a Canadian canal, the bassist killed in a crash in Toots Johnson's band, and Russell Wooding's death in a fire. These are tied to the Chu Berry stories only by the motif of sudden death on the road, so the cluster is a tight core with a looser fringe.
threads: The Youngstown crash and how it happened
Chu Berry's injuries, delirium and death
Cab Calloway announcing the death in Montreal and hiring a replacement
Keepsakes and aftermath: the pipe, the watch, the bus fire
Other musicians killed in car crashes or fires (Speed Webb's arranger, Toots Johnson's bassist)

communities.name: Mutes: homemade tricks and who invented them
communities.parent_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition
communities.narrative: Trumpet and trombone players across several collections tell how brass mutes came into jazz. Most of the stories are set between about 1910 and the 1950s, in New Orleans, Chicago, Harlem and New York. Early players improvised mutes from whatever was at hand: derby and felt hats, toilet plungers, tin and coffee cans, glasses, cuspidors, coconut shells, kazoos, eggshells and cigarette tins. Manufactured cup, Harmon and bucket mutes came later. The tellers largely agree that the effects began with New Orleans players such as Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Joe Oliver and Freddie Keppard. They disagree about who was first, and several claim priority. Johnny DeDroit says he invented the cup mute in 1917. Briggs recalls Johnny Dunn claiming the same discovery. Herman Autrey says he was muting before Jonah Jones, and Clark Terry says St. Louis players pulled the stem out of the Harmon mute before Miles did. The tellers are mostly trumpeters, with some trombonists, and they also describe how they learned the sounds, such as the plunger wah-wah and the Embers-era muted style. One group of segments is a near-duplicate run of Vic Dickenson on Frankie Newton's homemade mute. A few samples drift into adjacent topics such as Basie's muted brass, musicians guarding their ideas, or interview business.
threads: Homemade and improvised mutes: derbies, plungers, cans, coconut shells
New Orleans originators: Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Oliver, Keppard and the wah-wah
Who invented the cup, Harmon and bucket mutes: rival priority claims
Learning and perfecting the plunger and wah-wah sound
Mutes as a personal trademark: Autrey, Jonah Jones, Frankie Newton and the Embers

communities.name: Bubber Miley, the plunger and the growl
communities.parent_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition
communities.narrative: Musicians tell where the plunger-mute "growl" sound of Duke Ellington's 1920s band came from and who passed it on. Garvin Bushell places its roots in New York around 1921-24, when he and Bubber Miley heard King Oliver's muted growl in Chicago (Miley later brought it to Ellington), and when trombonist Charlie Irvis supposedly invented the growl on trombone. Lawrence Brown credits Miley's plunger trumpet and Irvis's trombone with the Jungle Band style. Sam Wooding sets the wa-wa and "wow-wow" trumpeters, Johnny Dunn among them, in Harlem. Vic Dickenson says he heard plunger playing from Ellington's band and from Joe Smith in Fletcher Henderson's band, and thinks Johnny Dunn used it. Cootie Williams and Quentin Jackson describe inheriting the plunger roles of Miley and Tricky Sam Nanton, learning them by listening to Nanton or to his records. Clark Terry and Howard Scott add dissenting or qualifying views: Terry denies that his half-valve style came from Rex Stewart, and Scott says Miley was not technically advanced. Tellers are mostly brass players from Ellington's and Henderson's circles, speaking about the 1920s and early 1930s. Vic Dickenson's three near-identical segments inflate the cluster.
threads: Origins of the growl: King Oliver, Irvis and Miley
Bubber Miley's plunger trumpet and the Jungle Band sound
Learning the plunger from Tricky Sam Nanton
Taking over the Ellington plunger chairs (Cootie Williams, Quentin Jackson)
Dunn, Joe Smith and other plunger players in Harlem and Henderson's band
Disputed influences and Miley's limits (Terry, Scott)

communities.name: The death and funeral of Buddy Petit
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: Musicians in this cluster tell about the illness and death of the New Orleans trumpeter Buddy Petit around 1931, and about the funeral that followed. George Lewis, who tells it most often, says Petit played his last jobs at Empire across Lake Pontchartrain, drank at a speakeasy, fell ill and was dead when the band came back. Others give different pieces: Sammy Penn describes two strokes, the second of which killed him, and Alex Bigard and Wilbert Tillman remember him weak and sick, with tuberculosis, hard drinking and exposure blamed. Kid Howard recalls playing the funeral with the Eureka Brass Band and his own band. Several tellers, including the interviewer with Lewis, Earl Humphrey and Joe Darensbourg, try to date the death through Louis Armstrong's 1931 visits and Chris Kelly's funeral, and some only heard of it years later. They disagree on details such as the year, where the last picnic was and the cause, but all treat his death as a landmark event among New Orleans players. A few samples drift to other people, such as a banjoist called Little Dad and another musician's funeral, which weakens the focus slightly.
threads: Last jobs across the lake at Empire and the sudden death
Illness: strokes, tuberculosis and hard living
The funeral and the brass bands that played it
Dating the death by Louis Armstrong's 1931 visits
Burial place and Petit's real name
Learning of his death years later

communities.name: Arranging and recording Randy Weston's Little Niles
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: The strongest strand in this cluster is Melba Liston listening to and discussing her arrangements of Randy Weston's music. She recalls Weston meeting her at Birdland around 1956 and having her turn Little Niles into an album with Johnny Griffin and Ray Copeland. She then compares the 1956 version with the 1973 Tanjah recording and the 1996 string versions, including Hi-Fly, and says Weston tells her only the choruses, string entrances and who solos where. Around that core are loosely related stories about how particular tracks were chosen, timed, arranged or sequenced on records. Orrin Keepnews describes LP side lengths and placing High Fly on side two, and Dave Brubeck explains Blue Rondo a la Turk and Columbia's choice of Take Five as the A side. Christian McBride talks about improvising his solo bass feature on Night Train, Paul Shaffer discusses versions of Cast Your Fate to the Wind, and Jackie Cain recalls a new East of Suez arrangement for Concord. The tellers are arrangers, producers and players across the 1950s to 1990s, and they share a studio-craft perspective but not one subject. Only the Liston and Weston material is tightly unified.
threads: Melba Liston arranging Randy Weston's Little Niles across 1956, 1973 and 1996 versions
Writing for strings and how Weston directs Liston
Choosing and sequencing tracks for LP sides and A-sides
Origins and arrangements of individual tunes like Blue Rondo and Cast Your Fate to the Wind
Last-minute or one-off studio arrangements and solo features

communities.name: Battle of the bands: beating the rival band
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews tell about "battles of the bands" (also called battles of music), head-to-head contests in which two or more bands played the same hall and the crowd, judged by its noise or its dancing, decided the winner. Most stories are set between about 1928 and 1938, in places such as Detroit's Graystone Ballroom, Kansas City, Hartford, Omaha, Flint, Buffalo and Cincinnati, and the rivals are the big names of the era: Bennie Moten, Count Basie, Chick Webb, Jimmie Lunceford, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Fletcher Henderson and Casa Loma. Tellers describe multi-band one-nighter tours, with Moten breaking up the night with "Moten Swing", as well as single famous contests like Basie against Lunceford in Hartford. They agree that these contests were serious business and that winning depended on tactics: letting the other band play first, saving the specials for the last set, a strong drummer or a crowd-pleasing vocal. They differ on what wins. Some stress swing and a driving beat over better arrangements, others stress arrangements or tone, and a New Orleans Dixieland band won a Kansas City contest by playing old-style jazz. The tellers are mostly big-band and territory-band sidemen and leaders, recorded at Rutgers and Tulane.
threads: Multi-band battle tours with Moten, Basie and Webb
Detroit Graystone battles with McKinney's Cotton Pickers and Casa Loma
Basie versus Lunceford in Hartford
Tactics for winning: ordering sets, drummers, vocals, arrangements
Territory-band and local rivalries (Omaha, Flint, Cincinnati, Buffalo)
Dixieland versus big-band arrangements as a contest

communities.name: Playing the Savoy Ballroom against Chick Webb
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Musicians from many bands recall the Savoy Ballroom in Harlem, mostly between the late 1920s and early 1940s, as the place where a band proved itself. Chick Webb's orchestra, with Ella Fitzgerald, is the house band and the one to beat. Visiting leaders and sidemen tell of "battles of music" against Webb, Goodman, Basie, Lucky Millinder and the Savoy Sultans. Count Basie, Jo Jones, Teddy Wilson, Buck Clayton, Mario Bauza and Erskine Hawkins describe packed halls, a springy dance floor and a crowd that judged the bands by how they swung. Some tellers go back to the Savoy's first years, with Fess Williams, the Savoy Bearcats and early Webb sidemen. Others recall auditions, arriving late for a first night, or being hired into Webb's, Millinder's or Teddy Hill's bands. Accounts of who won differ: Basie calls it no battle, Horace Henderson says his band beat Webb in Chicago, and Quinn Wilson says Webb always won at home. A few segments drift to related scenes, such as the Rhythm Club, the Harvest Moon Ball and unrelated bands, and one is only interview logistics.
threads: Battles of the bands against Chick Webb (Goodman, Basie, Hampton, Hines)
The Savoy's early years and house bands (Fess Williams, Savoy Bearcats, Webb)
Dancers' favorites: the Savoy Sultans, Millinder and Erskine Hawkins
Joining and auditioning for Webb, Millinder and Teddy Hill at the Savoy
The room itself: crowds, springy floor, manager Charlie Buchanan, broadcasts
Out-of-town bands booked into the Savoy (Jay McShann, Collegians, Benny Carter)

communities.name: Joining the big bands: Henderson and the swing-era circuit, 1928-36
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they got into, moved between, and left the Black big bands of the late 1920s and mid-1930s. Fletcher Henderson's orchestra is the strongest pull, and Horace Henderson's band, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Les Hite, Earl Hines, Claude Hopkins and Fats Waller's group recur around it. Typical stories are about being recommended by a friend, subbing for Don Redman, or swapping places in a trade such as the Big Trade of Carter and Jimmy Harrison for Procope and Benny Morton. The settings are mostly New York and Harlem, with Roseland and the Dunbar Palace, plus Chicago, Philadelphia and Los Angeles clubs like the Club Alabam. Tellers also work through personnel and chronology, often with an interviewer checking dates against reference books. The cluster is loose at its edges. A few segments are about Los Angeles bandleaders, New Orleans small bands, or a 1959 Chicago job, and they share only the general theme of who joined which band when. The tellers are mostly sidemen and arrangers of the swing generation.
threads: Joining Fletcher Henderson's band
Subbing for and replacing Don Redman
Personnel swaps and recommendations between bands
Sorting out dates and band chronology
Los Angeles and Harlem bandleaders and clubs
Horace Henderson and the Dunbar Palace scene

communities.name: Making the record: albums, tunes and credits
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians across eras tell the story of how a particular record came to be made: whose idea the album was, who wrote or arranged the tunes, how the session went, and who got the credit. The settings run from Sippie Wallace's first sessions in the 1920s and Lawrence Harris's 1933 date, through the 1940s Capitol and Columbia dates, 1950s-60s LPs by Golson, J.J. Johnson, Abbey Lincoln and Kenny Burrell, New Orleans rhythm-and-blues sessions with Bartholomew and Toussaint, and 1990s-2010s CDs of original compositions. Tellers are mostly leaders, arrangers and sidemen, and they share a focus on practical details: producers' and labels' marketing ideas, album concepts, title changes, composer credits, pseudonyms and unrehearsed studio work. They differ in scale and period, from big-label budgets and RCA freedom to small-label or self-conceived projects, and in outcome, since some albums sold poorly or were only partly released. The common thread is album and session provenance rather than any one musician, place or style, so the cluster is real but loose.
threads: Whose idea the album was: producers, labels and concepts
Who wrote and arranged the tunes, and who got credit
Studio sessions with little rehearsal
Naming songs, titles and pseudonyms on records
Albums that sold poorly or were only partly released
Recording one's own compositions in later years

communities.name: Joining a new band: the sideman's job-hopping path
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Across about a hundred interviews, musicians tell how they got a particular chair in a particular band, and then moved on to the next one. The stories are mostly set between 1925 and 1949, with outliers from 1913 and the 1970s. They follow the circuit of territory and dance bands through Detroit, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Pittsburgh, Buffalo, Chicago, New York, Florida and New Orleans. The bands named include the Jean Goldkette orchestra, Horace Henderson's Collegians, Troy Floyd, Leonard Gay, Step Wharton, Al Sears, Celestin, Snookum Russell and Nat Towles. The usual pattern is a recommendation, a call from a leader, an audition or a replacement for a departing player. The tellers vary widely: New Orleans players, big-band sidemen, arrangers, singers and later bebop players. What they share is the mechanics of hiring and moving between bands, not one band, place or event. Because no single subject holds the samples together, the cluster is only loosely coherent.
threads: Getting recruited into the Goldkette orchestra and Detroit bands
Territory and big bands on the Midwest circuit (Cleveland, Cincinnati, Detroit)
Replacing a player or being recommended and auditioned for a chair
Leaving New Orleans for jobs in other cities
Leaving school or hometown for a first professional band

communities.name: Sideman jobs in 1930s territory and Philadelphia bands
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: These are musicians' accounts of joining, leaving and moving between working bands in the late 1920s and 1930s, mostly the second-tier territory and local bands outside the famous names. The largest strand is Philadelphia, where Al Hall, Tom Whaley, Ram Ramirez and Jonah Jones recall local groups, Bill Doggett's big band, Stuff Smith's stranded band and Lil Armstrong taking it over. Another strand is Speed Webb's band, which Vic Dickenson and Teddy Wilson describe forming around a movie appearance and a lineup that included Roy Eldridge and Gus Wilson. Others recall Midwest and Detroit-area bands such as Zack White's, the Cotton Pickers lineage and the Jeter-Pillars orchestra at the Plantation. The tellers agree on the pattern of band-hopping, naming and personnel, and on the mix of ballrooms, radio and one-nighters. They do not share one event, and a few samples fall outside the period, such as Wilbur Ware in 1961 and Breaux in New Orleans, so the cluster is a loose family of band-personnel stories.
threads: Philadelphia local bands and Bill Doggett's big band
Joining Speed Webb's band with the Eldridges and Teddy Wilson
Stuff Smith's stranded band and Lil Armstrong taking over
Midwest bands: Zack White, Jeter-Pillars, Cotton Pickers
Band names, lineups and who played where

communities.name: Territory bands of the Southwest: Holder, Kirk, Blue Devils, Moten
communities.parent_name: Battling at the Savoy Ballroom
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the shifting, hand-to-mouth world of the Southwest and Kansas City territory bands around 1927-1934, when bands formed, split, were taken over and dissolved with startling speed. The clearest shared story, told by Budd Johnson, Eddie Durham, Mary Lou Williams, Buddy Tate and Ernie Fields, is how bandleader T. Holder ran off with or gambled away the payroll, and the men voted Andy Kirk in as leader of the Twelve Clouds of Joy (Johnson adds a variant in which Jesse Stone takes over). Around it sit related accounts of Walter Page's Blue Devils, the Bennie Moten band splitting so that Thamon Hayes could form the Kansas City Rockets, and the break-up of Alphonso Trent's band into Jeter-Pillars. Tellers agree on the pattern of short stints, poor pay and players moving between Oklahoma City, Dallas, Tulsa and Kansas City, and they differ on details such as who led the Blue Devils and exactly when each change happened. Several samples drift to adjacent bands (McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Detroit and Baltimore, Cab Calloway personnel, Louisville and Pittsburgh groups) that share only the era and the band-hopping theme.
threads: T. Holder absconds with the pay and Andy Kirk takes over the Clouds of Joy
Walter Page's Blue Devils: personnel, leadership and break-up
Bennie Moten's band splits and the Kansas City Rockets form
Players hopping between short-lived Southwest bands and cities
McKinney's Cotton Pickers and other Eastern bands of the early 1930s

bands: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

communities.name: First paid gigs and getting started on the bandstand
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection and nearly every era, from New Orleans bandleaders in 1909 to teenagers in the 1970s and 1990s, recall the first time they were paid to play. The pay is usually small and remembered exactly: three, five, twelve, fifteen or twenty-five dollars, or 75 cents for a root beer job. The first jobs are modest too: school and kids' dances, weddings, lawn parties, settlement houses, roadhouses, pizza parlors and teenage bands. Many tell it as being brought in by a schoolmate, an older player, a teacher or a parent, and several describe sitting in or talking their way onto a bandstand. Parents show up as chaperones, as a push toward music over the steel mills, or as the person who insists the bandleader pay up. The tellers agree that the first job was about experience, getting started and learning the working rules rather than the money. They differ mainly by period and idiom: early jazz and territory bands, swing-era dance bands, and later rock, R&B and pop bands. A few samples drift to related career-start stories, such as a recording-studio apprenticeship, hustling in after-hours clubs and a bit of interview housekeeping, so the cluster is mostly but not entirely about the first gig.
threads: First paid gig and what it paid
Teenage bands, school dances and kids' jobs
Being brought in by an older player, teacher or schoolmate
Sitting in and talking your way onto the bandstand
Parents: chaperones, support and demanding pay
Roadhouses, clubs and the first working band

communities.name: Trumpet range, high notes and who taught whom
communities.parent_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about trumpeters and cornetists by their range, tone and teachers. The recurring concerns are who could hit the high notes, how they trained to do it, and who taught whom. In the New Orleans and Crowley accounts, Lawrence Duhé, Norman Brownlee and Monk Hazel trace a teaching line from Manuel Manetta (also spelled Mineta or Moneta) to Emmett Hardy and Turk Rene, and from Professor O'Jay to E.T. Thomas. A family member describes a brother's held notes and reading ability in the WPA band. Later bebop-era and modern players (Howard McGhee, Jacques Butler, Teddy McRae, Ken Poston) dwell on high C's, big sounds and unreachable players such as Fats Navarro, Cat Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie and Maynard Ferguson. Others praise a teacher's harmonic knowledge or note a mouthpiece habit. The samples span roughly 1910 to 1970 and several collections, but they do not share one story. They are portraits of individual trumpeters joined loosely by range and technique, so the grouping is only partly coherent.
threads: Manetta's pupils: Hardy, Rene and the High Society cornet line
Local trumpet teachers and prized pupils in Crowley and New Orleans
High C's and extreme range: Cat Anderson, Navarro, McGhee
Playing along with records and measuring oneself against Dizzy, Maynard and Chet
Mouthpiece, lip and training behind a big sound

communities.name: Grieving the dead: deaths of family and colleagues
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: Musicians tell of the deaths of people close to them and of how they lived through the loss. The cluster is set mostly between the 1920s and the 1990s, with a few accounts reaching into the 2000s, and it draws on New Orleans, New York and Los Angeles interviews alike. Most tellers describe a mother, wife, son, brother or twin dying, often of a heart condition, cancer, a stroke or a sudden collapse. Others recall the deaths of bandmates and friends such as the Dorseys, Thad and Elvin Jones, Pat Patrick, Bill Barron and Pearl Bailey. Some stories are about the event itself, such as a death on stage, a wake or a memorial service. Others are about the aftermath: Monk Montgomery losing the will to play after his brother's death, Vi Redd turning to therapy, prayer and church, and Hank Jones saying a brother's death never brings closure. The tellers agree on the shock and the sense of loss. They differ in whether they go back to work at once or withdraw from music. A few segments, such as the Lee Collins arrival and the Clarence Williams kinship story, only touch on a death in passing, so the shared subject is strong but not perfectly uniform.
threads: Death of a mother, father or spouse
Losing a brother, twin or son
Deaths of bandmates and fellow musicians
Illness and sudden death (heart, cancer, stroke)
Wakes, memorials and funerals
Grief, faith and going back to work

communities.name: Depression-era hard times and the WPA band
communities.parent_name: The Depression years and the WPA band
communities.narrative: Musicians looking back on the 1930s, mostly in New Orleans, tell about making a living through the Depression. The strongest and most concrete strand is the WPA music project: a huge band of roughly 100 to 135 players that rehearsed at places like the Fifth Ward Club on Dumaine Street, was led first by Louis Dumaine and Gilbert and then by Professor Martinez, and was thinned by reading tests and auditions until only about 35 to 40 remained. Players describe the rules (daily reporting, three-hour jobs, permission for outside work), pay of about 25 dollars a week, and concerts in schools, hospitals, parks and City Park. Some men were in it, some were refused or never joined, and some went back to scuffling afterward. Around that core sit wider Depression memories: nightly pay of one to four dollars, plentiful but cheap pick-up and small-band work once beer returned in 1933, funeral jobs, day jobs, and the busiest bands such as Sidney Desvigne's. A few tellers, including Chicago, New York and non-jazz interviewees, add food, prices and soup-line recollections, and a handful of segments only touch the Depression in passing, so the cluster is anchored on the WPA band but loosens at the edges.
threads: Inside the WPA band: size, directors, tests and rules
WPA pay, hours, outside jobs and park concerts
Nightly wages and pick-up band work in the Depression
Busiest bands and big names of the 1930s
Food, prices and everyday scarcity
Scuffling after the WPA ended

communities.name: Day jobs: working outside music to get by
communities.parent_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music
communities.narrative: Musicians from many eras and collections describe the non-music jobs they held alongside, or instead of, playing. The stories are set mostly in New Orleans from the 1910s through the 1940s, with later versions from New York, Chicago and Los Angeles up to the 1970s. The tellers agree that music alone rarely paid steadily, so players worked as clerks, laborers, tradesmen, longshoremen, bank and insurance employees, hospital typists or public servants, and arranged their hours so they could still play at night. They differ on what the day job meant. For some it was a sideline that made music a pastime. For others it meant quitting music for decades, as with Dawson, Leclere and Eddie Marrero. A few kept it to keep the music pure, as Sheila Jordan did. A smaller group, including Carmen Lundy, Art Baron and Mike Wofford, say they never or hardly ever needed one. Older New Orleans traditional players and younger bebop and vocal musicians both tell it, and the tellers' trades are named in detail.
threads: Day jobs held alongside nightly gigs
Quitting or leaving music for steady employment
Trades and labor: bricklayer, riverfront, cotton mill, lumber yard
Office, bank, insurance and public-service careers
Musicians who never needed a day job
Lean years and the Depression

communities.name: Making a living: lean years and freelance struggle
communities.parent_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music
communities.narrative: Musicians, and a few jazz writers, describe how hard it was to earn a steady living from jazz, especially in lean stretches after leaving a famous band or job. Charles McPherson recalls the tough years after leaving Mingus, Frank Foster the roughly 22 years of "freelance starving" around his Basie work, and Mary Lou Williams the 1963-70 years when she lived on royalties and friends. Dan D'Imperio, Jimmy Scott and Richard Wyands describe thin work, no steady income and slow years in New York or Cleveland. Others, such as Big Bill Thompson, JJ Johnson (the Sperry Gyroscope job), Louis Cottrell and Albert Artigues, rely on day jobs, commission work or occasional spot gigs. A second strand comes from jazz writers (Nat Hentoff, James Lincoln Collier, Frank Alkyer, Peter Vacher) who say freelance writing is as precarious as playing. The stories run from the 1910s-20s to the 1990s but mostly cluster in the 1960s-80s. The tellers agree that jazz rarely paid reliably, and they differ in whether they coped with side jobs, spouses' incomes, royalties or writing.
threads: Lean years after leaving a big-name band
Freelance starving and no steady income
Day jobs and side work to survive
Surviving on royalties, friends and family support
Jazz writers' precarious freelance careers

communities.name: Name-checking local musicians when the interviewer asks
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: These are short exchanges in which an interviewer reads out or raises names of local musicians and the interviewee says what he or she knows of each. The answers are brief: who played what, who taught whom, who was in which band, and where someone lived or worked. They are mostly set between about 1890 and 1930, and the places are Mississippi and the Gulf South (Jackson, Tylertown, Mobile, Brookhaven), New Orleans and its country parishes, and Dallas. The tellers range from New Orleans brass and jazz band men (Brunies, Love, Robinson, Phillips) to Mississippi and Louisiana blues guitarists (Babe Stovall, Butch Cage) and swing-era players (Don Albert, Quentin Jackson). Most come from the Tulane collection, with a few from Rutgers, Hamilton and the Smithsonian. The sample has no single event or subject. What the segments share is the interview mechanic of prompted recall of other players, and several answers are thin or garbled by transcription. They read as scattered fragments of local musical networks and not as one story.
threads: Interviewer reads a list of names and the musician comments on each
Who played with whom in the bands (Sam Morgan, Pickwick, Zack White)
Guitarists and blues players around Mississippi and Louisiana
Teachers, family ties and neighbourhood connections among players
Towns and country parishes where bands played
Thin or garbled answers about half-remembered musicians

venues: Home for the Aged (Sive des Vieillards)

communities.name: Favorite trombonists and who played the slide
communities.parent_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how
communities.narrative: Musicians across many interviews, mostly New Orleans players but also swing-era and later bandleaders and educators, talk about trombonists: who they admired, who was in town, and how the instrument was played. The oldest strand is early New Orleans, roughly the 1900s to 1920s. Eddie Summers, Eddie Morris, Ike Robinson, Jim Robinson and Peter LaCaze name players such as Harrison Bradley, Boots Young, Frankie Dusen, Earl Humphrey and Moise French, often noting who read music and who faked by ear. Later tellers, including Wycliffe Gordon, Slide Hampton, Quentin Jackson and Phil Mead, list their own influences: Jack Teagarden, Tommy Dorsey, J.J. Johnson, Lawrence Brown, Urbie Green and Carl Fontana. A smaller group covers technique and the instrument itself, such as ballad playing, valve versus slide, and the trombone chair in big-band books. A few samples only mention a trombonist in passing, for example Harmonica players, bass players and minstrel bandleaders, so the edges are loose. The tellers agree that Teagarden and J.J. Johnson were touchstones, and they differ mainly by era and city.
threads: Early New Orleans trombonists named and ranked (Dusen, Bradley, Humphrey, Boots Young)
Jack Teagarden and Tommy Dorsey as idols
Later players listing influences (J.J. Johnson, Lawrence Brown, Urbie Green, Fontana)
Reading versus faking: how trombonists learned and played
Trombone technique and role: ballad solos, valve versus slide, big-band chairs
Trombone chairs in big bands and bands that dropped the trombone

communities.name: Jazz musicians in film and TV studio work
communities.parent_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring
communities.narrative: Across about 180 interviews, jazz musicians describe their dealings with the movies and television: appearing on screen, playing on soundtracks, scoring pictures and TV shows, and working the Hollywood studio scene. The stories are set mostly in Hollywood, Los Angeles and New York, from the 1930s film shorts and 1940s musicals (Cabin in the Sky, A Song Is Born, band shorts for Universal and Snader) through the 1950s and 60s soundtrack and scoring boom (The Man with the Golden Arm, The Pawnbroker, Repulsion, The Learning Tree) to 1970s-80s TV themes, residuals and later films. Players such as Red Callender, Leonidas Raymond Young and Benny Carter describe studio calls, conductors and orchestrators, while others (Bubbles, Bobby Hutcherson, Al Hall, Slam Stewart) recall small on-screen roles or playing behind a star. Arrangers and composers like Benny Carter, Oliver Nelson, Chico Hamilton and Tom Scott talk about deadlines, working with directors and how film writing differs from jazz. The tellers disagree on whether film work is a worthwhile broadening or a distraction they avoid (Kenny Burrell, Ron Carter), and Mingus raises the exclusion of Black players from studio jobs. A few samples drift to documentary-making, film depictions of jazz history and film-editing careers, so the edges are loose.
threads: Appearing on screen: small film roles and band shorts
Playing on soundtracks and in studio orchestras
Scoring films and TV: directors, deadlines, orchestrators
Residuals, TV themes and the money in studio work
Race and access to Hollywood studio jobs
Documentaries and films about jazz

communities.name: Falling ill: hospital stays and health that stopped the music
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives tell about being taken ill and what it did to their playing and their work. Most of the stories are anchored by a diagnosis or a hospital: strokes, heart attacks, tuberculosis, cancer operations, Bell's palsy, pneumonia, hypertension and diabetes. They are set mostly between the 1930s and the 1970s, in New York, Chicago and New Orleans, with a few from the 1990s. The tellers agree that illness cost them work, whether a lost engagement (Nellie Lutcher's infected tooth), a stretch off the horn (Bob Shoffner's lip cancer, Quentin Jackson's palsy, Higginbotham's retirement) or a forced end to playing (Charlie Holmes). They differ in tone and in who tells it. Some describe their own bodies in detail, such as Wilbur Ware's TB and Arnett Cobb's repeat spinal operation. Others recount a colleague's decline, as with Ory at the 1972 festival, Celestin's last illness, and Ellington and Dr. Logan's deaths. The Zutty Singleton interviews are told largely through his wife Marge, who nursed him and refused a spinal tap. A few segments only touch on illness, for example a record date made with a fever or a hand injury from a bass.
threads: Strokes, heart attacks and hypertension
Tuberculosis, pneumonia and lung illness
Cancer and surgery, then the long recovery
Bell's palsy, lip trouble and being unable to play
Marge Singleton nursing Zutty at home
Watching a colleague or bandleader fail, as with Ory, Celestin and Ellington

communities.name: What musicians made of the avant-garde
communities.parent_name: Playing with and hearing Coltrane
communities.narrative: Across 29 interviews, mostly from the Hamilton and Smithsonian collections, musicians give their verdict on the avant-garde and free jazz that emerged around Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane and George Russell, and on the AACM and loft scenes that followed. The stories are set from the 1950s into the 2000s, with most placed in the 1960s and 70s. The tellers mostly respect the music, but many attach a condition: it should be rooted in tradition and the basics. Slide Hampton liked Ornette but wanted him grounded, Hank Jones says yesterday's avant-garde becomes standard, and Bill Watrous says playing outside needs roots. Art Farmer explains the appeal as relief from increasingly complex harmony. Some played in it themselves. David Baker dates his avant-garde period to the Russell years, and Michael Moore remembers the loft scene before returning to songs and tighter forms. Michael White says it let him express feelings that tradition could not, and Longineu Parsons calls it spiritual. A few samples drift to other subjects, such as studio work on one-chord grooves and a band's frustrations in the 1950s.
threads: Why Ornette's freedom appealed, and Coltrane and Russell's ideas
Respect for free playing, but rooted in tradition and the basics
Musicians' own avant-garde periods and loft scenes
AACM, Chicago and Europe's support for free music
Free jazz as spiritual expression and a reflection of the times

communities.name: Remembering John Coltrane and his circle
communities.parent_name: Playing with and hearing Coltrane
communities.narrative: Most of these stories are about John Coltrane. He appears in 142 of the tagged people mentions, and the John Coltrane Quartet is the top band facet at 34. They are told by musicians who played with him, heard him, or measured themselves against him. The samples are mostly set between the late 1950s and 1967, in New York, Philadelphia, Los Angeles and Chicago. Elvin Jones, Roy Haynes and McCoy Tyner speak from inside the band. They describe the quartet's discipline, the Gothenburg duet "Chasin' the Trane", the spiritual turn after A Love Supreme, and the arrival of Pharaoh Sanders, Archie Shepp and Rashied Ali. Tyner explains why he left the avant-garde direction. Peers such as Frank Foster, Charles Lloyd, Kenny Burrell, Red Holloway and Big Nick Nicholas tell personal encounters at the Five Spot, Birdland and Prestige sessions. They stress his humility, devotion and blues foundation. Later players such as Dave Liebman and Branford Marsalis reflect on his spirituality and legacy, and a few dissenters, such as Kenny Davern and Benny Carter, prefer other lineages. A looser fringe widens to Eric Dolphy, Ornette Coleman and Cecil Taylor, where the shared subject is the early-1960s new music rather than Coltrane himself.
threads: Playing in the Coltrane quartet: Elvin, Tyner and Haynes on the music
Hearing Trane live at the Five Spot and Birdland
Coltrane the person: humility, devotion, practicing
Spirituality and the late avant-garde turn, and why sidemen left
Eric Dolphy, Ornette Coleman and Cecil Taylor in the new music
Influence and dissent: sheets of sound and doubters

communities.name: Friends lost: remembering musicians who died
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, New York and elsewhere stop mid-interview to remember colleagues and friends who have died, often listing names as they go. The deaths range across the century: Ladnier dying at Mezz Mezzrow's house in 1939, Charlie Christian's final illness in 1941-42, the Amsterdam Club's nineteen members lost in 1965, and the musicians who died in the 2020 pandemic. Tellers such as Kenny Clarke, Zutty Singleton, Herb Ellis, Benny Golson, Quincy Jones and Russell "Big Chief" Moore dwell on early deaths, especially Christian at 23 and Coltrane, and on the sense of being one of the few left. Some tellers frame the loss as a tribute to a musician's influence or reputation, while others give a plain roll-call of friends gone or news of a friend's illness. The cluster is small and loosely bound. A few samples drift to a prison inmate's death and to a bandleader's illness, and the shared thread is mourning rather than any one event or place.
threads: Lists of friends and colleagues who have died
Charlie Christian's early death and influence
Coltrane and other musicians lost too young
Club and society funerals and deaths of members
Illness and death in recent decades, including the pandemic
Deaths among fellow band members and sidemen

communities.name: Last illness and death of a fellow musician
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how a colleague, bandleader or friend sickened and died, and what they did or felt when they heard. Most stories are set between the 1930s and the 1990s, with a few reaching to 2000 and 2009. The scenes are in New York, Chicago, New Orleans and San Francisco, and on the road or abroad. Tellers give clinical detail: strokes, heart failure and heart attacks, pneumonia, consumption, kidney trouble, diabetes and misdiagnosis after surgery. Some stories are firsthand deathbed or hospital visits (Wettling, George Lewis, Dizzy Gillespie). Others are secondhand or rumoured accounts, such as how Slim died or how Woody Shaw was killed. Tellers dispute causes (Moten's scalpel slip against a heart attack, Burnell's dropsy against a police beating) and mention concealed illness (Joe Williams hiding his condition so he would keep getting booked). The stories also cover the aftermath: funerals, benefit concerts, last recordings and final gigs, and one musician who stopped playing for months. They come from veterans of New Orleans jazz, swing bands and bebop, and from younger players recalling mentors and peers. The Basie, Webb and Goodman orbits are especially visible.
threads: Final illness and cause of death, including disputed causes
Hospital visits and deathbed scenes
Learning of a death from afar
Hidden or neglected health problems
Funerals, benefits and last recordings or gigs
Dying on the way to or after a job

communities.name: Serving on NEA panels and lobbying for jazz funding
communities.parent_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards
communities.narrative: Musicians recall sitting on National Endowment for the Arts panels and other advisory bodies to win public money and recognition for jazz, mostly from 1968 through the 1980s, with a few later echoes. David N. Baker says that from 1968 he argued Basie and Woody Herman bands deserved subsidy like symphony orchestras, with Cannonball Adderley backing him. He later chaired the Kennedy Center jazz advisory committee, joined the National Council on the Arts and helped found the National Jazz Service Organization. Jimmy Owens tells the most detailed version: he served on the NEA Jazz Folk Ethnic panel from 1972 to 1976, and the jazz budget grew from $5,000 to hundreds of thousands of dollars. He started programs such as travel study and composer grants, and he reassured doubtful Harlem musicians that applying for grants worked. His 1986 speech to the Congressional Black Caucus helped lead to House Resolution 57, which named jazz a national treasure. Jackie McLean and Vi Redd describe panel service more briefly, McLean to keep Washington connections and bring funds to Hartford institutions, and Redd as years of travel with Benny Powell. The tellers are educator-performers who treat panel work as a duty to the music. A couple of samples drift to related funding and organizing topics: Dave Robinson's 2000s educators' network and kit, and Owens's failed CBA publishing company.
threads: Baker pressing the NEA to subsidize jazz bands like orchestras
Jimmy Owens on the NEA jazz panel: budget growth and new grant programs
Explaining grants to skeptical musicians and working with state arts councils
Kennedy Center, National Council on the Arts and the National Jazz Service Organization
The 1986 Congressional Black Caucus and jazz as a national treasure
Panel service to bring money home to schools and societies

communities.name: Getting the call: auditioning for a bandleader
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Musicians from across the swing, bebop and later big-band eras tell how they landed a job in a named leader's band, and the story almost always turns on an audition or a tip passed along by someone else. Most are set between the late 1930s and the early 1990s, with a few earlier or later. Frank Foster's account of reading about Basie in Down Beat, leaving the army and auditioning at Detroit's Graystone Ballroom for Count Basie in 1953 is the most repeated version. Maynard Ferguson's band supplies several parallel stories, where a friend, a sit-in or a recommendation leads to a telegram, a borrowed baritone or a tape (Diblasio, Militello, Johnstone). Others tell of auditioning for Dick Stabile, Kai Winding, Disney in Miami, Sauter-Finegan or Jack Teagarden, or of filling in after an accident or a departing player. The tellers agree that getting hired rested on connections, being ready and a rough first read of the charts, and they differ mainly in which band and which route in. They are mostly sidemen, often horn players, though a few are drummers and guitarists.
threads: Frank Foster's Detroit audition for Count Basie
Joining Maynard Ferguson's band through a tip, a tape or a sit-in
Auditioning for a leader and flubbing the sight-reading
Replacing a departing or injured sideman
Recommendations and connections that open the door
Sitting in and being hired afterward

communities.name: Jam sessions in Los Angeles and Central Avenue
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the after-hours and Sunday jam sessions that made Los Angeles a jazz town, mostly from the 1930s through the late 1940s. The core of the cluster is Central Avenue and its neighbours: the Dunbar Hotel clubs, the Apex and the Alabam, Watts church sessions, Jack's Basket, the Trouville, Billy Berg's and the Toddle House. Visiting big-band men from the Lunceford and Ellington orchestras sat in alongside local players such as Nat Cole, Lee Young, Wardell Gray, Dexter Gordon, Hampton Hawes and Don Byas. Nellie Lutcher, John Simmons and Leonidas Raymond Young tell it from the inside, describing sessions in private houses, Sunday sessions run by Lee Young (with a $500 union fine after one), and tenor duels that tested everyone in every key. A minority of samples drift to jam sessions elsewhere (a New York hotel and a Village loft, a Paris-era after-hours scene, a Louisiana house) and share only the practice of jamming, not the Los Angeles setting. Tellers broadly agree that jamming was where players proved themselves, met each other and found work.
threads: Central Avenue clubs and after-hours jamming
Sunday sessions run by Lee Young and the Nat Cole trio
House sessions at Nellie Lutcher's home
Tenor duels: Wardell Gray, Dexter Gordon, Don Byas
Visiting big-band players sitting in

communities.name: Writing the book: musicians as authors
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about writing books: memoirs, autobiographies, novels, essays, instructional texts and jazz scholarship. The stories run from the 1970s to the 2020s, told mostly late in careers and often at the end of an interview. Count Basie in 1977 and Jimmie Crawford and Sammy Price in the 1970s say a book is underway and decline to give details because they are saving them for it. Later figures, including Artie Shaw, Annie Ross, Jimmy Heath, Howard Levy and Gunther Schuller, describe how the memoir was built, how long it took, and how publishers like Oxford rejected or accepted it. Others tell how they came to write at all. David Baker needed teaching materials. Bill Crow was asked by Gene Lees and Sheldon Meyer. Bud Freeman was encouraged by a newspaper editor. Alongside these is a looser strand of future plans, such as unwritten books, orchestral pieces and string projects, which drifts from writing prose toward writing music. The tellers agree that writing is a late-life project to set the record straight. They differ on whether it is a memoir, a teaching text or fiction, and on how hard publishing was.
threads: Memoirs and autobiographies in progress, and what the author is saving for the book
How the book got written: ghost writers, diaries, decades-long drafts
Publishers, editors and rejections (Oxford, Sheldon Meyer)
Teaching books, essays and jazz scholarship by musicians
Novels, fiction and plays by musicians
Future plans and unwritten projects, including compositions

communities.name: Commissions and pieces written in response to events
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about works that were commissioned or composed in response to a larger event or cause, and about what they hoped the music would say. The clearest core is commissioned and occasion pieces: Toshiko Akiyoshi's Hiroshima piece, premiered on August 6, 2001 and shaped around hope; George Russell's It's About Time, commissioned for Stockholm; Ramsey Lewis's Lincoln work for Ravinia; Slide Hampton's African suite for the Chicago Jazz Ensemble; and Yusef Lateef's African-American Epic Suite. A second strand is music answering historical or political events: Coltrane's Alabama after the church bombing, and its influence on Josephine Davies, plus pieces prompted by 9/11 and by war from Tom Varner and Chazz Frichtel. Tom Varner and Ran Blake also imagine hypothetical pieces for the January 6 anniversary. Johnny Wiggs's Congo Square, written to evoke enslaved people singing, belongs here too. Tellers mostly agree on turning struggle into hope or reflection, and differ in how directly they treat the event. The tail of the cluster drifts into loosely related future-project talk, such as hoped-for commissions, long-term goals, Covid livestreams and songwriting. These are 2020s and 2000s forward-looking remarks that do not fit the commission or event theme.
threads: Commissioned works and premieres (Hiroshima, Stockholm, Ravinia, Chicago)
Coltrane's Alabama and music answering injustice
Pieces written after 9/11 and about war
Imagined pieces on January 6
Suites about African and African-American history

communities.name: The Basie rhythm section and Freddie Green
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Musicians from several generations talk about what made the Count Basie band's rhythm section distinctive, mostly in the 1930s through the 1960s with roots in Kansas City. The recurring figures are Basie at the piano, guitarist Freddie Green, bassist Walter Page and drummer Jo Jones. Tellers such as Buddy Tate, Clark Terry, Billy Mitchell, Buddy DeFranco, Bucky Pizzarelli and Phil Schaap praise Green's steady four-four chording and Basie's economical comping, his sense of space and tempo, and his leadership from the keyboard. Players who worked in the band describe it as a well-oiled machine, while outside listeners and guitarists analyze why it worked. Danny Barker traces the lineage back to King Oliver and Bennie Moten, and other samples set the Basie section beside other tight units, such as Benny Carter's and the Jimmy Jones-Denzil Best trio. A few segments drift into rhythm sections in general rather than Basie's, so the core is strong but the edges are looser.
threads: Freddie Green's four-four rhythm guitar
Basie's spare piano and leading from the keyboard
Page, Jones and Green as a unified section
Basie's sense of tempo and space
Roots of the Basie sound in Kansas City and King Oliver
Other bands' rhythm sections compared

communities.name: Harlem bandstands: Charlie Johnson and Small's Paradise
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Most of these stories are set in Harlem and Atlantic City between the early 1920s and the early 1930s. They are about who played in which New York band and club. The strongest thread is Charlie Johnson's orchestra at Small's Paradise. Benny Carter, Benny Waters, Happy Caldwell, Teddy McRae, Doc Cheatham and Don Albert each place themselves in the band or recall its sidemen, such as Jabbo Smith, Edgar Sampson and Jimmy Harrison. Waters is pressed by interviewer Schaap on whether Johnson's band or Elmer Snowden's was at Small's first, and on whether the 'Paradise' name came from Atlantic City. Around that core sit related Harlem band-and-club recollections: Snowden handing the Nest Club job to Cliff Jackson, Sam Wooding's orchestra at the Nest, Horace Henderson's Dunbar Palace men, and Sonny Greer and Bricktop at Baron Wilkins'. A few samples drift off the theme. Bunk Johnson's band at a 1940s ballroom, Keppard with Tim Brown in 1919, and a late-1930s hotel sextet are loosely related at best. The tellers are mostly New York swing and big-band sidemen, with some New Orleans players who passed through. Their accounts agree on the band's importance and differ on exact dates and sequence.
threads: Joining Charlie Johnson's band at Small's Paradise
Atlantic City summer engagements and the 'Paradise' name
Snowden, Cliff Jackson and the Nest Club band succession
Who played in the Harlem club bands and sidemen lineups
Other 1920s New York engagements: Baron Wilkins', Coconut Grove, Dunbar Palace

communities.name: Billy Berg's and the Los Angeles club scene, 1940s
communities.parent_name: Going west: moving to and working in California
communities.narrative: Musicians recall Billy Berg's, the Los Angeles nightclub that moved among several addresses (Pico, La Cienega, Beverly, Hollywood Boulevard, finally Vine Street), as the hub of the 1940s Hollywood scene. Tellers such as Vic Dickenson, Joe Turner, Zutty Singleton, Barney Bigard and Trummy Young remember working there or around it in bands with Slam Stewart, Slim Gaillard, Roy Eldridge and Leo Watson. Others, including Art Farmer, JJ Johnson and Chico Hamilton, remember it as the place where Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker opened in late 1945. They disagree on how it went: Farmer says the engagement failed commercially and Bird stayed behind in California, and Hamilton says Bird and Diz were on Central Avenue first and Berg's started later. Around this core the stories spread to neighboring Los Angeles rooms (the Swing Club, Swanee Inn, Trouville, Capri and Finale Club) and to Howard McGhee's band and Teddy Edwards's recollections of 1945-46. A few segments drift to loosely related LA scenes, such as after-hours singing during Jump for Joy and George Bledsoe at the California Club.
threads: Billy Berg's moving from address to address, down to Vine Street
Bird and Diz open at Berg's, 1945-46, and why it faltered
Slim and Slam, Leo Watson and the house-band regulars
Howard McGhee's band at the Swing Club and Finale Club

communities.name: Joining Lionel Hampton's band: how musicians got the call
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell how they came to play with Lionel Hampton, and what the band was like from the inside. Most stories are set between the mid-1930s and early 1960s, with the strongest cluster in the 1940-48 big band years. They are told in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Detroit, at venues such as the Grand Terrace, the Apollo and the Paradise Theater. The tellers describe the recruiting moment: a wire or phone call, a message handed over at a club, a visit to hear a young player, or an audition on the job. They also describe who was in the sections (Dexter Gordon, Illinois Jacquet, Arnett Cobb, Joe Newman, Ernie Royal, later Clifford Brown) and the swap of players when someone left. Sidemen such as Joe Wilder, Teddy McRae, Arnett Cobb and Charles Thompson give personnel and pay details. Others, such as Andrew Blakeney, Reb Spikes and Quinn Wilson, go back to Hampton as a young drummer in 1920s-30s Los Angeles. Some later players, from the 1950s to the 1980s, tell the same kind of story. A few samples only touch Hampton, or not at all, so the cluster is a loose majority rather than a pure one.
threads: Getting the call: wires, phone calls and club messages from Hampton
The 1940-46 band: Gordon, Jacquet, Cobb and the sax and trumpet sections
Replacing a departing player and sitting in the chair
Hampton as a young drummer in 1920s-30s Los Angeles

Hampton as showman and vibes influence

communities.name: Working for Lionel Hampton: pay, Gladys, and quitting
communities.parent_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band
communities.narrative: Musicians who passed through Lionel Hampton's orchestra, from his early 1940s band through the 1950s and into his late-1980s years, tell remarkably similar stories about what it was like to work for him. The dominant thread is money: Howard McGhee quit over ten dollars a night, Charles Mingus says he was promised $400 a week and cut to $125 by Gladys Hampton (and was never paid for his arrangements), Benny Golson left when his pay fell to $19, and Joe Wilder and David Baker describe poor pay, hard conditions and constant turnover. Gladys Hampton, who ran the band's business, appears as the person who set and cut wages and settled disputes. A second strong episode is the 1953 European tour, where Art Farmer, Annie Ross, Monk Montgomery and Golson recall the sidemen (Quincy Jones, Gigi Gryce, Clifford Brown and others) secretly recording in Sweden, Hampton's threats and firings, and the cliques inside the band. Tellers agree that Hampton was a showman who insisted the public paid to see him; they differ in tone, from Wilder's lasting resentment to Slide Hampton's more affectionate view of a strong band led by a contradictory egomaniac. The tellers are mostly sidemen and arrangers, with a few later players such as Magnarelli recalling Hampton in old age.

The 1953 Europe tour and secret recordings in Sweden
Hampton's ban on outside recording and the firings

communities.name: Union cards, locals and the musicians' union
communities.parent_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1910s to the 1990s tell stories about the American Federation of Musicians and its locals, above all New York's Local 802, Chicago's local, and Los Angeles's Black Local 767 and white Local 47. The most common story is getting a card: reading or audition tests, six-month or three-month waiting periods for transfers, and cards that kept a player from a job, as with Cootie Williams, Milt Hinton and Buddy Tate. Others tell of the union as an enforcer, with fines for sitting in, back pay hearings, and pay for missed dates. The Black locals and the long fight to merge 767 into 47 get their own accounts, and New Orleans players say there was no union for them. Tellers differ on value. Some praise a local's flexibility or its drives for scale and death benefits, while later players such as Herman Autrey, Ernie Fields and Johnny Varro call the union weak, indifferent or without a pension. The tellers are mostly big-band sidemen and bandleaders working in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles, plus New Orleans and Oakland players. A few samples drift to related matters such as the cabaret card system, the Clef Club's Masonic rule and ASMAC.
threads: Getting a union card: tests, waiting periods and transfer rules
Segregated locals: Local 767, Local 47 and the merger
Fines, back pay hearings and the union as enforcer

communities.name: Playing with and hearing George Lewis
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Musicians and listeners from many interviews (31 across Tulane, Rutgers, Hamilton and the Smithsonian) mention George Lewis, the New Orleans clarinetist, usually as one name among the bands and bandleaders around him. Most of the stories are about working with him or hearing him. Abbie Williams recalls playing with Lewis around 1945. Sid Davilla describes hiring him for club dates. Kid Howard describes first playing with him before Bunk Johnson. Allan Jaffe covers his absence at the start of Preservation Hall, and the visitors of 1963 recall his sets there as the most inspiring. A second strand reaches back to Lewis in the 1910s and 20s in the Buddy Petit and lake-country bands, and in Bunk Johnson's New York engagement. Beyond that the cluster drifts: several samples, such as Abby Foster on the White Carnations records and Chester Zardis on George Washington and the Covington band, are about other bandleaders or a different 'George' and share only the name. The tellers agree Lewis was central to the revival era, but the cluster is a loose gathering around his name and not one single event.

Lewis's early years with Buddy Petit and lake-country dance bands
Hiring and hearing Lewis in clubs and at Preservation Hall

communities.name: Who wrote it: arranger credit and Glenn Miller's hits
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians from big-band circles tell stories about who really wrote or arranged a famous swing tune, and who got the credit and money. The strongest strand is Glenn Miller's "In the Mood". Higginbotham, Kenny Clarke, Charlie Barnet and Georg Brunis each credit someone else (Joe Garland, Eddie Durham, Wingy Manone, or a stranger at a Lincoln Hotel rehearsal) and say Miller got the fame. Related tales cover Eddie Durham's "Wham" with Miller taking half the writer credit, Basie arrangements carried to Miller's band, and Buddy DeFranco on the origins of "Moonlight Serenade". Other tellers apply the same question to other bands: Walter P. Thomas writing the "Minnie the Moocher" intro for Cab Calloway overnight, Erskine Hawkins's head arrangements such as "Tippin' In", Lunceford's "Yard Dog Mazurka" with Roger Segure, and "One O'Clock Jump" renamed on air in 1936. The setting is mostly 1930s-40s swing-era bands in New York and on the road. The tellers agree that arrangers were often uncredited, and they disagree on specific attributions. A few samples (Juber on altered guitar tunings, DeDroit on stock arrangements) fit only loosely.

Eddie Durham and Basie arrangements going to Glenn Miller
Writing Cab Calloway's 'Minnie the Moocher' arrangement

Origins of Glenn Miller's signature sound

communities.name: Louis Armstrong as colleague, boss and legend
communities.parent_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong
communities.narrative: Musicians from many bands and collections tell stories in which Louis Armstrong is the common presence, from the 1910s New Orleans riverboats and Pete Lala's through Chicago (Erskine Tate's Vendome pit band, the Sunset Cafe, Joe Glaser's early backing), Fletcher Henderson's band in New York in 1924-25, and the Hot Five and Hot Seven records. The tales then run on to the big-band and All Stars years of the 1930s-60s. Some tellers worked for him, such as John Simmons and Big Sid on the 1940s bus tours, Trummy Young, and Zutty Singleton. Others heard him, sat in with him, recorded with him (Happy Caldwell, Sippie Wallace, Jacques Butler on Paris Blues) or were advised by him on lips and high notes. Recurring concerns include his lip trouble, his early training at the Waifs' Home, Joe Glaser's management and money handling, his reputation (no 'Uncle Tom', changing jazz through his records), and road-life anecdotes. The tellers agree on his stature and generosity but differ in which period and relationship they recall. The shared factor is the person rather than a single event, so the cluster is a loose portrait gathered from many angles, not one story.

Armstrong with Henderson, Russell and Chick Webb in New York
On the road with the Armstrong band and All Stars: buses, Big Sid, Velma
Joe Glaser, money and management

communities.name: Why the big bands died, 1945-1955
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Musicians from Basie, Hawkins, Calloway and Ellington sidemen to younger players like Bob Wilber and Lanny Morgan explain how the big-band business collapsed in the late 1940s and early 1950s. The story is set mostly between 1945 and 1952, with New York, the Savoy Ballroom and the road as the backdrop. Tellers agree on the symptoms: dance halls and theaters closing, guarantees disappearing, and leaders such as Basie, Hawkins and Calloway cutting down to six pieces, hotel jobs or a single act. They disagree on the cause. The reasons offered include the 20 percent ballroom tax, travel and payroll costs, the recording ban, television and radio, bebop, the rise of Louis Jordan's small rhythm-and-blues groups, singers like Sinatra, package shows, and later rock and roll. A smaller tail looks ahead and asks whether big bands can return, with Pete Fountain, Ernie Fields and Ira Gitler mostly doubting it on cost grounds. A few outliers drift off the subject, such as Howard Mandel on Down Beat and Herman Autrey on the Saints and Sinners, plus some 1930s ballroom background.
threads: Basie, Hawkins and Calloway break up their bands (1950-52)
Money and logistics: ballroom tax, travel costs, lost guarantees
Changing tastes: bebop, Louis Jordan, singers, television, rock
Musicians pushed into small groups and Dixieland work
Will big bands ever come back?

communities.name: Violinists in New Orleans bands and beyond
communities.parent_name: Fiddlers and reading violinists of New Orleans
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews, mostly Tulane's Hogan Archive, talk about violin players and what the fiddle meant in early New Orleans music. The core is the 1900s to 1920s. Tellers name and rank the reading violinists of the downtown Creole bands, chiefly Peter Bocage, Manuel Manetta, John Robichaux, Armand Piron, Paul Dominguez and Herbert Lindsay (called Fiddle Up, famed for his double stops). Others cover Max Fink and Oscar Marco, who played in theaters and at carnival balls. They agree that these violinists read at sight, often led or taught the bands, and sometimes acted as bosses. Several, such as Johnny DeDroit and Chink Martin, explain why violins faded from dance bands: they did not suit two-beat jazz and could not be heard before amplification. A smaller group looks outside New Orleans at jazz violinists such as Joe Venuti, Stuff Smith, Eddie South and Ray Perry, and at Heifetz's remarks on Venuti. Some segments are only loosely related, such as a photograph's provenance and a vibes trio plan.
