threads: Ranking the reading violinists: Bocage, Manetta, Robichaux, Piron
Violin-led string bands, theaters and carnival balls
Why violins faded from dance bands
Joe Venuti, Stuff Smith and other jazz fiddlers
Heifetz and the classical view of jazz violin

communities.name: Who played what: instrumentation of early string bands
communities.parent_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation
communities.narrative: In this cluster, musicians describe the makeup of early bands: which instruments were in the lineup, which were left out, and what that did to the sound. The tellers are mostly New Orleans players, with a few from Chicago, Baton Rouge and Texas. They place the stories mainly between 1900 and the late 1920s, with some later outliers. Many describe "string bands" built on guitar, banjo, violin, mandolin and string bass, often with no piano, clarinet or trombone. Several say there were no tubas until about 1920 and that guitar gave way to banjo because it could not be heard against brass. Others contrast brass bands with string bands, or describe players doubling on several instruments. Some segments work through a photograph and name the members and their instruments (the Superior Band, the Six and Seven Eighths, the Owls, the Ringside Orchestra). The tellers agree that early lineups were small, flexible and varied. They differ on which instruments came first and which were dropped, and a few later or non-New Orleans segments, such as Hines's strings band, Bill Boyd's band and an amplified cello group, only loosely fit.
threads: Guitar, banjo and violin: what counted as a string band
No tuba, no piano, no clarinet in the earliest lineups
Brass band versus string band and instrument doubling
Naming band members and instruments from photographs
Lineups of specific bands: Superior, Six and Seven Eighths, Owls, Ringside
Later or outside examples of unusual instrumentation (Hines, Boyd, cello group)

communities.name: Who played what: band size and instrumentation
communities.parent_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation
communities.narrative: Musicians across 74 interviews, mostly from Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive with a share from Rutgers and the Smithsonian, tally who was in the band and which instruments it carried. The core of the story is New Orleans brass bands, dance bands and society orchestras from the 1890s to the 1920s. Jim Robinson, Papa Jack Laine, Bat Stecklet, Punch Miller, Emile Barnes and Danny Barker give band sizes (five to seven for dance bands, ten to eighteen for marching bands) and name the horns used: cornets, E-flat and alto horns, valve trombone, baritone and tuba. The tellers agree that early bands had no saxophone and rarely a piano, and that violins gave way to wind instruments. They differ on size, and on whether a given band counts as jazz. A smaller group carries the question to later big bands and Latin ensembles: Cootie Williams, Zilner Randolph, Mario Bauza, Candido Camero, Eddie Sauter and Bill Kirchner. The samples are tightly tied to instrumentation, but the later swing and Latin examples and the odd item such as the Boston union hangout fall outside the New Orleans core.
threads: Early New Orleans brass bands: size and instruments
Dance bands and the five-to-seven-piece jazz combination
No saxophone, no piano: what early bands lacked
Society orchestras and show bands, 1910s-30s
Big bands growing into sections, plus Latin conjuntos and later ensembles

communities.name: Not listening to their own old records
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections reflect on how they relate to their own recordings after the fact. The dominant story is avoidance: Sheila Jordan, Steve Turré, Joe Wilder, Helen Humes and Ken Peplowski say they rarely or never play their own records. They are too self-critical, the records could always have been better, and they hear rough edges and humiliations. Dick Katz recalls embarrassing record dates, and McBee calls himself his worst critic and tells of not recognising himself on a 1977 record his wife put on. A few tellers differ. Vic Dickenson names records he likes and one with a response vocal he disliked, and Jackie Cain describes how listening again led to re-recording 'East of Suez'. Al Gallodoro's re-recording of Czardas faster seven years later and Howard R. Scott's talk of his last record fall at the edges. Most of the stories are undated, reflective asides from working musicians looking back at their discographies, not tied to one period or place.
threads: Never playing their own records
Being their own worst critic
Embarrassing or regretted record dates
Picking favorite records and disliking parts of them
Re-recording or revisiting old albums
Hearing themselves unexpectedly on TV or on old records

communities.name: Starting that first neighborhood or school band
communities.parent_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from across the country remember how they first played in a band as boys and girls, usually in the 1920s and 1930s and occasionally later. The band forms among neighborhood friends, brothers and school classmates, or around a school band director. Bigard is recruited by a neighbor, Jacques Butler organizes a band with the Walker family, Henry Russ plays in Tillman's band with boyhood friends from the Sixteenth Ward, and Joe Watkins runs yard parties with a kazoo player named Frog. School settings include the Booker T. Washington and Manassas bands, Sy Jenkins's high school weekend band, Helen Humes's little school band, and Major N. Clark Smith's Chicago Defender boys' band. The tellers agree that these were informal, enthusiastic, often unpaid first ensembles built from friendship and a bit of luck. They differ on whether the pull came from a friend or relative, an older mentor, or a school program. The speakers come from New Orleans, Chicago, Kansas City, New York and Missouri, and many later became professionals. The cluster is loose, though. The samples share the theme of first bands but are set in many different places and circumstances.
threads: Neighborhood friends forming a first band
School and high school bands and their directors
Recruited by a neighbor, relative or manager
Yard parties, first unpaid gigs and early rehearsals
Boys' bands under older mentors

communities.name: Going broke: why the band folded
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews tell how a band they led or played in ended because the money ran out. The settings range from a WPA band cut back around 1938, through Don Albert's 1940 breakup and the late-1940s collapse of Billy Eckstine's big band, to the late-1950s end of the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra and the short-lived early-1960s and 1972 groups of Pete Barbutti and Jack DeJohnette. The causes differ. Some bands were sunk by bad bookers or managers, some by owners handing a booking to a bigger name such as Dizzy Gillespie, and some by debts, a tax on gate receipts or the cost of touring. What the tellers share is the aftermath: leaders paying sidemen out of their own pockets, running up large debts, and going solo or leaving the business. The tellers are mostly bandleaders, sidemen and arrangers, and the setting is New York as well as Texas, New Orleans and the West. Only ten samples are in this pack, but nearly all of them fit one subject.
threads: Bad bookers and managers wrecking a band
Leaders paying sidemen out of pocket
Debts and taxes ending the big band
Losing a booking to a bigger name
Record deals and tours that could not be financed

communities.name: Changing bands: joining, quitting and replacing in the big-band years
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Sidemen from the swing era into the early 1960s tell how they moved between name bands: who recommended them, who they replaced, why they quit, and what the new boss was like. The recurring leaders are Woody Herman, Charlie Barnet, Red Norvo, Teddy Powell, Glenn Miller and Earl Hines, with New York (Nola Studios for auditions, the Apollo, Broadway, Glen Island and the Meadowbrook) as the usual setting. Most stories are set between about 1933 and 1960. Tellers agree that jobs came through personal recommendation, as with Ralph Burns getting Flip Phillips and himself into Herman's band and Leeman getting Chubby Jackson into Barnet's. They differ in the reasons for leaving. Some left over the music, as Wayne Andre did over strictly written parts. Others left over management or leader problems, as Gil Evans did when MCA put Skinny Ennis in front of his band. Others left over quarrels, pay or a drafted colleague's chair, and Quinn Wilson's accounts of Earl Hines personnel turnover are a related case. The subject is the churn of personnel and not any single band, so the samples share a pattern more than one story. The tellers range from trumpeters and saxophonists to pianists and drummers.
threads: Getting hired on a colleague's recommendation (Ralph Burns, Chubby Jackson)
Leaving one name band for another (Norvo to Thornhill, Powell to Herman)
Replacing a drafted or departed player
Bandleader as boss: absences, pay, takeovers
Personnel turnover in the Hines and Herman bands
Auditioning in New York studios

communities.name: Managers, bookers and agents: who ran the business
communities.parent_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work
communities.narrative: Across 189 interviews, musicians tell stories about the people who handled their business: personal managers, road managers, booking agencies and bookers. The tellers span the 1920s to the 1990s, with most stories set between the 1930s and the 1990s. They cover swing-era bandleaders such as Roy Eldridge, Cootie Williams, Jay McShann and Ernie Fields, vaudeville dancers such as John W. Bubbles, singers such as Maxine Sullivan and Horn Shirley, and later artists such as Carla Bley and Maria Schneider. The agents themselves also speak, notably Walter P. Thomas and John Levy. Joe Glaser, Billy Shaw, Moe Gale, MCA and William Morris recur as the gatekeepers of work. The tellers agree that the arrangement mattered. Commissions of 5 to 50 percent, binding contracts and handshake deals shaped a career, and a manager could be a protector or an exploiter. They differ on trust. Some praise Glaser or Levy as honest and straight-talking. Others recount split commissions, a manager who sold a contract, or a five-year deal signed behind a partner's back. A minority say they never had a manager and booked themselves.
threads: Joe Glaser and the big agencies: Shaw, Gale, MCA, William Morris
Commissions, contracts and handshake deals
Exploitative managers and breaking away (Nazarro, Sam Beers)
Road managers and tour coordination
Agents' own accounts: Walter Thomas, John Levy, Ruth Bowen
Managing yourself: booking your own band

communities.name: Bunk Johnson: early playing, decline and 1940s comeback
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Nearly every segment is about one man, the New Orleans trumpeter Bunk Johnson, as remembered by 37 different interviewees, mostly in the Tulane (Hogan) collection with a few from Rutgers and the Smithsonian. The tellers place him at several stages. As a young player in Superior, Eagle and country bands (c. 1900-1920) he was a soft, sweet, good reader, sometimes compared with Bolden and Keppard. Then comes his wandering through Alexandria, Houston, Crowley, New Iberia and Kansas City, and his disappearance to a rice farm. The 1937-1945 rediscovery follows: collectors found him, bought him teeth and a horn, and brought him to New York and Chicago with George Lewis, Jim Robinson and Baby Dodds. Tellers agree on his sweet tone, his drinking and his generosity. They disagree about how good he was late in life, with some saying the false teeth cost him power, and about whether he was only a sit-in substitute or a real leader, and the rumor that he taught Louis Armstrong comes up as well. Several speakers, such as Emmanuel Sayles, only say they never played with him, and a few segments drift into tangents (Billie Pierce's trio, the Alexandria Red Book bands), but the subject stays the same.
threads: Bunk's soft, sweet style and reading in the early New Orleans bands
Travels and wandering: Alexandria, Houston, Kansas City, Chicago, New York
Drinking, lost teeth and decline before the revival
The 1937-45 rediscovery by collectors and the New York and Chicago band with George Lewis
Sitting in versus leading, and the rumor that he taught Louis Armstrong
Later-life character: generosity, no home, age at death

communities.name: Who played in the early New Orleans bands
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Musicians reconstruct band personnel from memory: who played in which early New Orleans jazz band, who replaced whom, and who was considered the best. The stories are set mostly between about 1900 and 1928, centered on New Orleans (Algiers, Franklin Street, Lincoln Park) with spillover to Chicago, Paris and California. The most recurring band is Buddy Petit's, remembered by drummers, guitarists and clarinettists as the most popular jazz band of the 1920s. Others include Buddy Bolden's band and its successor the Eagle Band under Frankie Dusen, the Superior and Imperial bands, the Young Olympia, and the French and White band. Tellers agree on a shared roster of names such as Big Eye Louis Nelson, Manuel Perez, Bunk Johnson and George Washington. They differ in how much they remember: some give full lineups, while others, such as Papa Jack Laine, know little. A few segments drift to related remembrances, such as New Orleans players in Chicago or Paris, or lists of earlier musicians heard.
threads: Buddy Petit's band and its personnel
Bolden's band and the Eagle Band lineup
Superior and Imperial bands, Big Eye Louis and Manuel Perez
Lists of early musicians remembered by name
New Orleans players who moved to Chicago or Paris

communities.name: Practice habits: how musicians keep their chops up
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection and from the 1930s through the pandemic year of 2020 describe whether and how they practice. Most samples are about daily routines: scales and arpeggios, Hanon, Czerny and Jackie McLean exercise books, long soft notes, working hard tunes slowly, and practicing in the head on buses and in hotels. Tellers disagree sharply about the value of practice. Buddy Tate, Hank Jones, Benny Waters and Wild Bill Davison say they practice as much as ever or more, and August Laurent warns that a player who stops loses fingers, lips and breath control. Buster Smith, Lou Donaldson, Harry Edison and J. C. Higginbotham say they never practiced scales or books, or hardly practiced at all, and instead stayed in shape by playing on the job. A smaller thread is set in 2020, when Victor Rendon, Ken Peplowski and Arthur Baron talk about staying ready or losing motivation while gigs were gone. A few samples have little to do with practice, such as Davison's nightly drive from New Jersey, Wallace Davenport's band changes, and Cozy Cole's session wrap-up. The core is old-school and modern players of horns, piano and drums talking about discipline and maintenance.
threads: Daily routines, scales and exercise books (Hanon, Czerny)
Never practiced: staying sharp by playing on the job
Keeping chops up with age and layoffs
Practice advice for students: slow tempos, small goals, long tones
Staying motivated and ready during the 2020 gig drought

communities.name: Breaking into New York vaudeville and Harlem stages
communities.parent_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows
communities.narrative: Musicians from several generations recall their first encounters with New York show business, usually through vaudeville acts, theaters and stage bookings. The earliest stories date from about 1901 to 1920: Roy Carew remembers New York winters before moving to New Orleans in 1904, Arnold Loyacano's band toured vaudeville as the Musical Rubes, and Garvin Bushell describes a failed act with Clarence Potter that ended in Hoboken. The 1920s stories centre on Harlem and the Keith circuit. Sonny Greer talks about the Wilbur Sweatman engagement with Duke Ellington, and Count Basie, pressed by interviewers, disputes how his debut as a vaudeville accompanist has been told. He says he accompanied acts in nightclubs, never in a theater pit, and that he replaced Fats Waller in Katie Crippen's traveling act. The latest stories are Marshall Royal's first Apollo crowds with Hampton in 1940-42 and Eddie Locke's 1954 arrival at the Apollo. The tellers agree that New York was the place to be tested, but their accounts differ in tone, from comic flops to prestigious Harlem bookings. The cluster is loose, joined more by setting and by the stage-act theme than by one shared event, and Basie's interview alone supplies several of the samples.
threads: Vaudeville acts and tours out of New York
Count Basie correcting the record on his early New York work
Harlem and the Apollo as a proving ground
Early arrivals in New York, 1900s to 1920s
Flops, breakups and bad bookings

bands: Ray Miller's Black and White Melody Boys

communities.name: Quitting the band over money and pay
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Musicians tell how they left or lost a band job because the money went wrong. In the 1930s and 1940s, mostly set in New York and on the road in Texas, Detroit and Washington, bands fold or men walk out over unpaid wages, short pay, deductions and loans refused. Doc Cheatham recalls McKinney's Cotton Pickers breaking up in Detroit when the bass player hid the music and demanded back pay. Eddie Barefield describes leaving the Cotton Pickers, who refused him his pay, and a brawl over a clarinet. Harry Fairconnetue and Lawrence Douglas Harris describe Texas and New Orleans bands that broke up as money ran short. Danny Barker quarrels over a Social Security deduction. Juan Tizol leaves Duke over a refused loan, and John Malachi leaves Jacquet over pay. The tellers agree that money was the usual reason. They differ on whether the leaver quit, was fired, or the whole band dissolved, as in Challis's account of Whiteman cutting the band and Ram Ramirez's account of the Rex Stewart band. The tellers are sidemen from both big-band and local territory bands.
threads: Bands breaking up over unpaid wages
Quitting over pay disputes and deductions
Leaving one leader for a better-paying job
Fired or downsized when bandleaders cut costs
Road hardships and transport troubles ending a band

communities.name: Giving notice: why musicians quit or were fired
communities.parent_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left
communities.narrative: Across 156 interviews, musicians tell the story of leaving a band, leader or employer: giving notice, quitting, being fired, or drifting away. The settings run from 1910s New Orleans spot bands and 1920s dance orchestras through the big bands of the 1930s and 40s, to the small groups and fusion-era bands of the 1960s and 70s. Ellington, Cab Calloway, Lionel Hampton, Miles Davis, Kid Ory and others recur as the band being left. The reasons given are fairly consistent: money and control over outside bookings (Arnett Cobb and Hampton), musical frustration or a repetitive repertoire, a leader's change of style, bad band behavior, a better job lined up, a wish for freedom or to lead one's own group, or personal and family pressure. Tellers differ on tone: some leave amicably and find a replacement at the leader's insistence, while others describe a humiliation, a dispute or a dismissal. The cluster is narrow in event but wide in setting, and a few samples (a photographer losing interest in a band, a record-label dispute) only loosely fit.
threads: Giving two weeks' notice and finding a replacement
Leaving a famous leader (Ellington, Calloway, Hampton, Miles) for money, freedom or a new job
Being fired or dismissed by a bandleader
Quitting over a humiliation, fight or band behavior
Leaving to start one's own band or to study
Early New Orleans bands breaking up and trombone replacements

communities.name: Life outside music: hobbies and pastimes
communities.parent_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant
communities.narrative: In these segments musicians are asked what they do when they are not playing, and they answer with hobbies, diversions and private pleasures. The commonest answers are fishing and hunting (Buster Smith, Theodore Leroy Bunn, Floyd Jones), photography (Rudy Van Gelder, Frank Foster, Jane Ira Bloom), painting and drawing (Marian McPartland, Yusef Lateef), reading and movies, and collecting, from Cliff Leeman's antiques and Civil War relics to Don Wolff's jazz films. Others mention cooking, sports, swimming, flying, Tai Chi, shopping, computers and bingo. The stories span roughly the 1940s to the 2020 lockdown, and they come from all four archives, mostly as a short stretch of an interview, often a sideline the interviewer prompts. The tellers differ in how much they have to say. Some are devoted to a pastime and say it helps their music, such as Piltzecker's flying and Bloom's Tai Chi. Others, like Slam Stewart and Sing Miller, say music is their only real interest. A few segments are loose: a bit of small talk about computers, or a lockdown inventory of reading, dog-walking and weight loss.
threads: Fishing and hunting as relaxation
Photography, painting and other creative sidelines
Reading, movies and film collecting
Collections and antiques
Sports, fitness and focus (swimming, Tai Chi, flying)
Music as the only real interest

communities.name: Hamilton College days: fraternities, tuition and what college gave them
communities.parent_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians and alumni, mostly interviewed for the Fillius Jazz Archive at Hamilton College, look back on their college years, chiefly the 1940s through the 1950s. The core of the cluster is Hamilton in Clinton, New York. Tellers recall why they chose it, what tuition cost (from $400 a semester around 1940 to about $1,100 with room and board in the 1950s), and the small classes and caring professors such as Dean Tolles and teacher Bobo Rudd. Fraternity life recurs: lax drinking rules, beer parties, house politics, and some later regret about what fraternities did to students. Many also describe what Hamilton gave them: how to think, independence, storytelling, and lasting alumni loyalty. Campus music runs through it as well, including the Catatonic Five, the WHC radio station and the music department. The edges drift to other colleges and schools, including Ole Miss, Hillsdale, Buffalo State and a television school, plus a few later-career echoes of a degree. Tellers agree that college was formative and affordable and that drinking was a constant. They differ by decade, with wartime and veteran classes sounding different from the 1950s ones.
threads: Choosing Hamilton and paying tuition
Fraternity life and drinking on campus
Professors, Dean Tolles and what Hamilton taught
Alumni loyalty and lasting friendships
Campus bands, radio and music at college
Other colleges and schools (Ole Miss, Hillsdale, Buffalo State, television school)

communities.name: Who played in the band: sidemen rosters
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: In these segments musicians reel off band personnel: who played which instrument, who sat in the sax or trumpet section, and who passed through before moving on. The tellers are mostly reed players, sidemen and bandleaders. They name Salvaggio's, Walter Barnes's, Doc Hyder's, Chick Webb's, Artie Shaw's and Ernie Fields's bands, and they recall teachers and band-mates such as Marshall Lawrence's trainees. The setting runs from the 1910s to the 1960s, with the strongest weight in the 1920s to 1940s, and moves between New Orleans, the Southwest and Mississippi, and New York big bands. The segments agree only on the form of the telling, a list of names attached to a band. Beyond that, little is shared: there is no common event or place, and a few, such as Purdie's favorite studio sidemen and Christophe's memory of David Jones and a Lutcher band photo, stray from one band's roster into general recollection of players.
threads: Band personnel lists by section (sax, trumpet)
Sidemen who passed through a leader's band
Early New Orleans and Louisiana band rosters
Big-band reed sections (Webb, Shaw, Ellington)
Players recalled by instrument and later career

communities.name: Life on the road shows: vaudeville, TOBA and tent shows
communities.parent_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows
communities.narrative: Musicians recall working in touring and staged shows rather than in clubs or dance bands: TOBA vaudeville, tent and medicine shows, minstrel and carnival companies, and theater revues. They are set mostly between the 1910s and the 1940s, with a peak in the 1920s. The places range from small Midwestern and mining towns to Chicago, Philadelphia and Harlem's big theaters, including the Apollo, Lafayette and Howard. Tellers describe how they joined a show (a sick pianist's replacement, a scout's offer, a show assembled in Boston), what they played or did on stage (pit bands, clowning, blackface comedy, dancing), and how little they were paid. The largest single block is Reb Spikes' detailed account of his own productions, such as Steppin' High, Rhythm Town and An American Rhapsody. Mary Lou Williams's account of the Buzzin' Harris show, and sidemen and dancers recalling Dr. Moon's medicine show, Rabbit's Foot Minstrels and the Whitman Sisters, add other angles. The samples agree on the theatrical, itinerant setting. They differ on whether the show is a hardscrabble circuit or a producer's stage project, and a few samples (Shuffle Along, theater house bands) drift toward big-city theater work generally.
threads: Joining and touring TOBA vaudeville and tent shows
Medicine shows, minstrels and carnivals
Reb Spikes's own stage productions and revues
Stars and acts on the theater circuit (Apollo, Whitman Sisters, Buck and Bubbles)
Pit bands and house bands in theaters
Clowning, comedy and dance as part of the band's act

communities.name: Blending, leading and balance in the ensemble
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians across many eras and idioms talk about how players fit together in a band: who leads, who stays under the lead, and how volume is shared out. The earliest tellers are New Orleans players such as De De Pierce, Emile Barnes and William Russell (relaying Jelly Roll Morton and Buddy Bolden). They describe how a band started a tune together, how the trumpet led and rested while others took choruses, and how bands played soft in the middle and loud on the last chorus. Later swing-era and modern players, including Snooky Young, Cootie Williams and Vic Dickenson (who has three near-identical segments), describe the lead trumpet or section lead setting the phrasing. In their account everyone else blends and balances beneath the lead, and only the lead should stand out slightly. Edmond Hall, Randy Sandke and Billy Bauer extend this to small-group roles, such as playing simple, sparse backing behind a lead (Kid Thomas) or obbligato versus unison heads, and to blending without crowding other players. The tellers agree that cooperation and restraint are the point. They differ in setting, from early New Orleans dance bands to big-band sections to bebop and Dixieland revival combos. The subject is loosely shared rather than a single story, and the period is mostly 1900 to 1938 only for the New Orleans material.
threads: Early New Orleans band dynamics: soft middle, loud last chorus
How the lead trumpet leads and the section blends beneath
Vic Dickenson on balancing volume in a section
Playing simple behind a sparse lead (Kid Thomas)
Front-line roles in Dixieland versus swing and bebop
Tone and not crowding other players

communities.name: Who controls the money: crooked leaders, managers and back pay
communities.parent_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, New York and the swing-era big bands tell stories about who handled the band's money and whether they were honest. Most are set between the 1910s and the 1960s, with a cluster in the 1920s-30s. Several describe leaders or managers who skimmed or withheld pay: Bob Lyons called crooked with money, Paul Whiteman collecting far more for Mildred Bailey than he paid her, and Buddy DeFranco's manager Lenny Lewis, who raised backers' money and kept half the take. Others show the corrective side: a band secretary keeping a job-and-pay record book to settle arguments, Marge arriving with her account books to collect months of back pay owed by Nick, and Bubbles certifying a check and opening his own bank account. Edgar Joseph and Eric Alexander offer the self-portrait, one boasting he pays his men before the job, the other admitting he is a poor businessman while difficult musicians get paid more. The tellers agree that money handling was a matter of character and trust, but the samples are anecdotes about different bands and not one shared event, so the subject holds together loosely.
threads: Crooked or underpaying bandleaders
Managers who raised money and took a cut
Collecting back pay and keeping the books
Paying the men on time
Bad business sense versus diva pay

communities.name: What swing is and how rhythm feels
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Most of the central samples are musicians trying to say what swing is, and most of them decline to give a neat definition. Rollins says he never had to learn it. Zeitlin and Dick Hyman say you can't define it, and Zeitlin says you point at examples. Foster ties it to tapping on two and four. Sidran calls it a heartbeat. LaLama and Chuck Israels describe it as togetherness and aligned accents. Marty Grosz says it can't be forced. Wilder and Bourgeau stress tempo and telling a band to slow down and swing. Tellers include jazz educators, drummers, pianists, bassists and singers, many interviewed by Monk Rowe at Hamilton. The story then spreads outward to rhythm feel in general. Latin and Afro-Cuban players explain clave, finding "one", and how swing eighths differ from straight Cuban articulation. Others trace the shift from swing to even eighth notes in pop and rock, and there are afterbeat and bebop rhythm remarks. A tap-dance subset, mostly Chuck Green on John Bubbles' cramp rolls and heel drops, and a few odd items (comic timing, a batanga rhythm) do not fit the swing-definition core. The period is mostly unspecified, and the samples that do give one range from the 1930s to 2006.
threads: Defining swing: feeling, heartbeat, two and four
What makes a band or rhythm section swing: tempo and accents
Clave, finding one, and Latin versus swing feel
Swing eighths giving way to straight eighths in pop and rock
Afterbeat and early rhythm sources (bebop, drum feels)
Tap dance rhythm: Bubbles' cramp rolls and heel drops

bands: Alex Torres and the Latin Kings

communities.name: U Street and Washington's Black nightlife strip
communities.parent_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene
communities.narrative: Most of the stories in this cluster walk through the clubs, theaters, hotels and hangouts of Washington, D.C.'s Black entertainment district, centered on U Street and the Howard Theatre area, from the mid-1930s through the 1950s. Jimmy Cobb, John Malachi, Clark Terry and Horn Shirley place venues such as the Crystal Caverns (Bohemian Caverns), the Jungle Inn, 2011, the Colonnade, Klors's rooming house, the 7th and T jam spot and Hot Dog Tim's half-smokes. Their accounts agree on the Caverns as the most prestigious room, on theater musicians jamming after hours, and on the pull of the street for working players. They differ in period and viewpoint: Malachi tells it as a 1936 job hunt that leads to a show band, Cobb as a 1940s after-hours circuit, and Shirley ranks the 1950s clubs by pay and prestige. A minority of segments apply the same kind of venue-by-venue tour to other cities, namely Kansas City's Vine Street and Eblon Theatre, Philadelphia and Atlantic City, Camden, and Indianapolis's Indiana Avenue. The tellers are mostly sidemen and bandleaders who passed through these strips as young working musicians. The D.C. core is solid, but the cluster loosens into a general theme of the Black entertainment street.
threads: Working the U Street clubs: Crystal Caverns, Jungle Inn, 2011
Howard Theatre area hangouts, jam spots and Tim's half-smokes
Ranking the D.C. rooms by pay and prestige
Kansas City's Vine Street hotels and the Eblon Theatre
Other cities' entertainment strips: Atlantic City, Philadelphia, Indianapolis

communities.name: Who pays the band, and haggling over wages
communities.parent_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1920s to the 1970s tell stories about the mechanics and politics of getting paid in a working band: who actually handed out the money, whether the leader, a manager, a road manager or a booking agency, and what happened when a sideman asked for more. Many are confrontations with leaders and managers. Joe Wilder gets a raise from Hampton and Joe Glaser and sees Millinder dodge paying for extra shows. Charlie Holmes is fired after speaking up to Irving Mills. The Lunceford band holds a sit-down over pay, and Sy Oliver resents his low wage. Others describe skimming and shorting. Snub Mosley's leader pockets a hotel raise, Desvigne cuts each man's pay, and agency bids such as MCA's undercut New Orleans leaders. A third strand is the other side of the table: managers and leaders explaining how they handled cash, expenses and fair splits (Mike Vax, Emile Barnes, Mark Soskin, Maxine Sullivan on her contract). The tellers are mostly big-band and New Orleans sidemen, with a few leaders and one singer. They agree that pay was opaque and often unfair, but differ on whether to push back or stay quiet. The specific incidents are tied to different bands and decades, so the common thread is the pay relationship rather than any one event.
threads: Asking the leader or manager for a raise
Band-wide confrontations over pay
Skimming, shorting and cheating on extras
Who actually handled the money: managers, road managers, agencies
Leaders and managers on fair splits and paying sidemen
Contracts, salary and withheld expenses

communities.name: What the job paid: wages, scale and band salaries
communities.parent_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope
communities.narrative: Musicians across the 1910s to 1960s, with a few later outliers, recall what they were actually paid and how that compared with others. Typical figures are $10 a night on Lunceford one-nighters, $50 to $75 a week for sidemen, and $125 to $150 for the best-paid bands. Basie, Ellington and Cab Calloway are repeatedly named as top payers, and Barnet is said to have outpaid Lunceford. Many tellers compare one leader or band's pay against another's. Others describe how the money was structured: union scale, percentage door deals, tips, guaranteed salaries versus pay only when the band worked, and per-chart or per-record fees. Tellers also describe leaders earning only slightly more than sidemen, raises negotiated by threat or walkout, and cheap living costs set against modest pay. Big-band sidemen, New Orleans and Kansas City club players, and later bebop-era and 1960s players all tell it, with New York, Chicago and New Orleans as the usual settings. The tellers agree that pay was low and uneven. They differ on which bands were generous and whether the work was worth it. The cluster is broad, so some segments only mention money in passing.
threads: Sideman weekly wages in the big bands
Which leaders paid best: Basie, Ellington, Cab, Barnet
Union scale, percentage deals and tips
Raises, bargaining and walking out over pay
Pay for charts, records and one-off jobs
Cheap living costs set against low pay

communities.name: Listing the bands I played in
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: New Orleans musicians, mostly interviewed for Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, answer the question of which bands they played in by reciting names and lineups. The stories are set between about 1900 and the 1930s, with most from the 1910s and 1920s. They cluster around the Tuxedo and Young Tuxedo bands, the Golden Rule band that became the Young Tuxedo, Imperial, Excelsior, Robichaux and Sam Morgan's bands, and Papa Celestin, Kid Rena and Foster Lewis and Dude's band. Tellers such as Joe Watkins, Cie Frazier, Ricard Alexis, Alphonse Picou and Emile Barnes trace their first band and the personnel who swapped in and out. A few segments are about identifying members in photographs, for instance the Tuxedo band of 1910 or the WPA band at the Italian Hall, and the interviewer sometimes supplies the names. The tellers agree on the band-hopping pattern but share no one event, venue or period, so this is a loose cluster of band-roster recollections rather than a single story.
threads: First band and how it was formed
Tuxedo and Young Tuxedo band lineups
Golden Rule band becoming the Young Tuxedo
Rosters of rival bands like Imperial, Excelsior and Robichaux
Identifying band members from photographs
WPA and police bands of the 1930s

communities.name: Who was in the band: recalling personnel lineups
communities.parent_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel
communities.narrative: Across hundreds of interviews, musicians are asked to name who played in a particular band, and they answer by reciting lineups: who was on trumpet, trombone, clarinet, piano, bass and drums, who replaced whom, and which brothers or relatives were in the group. The largest share is set in New Orleans in the 1910s to 1930s and concerns bands such as Sam Morgan's, Jack Carey's, Kid Rena's, Sidney Desvigne's, the Tuxedo and Eureka brass bands, and smaller local groups. A smaller share comes from New York, Chicago and big-band settings, including Cab Calloway, Chick Webb, Rex Stewart, the Cotton Club band, Lionel Hampton and Horace Henderson's Swingland revue. Many of these exchanges are prompted by the interviewer or by looking at band photographs, so the tellers piece the roster together from memory and sometimes admit they cannot recall everyone. They agree that a band is defined by its members, but they differ in how much detail they remember and in whether they treat the band as a steady unit or a shifting pool of players. A few samples drift to related topics such as photographs, the King of Siam's band, or a recording session, but these still turn on who the players were.
threads: New Orleans dance and brass band rosters (Sam Morgan, Jack Carey, Tuxedo, Eureka)
Identifying players in band photographs
Big-band personnel in New York and Chicago (Calloway, Webb, Cotton Club, Henderson)
Who replaced whom: genealogy of band membership
Naming the bands a musician played with over a career
Personnel on recording sessions and later touring bands

communities.name: Working the riverboats with Fate Marable and the Streckfus Line
communities.parent_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable
communities.narrative: These are stories of playing, or hearing, bands on Mississippi River excursion steamers, above all the Streckfus Line boats (Capitol, St. Paul, J.S., Sidney) and Fate Marable's band, in the 1910s through early 1930s. They are set mainly in St. Louis and New Orleans, with stops up and down the river at Rock Island, Memphis, Cincinnati and Peoria. Sidemen such as Pops Foster, Emmanuel Sayles, Louis Nelson, Zutty Singleton and Joe Darensbourg recall the lineups, the pay (about $25 a week plus board), the sleeping quarters and the steam calliope played before departure. They also describe the discipline of Marable's strict reading band with stock arrangements. Other bands tied to the boats, such as those of Sidney Desvigne, Charlie Creath, Dewey Jackson and Piron, come up as rivals or successors. Some tellers never worked the boats and know them only as listeners or from hearsay. A few segments drift off the subject, including a modern jazz cruise, a Lake Charles resort band and Vic Dickenson's 1931 Missouri River boat trip.
threads: Fate Marable's band: lineups, discipline and alumni
Streckfus steamers Capitol, St. Paul and J.S.: routes, crowds and rival bands
Steam calliope and hearing the boats from the levee
Boat life: pay, board, sleeping and reading stock arrangements
Desvigne, Creath, Dewey Jackson and Piron bands on the river
Other river and excursion boat gigs outside the Streckfus orbit

communities.name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline
communities.parent_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans and beyond tell stories about Joe "King" Oliver, from his youth as a brass-band cornetist to his last years. Early accounts, mostly from New Orleans people such as Doc Souchon, Eddie Dawson, and Mrs. McCullum (who insists her husband George taught him), place him in the 1900s-1910s. He is a teenager chewing tar, a riverfront worker and butler who bought his first cornet, and a player learning to read dance music before he left for Chicago. Players who worked with him in the 1920s, including Bob Shoffner, Darnell Howard, Louis Armstrong, Sippie Wallace, and Muggsy Spanier, remember a gentle, joking, businesslike leader with a huge appetite. They also remember the Lincoln Gardens band with the Doddses and Armstrong, and the rift among New Orleans musicians in Chicago. Later tellers, including Leonard Phillips (who gives ten segments), Vic Dickenson, Joe Thomas, Buddy Tate, and Bud Freeman, describe his decline in the 1930s. The details are bad teeth, a cataract, stomach trouble, selling clams in Savannah, and a poolroom job. Many tellers only heard him or knew him from records, so the stories vary a great deal in depth and firsthand knowledge.
threads: Oliver's New Orleans youth, teachers and first cornet
Leaving for Chicago and the Lincoln Gardens band with Armstrong
Working for Oliver: humor, appetite, easy leadership
Physical quirks: the bulging eye, teeth, cataract, stomach
Decline and last sightings in the 1930s (Savannah, Nashville)
Musicians who only heard him or knew him from records

communities.name: Teachers' lessons on keeping time
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Across nearly twenty interviews, musicians recall how a teacher or mentor taught them to feel and keep time. The best-known version is the New Orleans and Bechet lineage. Louis Cottrell Jr. and Ernie Cagnolatti describe Tio's and Metoyer's French-method habit of tapping the foot, like an imaginary needle, until the beat is felt internally. Bob Wilber and Robert Lewis recall Sidney Bechet's 1940s lessons on variations, scales and swing, with the advice to carry your own rhythm section in your head. Drummers such as Louie Bellson recall Big Sid Catlett and Jo Jones on brushes and never losing "one", and Murray Spivack on rudiments and the practice pad. Jimmy Maxwell tells of Cootie Williams's foot-marching cure, and Sam Wooding tells of Will Marion Cook teaching him to retard for a singer. Later teachers such as Alan Broadbent and Sherrie Maricle pass the idea on, using slowed-down recordings and push/pull drum studies. The tellers agree that time is a feeling in the body, not an intellectual exercise. They differ in method: foot-tapping, counting systems, rudiments, listening to records. The cluster is loosely held together, since a few samples are about technique or conducting rather than time.
threads: Foot-tapping to internalize time (Tio, Metoyer, Cootie Williams)
Sidney Bechet's lessons on swing and rhythm
Drum teachers: brushes, rudiments, never losing one
Teaching the feeling of time with recordings and push/pull
Retarding and following a singer

communities.name: Saxophonists remembered: alto, tenor and baritone players
communities.parent_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers brief asides in which musicians talk about individual saxophonists they worked with, heard or hired, mostly alto, but also tenor and baritone. The stories run from the 1920s-30s to about 1963 and are set in New Orleans, Kansas City, Lake Charles, New York and California. Tellers include New Orleans players (Kid Thomas Valentine, Clarence Vincent, Don Albert, Red Tyler, Ernie Fields, Tim Kelly) and bandleaders and sidemen from elsewhere (Count Basie, Cootie Williams, JJ Johnson, Jimmy Cobb, George Handy). Most are short portraits of one player: Joe Harris, Louis Warnick, Leonard Fields, Leroy Cooper, Earl Bostic, Cecil Payne, Boyd Raeburn. They agree on little beyond the instrument. Some praise a player's tone or versatility, such as Cottrell's tenor or Cooper's willingness to play any dance music. Others note neglect (Fields never hired by the big bands) or criticize (Raeburn as a poor saxophonist). There is no single event or shared narrative, only the recurring habit of sizing up a saxophonist by style, section role and employers.
threads: Portraits of individual New Orleans alto saxophonists and the bands they worked with
Tenor and baritone players: tone, section roles and switching instruments
Rhythm and blues saxophonists such as Earl Bostic, Leroy Cooper and Earl Batiste
Overlooked or criticized players: Leonard Fields, Boyd Raeburn
Bandleaders on their saxophone sections: Basie, Cootie Williams, Don Albert

communities.name: Remembering Sidney Bechet: boy, bandmate, exile in France
communities.parent_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds tell stories about one man, the clarinetist and soprano saxophonist Sidney Bechet. Almost every segment is tagged to him, and most are character portraits. The earliest tellers are New Orleans contemporaries, such as Laurent, Dawson, Barnes, Manetta and Glass. They remember him as a boy with a cheap flute or wired-up clarinet, asleep on the Smoky Mary to the Milneburg picnics, and cutting heads with other clarinetists. A second group worked with him in the 1920s to 1950s: Noble Sissle's band in Paris, Blue Note dates, Jimmy Ryan's and the 1958 Brussels Fair. They describe a daring and dominant player. Some call him reserved, selfish or untrustworthy, while others call him agreeable and a friend. A third strand covers his years in France, with his villa, his statue, his weapon-laden Lincoln and his demanding letters. A last strand is admirers who heard his records or saw him play, including Buster Smith, Juan Tizol and Joe Segal. The tellers agree on his great musicianship and differ on his temperament.
threads: Bechet as a boy in New Orleans: flute, clarinet, Milneburg picnics, cutting contests
Playing for and with him: Sissle's band in Paris, Jimmy Ryan's quartet, Blue Note dates, the Brussels Fair
His temperament: daring and generous to some, selfish, reserved and quarrelsome to others
Life as an exile in France: villa, car, letters and fame
Hearing and idolizing Bechet on records and in person

communities.name: Saxophonists they admired and how they sounded
communities.parent_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection talk about the saxophone players they heard, admired or learned from, and rate them by tone, style and influence. The talk runs from 1920s New Orleans altoists such as John Handy, Son Johnson and Oliver Alcorn, through the Basie and Lunceford alto and tenor sections (Earle Warren, Tab Smith, Willie Smith, Hilton Jefferson against Hodges and Carter), to the Texas and Southwest honking tenor sound (Illinois Jacquet, Arnett Cobb, Sam Taylor, King Curtis). It continues into modern players: Woody Herman on his section men, Frank Tiberi, Gregory Herbert, Nick Brignola and Serge Chaloff, Jackie McLean on other altoists, and Liebman on Wayne Shorter. Tellers mostly agree that the great saxophonists had a distinctive tone and kept their own style rather than copying others, though they differ on who set the model, such as David Jones teaching New York players legato or Jacquet starting honking. The accounts are brief opinionated comparisons, not extended narratives, and they cover about 1920 to the 1990s. Because the cluster is a list of players rather than one event, it holds together as a subject (judging saxophonists) but not as a single story.
threads: Early New Orleans alto and sax players
Big-band sax sections: Basie, Lunceford, Herman
Texas and Southwest honking tenor sound
Baritone and tenor giants in the Herman Herds
Alto rivalries and Hodges/Carter comparisons
Staying your own player versus copying influences

communities.name: Coleman Hawkins: the father of the tenor
communities.parent_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists
communities.narrative: Musicians from every generation tell stories about Coleman Hawkins, the man and the model. Older players such as Garvin Bushell, Russell Procope, Benny Carter and Artie Shaw recall hearing and sitting beside him in the Fletcher Henderson band in the 1920s and 30s. Many say his sound and chord sense set him apart, and that his Stampede solo eclipsed other tenor players. Others tell of the 1939 return from Europe and "Body and Soul", with Walter P. Thomas, Teddy Wilson and Howard McGhee agreeing it answered those who had written him off. Peers and younger players, including Big Nick Nicholas, Bud Freeman, Kenny Burrell, Sonny Rollins and Branford Marsalis, describe his personality: private, argumentative, money-minded, stylish with his cars and clothes, and still changing late in life. They broadly agree he made the tenor saxophone respectable and is the father of tenor soloists. They differ on the details, such as Benny Carter's influence on him, his standing against Lester Young and Chu Berry, and any rivalry in Europe. A few samples drift to other saxophonists or unrelated topics, but most circle him.
threads: Hearing Hawkins with Fletcher Henderson and the Stampede solo
The 1939 return from Europe and 'Body and Soul'
Hawkins the person: loner, argumentative, stylish, generous with advice
Idol and teacher for later tenor players
Hawkins among peers: Benny Carter, Chu Berry, Ben Webster, Lester Young
Playing and sitting in with him on 52nd Street and in sessions

communities.name: Wrestling with the slide trombone
communities.parent_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers musicians talking about the trombone as an instrument: how it is played, what makes it hard, and how they came to it. The strongest thread is technique. Vic Dickenson says the slide can bend between positions like a voice or cello and that he never had a lesson, Oscar "Chicken" Henry explains alternate positions and wrist vibrato, and Trummy Young says he is still learning because a slide has no markings. Players also describe Jack Teagarden as a flexible trombonist who made his own mouthpieces and mutes. A second thread is physical and personal. Slide Hampton and Al Wynn both played left-handed, and Wynn took months to turn the horn around in 1920s South Bend. Maxine Sullivan, a singer, tells the story of taking up valve trombone in the 1950s, being pushed onto the bandstand, and being told by a critic to stick to singing. Other tellers cover why the trombone suited Delfeayo Marsalis's role in a New Orleans band, JJ Johnson's trombonium recordings, and the shortage of trombonists. The stories span roughly the 1920s to the 1990s and come from many collections. A few samples, such as Ba Ba Ridgley on vamping bass figures, only loosely fit.
threads: Slide technique: positions, quarter tones, wrist vibrato
Playing left-handed and turning the horn around
Maxine Sullivan taking up valve trombone and the 'stick to singing' review
Teagarden and others as trombone innovators and tinkerers
Why the trombone: personality, difficulty, and scarcity of players

communities.name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band
communities.parent_name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans and the Mississippi coast remember Chris Kelly, the trumpeter who led the city's most famous blues dance band in the 1910s and 1920s. Nearly everyone calls him the blues king: no one played the blues like him, using a plunger, derby or silver mute and sometimes drawing a crowd from a dance-hall window. The tellers are mostly sidemen and rivals from Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, including Kid Howard, Jim Robinson, Ike Robinson, John Casimir, Louis Gallaud and George Lewis. They list his changing personnel, mostly a six- or seven-piece band with no piano and no written arrangements, and the halls he played, such as the Bulls Club, Economy Hall and Turtle Back Hall. They also recall his habits: he was a poor dresser, did not read music, and double-booked jobs and sent substitutes (Howard and Peter LaCaze among them). He is compared with Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and Kid Rena, and some tellers date his death to the 1920s and others to 1947. Accounts differ on his band's lineup and on how he ranked against his rivals, but they agree on his blues playing and his hold on the local dance circuit.
threads: Kelly's plunger-muted blues trumpet and tunes
Band personnel and instrumentation over the years
Dance-hall jobs: Bulls Club, Economy Hall, Turtle Back Hall, Mississippi towns
Double-booking and substitutes, including Kid Howard taking over jobs
Rivalry and comparison with Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and Kid Rena
His appearance, character and death

communities.name: Picking up the clarinet and doubling on other instruments
communities.parent_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear
communities.narrative: Musicians describe how they came to the clarinet, usually as a second or third instrument, and how they spread across several horns to stay employable. Most stories are set from the 1900s to the 1950s, with a few from the late 1960s and one from 2025. They come mostly from New Orleans players (Tulane) and from Hamilton, Rutgers and Smithsonian interviews. Several tellers were pushed into it by a mentor or bandleader: Johnny Dodds urged Manetta, Joseph Rene urged a young George Lewis, Gunable insisted on it for McRae, and Lorenzo Tio Jr. lent Cottrell a C clarinet. Others took it up out of practical need, as Darnell Howard did after finding Bechet's saxophone in pawn, or because it opened work, as with Altman's folk and Dixieland gigs. McRae calls it the natural double for any reed man. Tellers agree that clarinet and saxophone move together, but they differ on the route. Some began on drums, flute or violin, while Laws and Jordan used clarinet to branch into flute or high-note saxophone work. A few segments only touch the theme loosely (Nicholas's Cairo symphony work, Bennett's return to classical lessons), so the cluster is a clear majority rather than a single tight story.
threads: Urged onto clarinet by a mentor or teacher
Doubling as a working necessity for reed players
Moving between clarinet, saxophones, flute and other horns
Starting on another instrument (drums, violin, flute) first
Formal clarinet study and classical technique

communities.name: Growing old and still playing: Eubie Blake and the ageless musician
communities.parent_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians
communities.narrative: In these stories, musicians talk about getting old and what music does for the body and spirit. Most are told in the 1970s and 1980s by veterans in their seventies, such as Sippie Wallace, Sammy Price and Doc Cheatham. A few are told by younger players in the 2000s and 2020. The tellers agree that playing keeps you young. Doc Cheatham says he will play until he cannot play another note, and Sippie Wallace says being active keeps her feeling sixteen at eighty. Chembo Corniel cites Candido, Lionel Hampton and Clark Terry as proof that music heals. Eubie Blake, still practicing at 96 with undimmed hands, is the shared example, named by several different interviewees. They differ in tone. Some are playful about arthritis, canes and false teeth, some reflect on death and enjoying each day (Phil Woods), and others note that age does limit playing for most people (Howard Scott). A few segments drift toward other subjects: Javon Jackson on keeping a daily schedule and exercise during a delayed recording project, and Pops Smith's long trumpet career in the Fletcher Henderson and Cab Calloway bands, which ends with his playing well into his eighties.
threads: Music as the fountain of youth
Eubie Blake still playing in his nineties
Never retiring: playing until the last note
Arthritis, canes, and joking about age
Facing mortality and enjoying each day
Older players who kept their ability, like Pops Smith

communities.name: Brawls, pistols and punch-ups on the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, Chicago, New York and the touring circuit tell anecdotes of violence breaking out around the music: dance-hall brawls, second-line fights, punches thrown at clubs and ballrooms, and guns drawn or carried. The stories run from the Buddy Bolden era (a Labor Day fight at Globe Hall) through the 1930s-50s (Golden Gate Ballroom, the Village Vanguard, Smalls Paradise, the Plantation), with most set in the 1940s. Tellers usually recount a specific incident with named people: a bandleader facing down a gunman, a bandmate who fights anyone who smiles at his girl, a tap star pulling a gold pistol on a drunk, a musician fired after an argument. The tone is often wry or admiring rather than grave, and several incidents end in reconciliation or comic aftermath, such as the club owner thanking the man who hit his brother-in-law. A few stories drift to adjacent troubles (a bandleader's breakdown in the snow, a slap over Sun Ra's music). Tellers are sidemen, bandleaders and entertainers across all four collections.
threads: Club and ballroom fights, owners and aftermath
Guns drawn or carried by musicians and stars
Bandmates with violent tempers and jealous quarrels
Funeral second-line and dance-hall brawls in New Orleans
Run-ins with police and cops paid off
Fired or slapped over personal and musical disputes

communities.name: Making hit records in the studio, Benson's Breezin' to Give Me the Night
communities.parent_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"
communities.narrative: The clearest core of this small cluster is George Benson's account of making his late-1970s crossover records, set mostly between 1976 and 1980 in Los Angeles studios. He describes Breezin' as a cheap, quickly made album (This Masquerade in one take, Bobby Womack's lick, Gabor Szabo's simple tune, Claus Ogerman's strings, Tommy LiPuma producing), then working with Donny Hathaway and Harvey Mason on The World Is a Ghetto, and finally Quincy Jones assembling an A team for Give Me the Night with Bruce Swedien and Rod Temperton, with Quincy persuading executives on release strategy. Around that core sit scattered recording-session stories from other musicians, such as Carla Bley's Dinner Music with Stuff, Ramsey Lewis recording Sun Goddess with Earth, Wind and Fire, McCoy Tyner adding harpsichord and celeste on Trident, and Marilyn Crispell's duo album on detuned pianos. What they share is only that a particular record was made in the studio and how: unusual instrumentation, producers, takes and overdubs. Beyond Benson, the tellers do not agree on a single story; the peripheral segments (Dick Hyman's MGM harpsichord sound, Johnny Mandel faking bad Japanese jazz records) are loosely related at best. The cluster is best read as a Benson studio-hit story surrounded by miscellaneous album-making anecdotes.
threads: Breezin': one-take This Masquerade, Szabo's tune, Ogerman strings and the low budget
Quincy Jones and Give Me the Night: Ivan Lins songs, Swedien, Temperton lyrics, release strategy
Cutting tracks live in one take with Donny Hathaway and Harvey Mason
Finding the tempo and groove on stage, as with On Broadway at the Roxy
Other musicians' album sessions: Stuff, Earth Wind and Fire, harpsichord and celeste, detuned pianos
Studio sound tricks and imitation, from harpsichord-piano records to faked Japanese jazz

communities.name: Movie stars in the Los Angeles clubs
communities.parent_name: Going west: moving to and working in California
communities.narrative: Musicians recall Los Angeles and Hollywood nightlife from about 1917 to the late 1940s, and the celebrities who turned up in it. Reb Spikes describes playing Baron Long's Tavern in Watts for Rudolph Valentino's dance act with Hollywood stars in the audience. Jimmy Rowles remembers Stokowski and many actors at the Capri around 1941, and Teddy Edwards names Ava Gardner, Orson Welles and Sonny Tufts in the clubs in 1945-46. Red Norvo and Marshall Royal tell of Al Rinker and Bing Crosby's early Los Angeles days, from the theater and speakeasy scene to after-hours crowds at the Apex. Bob Coquille and Eddie Alley connect the same idea to photographs of celebrities at the Famous Door and Purcell's in San Francisco's North Beach and a New Orleans venue. The tellers agree that film people were a regular part of the audience, but the stories differ in decade and city, and several are really about one person, mainly Crosby, rather than about the stars as a crowd.
threads: Hollywood stars in the club audience
Bing Crosby and Al Rinker's early Los Angeles days
Watts and Los Angeles nightspots of the 1920s-30s
Photos of celebrities at clubs in San Francisco and New Orleans
Young musicians and film stars on the 1940s scene

communities.name: Favorite recordings and desert-island records
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: In these segments musicians, and a few critics and producers such as Nat Hentoff and Delfeayo Marsalis, are asked to pick their own favorite records. The prompt is usually an interviewer's standard question: which of your albums are you proudest of, which would you take to a desert island, which are your best recent sessions. Most tellers list titles and sidemen in a quick run. Kenny Barron, Phil Woods, Jack DeJohnette, Buddy Tate, Sammy Price and Elvin Jones name their own albums and say why they like particular dates. Hentoff, Vince Lateano, Vincent Pelote and Milt Fillius name records by others, often Ellington (Ellington at Fargo comes up repeatedly), Basie, Armstrong, Coltrane and Monk. The tellers mostly agree that the favorite is the recent one or the next one, as Joe Williams and Bob Magnusson put it, and that the choice rests on the playing partners or the writing. They differ on whether they listen to their own records at all: Joe Temperley rarely does. The stories span the 1930s to the early 2000s, and the interviews come from all four archives, with Hamilton and the Smithsonian the largest contributors. The cluster is large and loosely edged, so a few segments drift into liner notes, a session anecdote or a record-listening scene.
threads: Favorite albums of their own as leaders and sidemen
Desert-island records and companions
Best recent work and the next record
Duo, trio and small-group dates chosen for the partners
Favorites by other artists: Ellington, Basie, Bechet, Coltrane
Liner notes, producing and listening back to old records

communities.name: Jingles and the New York studio grind
communities.parent_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life
communities.narrative: Jazz musicians in New York, and later Los Angeles, tell how commercial studio work, above all advertising jingles, paid their bills from the 1950s into the 1980s. The stories are set in the busy 1960s and 70s, when a first-call player could do several record dates, a Broadway show and a network or Tonight Show staff job in a single day. Contractors booked sessions by late-night phone calls or the Radio Registry. Agencies such as BBDO supplied the products: Pepsi, Ivory Soap, Doublemint, Halo Shampoo, Coca-Cola, Rice-a-Roni. The tellers agree that the money was very good, especially once union scale, double scale and residual checks every 13 weeks are counted. They differ on what it did to them. Burrell, Watts and Lateef felt it taught craft but stalled their growth as artists, so they stepped away. Bernhardt, Leonhart and Pizzarelli treated it as steady, respectable work that supported a family. Hamilton and Spinozza built their own jingle businesses. Tellers are mostly guitarists, bassists, horn players, arrangers and singers who were hired as reliable session players. A few samples, such as Muzak production and sidemen's hardships, drift toward the wider commercial music economy.
threads: Writing and scoring jingles: Hamilton, Spinozza, Torkanowsky and the ad agencies
Getting the calls: contractors, referrals, Radio Registry and staying on lists
Money: union scale, double scale, residuals and pensions
A typical studio day: stacked dates, Broadway shows and network staff jobs
Craft versus soul: choosing or leaving studio work to play real jazz
Specific campaigns and sessions: Pepsi, Ivory Soap, Doublemint, Coca-Cola, Halo

communities.name: Bad men, vice and the Battlefield district
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the rough, vice-ridden side of early New Orleans, above all the Battlefield neighborhood around Franklin, Rampart, Gravier and Basin Streets, set mostly between 1900 and the 1920s. Eddie Dawson, who lived there for decades, anchors the cluster. He tells of the Robert Charles riot, policemen beaten and disarmed by dice players, the two red-light districts, and notorious figures such as Black Benny, Aaron Harris, Sawadick and violent women like Mary Jack the Bear. Charlie Love, Lemon Nash and Lee Collins add the district's gangs, shootings, gamblers, tough fish fries and saloons such as the Nancy Hanks and the Big 25, along with the old Chinatown and opium. A smaller strand moves beyond New Orleans to pimps, prostitution and why women went for musicians. It includes Tex Stephens on Iceberg Slim in Washington, Zutty Singleton on musicians who were also pimps, and Will Shade on violence on Beale Street in Memphis. The tellers agree the district was dangerous and colorful. They differ in vantage point: neighborhood residents describe local characters and episodes, while others talk about the sex trade in general terms.
threads: Battlefield neighborhood and its tough characters
Dice games, police and the Robert Charles riot
Red-light districts, saloons and the Big 25
Pimps, prostitution and musicians' appeal to women
Chinatown, opium and gang violence
Comparable vice on Beale Street and elsewhere

communities.name: Going west: musicians in Los Angeles and California
communities.parent_name: Going west: moving to and working in California
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell about coming to, working in, or leaving California, mostly Los Angeles, with San Francisco and the Bay Area as a secondary pole. The earliest stories come from the 1910s and 1920s, when Kid Ory's New Orleans men migrated west. They are followed by the Central Avenue scene of the late 1920s to 1940s: the Dunbar Hotel, Apex Club, Club Alabam, Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club, and bandleaders Curtis Mosby and Les Hite. Later tellers describe postwar and 1950s moves: West Coast jazz clubs like the Haig and Hillcrest, studio and string-chart work, and recording dates. The 1960s and 1970s bring television jobs, with the Tonight Show and Merv Griffin pulling New York players out to Hollywood and Burbank. Tellers agree that the weather, the work and the musical community drew them; they differ on whether they stayed, with Ory preferring the Bay Area to smoggy LA, Teddy Edwards finding LA collapsed in 1946, and Zutty Singleton's wife hating the move. The shared thread is the California move, but the samples vary widely in era and subject, from New Orleans migrants to Latin bands, big-band leaders and TV-era studio players.
threads: New Orleans musicians migrating west with Kid Ory, 1910s-20s
Central Avenue clubs and bandleaders: Dunbar, Apex, Club Alabam, Curtis Mosby
Moving from New York to LA for TV and studio work (Tonight Show, Merv Griffin)
1940s-50s West Coast jazz scene and touring bands playing Los Angeles
Weather, homesickness and whether to stay in California

communities.name: Alfred Lion, Frank Wolff and Blue Note
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians and friends of the label tell how Blue Note Records was run and who was around it. Lorraine Gordon recalls meeting Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff at Jimmy Ryan's on 52nd Street in the early 1940s. She describes Lion fleeing Germany with a large record collection, the Lexington Avenue office, and the First Avenue apartment full of records. She also describes Wolff keeping the label going while Lion was in the Army, and Ike Quebec acting as Blue Note's guide into Black jazz circles. Lou Donaldson tells of Lion asking at Minton's whether he could play like Parker, and of bringing Blue Mitchell and Horace Silver to the label. Rudy Van Gelder, Tiny Grimes, Wilbur Ware and Art Hodes add how Lion found his engineer, how sessions were arranged, and the Village aficionado scene. The tellers agree that Lion was the central figure, and their accounts range from the 1940s to 1957. One sample, Machito on the Roost label's Cubop City session, is about a different label and is off-topic.
threads: Lorraine Gordon on Lion, Wolff and the early Blue Note offices
Ike Quebec as Blue Note's guide and session friend
Lion recruiting players for Blue Note (Donaldson, Silver, Mitchell)
How Lion found Rudy Van Gelder
Blue Note recording dates in the 1940s and 50s
Lion and Wolff in the Village aficionado scene

communities.name: Who really wrote Duke's hits? Mood Indigo and credit
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians from Ellington's circle and beyond argue over who actually composed Duke Ellington's famous tunes, above all "Mood Indigo" and "Sophisticated Lady". Barney Bigard says he gave Duke the second half of "Mood Indigo" and laughs at Duke's story of writing it in fifteen minutes while his mother made breakfast. New Orleans voices, including Louis Tio, Hilda Taylor and Zutty Singleton, trace the tune back to Lorenzo and Papa Tio, who taught Bigard. Others, including Marshall Royal, Russell Procope, Milt Hinton and Cootie Williams, describe Duke as a hustler who borrowed ideas from his sidemen and put his name on their work. They also note that Irving Mills's name appears on much of the early music. Red Callender and Hinton extend the question to "Night Train" and "Cottontail". The tellers agree that credit was murky and that Duke did compose good numbers. They differ on whether the theft was real or fair. The stories are set mainly in the 1920s to 1950s and come mostly from Rutgers interviews. One outlier, Alberta Hunter on Porter Granger, shares only the theme of uncredited songwriters.
threads: Bigard's claim on Mood Indigo
The Tio family as the source of the tune
Sophisticated Lady and the sidemen who shaped it
Irving Mills's name on Duke's music
Night Train, Cottontail and other disputed credits
Duke as a hustler borrowing from his band

communities.name: Who was the best trumpeter: Creath, Perez, Oliver and Keppard
communities.parent_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds talk about the trumpeters and cornetists they heard coming up, and about who had the best tone. The stories fall into two camps. In the New Orleans camp, Manny Gabriel, Ray Lopez, Isidore Barbarin and Joe Darensbourg weigh Manuel Perez, King Oliver, Freddie Keppard, Kid Rena and Kid Thomas against each other. Barbarin, pressed to pick, declines and says both were good. In the St. Louis camp, Clark Terry, Ed Allen, Bob Shoffner and Joe Thomas praise Charlie Creath, the 'King of Cornet', for his individual tone, his blues playing and his sharp dress. Creath worked the riverboats and led bands around St. Louis. Terry also traces a St. Louis trumpet tradition from Creath through Joe Gustave's students, who used Heim mouthpieces. Zutty Singleton adds a qualification: Creath's band played northern stock arrangements rather than New Orleans style, though he was known as a soulful blues player. A few outliers, such as Armand Hug on cornet players and Pierre Merlin on his influences, fit only loosely. Most stories are set between the 1910s and the early 1940s. Tellers agree that tone and blues feeling were what set trumpeters apart, and they disagree about whom to rank first.
threads: Charlie Creath as St. Louis's King of Cornet
The St. Louis trumpet sound and Heim mouthpieces
Comparing Perez, Oliver, Keppard and Kid Rena
Early trumpet players musicians heard coming up
Declining to name the best player
Creath's band: northern stock arrangements and riverboat work

communities.name: Remembering King Oliver: tone, mutes and Louis
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, Chicago and elsewhere recall hearing and playing around Joe "King" Oliver, mostly in the 1900s to early 1920s. The stories center on his sound: a big, dirty, growling tone worked with mutes, long wind, and a blues break that caught younger players. Several tell how he drew crowds away from rival bands at picnics and street corners in New Orleans, including the dozens-style insults traded with a neighboring player. Others follow him to Chicago, where Ed Garland sent for him to open the Royal Garden, and to the 1923 band with two cornets, where he signalled Louis Armstrong's breaks by fingering the valves. Tellers often compare Oliver with Armstrong and say Louis learned from him. They differ in emphasis: Alberta Hunter stresses his soft playing and his one eye, Fred Moore tells of the brick and the pistol at rehearsals, and William Russell passes on Johnny Dodds's theory of why the band broke up. The tellers are trumpeters, clarinetists, bandmates and a singer, plus collectors such as Al Rose and Russell.
threads: Oliver's tone, mutes and long wind
Drawing crowds and rivalry in New Orleans
Chicago: Royal Garden and the 1923 band
Oliver compared with Louis Armstrong
Rehearsal discipline: the brick and the pistol
Why the Oliver band broke up

communities.name: Embouchure, breath and the brass player's lip
communities.parent_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing
communities.narrative: Brass players, mostly trumpeters and a few trombonists, talk about the physical craft of playing: how to place the mouthpiece, build and protect the lip, and breathe. The stories run from the 1910s to the 1990s and come from New Orleans, New York and Chicago players alike. Many centre on teachers and methods. Metoyer's non-pressure system, as relayed by Ernie Cagnolatti, Hilda Taylor and Mrs. Metoyer, is one. Gunable's mouthpiece-only exercises, which Teddy McRae credits for his tone, are another, along with Perkins' trombone method. Others are about the lip itself: swelling, blisters, calluses, a sore "iron lip", pacing practice to avoid spasm, and the fear that dental work or false teeth can end a career (Dickenson on Jabbo Smith and Sandy Williams). Breathing gets its own thread, with circular breathing demonstrated by Clark Terry, Budd Johnson and Buster Bailey, and with diaphragm and stomach breathing. Players agree that endurance and lip health matter. They differ on pressure versus non-pressure playing, on shallow versus standard mouthpieces, and on whether to chase the high register. A few stray segments on conga stamina, phrasing and articulation sit at the edges.
threads: Non-pressure playing and teachers' embouchure methods
Lip care, swelling, wear and dental fears
Mouthpieces: choosing, switching and modifying
Circular and diaphragm breathing
Endurance, practice routines and the high register

communities.name: Freddie Keppard: power, secrecy and rivalry with Oliver
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Musicians in New Orleans, Chicago and elsewhere remember the cornetist Freddie Keppard, mostly as he sounded in the 1910s and 1920s. Tellers range from fellow band members (Darnell Howard, Lillian Hardin Armstrong, Bob Shoffner, Omer Simeon, Roy Palmer) to players who only heard him or knew him by reputation (Steve Angrum, John Pope, Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote). They agree that he was loud, powerful and ragged, with a big tone and plenty of drive. Several add that he was a gifted player who did not read well, or who read faster than Oliver. Recurring details are the handkerchief he held over his valves to hide his fingering, his fear that others would steal his ideas (which is why he recorded only once), his heavy drinking, and the Original Creole Orchestra's Orpheum circuit tour. The most common frame is comparison. Keppard is set against Joe Oliver, Buddy Bolden, Bunk Johnson and Louis Armstrong, with Oliver as the muted, organized cabaret player and Keppard as the open-horn power player. Opinions split on who was better. A smaller strand, told by Eddie Dawson, places Keppard in the Storyville district, where he got permission to play cornet in the brass ban at Harry Parker's.
threads: Loud, powerful, ragtime-rooted trumpet style
Handkerchief over the valves and fear of being copied or recorded
Keppard versus Joe Oliver, Bolden, Bunk and Armstrong
Keppard's bands: Original Creole Orchestra, Orpheum circuit, Chicago dance halls and cafes
Storyville brass ban and Harry Parker's
Heard only by reputation or missed entirely

communities.name: Who were the great clarinetists of New Orleans
communities.parent_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals
communities.narrative: Musicians across the Tulane, Hamilton and Rutgers collections answer the same question: who were the best clarinet players they heard, worked with or learned from? The stories are set mostly in New Orleans between about 1900 and the 1930s, with some Chicago and New York players. Interviewees list and rank players, often weighing tone, originality, reading ability and instrument (Albert-system or C clarinet). The names that recur are Lorenzo Tio, George Baquet, Alphonse Picou, Big Eye Louis Nelson, Johnny Dodds, Jimmie Noone, Sidney Bechet and George Lewis, along with less-remembered players such as Isidore Fritz, George Boyd, Yellow Nunez and Zeb.
