Older New Orleans players (Barnes, Duhé, Garland, Barbarin) describe the early generation, while revival-era and Chicago-scene interviewees (Hodes, Chace, Ashcraft, Wilber) compare Dodds, Bechet, Teschemacher and Goodman and ask who influenced whom. A few segments drift to other subjects, such as a bassist's account of playing with Kenny Davern, but most share the clarinet-ranking subject.
threads: Ranking the early New Orleans clarinetists: Tio, Baquet, Picou, Big Eye Louis
Tone, reading and technique: what made a clarinetist good
Forgotten and local clarinetists few people recall: Fritz, Boyd, Nunez, Zeb
Dodds, Noone, Bechet and the Chicago clarinet lineage
George Lewis and the revival-era comparisons
Influences and models: Tio, Goodman, Bigard, Shaw

communities.name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the tools of tone
communities.parent_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear
communities.narrative: Reed players talk about the physical gear that shapes their sound: cane and plastic reeds, mouthpiece facings, ligatures, and the make of horn. The most central stories are from later saxophonists and clarinetists such as Sam Kininger, Scott Hamilton, Harry Allen, Eric Alexander and Buddy DeFranco, who discuss reed strength, custom mouthpieces and Selmer, King or Conn horns, including Cannonball Adderley's switch to Selmer. Older New Orleans and swing-era players tell related stories set between about 1910 and 1960. Emile Barnes and Edmond Hall weigh plastic reeds against cane, and Alphonse Picou and Joseph Thomas compare Albert-system and Boehm clarinets. Around this core are stories about changing or doubling instruments, such as alto to tenor, clarinet to saxophone, or drums to tenor. There are also reflections on why the clarinet is hard or fading and why the soprano saxophone is disliked. The tellers agree that reeds and mouthpieces matter more than the horn, and that a player's sound is personal. Some, like Jackie McLean and Jerry Bergonzi, say equipment is not the real answer. A minority of samples are only loosely connected, such as a fan letter about tone or a brother's recording career, so the cluster is mostly about gear and instrument choice, with some drift.
threads: Reed strength, cane versus plastic reeds
Mouthpiece facings, custom mouthpieces and chasing a sound
Choice of horn: Selmer, King, Conn and Buffet
Albert-system versus Boehm clarinets
Switching or doubling instruments (alto to tenor, clarinet to sax)
Why the clarinet and soprano sax are hard instruments

communities.name: What I'm writing now: late-career composing projects
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Established jazz musicians, interviewed mostly from the late 1970s into the 2000s, describe the pieces they are currently composing or hope to compose. The talk is of work in progress rather than of the past: Red Callender writes daily on a piece called Jazz Travels and sends tuba ensemble pieces to New York, Ram Ramirez works on the suite "Hills of New York", Melba Liston revises her first trombone, trumpet and strings piece, and Bob Magnusson and Magnarelli mention upcoming records and writing from the piano or horn. Mingus, by contrast, looks back on symphonies and string quartets he never managed to write the way he wanted. Several tellers are modest or uncertain about the work. Ramirez says he is not a real songwriter, Sheila Jordan doubts she wrote her own heavy lyrics, and Ramsey Lewis cannot recall the movement titles of Colors. A few segments drift to related subjects: Woody Herman's search for band writers, Lorraine Feather's grammar blog and musical, and Nancy Wilson on great lyrics. The shared thread is a composer's present-tense account of unfinished writing, but it is loose and spread across many interviews.
threads: Extended works in progress: suites, symphonies and string pieces
Plans for new records and publications
Writing lyrics and songs, and doubting one's own
Commissions and pieces written for other players or bands
Unfinished, unperformed or forgotten compositions

communities.name: Trumpeters talking about other trumpeters
communities.parent_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players
communities.narrative: In this cluster musicians are asked, or volunteer, to size up other trumpet players: who had an original style, whose sound and feeling they admired, and who never got a fair chance. The stories mostly look back at players of the 1920s through the 1950s, such as Billy Douglas, Jabbo Smith, Red Allen, Bunny Berigan, Freddie Webster, Harold Baker, Buck Clayton and Doc Cheatham. They also reach forward to Woody Shaw, Freddie Hubbard and Art Farmer. Louis Armstrong, Dizzy Gillespie and Miles Davis are the names most often tagged. The tellers agree on praise for sound, warmth, soul, vibrato and ballad playing, and they often judge a player against another, as when Berigan is said to have warmth that Harry James lacked. They differ on whether comparison is fair, since Joe Thomas refuses to compare players and Don Albert argues against calling Douglas a copyist. The tellers are largely trumpeters, along with some saxophonists, bassists and drummers, in interviews from all four archives, and Stanley Dance's prompting in several of them gives the segments a common shape. The subject is shared, but each segment is about a different player, so this is a loose genre of talk rather than one event.
threads: Praise for a trumpeter's sound, warmth and feeling
Originality versus copying a style
Ballad playing as the test of a musician
Favorite players named when asked by an interviewer
Overlooked section trumpeters in big bands such as Ellington's and Gillespie's
Comparing two players, such as Berigan and James

communities.name: Who were the great trumpeters: musicians rank their favorites
communities.parent_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players
communities.narrative: Across nearly 200 interviews, musicians talk about trumpet and cornet players they heard, worked beside or admired, judging them by tone, power, reading ability and style. Most of the stories are brief portraits or rankings: a favorite trumpeter, who had the sweetest or loudest sound, who was a first-chair section man rather than a soloist, and who is now forgotten. The New Orleans tellers (Laine's players, Tom Albert, Parenti, Sbarbaro, Dejan, Little Dad Vincent) reach back to the 1890s-1910s and name Manuel Perez, Buddy Petit, Kid Rena, Bunk Johnson, Lawrence Vega and Emmett Hardy. Big-band sidemen such as Quentin Jackson, Charlie Holmes, Horace Henderson and Lawrence Brown recall the 1920s-40s sections of McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Chick Webb, Lunceford and Ellington, with Rex Stewart, Bobby Stark and Paul Webster. Later players such as Slam Stewart, Dave Liebman and Picky Brunious weigh Roy Eldridge, Dizzy Gillespie and Randy Brecker. The tellers agree on judging trumpeters by tone and power, but they disagree on who ranks highest, and the cluster is a set of portraits more than one shared event.
threads: Favorite trumpeters and who was best
Old-time New Orleans cornetists and Laine's players
Big-band trumpet sections: McKinney's, Webb, Lunceford, Ellington
Tone, power, high notes and mutes
First-chair readers versus hot soloists
Forgotten and overlooked trumpet players

communities.name: Cornet versus trumpet, and horn gear talk
communities.parent_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns
communities.narrative: Musicians talk shop about the physical instrument: which horn to play and how to set it up. The strongest strand is cornet versus trumpet. Spanier, McPartland, Ecklund, Isaiah Morgan and Sharkey Bonano prefer the cornet's rounder, mellower tone and conical bore, and some say they disliked the trumpet's feel. Ecklund argues the mellow sound comes from the bore, not the horn's age. A second strand is trombone setup. Roy Palmer and Oscar "Chicken" Henry cover bell size and bore, slide weights, how to hold the horn, slide lubricant, upkeep, and a homemade wire-ribbon collar protector. Smaller items include mouthpiece choice and duplication, handmade horns and collections, and low versus high pitch for dance halls and street work. The tellers mostly agree on tone and practicality. They differ by instrument, and the cornet and trombone discussions share a theme but not a single story. Most are New Orleans and Chicago-style players, mainly from the Tulane collection, and few of the segments are tied to a particular period.
threads: Cornet vs trumpet tone and bore
Trombone bell size, bore and holding the horn
Slide lubricant and instrument care
Mouthpieces and having them copied
Handmade horns and collections
Pitch standards for dance halls and street

communities.name: Cornet or trumpet: the horns they owned and played
communities.parent_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, Chicago, New York and beyond talk about the physical horns they played: cornets, trumpets, flugelhorns, mellophones and trombones, and the makers behind them (Conn, Buescher, King, Martin, Selmer, Olds, Benge, Harry B. Jay, Monette). The stories are mostly inventories and anecdotes. A player lists the horns he bought, traded, lost or had stolen. He recalls the moment he switched from cornet to trumpet, or back. He explains how the two instruments differ in tone, shank, bore and how hard they are to blow. Older New Orleans and Chicago players, set mainly in the 1910s to 1930s, remember E-flat and B-flat cornets, gold-plated band instruments and trades at conventions. Later players such as Clark Terry, Art Farmer and Woody Herman cover the 1950s to 1990s: flugelhorns, mouthpieces, the flumpet, endorsement deals and custom-built horns. Tellers agree that the choice of horn shapes tone and style, and some argue that older instruments sound better. A few segments drift into adjacent topics, such as buying property or the piano on advertising trucks, but most share the subject of instruments and their makers.
threads: Cornet versus trumpet: tone, shanks and switching
Inventories of horns bought, traded, stolen or lost
Makers and brands: Conn, Buescher, King, Martin, Selmer, Benge
Flugelhorn and the flumpet: Miles, Clark Terry, Art Farmer

communities.name: Kid Rena and Buddy Petit: comparing New Orleans trumpet kings
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Musicians from many walks of New Orleans life compare the city's great early trumpeters, with Kid Rena at the center and Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Louis Armstrong and Punch Miller as the usual yardsticks. The stories are set mostly in the 1910s to 1930s, in the second lines, street-corner truck battles, ballhouses and bars of New Orleans, and in the Gypsy Tea Room band of the early 1930s. Tellers agree that Rena had a big, sweet, clean tone, a command of the high register and every key, and great stamina, and that he stayed in New Orleans rather than follow Armstrong to Chicago. Petit is remembered as a clean, accurate, ballhouse-blues player, Kelly for his plunger-mute blues, and Armstrong as the model many trumpeters imitated. Tellers differ on rankings and on details such as Rena's volume, which Punch Miller blames on a small-cup mouthpiece. The tellers are drawn from many interviews, mostly in the Tulane collection and mostly horn players, drummers and bassists who heard these men in person. A few segments drift to other trumpeters, such as Kid Kyfer, Papa Celestin, Evan Thomas and Alvin Alcorn.

Rena versus Buddy Petit: who was the better player
Chris Kelly's plunger blues and Armstrong's influence

communities.name: Remembering Buddy Petit, the unrecorded trumpeter
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Nearly every story here is about one man: Buddy Petit, the New Orleans trumpeter who lived across Lake Pontchartrain (Mandeville, Covington), led a small head-arranging band in the 1910s and 1920s, and died young in 1931 without ever making a record. Fellow musicians such as Punch Miller, Kid Howard, Chester Zardis, Albert Burbank, Louis Nelson, Edmond Hall and Ba Ba Ridgley describe how he played. They remember a soft, sweet, round tone, a middle-range style with few high notes, playing mostly by ear, mutes, triple-tonguing, long held notes and plenty of blues. Tellers agree he was a great player who has been lost to history, and that drink, lateness and unreliability hurt his career. They disagree on how he compares with Armstrong, Bunk Johnson, Kid Rena and Sam Morgan, and on whether he read music. Several also recall working with him, subbing for him, or seeing him at rehearsals, parades and excursion-boat jobs. A few segments are only loosely attached, such as a Bocage passage on second-lining, a Palmer passage on trombonists, and an interviewer's request for a portrait.
threads: How Petit played: tone, mute, range and style
Comparisons with Armstrong, Bunk Johnson, Kid Rena and Sam Morgan
Playing in his band and subbing for him
Drink, lateness and his life across the lake
Never recorded: the lost sound and the listening debates

communities.name: Remembering Buddy Bolden: loud horn, lost mind
communities.parent_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans tell stories about Buddy Bolden, the legendary cornetist of roughly 1895 to 1907, who by the 1920s and 1930s was a half-forgotten figure. Most tellers were children or young players who heard him once or twice at Lincoln Park, Johnson Park, West End or the dance halls. Others, including Kid Ory, Peter Bocage, Fess Manetta and Ed Garland, knew his band or played with it. They agree he was extremely loud, a rough blues and ragtime player who drew dancers. His tunes included Funky Butt and The House Got Ready, and his sidemen included Willie Cornish, Frank Lewis, Brock Mumford and Frankie Dusen. They also recall a rivalry with John Robichaux's more polished orchestra, which played the other park. Many have only second-hand talk to offer, and William Russell and Albert Nicholas question how much of the legend is reliable. They differ on his tone and power, and several recall his breakdown, his confinement and the story of the poisoned trumpet. A few segments drift to neighbouring figures such as Bunk Johnson, Bigfoot Willis, the Magnolia band and the Olympia band, but the cluster is overwhelmingly about Bolden.
threads: Hearing Bolden as a child at Lincoln Park, Johnson Park and West End
Bolden's band: personnel, size and the Eagle Band afterward
Loudness and style: blues, rags and tunes like Funky Butt
Bolden versus Robichaux: rough music against polished
His breakdown, confinement and the poisoned-trumpet story
Legend and doubt: second-hand talk, missing cylinder and photograph

communities.name: Retirement, aging and still playing
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: In the closing stretch of their interviews, musicians talk about where life has left them: whether they have retired, how much they still play, and what is next. Most are in their seventies or later and say they are semi-retired or choosing their work carefully. Joe Wilder says offers are fewer and he can now decline jobs he would not enjoy. Bob Hardaway and Norris Turney describe mostly retired lives built around occasional gigs, Japan trips or a festival. Others refuse to stop at all (Machito, Doug Carn, Adam Nussbaum with Elvin Jones and Milt Hinton as models). Health and the body come up often, whether failing sight, dental trouble, disability or good luck with health. Pensions, family, grandchildren, quiet time and Covid-era routines also appear. The tellers span the 1970s interviews through to the 2020s and come from every collection, and many of these segments are the last thing said before the interview ends. They agree that music stays a source of pleasure and purpose, and differ on whether they have stopped, slowed down or never will.
threads: No retirement: musicians who keep playing for life
Semi-retirement and choosing which jobs to take
Health, eyesight and physical limits in old age
Pensions, family, grandchildren and quiet home life
Future plans and closing reflections at the end of the interview
Staying connected to music without playing (clubs, festivals, teaching)

communities.name: Dick Gibson's jazz parties and their offshoots
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians describe the invitation-only jazz parties that Denver businessman Dick Gibson began in 1962 in Aspen, Colorado, and that later moved to Vail and the Broadmoor Hotel in Colorado Springs. Players such as Cliff Leeman, Trummy Young, Gus Johnson, Buddy Tate and Victor Moore tell how they were invited, often through a friend like Jack Lesberg or Leeman. They explain how Gibson paid their way, posted daily set slips, mixed combinations on the fly, and reunited old friends such as Teddy Wilson, Ralph Sutton, Milt Hinton and Flip Phillips. Leeman, who played them for years, supplies the most detail: the party's growth, the lavish hospitality, and spin-offs like the Odessa, Texas party founded by Dr. Fulcher, plus Midland and Manassas. The tellers agree the parties are a warm social reunion, and later speakers (Masso, Frishberg, Hofmann) extend the topic to jazz parties in general. A minority of samples drift to unrelated festivals, tributes and New York club gigs (Bix society, Montauk, Whitefish, the West End), so the core is Gibson's circuit, set mostly in the 1960s to 1980s.
threads: How Gibson started the parties in Aspen in 1962 and grew them to Vail and the Broadmoor
Getting invited and paid: Lesberg, Leeman and Gibson covering expenses
Lineups, set schedules and playing with Teddy Wilson, Sutton and Hinton
Odessa, Midland and Manassas parties as offshoots
Parties as reunions of old friends and Gibson as patron
Other jazz festivals and tributes (a loose fringe)

communities.name: Dances and dance tempos musicians played for
communities.parent_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets
communities.narrative: Musicians from many regions, but above all New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, talk about the dances they played for and the repertoire that went with them. The earliest tellers, set around 1890-1920, recall quadrilles and their called figures, waltzes, mazurkas, schottisches, polkas and two-steps. They name the newer ragtime-era fads: the turkey trot, bunny hug, grizzly bear, shimmy, buck dance and Charleston. Others describe the dance halls, tonks, balls and picnics where this was played, and what reading bands played compared with blues bands such as Bolden's. Later tellers, from the 1930s to the 1950s and a few from later decades, shift to swing-era and Latin dancing (tea dances, cha-cha, rumba, mambo). They also talk about keeping tempos right for dancers and simplifying arrangements for them. The tellers agree that dancing shaped what bands played and how fast. They differ on whether the old waltz and quadrille repertoire was easy or hard, and on how much jazz was played versus sweet dinner music. A few segments stray into religious attitudes to dancing, a singer's recollections and transcript noise, so the cluster is only loosely unified.
threads: Quadrilles, waltzes and the old dance repertoire
Ragtime-era dance fads: turkey trot, bunny hug, grizzly bear, Charleston
Dance halls, tonks and balls where bands played
Keeping tempo for dancers and playing danceable swing
Latin dance crazes: rumba, cha-cha, mambo
Church and family attitudes to dancing

communities.name: Learning the bass with little or no teacher
communities.parent_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique
communities.narrative: Bassists from many regions and generations describe how they came to the instrument, and most agree that formal teaching was scarce. Many were self-taught or taught by ear, often crossing over from tuba, violin, guitar, mandolin, banjo or ukulele and carrying fingering and tone ideas with them. They learned from method books, charts pasted on the instrument, or by watching older bassists. In New Orleans, Simon Marrero gave Albert Morgan reading and bowing lessons and a method book. In Los Angeles, Henry Kimball and a Local 47 official who had played with Whiteman taught Ed Garland to bow. Others report improvising their first instrument, such as Pavageau's soapbox and barrel bass, or buying a bass because a club needed one. The period runs from about 1905 to 1960, mostly the 1910s to 1940s. Tellers differ on bowing: some mastered it, others only plucked and resisted classical technique in favor of their own jazz approach. A few segments about violin and banjo students or popular tunes in lessons sit at the edges and are about teaching generally, not bass.
threads: Self-taught from books, charts and ear
Moving to bass from tuba, violin, guitar or banjo
Older bassists showing fingering and bowing
Learning to read and bow, or refusing to
Improvising a first bass from scrap materials

communities.name: Where to live: moving, staying, leaving New York
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations tell how and why they chose where to live, most often in relation to New York. Some left the city for a house in Connecticut, Montclair, Woodstock, Hartwick, Hartford, Syracuse or the Poconos, usually citing family, schools, safety, a mother or wife, or burnout. Others chose a different scene over New York, such as Los Angeles for film and TV scoring, San Francisco, San Diego, Denver, Seattle, Toronto or Rome. A few stayed in New York on purpose because the staff and recording work was there and they could raise a family. Immigrants such as Paul Shaffer, Rossano Sportiello and Nicki Parrott describe the move to the US, including visas and citizenship. The stories mostly date from the 1960s through the 1990s. Tellers agree that the decision was driven by family and work as much as by music. They differ on whether leaving New York meant escape and relief or a loss of centrality. The cluster is loosely held together by the practical, domestic side of relocation, and a few samples drift into other topics such as career goals or travel.
threads: Leaving New York for a house upstate or in Connecticut
Choosing the West Coast or another city over New York
Staying in New York for work and family
Moving for a spouse, parent or children
Immigrating to the US and getting visas
Burnout and leaving the New York scene

communities.name: Landmark jazz concerts: Carnegie Hall and beyond
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: Musicians and producers recall the staged jazz concerts of roughly 1938 to 1947, when jazz moved from dance halls and clubs onto the concert stage. The centre of gravity is Carnegie Hall: Count Basie, Teddy Wilson and Joe Turner remember Benny Goodman's 1938 concert and John Hammond's Spirituals to Swing blues show, and Mario Bauza recalls Gillespie's September 1947 concert with the Afro Drums Suite. Wilson and an interlocutor argue over which came first and the exact dates, so the tellers do not always agree on chronology. A second strand is the revival-era concert scene outside New York. New Orleans figures (Edmond Souchon, August Lanoix, Abbie Williams) describe Scoop Kennedy's National Jazz Foundation concerts of the early 1940s and the 1944 and 1946 shows with Bunk Johnson, Sidney Bechet and Pops Foster, and Carl Rinker recalls wartime concerts in Chicago halls. Producers such as Al Rose, who brought Spanier, Bechet and Baby Dodds to Carnegie Hall and on an Ivy League tour, and Benny Carter, who recalls a 1942 Goffin and Feather gathering, tell it from the organiser's side. The stories mix the artists who played, the promoters who staged the concerts and the occasions they marked, and are looser in the smaller New Orleans and Chicago examples than in the Carnegie ones.
threads: Goodman's 1938 Carnegie Hall concert and Basie's debut
Hammond's Spirituals to Swing and the first blues concert
National Jazz Foundation and Bunk Johnson concerts in New Orleans
Producers and promoters staging jazz concerts (Al Rose, Goffin and Feather)
Gillespie's 1947 Carnegie Hall concert
Wartime benefit and revival concerts in Chicago

communities.name: Memorable gigs and comebacks at Carnegie Hall
communities.parent_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers stories in which musicians single out a particular concert or gig as a high point, most often at Carnegie Hall, which dominates the venue facets by a wide margin. Most are set between the 1950s and the 1990s, with a heavy concentration in the 1970s, when George Wein's Newport-in-New York programs, tribute concerts and anniversary shows put veteran players back on a major stage. Several tellers describe comebacks or returns: Jess Stacy, Helen Humes (coaxed in by Stanley Dance), Spiegle Willcox and Chuck Green at the Apollo each describe being pulled back into public performance and met with standing ovations or rave reviews. Others recount band reunions and anniversary concerts such as Woody Herman's 1976 alumni show, the Jazztet reunion, Goldkette and Whiteman revivals and the JATP anniversary. Sidemen and younger players, including Mcbee, Magnarelli and Ray Ricker, answer the standard question of what their best or most memorable gig was. The tellers agree that the occasion mattered and the audience response was warm, but they differ in what it meant: vindication for a veteran, a first appearance, or simply a favorite night. The edges are loose, since a few samples (a 1919 command performance in London, the founding of the New York Pops, a Telluride jam finale) share only the idea of a notable performance, not the venue.
threads: Veteran comebacks on the Carnegie Hall stage (Stacy, Humes, Willcox)
Newport-in-New York and George Wein tribute concerts, 1972-74
Band reunions and anniversary concerts (Woody Herman, Jazztet, Goldkette, Whiteman)
Answering 'what was your best gig?' (Frishberg, Hall, Magnarelli, Ricker)
Standing ovations and press reviews after a big concert
Other landmark performances: Apollo youth fund show, London command performance

communities.name: The color line at the Cotton Club and Harlem nightlife
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: The core of this cluster is the Cotton Club in Harlem, mostly in the late 1920s and 1930s. Musicians such as Jimmie Crawford, Sonny Greer, Ram Ramirez, Charlie Holmes, Benny Carter and Alberta Hunter describe a club with a Black show and band but a white clientele, owned by the mob. Black patrons were excluded outright or priced out, with Bill Robinson the frequently cited exception. Tellers differ on how strict the policy was. Russell Procope walked in without being sure, Holmes says Black patrons could enter if they could pay, and Howard R. Scott recalls no discrimination as a professional. Around this core, speakers contrast Harlem spots that welcomed Black audiences (Small's, the Rhythm Club, after-hours joints) with white-only or downtown venues, and mention Cafe Society as the first integrated club. The outer part of the cluster drifts into who owned and ran New York nightclubs (Birdland, the Paradise, Morocco, Club Zombie), including mob ownership, and a few unrelated items such as Quincy Jones on Castro and Daryl Sherman on Waldorf audiences.
threads: Cotton Club's segregated policy and Bill Robinson as the exception
White patronage of Harlem and after-hours joints
Harlem clubs welcoming Black audiences versus downtown white-only rooms
Cafe Society and integrated clubs
Mob and other ownership of New York nightclubs (Birdland, Paradise, Morocco)

communities.name: Why the club closed: nightclub failures and finances
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians across many interviews tell how a particular nightclub or band engagement came to an end. The stories are set mostly between the 1940s and the 1960s, in cities such as Denver, New Orleans, Kansas City, Buffalo and New York. The reasons vary: owners die or sell out, management goes into receivership, cheaper acts or big-name replacements drain the business, investors push for gambling and gimmicks, strict dress rules drive away neighbourhood customers, or a fire or killing ends the run. The fullest account is Horace Henderson's history of Denver's Clef Club, a nonprofit bottle club that was closed by the Colorado legislature, with details of rent, memberships and hotel pressure. Hayes Pillars on the Plantation clubs, Lionel Ferbos on the Melody Inn, and club owners and bandleaders such as Annie Ross, Don Albert and Reb Spikes tell similar stories. The tellers agree that club ownership is precarious and that business, more than music, decides the outcome. Their accounts differ in whether they blame owners, money, politics or bad luck. Some samples, such as the tap dancer's account of a declining Hotcha Club, sit only loosely inside this theme.
threads: Clef Club in Denver: bottle club, finances and legislative closure
Plantation and Riviera clubs: swapping bands and a declining business
Owners who sell, die or go broke
Failed ventures by musicians who became club owners
Investors, rules and gimmicks that drove customers away
Fires, receiverships and sudden closings

communities.name: Wakes, funerals and burying the dead
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians and family members describe the customs surrounding death in New Orleans Black and Creole communities. Joseph Rene gives the fullest account of the old ways: bodies laid out at home on a cot-like stretcher until the undertaker brought the coffin, the veil, flowers and three candles (now electric bulbs), all-night wakes with red beans and rice, beer, wine and coffee, and society or lodge suppers. Others add the order of a church funeral service, wakes at the funeral home with no drinking, the church bell tolled for a death, and burying people in favorite suits or Masonic caps. Carolyn Buck's segments are more personal: she tells of her husband's premonition, his planned funeral music, choosing a shared grave with his late wife and mother, and the moment of his death in December 1968. A stray radio sermon recorded over a tape end also falls in. The subject is shared, but the cluster is small and mixes general custom with one widow's private account. Almost all the stories come from Tulane's Hogan archive, with a few from Hamilton and Rutgers.
threads: Laying out the body at home and old embalming practice
Wakes: food, drink and lodge suppers
Order of the funeral service, dress and burial customs
Church bell tolled for a death
Carolyn Buck's account of her husband's final illness, death and burial
Stray religious radio sermon

venues: Prayer Tower Church of God in Christ

communities.name: What a bassist owes the band: foundation, not solos
communities.parent_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique
communities.narrative: Bassists, and the bandleaders and players who work with them, talk about what the bass chair is for. The shared view is that the bass is the foundation: it supplies the bottom note, keeps good time and a good sound, and directs the band. Tellers range from New Orleans players such as Pops Foster and McNeal Breaux to modern bassists such as Ron Carter, Percy Heath and Rufus Reid. Many of them warn against over-soloing and against playing too high in the register. Several, including Carter and Ray Conniff, complain that younger players take guitaristic habits into the bass or write from the guitar. Percy Heath describes building a walking line on Walter Page's model, with strong and weak beats and implied harmony. Mario Bauza makes the same point from the Afro-Cuban side: Latin arrangers who ignore the bass foundation lose the band's sound. A few accounts are personal, such as Quinn Wilson's reluctant first bass solo and Foster defending his two-beat rhythm to symphony bassists. The sample is small and does not name a period.
threads: The bass as foundation: bottom note, time and sound
Against over-soloing and playing high in the register
Walking-bass concept and Walter Page as model
Complaints about guitaristic habits in younger bassists and writers
Bass in Afro-Cuban arranging and Bauza's rhythm-section insistence
Early bass solos and defending two-beat style

communities.name: Taking up the bass, often by necessity
communities.parent_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique
communities.narrative: Across 24 interviews, mostly New Orleans musicians from the Tulane collection with some from Rutgers, players tell how they came to the bass. The setting runs from the 1920s to about 1970, with most stories in the 1920s to 1940s. The recurring pattern is need. A bass player failed to show at a funeral, bass players were scarce in a band, or there were too many trombones, so someone was handed or lent an instrument and learned on the job. Clark taught himself from a fingering chart, Lanoix borrowed a bass for 75 cents, and Stevenson moved over from trumpet at the Gypsy Tea Room. Others bought their own, such as Butler on a six-dollar down payment and Mitchell on credit. Some tell odd-instrument stories: Mangiapane and Kimball play left-handed or backwards on borrowed basses. Coquille adds a later chapter on switching to electric bass around 1970. The tellers agree that bass was rarely a first choice. They differ in how they learned, whether by watching other players, teaching themselves or being picked by a bandleader.
threads: Drafted onto bass when no player showed up
Switching from trumpet, guitar or trombone to bass
Borrowing or buying a first bass on credit
Teaching yourself by watching and fingering charts
Playing left-handed or backwards on a borrowed bass
Moving from string bass to electric bass

communities.name: Bass players: Blanton, Pettiford and the jazz bass
communities.parent_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, Chicago, New York and the West Coast talk about the string bass and the people who played it. The most frequent thread is Jimmy Blanton, discovered in St. Louis in 1939 and hired by Ellington. Tizol, Clark Terry, Lawrence Brown, Mingus and Richard Wyands all recall how he changed the instrument and why early microphones never captured his tone. Around him sit Oscar Pettiford, Ray Brown, Slam Stewart, Walter Page and the New Orleans slap bassists Pops Foster and Wellman Braud, who anchored the Ellington and Russell bands. The tellers also trade practical bass talk: instruments they own or were given, taping fingers against blisters, carrying a bass on streetcars, the move from acoustic to electric, and long-scale or plywood basses. Many segments are shorter mentions of a bassist who joined a band or was recommended. The tellers agree that the bass player defines a band's time and sound. They differ on which players mattered most, and the period runs from the 1910s to the 1960s with a few later reflections. Not every sample fits this subject; a minority are only incidental mentions of a bass player.
threads: Jimmy Blanton's arrival in Ellington's band and his revolution on the instrument
Great bassists compared: Pettiford, Ray Brown, Slam Stewart, Walter Page
New Orleans slap bass: Pops Foster and Wellman Braud
The instrument itself: owning, carrying, amplifying, and electric versus acoustic
Bassists joining or being recommended to bands

communities.name: Learning chords and improvising by ear
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans players to college-era and later-generation jazz educators describe how they first picked up harmony and improvisation, mostly in settings between the 1920s and the mid-1960s. Many learned by ear and by rote, working out changes from older players, from visiting big bands, or from records, as Benny Carter did while learning his instrument, and as Lester Young was said to run intricate patterns without knowing chord names. Others came to chords more formally, relating guitar chord symbols to the harmony (Joe Wilder), playing through fake books with an accordion trio (Bobby Militello), or taking a college music appreciation course (James Lincoln Collier). Jam sessions and bandstand call-outs of tunes and keys, such as being forced to play I Got Rhythm in B-flat, appear as a proving ground. The tellers agree that chords were absorbed from other players more than taught, but they differ on whether this happened by ear or from written symbols. Because the samples also include a few loosely related items, such as a carnival job, a college band's repertoire and a Cuban and Irish comparison of oral learning, the cluster hangs together only around the general theme of learning harmony.
threads: Learning changes by ear from older players
Chord symbols, fake books and formal study
Learning to improvise on the instrument
Visiting big bands and jam sessions as classrooms
Oral learning compared across traditions

bands: Clyde Kerr and William Houston's band

communities.name: Learning tunes: records, fake books, and the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Musicians across many eras describe how they built a working repertoire of tunes. The sources vary: taking songs off records or the radio, learning lines by ear phrase by phrase, studying the illegal fake books and card-service lead sheets of the 1950s and 60s, and learning on the bandstand as songs are called. The settings run from New Orleans bands of the 1910s-20s working up hit tunes from records, through 1950s-60s New York and Tristano's circle, to 1970s-90s sessions where leaders like Ellis Marsalis or Thad Jones called unfamiliar tunes with no rehearsal. Tellers agree that repertoire is learned socially and under pressure, and that faking and following the changes is a survival skill. They differ on method: some stress root movement, chords and then melody, some memorizing lyrics, and bassists note they cannot fake a tune the way others can. Most tellers are rhythm-section players, especially bassists, with some horn players and a bandleader (Fleck) describing teaching tunes by ear.
threads: Taking tunes off records and the radio
Illegal fake books and card-service lead sheets
Learning songs on the bandstand when they are called
Faking it and the humiliation of not knowing a tune
Tunes every musician must know at a session
Teaching new tunes to a band by ear

communities.name: Bass and drums: locking the rhythm section's time
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and scenes talk about how the bass and drums, and the rest of the rhythm section, share the job of keeping time. Most tellers are drummers and bassists, from Dixieland and New Orleans players such as Johnny St. Cyr and Ed Garland, who stress four beats or first and third, to modern players such as Walter Booker, Ed Soph, Marty Morell, Nicki Parrott and Jerry Bergonzi. They agree that the bass and drums must act almost as one person on the beat, giving soloists and the front line a steady foundation. They differ in emphasis. Some give rules, such as knowing the tunes and the changes, or the bass outlining the chords with roots and thirds. Others describe feel and negotiation, such as adjusting to bassists who play behind or on top of the beat, dragging, or time as a consensus of the whole section. The stories are mostly not tied to a date, and a few stray into parade bass-drum duets and Sun Ra's rhythm approach, which sit at the edge of the main subject.
threads: Bass and drums as one unit on the beat
Defining each player's role in the rhythm section
Adjusting to different bassists and drummers (behind, on top, dragging)
Dixieland rhythm: four beats, down strokes, first and third
Knowing the tunes and changes; bass lines outlining harmony
Playing behind bass solos and reading a gig

communities.name: How New Orleans drummers set up and play
communities.parent_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used
communities.narrative: Drummers, mostly from New Orleans, explain the craft of their instrument: how they set up the kit, hold the sticks, work the pedals and keep time. The stories are told by street and parade drummers (Alex Bigard, Henry "Sleepy" Robertson, Louis Barbarin, Joseph Rene) and by dance-band and later swing and modern players (Ray Bauduc, Louie Bellson, Jimmy Cobb, Jack DeJohnette, Slide Hampton's circle). They cover sticks, rolls and wrist control, practice pads, tuning and sizing the snare and bass drums, and foot technique and stool height. Cymbals, sock cymbals, hi-hat and brushes come up too. Joe Watkins supplies the largest single thread: he plays left-handed and left-footed, learned it from Henry Martin, and followed George Lewis's advice to use a high stool and skip the hi-hat. Other tellers recall left-handed New Orleans drummers such as Snaggs Jones, Monk Hazel and Emmett Rogers. The tellers agree that the drummer's job is steady time and that technique is learned by watching older players. They differ on the parade-versus-dance divide and on modern versus traditional approaches, such as Bauduc's melodic style against modern drummers. The sample is mostly Tulane interviews, with a few from the Smithsonian, Hamilton and Rutgers, and no single period dominates.
threads: Left-handed and left-footed drummers and set-ups
Sticks, grip, rolls, wrist work and practice pads
Parade drumming: bass drum, snare and marching beat
Foot technique, stool height and the hi-hat question
Tuning drums, cymbals and brushes
Time-keeping and personal drum styles

communities.name: Writing the score: pencil, Finale and arranging habits
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Arrangers and composers describe how they physically put music on paper and how that changed with technology. The largest group of tellers, mostly from later interviews with working arrangers, compare pencil-and-score-pad writing with notation software such as Finale, Sibelius and Dorico, or the Synclavier. Several say they still prefer pencil and write faster by hand. Some use software only to extract parts, and John LaBarbera tells students not to trust playback. Others describe older craft habits: writing transposed scores, neat manuscript, working with copyists, and the thrill or cringe of first hearing an arrangement played. A smaller strand, led by Horace Henderson, covers 1930s-40s swing arranging choices, such as sketching chorus plans, varying out choruses and altering bridges. Other samples drift into how individuals composed, such as Charlie Love's dreamed-up pieces or Hal Galper's melody-first method. The tellers agree that hands-on writing mattered, and they differ on how far to trust software.
threads: Pencil and paper versus Finale, Sibelius and Dorico
Writing transposed scores and working with copyists
Hearing your arrangement played for the first time
Planning chorus structure and swing versus ballad arrangements
How individual composers conceive and sketch pieces

communities.name: Touring abroad: Japan, South America, Haiti
communities.parent_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan
communities.narrative: These are stories of overseas tours, told by musicians from many eras. The best-known thread is the 1966 Japan trip. Jimmy Owens went first with Herbie Mann, then on a drummers' tour with Art Blakey, Elvin Jones and Tony Williams. Owens, Elvin Jones and George Wein all describe the drug arrests that cut it short, including Elvin's arrest in Hokkaido and Kenny Clarke's deportation. A second thread is South America. Garvin Bushell played Buenos Aires and Montevideo in 1927, Cab Calloway's band toured there in 1951, David Albert Francis led a band there in 1954, Eddie Barefield directed a revue in 1959, and Woody Herman made a State Department tour in 1958 that used his band poorly. A third thread is Billy Taylor, Budd Johnson and Kenny Dorham touring Haiti in the mid-1940s, with voodoo drums at night. Konitz's 1965 European tour with Bill Evans and Bushell's 1927 European and Cairo dates round it out. The tellers agree that foreign tours were memorable and often chaotic, but they do not share one event. The places, decades and bandleaders vary widely, so what holds the cluster together is the touring abroad, not a single story.
threads: 1966 Japan tours and the drummers' drug arrests
South American tours from the 1920s to 1959
State Department tours and band mismanagement
Haiti tour with Billy Taylor and Budd Johnson
European tours in the 1920s and 1960s

communities.name: Max Roach and the bebop drummers of the 1940s
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds, including bandleaders, pianists, bassists and drummers, talk about the drummers who shaped 1940s New York jazz, with Max Roach at the center. Benny Carter recalls how Roach's innovative drumming made it hard for the big band to find the one after his solos. Benny Golson, Slide Hampton and Hank Jones describe him as an adventurous, melodic drummer who made the drums a musical instrument, and Jones places him on 52nd Street with Coleman Hawkins and the Parker-Gillespie group. Around him are stories of Kenny Clarke and the shift from bass-drum quarter notes to ride-cymbal timekeeping, which let bassists be heard, and of Dave Tough, Cliff Leeman, Shelly Manne and the lists of New York drummers. The tellers largely agree on Roach's and Clarke's importance, but they come at it from different angles, and some segments are really about bebop's founders, Ellington voicings or a disputed rhythm-section story. The cluster is therefore a loose gathering of drummer portraits and comparisons rather than one single event.
threads: Max Roach's innovative, melodic drumming
Kenny Clarke and the move to ride-cymbal timekeeping
Drummers on 52nd Street and in New York in the 1940s
Comparing drummers across eras and styles
Other drummers: Dave Tough, Cliff Leeman, Shelly Manne

communities.name: Copying Louis versus finding your own sound
communities.parent_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels
communities.narrative: Musicians from several generations talk about imitation and originality: how much to borrow from an idol, and when to stop. Players such as Mike De Lay, Bob Watts and Wild Bill Davison describe following Louis Armstrong or Bix Beiderbecke note for note, or taking only a few licks, before finding their own style. De Lay is told by the old violinist Robichaux in 1930 to develop his own sound, and Watts builds a gut-bucket style that made his name across Texas. Others judge the copyists. Watts says Red Allen copied Louis too closely to rise, Davison condemns Red Nichols for copying Bix, and Joe Darensbourg and Kenny Davern complain that today's players clone George Lewis, Johnny Dodds, Armstrong or Clifford Brown. Harry "Sweets" Edison's remark about being an originator rather than an imitator is quoted twice. The tellers broadly agree that individuality marked the older New Orleans players, though Joe Lyde's account of Ken Colyer copying Bunk Johnson from records, with little American jazz available in England, shows imitation as a route into the music. The period is mostly the 1920s to 1940s, told by Tulane, Hamilton and Rutgers interviewees. Several samples are interviewers' questions or quotations rather than first-person stories.
threads: Following Armstrong or Bix note for note, then breaking away
Elders advising a young player to find his own style
Condemning copyists such as Red Allen and Red Nichols
Modern players cloning the old New Orleans masters
Sweets Edison on being an originator
Imitating records abroad, as with Colyer and Bunk in England

communities.name: Drummers on their kits: drums, cymbals and tuning
communities.parent_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used
communities.narrative: In this cluster, drummers talk about their own equipment: what makes their kits, how big the bass drums and cymbals are, and how they keep the drums in tune. The tellers are mostly New Orleans drummers from the Tulane (Hogan) interviews, with a few from Hamilton, Rutgers and the Smithsonian. Several name makers and sizes: Ludwig, Leedy and Conn drums, Zildjian and Turkish cymbals, 18- to 21-inch cymbals and a 26-inch bass drum. Care and tuning come up repeatedly. One drummer puts a light bulb inside the bass drum to keep the head dry and tight in damp weather. Others loosen or tighten the heads with the weather, or say which pitches they tune the snare and bass drum to (F and D). Many of these segments are recorded as show-and-tell, with the interviewer looking at the kit in the room. The tellers differ mainly on preferences: bigger bass drums versus smaller ones for combos, and which cymbals suit a big band versus a small group. The stories have no fixed period, and no places or venues are tagged.
threads: Makes and models: Ludwig, Leedy, Conn, Zildjian
Bass drum and cymbal sizes
Tuning the snare and bass drum
Keeping heads dry: lights in the bass drum and weather
Choosing cymbals for big band versus small group
Showing the kit during the interview

communities.name: Early drum kits, sock cymbals and the hi-hat
communities.parent_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used
communities.narrative: Drummers recall how the trap set was built and how its equipment changed. Tellers from New Orleans (Hogan), New York and Chicago describe their first kits from about 1905 to the 1920s. These were homemade or wooden foot pedals, big rope-tension or folding bass drums, a single small or Chinese cymbal, cowbells, wood blocks and tambourines. Many say they never saw a sock cymbal or hi-hat until they reached New York or Chicago around 1930. Several credit Kaiser Marshall, Cuba Austin and Jo Jones with the low sock cymbal and then the raised high-hat, and they disagree on who came first. Later stories cover Louie Bellson's double bass drum kit (1938-40), Zildjian and Paiste cymbals, drum brands, sticks and brushes, and how kits grew by the 1960s and 70s. The tellers are mostly older New Orleans drummers, plus swing-era and studio drummers who compare old equipment with new. A few segments drift to washboards, novelty instruments and guitar picks.
threads: First homemade drum sets, wooden pedals and folding bass drums
Who first used the sock cymbal and high-hat
Cymbals: Chinese, Zildjian, Paiste and the cymbal beater
Bellson and the double bass drum kit
Brands, sticks, brushes and how kits grew
Washboards and novelty percussion

communities.name: Colour lines and exclusion in schools, towns and Black society
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds tell of their first or sharpest encounters with prejudice, mostly in the 1920s through the 1950s, with a few later reflections from the 1970s. The most concrete stories are about being shut out of institutions and public places. David Baker is expelled from Butler's Arthur Jordan Conservatory for dancing with a white girl and later meets sundown dating rules at Lincoln University. Curtis Fuller is turned away from the Catholic University of Detroit. Sheila Jordan's principal tells her not to associate with "colored girls". Tex Stephens describes Canal Street shops that would not let Black customers try on hats, and Charles Thompson recalls being refused service at a restaurant with his light-skinned father. A second strand concerns colour and class divisions inside Black communities: Danny Barker on society rivalries, Milt Hinton on the Blue Vein Society, and Sonny Greer being snubbed by Howard University girls. A smaller strand covers how prejudice is taught or passed on, including Jon Hendricks's father's teaching of universal brotherhood, Gil Evans on parents conditioning children, and Machito's first experience of discrimination in Cuba. The tellers are Black and white, American and Cuban, and they differ on whether prejudice came from outside the community or within it. The shared material is the lived experience of the color line, with specific places, schools and institutions as the setting.
threads: Barred from white schools and conservatories
Segregated shops, restaurants and public spaces
Colour and class snobbery within Black society
Parents teaching tolerance or racism
Discrimination outside the US, as in Cuba

bands: Smokey Smith and His Harlem Aces

communities.name: Who wrote it? Tune credit, copyright and stolen compositions
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1910s to the 1960s tell about disputes over who actually composed a tune and who got the credit and the money. The strongest cases come from early New Orleans: Nick La Rocca says he copyrighted tunes under his own name because bandmates took the royalties, and Papa Jack Laine answers that La Rocca claimed tunes he had learned from the band. Sbarbaro describes tunes written collectively, with royalty confusion cleared up in 1937-38. Georg Brunis traces Tin Roof Blues from Rusty Rail Blues through Melrose's retitling to royalties split among many names. Roy Carew, Irwin Leclere and Joe Darensbourg talk about others claiming Fickle Fay Creep, Jelly Bean, Camel Walk and Blues for Jimmy. Later players such as Juan Tizol, John Collins, Horace Henderson and Abbey Lincoln describe publishers, lost royalties, unpaid co-writing, added bars and lyrics written without permission. Cosimo Matassa, a recording-studio owner, explains how a publishing contract put his name on a song. The tellers agree that credit and royalties were routinely misassigned. They differ in who they blame: bandmates, publishers, collaborators or rival claimants. A few samples, such as Tizol's count of his tunes and Laurent's list of copyrighted songs, are looser fits.
threads: Early New Orleans bands disputing who composed Original Dixieland Jazz Band-era tunes
Tracing a tune's origin and retitling (Tin Roof Blues, Fickle Fay Creep, Tiger Rag)
Publishers, contracts and royalties that never arrived
Collaborators or others taking credit and money for co-written tunes
Counting and listing one's own copyrighted compositions
Lyrics and tunes used without permission

communities.name: Writing for strings and the orchestra
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Composers, arrangers and players talk about the craft of writing for orchestras and string sections. Most of the stories are about how to treat the orchestra: John Altman writes to the players he has, from a community orchestra to the LSO and Royal Philharmonic, and composes with specific instruments such as the English horn in mind. Paquito D'Rivera says to write for what strings and horns can actually do. Alan Broadbent describes the struggle to treat the orchestra as an instrument, as Nelson Riddle and John Williams did. Eddie Sauter advises thinking like a musician and consulting the player, and Rob Mounsey tells of a violin part that went out of range because of an unproofread transposition. Jim Hall and Johnny Mandel describe writing for strings with guitar or by ear, and Mandel admits he does not play strings. Slide Hampton, Chuck Israels and Pete Candoli add related remarks on arranging versus composing, writing for ensemble interplay and writing for trumpets in the studio. The samples carry no dates, and the tellers are mostly arrangers and composers working in jazz, film and studio settings. The stories share a loose craft theme but are not one tightly bounded narrative.
threads: Writing within each instrument's range and limits
Treating the orchestra as an instrument
Writing for strings and consulting players
Arranger versus composer
Film and studio orchestra dates
Writing for ensemble interplay rather than solos

communities.name: Jam sessions: sitting in and trading ideas
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Most of these stories are about the jam session as an institution: after-hours or midnight gatherings where musicians sat in, tested each other and learned. Tellers from the 1920s through the 2010s describe it as a training ground and a kind of seminar. Players traded ideas and styles, called standards like Basin Street and Stardust, and played without audience pressure. Venues and scenes named include Harlem sessions, Minton's and Monroe's, the Nest, Jimmy Ryan's and the union hall. Older players such as Vic Dickenson, Horace Henderson, Trummy Young and Al Hall stress learning and being heard by peers. They say it has become harder to sit in as standards rose. Later voices such as Ray Blue, Rick Margitza, Bill Dobbins and George Wein say there are fewer places to jam. They add that sessions are conservative and standards-based, and that young players must come prepared and learn the tradition. A few samples are off-topic: an amateur-contest winner at the 81 Theater, and Hubert Laws taking Julius Baker to hear the Jazz Messengers at Birdland.
threads: Jam sessions as the training ground and a seminar for exchanging ideas
Sitting in: getting called up, standing in line, being challenged
Famous sessions in Harlem, Minton's, Monroe's, Jimmy Ryan's
How sessions ran: standards, long solos, post-tune discussion
Jam sessions today: fewer venues, conservative, young players unprepared

communities.name: Where we played: New Orleans clubs and nightspots
communities.parent_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews answer the interviewer's recurring question, "where did you play?", by naming and placing nightclubs, cabarets, halls and cafes, mostly in New Orleans. The settings run from the 1900s-1920s Bucktown, Basin Street, Franklin Street and West End spots through the 1930s-40s Decatur Street, Bourbon Street and French Quarter rooms to the 1960s Red Garter and Preservation Hall era. The stories are mostly lists and locations: who owned a place, what the rooms looked like, who the house band was, and what it was like to work there (the dark 25, the Dew Drop's front and back rooms, the Silver Slipper, the Grunewald and Cobb's Tea Room, Club Desire). Tellers agree that these small clubs were the everyday working world of local players, and some contrast them with the rougher tunks and the Tenderloin that they avoided. They differ in period, in whether the clubs were Black or white, and in how much detail they recall. A few segments, such as Clark Terry on the Club Riviera and Pete Fountain's plans for a Jefferson Parish club, step outside the pattern. The subject is a loose one, a shared question with many individual answers, so this is a mixed cluster.
threads: Listing the clubs a musician played
Basin Street, Franklin Street and Bucktown early spots
French Quarter, Bourbon Street and Decatur Street nightlife
Club owners, house bands and room layouts
Rough tunks and places musicians avoided
Later clubs: Dew Drop, Club Desire, Red Garter

communities.name: Storyville's cabarets, saloons and the district at night
communities.parent_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene
communities.narrative: Musicians recall working in and around New Orleans' red-light district, Storyville, and the cabarets and saloons that surrounded it, mostly in the 1900s through the 1920s. The stories centre on Basin, Rampart, Franklin, Iberville and Canal Streets, and on particular places: Tom Anderson's saloon and Annex, Lulu White's, Pete Lala's, Gertrude Dix's and later the 25 Club and Honeysuckle Inn roadhouses of Prohibition days. Tellers such as Fess Manetta, Ed Garland, Paul Barbarin, Kid Ory and Joe Watkins describe the physical layout of the halls, the bandstands and string bands, the dancers' costumes, the cribs, the tips and the pay. They also cover who the customers were, the gambling, and how the district was closed and kept going afterward. Tellers differ in vantage point: players inside the houses, boys and vendors who only passed through, and interviewers pressing for detail. A few samples come from other cities (Atlantic City, Memphis, St. Louis, Buffalo), and some are fragments or reel-change mechanics, so the cluster loosens at its edges.
threads: Tom Anderson's saloon and the Basin/Rampart Street cabarets
Lulu White's, Pete Lala's and the houses: layout, shows and girls' costumes
Playing piano and string bands in the district: pay, tips, back doors
Storyville's closing and the district staying open into the 1920s
Prohibition roadhouses like the 25 Club and Honeysuckle Inn
Red-light districts and bawdy-house gigs in other cities

communities.name: Making the record: album sessions and how they came together
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: Musicians describe how a particular album or recording session came together: who was chosen, how long the session ran, whether the music was rehearsed, and who produced it. The stories span from the 1950s (Cliff Leeman's first Decca date and its album series, Lee Konitz on the 1959 Giuffre saxophone-section album, Jeanette Kimball recording Marie Laveau with Papa Celestin's band) through the 1980s and 1990s (Kenny Barron's Scratch session in Paris, Jon-Erik Kellso's two-session albums, Eiji Kitamura's one-day Los Angeles session, Branford Marsalis's last session with Kenny Kirkland) to the 2010s-2020s (Rick Margitza's Sacred Hearts, Ruthie Foster's Healing Time recorded live in New Orleans). The tellers agree that these were specific, memorable projects and often stress friends playing together or a loose, unrehearsed approach. They differ widely in method, from a single day to four days of tracking overdubbed over four years, and in who led the project: a bandleader, a producer or the sideman. Because the samples are individual album anecdotes with no common place, era or style, the link is the shared kind of story rather than one subject.
threads: Unrehearsed sessions with friends
One-day or two-session albums
Who chose the players and led the project
Producers, labels and series of albums
Live and overdubbed recording methods
Final or memorable sessions

communities.name: What arranging is: craft, orchestration and learning to write
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Arrangers, composers and bandleaders reflect on what the craft of arranging actually is and how they learned it. Toshiko Akiyoshi, Bill Holman and Slide Hampton each take up the line between arranging, composing and orchestrating. Akiyoshi says they are the same thing for her, Holman calls a good chart a composition, and Hampton defines the three as separate crafts. Others describe how they learned to write: Hampton from the Tchaikovsky scores of The Nutcracker and Peter and the Wolf, and later regretting that he never studied formally; Don Menza from records and scores; Marty Sheller by treating music like a language built from a lifetime of listening. A second strand is practical orchestration. It covers giving every player an idiomatic part, balancing instruments, writing plain note values for strings so they swing, the poor arrangements pops orchestras get, and computer-written parts that ignore a player's breathing. The samples are mostly undated and come from many interviewees, mainly in the Hamilton College and Smithsonian collections. Chuck Israels on Bob Brookmeyer's advice to delay the solo and Joseph Daley on Mingus's graphic scores sit at the edge, since they concern compositional form and notation more than arranging itself.
threads: Arranging versus composing versus orchestrating
Teaching yourself to write from scores and records
Writing idiomatic parts for strings and orchestra players
Studying with mentors and the limits of formal training
Pops orchestras and computer-written parts
Unconventional notation and compositional form

communities.name: Fights, shootings and danger at dances
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews tell about violence breaking out where they worked: dance-hall brawls, shootings, knife and razor threats, police raids and arrests. Most stories are set in New Orleans from the 1910s to the 1940s, in halls and social clubs such as Funky Butt Hall, Nelta's Hall, the Tuxedo and the Irish Channel dances, and in Milneburg and Delacroix Island. A strong core tells how the band coped: playing low blues that provoked or broke up fights, switching tempo, or running for cover. Others carry the theme beyond New Orleans to Dallas, Chicago, St. Louis, New York and Los Angeles, and into the 1950s with Mingus, Cobb and Sheila Jordan. Tellers agree that the work was rough and that the music was part of the trouble and the cure. They differ in tone, from comic anecdote (a bass player stuck in the rafters) to real danger (killings, a poisoned bottle). The edges stray into hoodoo curses, Mardi Gras revenge violence, a holdup beside Art Hodes, and a teaching job at a behavioral center, which only loosely share the subject.
threads: Brawls and shootings at New Orleans dance halls
Slow blues that started or stopped fights
Police raids, arrests and nights in jail
Rough clubs and gangster-run venues outside New Orleans
Street violence, holdups and muggings on the road
Curses, hoodoo and revenge tales

communities.name: How arrangers write: for the players and the band
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Arrangers and bandleaders from across the swing, big-band and later jazz-education worlds describe how they put a chart together and what they keep in mind while doing it. The strongest shared idea is writing for the people who will play the part. Horace Henderson learned the band's soloists and writes simply for slow readers. Yusef Lateef says unplayable parts never get heard. Louie Bellson studied the other instruments to know their ranges and writes rests so the band is not at fortissimo all the time. Melba Liston, Ellen Rowe and Zilner Randolph differ on method. Liston thinks long, writes nearly straight through, edits repeatedly, and adds dynamics and shadings. Rowe works by hand with voicings tried at the piano. Randolph hears the whole band in his head. Others add craft lessons such as John LaBarbera's early mistake of writing too much, Buster Smith's choices for voicing brass and reeds, and Bucky Pizzarelli's praise of favorite arrangers. The stories are mostly undated reflections, with a few anchored to the 1930s or 1960s-70s. About half are the arrangers' own accounts of method, and the rest are tributes to or lessons from other arrangers.
threads: Writing within the players' abilities and ranges
Working method: at the piano, by hand, or in the head
Dynamics, rests and leaving space in a chart
Voicing brass and reeds and thinking in colors
Early arranging mistakes and lessons from mentors
Favorite arrangers and their influence

communities.name: Voicing for horn sections: how arrangers write for horns
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Arrangers and players explain, in practical terms, how they voice and score parts for horn sections of different sizes. Buster Smith describes building chords down from the trumpet lead, with the second part a fifth below, the baritone on the tonic, brass spread wider than the saxes, and flatted fifths placed in the middle. Studio and R&B writers such as Tom Malone and Jerry Hey stress unisons and keeping the horns out of the vocalist's way, treating them as frosting around the singer. Others, including Slide Hampton, David Weiss, Marty Sheller and John LaBarbera, talk about getting a big sound from three to five horns, and about borrowing ideas from Thad Jones and Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. Johnny Mandel and Lou Marini discuss saxophone voicings and inner parts, and Gil Evans and Bill Holman describe balance and writing for the individual player. The tellers agree that voicing is learned by ear and by imitating other arrangers, and they differ mainly in idiom: swing-era block voicings, bebop-era sextets, and pop and R&B horn writing. The stories cluster in the Hamilton and Rutgers interviews, and most are not tied to a dated period. A few outliers, such as the Wilbur Ware and Art Baron segments, touch only loosely on arranging.
threads: Building chords from the lead: Buster Smith's top-down voicings
Horns behind the vocal: unisons and staying out of the singer's way (Hey, Malone, Hunter)
Getting a big sound from three to five horns (Blakey, Thad Jones, Sheller, Weiss)
Saxophone section voicings and inner parts (Mandel, Marini, drop twos)
Learning to arrange by ear and borrowing from other arrangers
Arranging for people and for voices (Holman, Siegel, Gil Evans)

communities.name: Where the beat sits: time, feel and who keeps it
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection and many eras talk about time itself: where the beat sits and who is responsible for it. The core of the cluster is the recurring question of playing on top of, ahead of, or behind the beat. Bassists, drummers and horn players weigh whether the distinction is real or just rushing and dragging. They answer with named reference points, mostly the Miles Davis quintet rhythm sections (Louis Hayes, Ron Carter, Tony Williams, Elvin Jones), Ray Brown, Basie and Ellington. Others say time is everyone's job, or that it comes from the drummer's ride hand or the bassist, and they describe locking in with some players and never grooving with others. A smaller strand is historical. New Orleans and Dixieland players discuss two-beat versus four-beat and fast double-time, and a few mention how fusion, Mingus or changing age altered their own sense of time. The tellers are mostly rhythm-section players, the stories are rarely tied to a dated period, and the topic is consistent while the particular answers differ.
threads: On top of, ahead of or behind the beat: is it real?
Who keeps the time: bass, drums or everyone
Miles Davis quintet rhythm sections: Hayes, Carter, Williams, Elvin Jones
Fast tempos, double-time and two-beat versus four-beat
Locking in with particular drummers and bassists
How fusion, Mingus or age changed a player's time
