communities.name: Dice, cards and losing the pay
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians from many bands and cities tell about gambling, mostly dice (craps) and cards, and what it cost them. The stories run from Sam Wooding learning to gamble with Charley Johnson in Atlantic City in 1915 to touring-band crap games and poker on the bus in the 1940s, with Lucky Millinder's orchestra and the Ink Spots at the center of the Francis and Gus Johnson tales. A recurring plot is losing a gig fee or paycheck (Jacques Butler kicked down the stairs at the Smart Set Social Club, Francis losing his suit money at the Adams Theatre) and then swearing off gambling for good; Danny Barker, Al Gallodoro and Wooding all tell versions of this. Others describe gambling as a livelihood or habit, such as Professor Longhair as a professional card player, T-Bone Walker losing the money thrown at him, and a club secretary gambling away dues. Cosimo Matassa adds the view from the house, explaining how gambling houses guard against cheating and the evolution of loaded dice. Tellers agree that gambling was everywhere around bands and travel, and differ mainly on whether it was a vice they escaped or a trade they practiced. A few stragglers, such as Chuck Green's galloping dominoes dice game that set choruses, are only loosely connected.
threads: Losing the pay and quitting gambling for good
Crap games and poker on the road with Lucky Millinder and the Ink Spots
Learning to gamble young in Atlantic City
Gambling as a living: card players and house rules
Loaded dice and how houses prevent cheating
Money gambled away from clubs and shows

communities.name: Rough rooms, brawls and the law around the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: This small cluster gathers stories of the violence and shady authority that musicians met while working in dance halls, saloons and clubs, mostly from the 1920s to the 1950s. The strongest thread is the Los Angeles Central Avenue detective Maceo Sheffield, whom Reb Spikes and Joe Darensbourg both describe as a huge Prohibition-era officer who raided bootleg joints and house-rent parties but let musicians go, and whom Sonny Clay's band commemorated on a record. Around that core sit tales of brawling bars and bouncers: Art Hodes on Chicago saloons and the Brass Rail, John Malachi on Happy Joe's, Jay McShann on Alligator in Ponca City, Johnny DeDroit on keeping the peace at dances, and Eddie Dawson on the Big 25. A separate strand, from Cosimo Matassa, concerns mobsters and gangster-run record labels in 1950s-60s New Orleans. The tellers agree that rough rooms and rough men were part of the working environment, but the places and decades differ widely, so the stories share a mood more than a single event.
threads: Maceo Sheffield, the Central Avenue detective who spared musicians
Brawls, bouncers and mickeys in saloons and dance halls
Rough bars where the band played with the doors closed
Mobsters and gangster-run record labels in New Orleans
Gambling dens and clubs of early New Orleans

communities.name: Studio drummer on 1950s hit records
communities.parent_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"
communities.narrative: The core of this small cluster is New York session drummer David Albert Francis, who accounts for most of the central samples. He and bassist Milt Hinton, who urges and prompts him, run through the hit records he played on in the 1950s and early 60s. The list includes Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue, Bobby Darin, the Platters, Brook Benton, Dinah Washington, Ray Charles, Jackie Wilson, Screaming Jay Hawkins, the Four Seasons and Clyde Otis sessions. His stories are about studio craft: the tape overdub rhythm for Perez Prado's Patricia, the cowbell on Love Is Strange, the 12/8 feel on I Put a Spell on You, brushes and a gospel feel behind Dinah Washington, and the first bass drum mike. Beyond Francis the cluster thins into other musicians' recording-date recollections: Ray Sherman's Capitol and Radio Recorders dates, Clarence Ford's Imperial sessions with Pee Wee Crayton and T-Bone Walker, and Al Gallodoro's album and TV work. Those tellers share the period and the idea of recording sessions but not Francis's rock, R&B and pop focus. The wider 85-segment cluster is set around 1950-54 and draws on Hamilton, Rutgers, Smithsonian and Tulane interviews.
threads: Francis's lists of hit sessions he drummed on
Inventing studio rhythms: Patricia overdub, Love Is Strange cowbell, 12/8 groove
Backing Dinah Washington, Ray Charles and R&B singers
Clyde Otis demo sessions and the rhythm section deciding the groove
Other musicians' 1950s record dates and label work

communities.name: Session players on pop and rock hit records
communities.parent_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"
communities.narrative: Jazz musicians, mostly New York and Los Angeles studio players, recall being hired for pop and rock recording dates, typically between the early 1960s and early 1980s, with a few later ones. The stories are about the sessions themselves: overdubbing horns, guitar or tuba onto an existing track, writing or transcribing horn charts from an artist's rough ideas, and playing a short solo on request. Artists named include Bruce Springsteen, Paul Simon, Burt Bacharach, Billy Joel, Mick Jagger, Neil Diamond, John Lennon and Frank Zappa. Many tellers say they did not know at the time that the record would be a hit, or only found out later by hearing themselves on the radio or in a bar. Others describe session mechanics: three-hour dates with overtime, producers who had written out or punched in the solo, stand-in vocalists, and a twenty-minute call that meant a long trip. The tellers agree that this was well-paid, anonymous work, and they differ mainly in which artist and decade they remember. The subject holds fairly well but the samples span many unrelated artists and eras, so it is a loose grouping rather than one event.
threads: Overdubbing onto hit records without knowing they would be hits
Writing and transcribing horn charts for rock artists (Springsteen, James Taylor)
Bacharach and 1960s New York pop dates
Paul Simon, Phil Ramone and the singer-songwriter sessions
Producer-constructed solos, stand-in vocals and studio mechanics
Finding credits later: hearing yourself on the radio or in a bar

communities.name: Playing the taxi dance halls: dime tickets and hostesses
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Musicians recall working in taxi dance (jitney) halls, mostly in New Orleans, with La Vida, the Astoria and the downtown halls around the One-Eleven named most often. They describe the same ticket system. Patrons bought dime or nickel tickets, the hostesses were paid by splitting the ticket take or on percentage, and the bands played short dances, often two choruses, with a waltz or slow number at regular intervals. The stories are set mainly in the 1920s to 1940s. The Depression is remembered as a time of low pay, and one later account comes from about 1960. Tellers agree that the halls were white-patronized and that the work was nonstop and tiring. They differ on pay, which one calls poor and another good but with brutal hours. They also differ on details such as how the job was landed, the personnel in the band, and the halls closing during the war. The tellers are mostly New Orleans players from the Tulane collection, with a few from Rutgers. One sample, about San Jacinto Hall badges and officers, drifts away from the taxi-dance subject.
threads: How the ticket system and hostess pay worked
Hours, fatigue and pay at La Vida and the Astoria
Band personnel and how musicians got the dance-hall jobs
Waltzes, slow numbers and the dance routine
Who the patrons were and how the halls closed

communities.name: Sunday picnics and bands at the Lake Pontchartrain camps
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews, mostly in the Tulane collection, remember the lakefront as a Sunday and weekend playground for New Orleans. Milneburg is the center of the story, with West End, Spanish Fort, Bucktown and later Lincoln Beach around it. The setting runs roughly from the 1900s to the late 1920s. People rode the "Smokey Mary" train or boats out to camps, pavilions and piers. Club-sponsored picnics, basket lunches, lawn parties and dances ran all day, with several bands playing at once and "bucking" each other, and the tellers recall pay of a dollar and a half up to seven dollars. They agree on the train, the competing bands and the camps. They differ on race. Some describe white and Black camps side by side, others a mixed band, and Howard asks whether the camps were Black or white. A few samples drift: Hug and Parenti mention Rappolo, and Kmen is an 1840s lake-hotel outlier. The tellers are mainly New Orleans players, both Black and white.

Milneburg camps, pavilions and lawn parties
Bands bucking each other, with pay and prices
Race and the Black and white camps side by side
West End, Spanish Fort and Bucktown resorts
Camp life: construction, floods and the lake being filled in

communities.name: Playing for gangsters in Harlem's clubs
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall working in the nightclubs, cabarets and private gambling games of 1920s and early-1930s Harlem, Brooklyn and Greenwich Village, where the owners, patrons and protectors were gangsters. The tellers include bandleaders and sidemen such as Sonny Greer, Tom Whaley, Howard Scott, Garvin Bushell, Danny Barker and Barney Bigard. They name the bosses and clubs: Owney Madden and the Cotton Club, Dutch Schultz and Connie's Inn, Casper Holstein's numbers racket, and Jack "Legs" Diamond at the loft clubs and the Kentucky Club. The stories share a pattern. The mob hired the band, paid or stiffed it, and sometimes put it in danger, with shootings behind the piano, holdups, a rival club vandalized and a bodyguard with a machine gun. The Baron Wilkins killing recurs, and tellers differ on who ordered it and how. Most describe the gangsters as courteous, generous tippers and decent employers. A few recall being cheated or threatened. A handful of samples from the 1940s and 1950s, and some interviewer commentary, fall slightly outside this core.

The Baron Wilkins killing and Harlem gang rivalries
Gangsters as bosses: tips, pay and cheating
Shootings, holdups and danger on the bandstand
Playing private dice games and Village mob clubs

communities.name: Playing for Capone: gangsters and Chicago clubs
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians who worked Chicago in the 1920s and early 1930s tell what it was like to play in clubs owned, fronted or protected by gangsters, above all Al Capone and his brother Ralph. The setting is the South Side, Cicero and roadhouses such as the Burnham Inn, along with Dreamland, the Plantation, the Sunset and the Royal Gardens. Tellers broadly agree that the mob ran most clubs, paid well and tipped lavishly, and left musicians alone as long as they played. They differ on the tone. Alberta Hunter and Milt Hinton recall kind employers, and Hunter says she will say only good things about them. Others tell of danger: playing at gunpoint, bombs, shootings, rival gangs seated on opposite sides, armed escorts through Capone territory, and a man left dead when the lights came back on. The tellers are mostly Black and white Chicago players, singers and bandleaders from New Orleans, Harlem and the Midwest. A few segments drift into the wider Chicago night life of after-hours spots, con men and pickpockets, or into side stories such as Ma Rainey being robbed.
threads: Capone-owned and mob-run clubs as workplaces
Big tips, good pay and gangster patrons
Violence in the clubs: shootings, bombs, gunpoint shows, gang wars
St. Valentine's Day massacre and Capone-era events
Wild Chicago night life, after-hours spots and con men

communities.name: Bootleg liquor, speakeasies and staged raids in Prohibition
communities.parent_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs
communities.narrative: Musicians recall Prohibition-era drinking as part of everyday life in the 1920s and early 1930s, from New Orleans and Chicago to Harlem, Cleveland and the Kansas-Missouri border. The stories are about where liquor came from and how it was sold: corn liquor and needle whiskey, home brew and chalk beer, canned whiskey thrown from rum-runners' boats, and Capone-supplied whiskey resold for rent parties. Tellers describe the places where it was drunk, including speakeasies, buffet flats, rent parties and country parties where musicians were sometimes paid in whiskey. Many agree that police were paid off and that raids were tipped off in advance or staged for show. They differ in how close they were to it. Some, like Joe Turner and Milt Hinton, sold liquor as teenagers, while others, like Russell Procope and Sam Wooding, say they stayed out of the raided places and rent parties. Tellers come from every archive, both Black and white and from several cities. A few samples drift to other subjects, such as the 1919 Chicago police shootings, top hat and tails fashion, and a Kansas college sitting on John Brown's route.
threads: Making, buying and selling bootleg whiskey and home brew
Speakeasies, buffet flats and rent parties
Police pay-offs and staged raids
Dry Kansas versus wide-open Missouri and bootleg towns
Teenage musicians selling liquor to earn money

communities.name: Who sat in the drum chair: changing drummers
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Musicians recall who played drums in their band and who replaced whom. The stories run from the 1910s and 1920s New Orleans bands of Sam Morgan, Isaiah Morgan, Chris Kelly and Clarence Vincent, through the 1930s Savoy Ballroom and Paul Whiteman circles, to the 1950s Paradise Club and the Modern Jazz Quartet's drum chair in the 1990s. Each teller lists a sequence of drummers, such as Rudolph, Sean and Roy with Sam Morgan, or Timmie Kennedy giving way to Kalil. Reasons for the change include a bandmate's war service or stroke, a leader wanting more experienced players, and a leader unwilling to take a friend's chair. A few tellers also mention bands that used no drums at all, like the Light Crust Doughboys. The tellers are mostly New Orleans players, with some swing-era and bebop-era musicians. They agree that the drummer was the position that changed most often, and that a leader's drummer was hard to replace. The cluster is small and its tight core is only ten segments, so the shared subject is a theme in the drum chair rather than one event.
threads: Sequences of drummers in early New Orleans bands
Replacing a leader's long-time drummer in swing-era bands
Drummer changes because of illness, war or a leader's choice
Hiring a more experienced drummer for visiting stars
Bands that used no drums

communities.name: Royalties, flat fees and who owns the tune
communities.parent_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song
communities.narrative: Musicians from every era and scene tell about the money that came from recording and writing, and how little of it reached them. The stories run from the 1920s (flat thirty dollars a record while the writer of Crazy Blues collected royalties) through the swing years, when tunes were sold outright to publishers for $25 or $50, to the 1950s and 60s, when sidemen got scale and leaders fought for advances and their own publishing. The tellers largely agree that session fees were one-time and flat, that publishers and managers such as Irving Mills, Feist or Bess Berman profited from tunes the band made up, and that credit and royalties often went to a leader like Basie or Ellington rather than to the actual author. They differ in temperament: some, like Red Callender, praise ASCAP's steady checks, others like Trummy Young chase arbitration, Machito calls chasing royalties foolish, and Chico Hamilton and George Avakian describe winning ownership and large advances. A few segments drift to bootleg and unauthorized recordings or to recording logistics, so the cluster is mostly one subject with a loose edge. Tellers include sidemen, band leaders, session players, producers and engineers across all four archives.
threads: Flat session fees versus leaders' and writers' royalties
Selling tunes outright to publishers and losing credit
ASCAP, BMI and publishing deals and catalog ownership
Advances, contracts and record-company bargaining
Bootlegs, unauthorized taping and unpaid recordings
Lawsuits and arbitration over disputed songs

communities.name: Johnny Mandel on writing songs with lyricists
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: The core of this cluster is Johnny Mandel's own interview, in which he traces how film and television themes became songs and who wrote the words. He recalls Emily from The Americanization of Emily, Quietly There and The Shadow of Your Smile from the 1960s, and the MASH theme, Suicide Is Painless, from 1969-70. He names his lyricists: Alan and Marilyn Bergman, Johnny Mercer, Peggy Lee, Morgan Ames and Dave Frishberg. He also describes setting finished lyrics to music, the Manhattan Transfer and Singers Unlimited vocal work, and later songs from the 1980s and 1990s. A few outside segments share only the loose idea of how a particular song or tune came about. Roy Carew recalls writing words for Morton's songs in 1938. Billie Pierce explains how Coconut Island became her theme song. Alicia Olatuja describes the melodic arc of Truth in Blue. Steve Allen tells how Gus Bivona's tune got its title. Toshiko Akiyoshi explains the Japanese titles on an LP. Jay Leonhart and Hubert Laws talk about starting to write songs and lyrics. The result is a strong Mandel core with a scattered fringe of other musicians discussing the origins of individual songs.
threads: Film and TV themes that became songs (Emily, Shadow of Your Smile, MASH)
Working with lyricists: the Bergmans, Mercer, Peggy Lee, Morgan Ames, Frishberg
Setting finished lyrics to music
Manhattan Transfer and Singers Unlimited vocal projects
Other musicians on how their own songs and titles originated

communities.name: Cosimo Matassa on studio design and multitrack recording
communities.parent_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology
communities.narrative: This is almost entirely Cosimo Matassa explaining the engineering of his New Orleans studios, from the late 1940s through the 1960s and 70s. He describes the early J&M board, which had no EQ, then the Rampart Street years of direct-to-mono recording. He covers the move to a bigger room with ice cooling at the Cosmo studio, then two-track mono, three-track tape and bouncing or overdubbing. He says he resisted multitrack because he preferred live playing, and that he did not get four-track until Camp Street around 1965, when others had eight to twelve tracks. He also covers a mixer upgrade, the isolated concrete studio floor, drum miking, live room versus dead room acoustics, control room layout and monitors, effects such as plates and tape delay, and recording with live audiences. Bunny Robyn's mastering work on the West Coast and Les Paul's multitrack experiments appear as side notes. Two outside samples, Rudy Van Gelder on control room design and Jonathan Scales on click tracks, touch the same studio-craft territory but are not part of Matassa's account.
threads: From mono to three-track: bouncing, overdubbing and resisting multitrack
Studio rooms and floors: Rampart, Camp Street, live versus dead acoustics
Miking drums and instruments, mixers and EQ
Control rooms, monitors and effects like plates and tape delay
Mastering and tape-machine lore: Bunny Robyn, Les Paul, Sea Cruise

communities.name: Dime dances, jitney dances and paying to dance
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Musicians describe how dancing was sold in New Orleans dance halls and neighborhood venues, mostly from about 1900 to the late 1930s. Early tellers such as Isidore Barbarin and Louis Jones recall calico balls with 25 to 40 cent admission and ten-man bands. Later tellers (Julius Handy, Bobby Johnson Jr., Russell Moore, Kid Thomas Valentine) explain jitney and dime-a-dance arrangements, where tickets bought dances with hostesses, as at the Music Box, Budweiser, Levita and La Vida. Charlie Holmes describes the same ticket-and-hostess system at big ballrooms, where bands alternated half-hour sets. Kid Howard says Black patrons would not pay to dance by the dance, while Kid Thomas Valentine remembers alternating white and colored nights in a tiny Marrero grocery. A few samples drift to related dance jobs, such as society and fraternity dances for white audiences, or are interview logistics that only mention jitney playing in passing, so the cluster is clear but not perfectly tight.
threads: Admission prices and calico balls around 1900
Jitney and dime-a-dance tickets and hostesses
Dance hall and ballroom practice: band size, set lengths, the slow drag
Who would pay: race, audiences and segregated dance nights
Small neighborhood dance jobs versus society and fraternity dances

communities.name: Getting the first gig after arriving in New York
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians from many places and generations describe the first break after they arrived in New York: the job, audition or sit-in that turned a newcomer into a working player. Most are set in the 1950s and 60s, with a long tail from 1938 into the 1980s and 1990s. They are told by sidemen, drummers, pianists, saxophonists and a few vocalists. Birdland comes up most often, along with Hickory House, Jazzmania and Brooklyn jam sessions. Typical moves are a telegram or phone call from a bandleader (Benny Golson's Jazztet for Roy McCurdy, Joe Marsala for Art Hodes), a jam-session introduction (Jackie McLean for Tolliver, Kenny Dorham for Sam Jones), or a replacement or sub chair (Out of the Blue, Gil Evans, Sun Ra). The tellers agree that one contact or one night opened the door, and that the first New York job was often a band chair, not a solo career. They differ in era and idiom, from big-band and swing-era hires to bebop-era and later fusion and jazz-rock settings. A few samples drift away from this: a 1915-20 account of jug bands and a 1997 first public engagement are only loosely related, which is why coherence is not higher.
threads: Telegram, call or audition from a bandleader
Sitting in at Birdland and jam sessions
Subbing or replacing someone in an established band
Joining Blakey, Moody, Golson and other sideman jobs
Big-band hires in the swing and bop eras
Freelancing and first record dates

communities.name: Discography checks: recalling sideman record dates
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: In this cluster, musicians are walked through a discography by an interviewer (often Brown, also Berger and Kirchner) and asked to recall particular sideman recording sessions. Hubert Laws dominates, working through his CTI, Creed Taylor and Van Gelder dates of the 1960s and early 1970s: Wes Montgomery, Milt Jackson, Mongo Santamaria, Helen Merrill, Mingus and others. Dave Liebman does the same for his early-1970s New York and Japan dates, and Bill Holman does it for 1950s big-band and studio dates. A few others, such as Benny Carter for 1933-34, Toshiko Akiyoshi for 1956 and Kenny Barron, are asked about a session or two. The tellers largely agree on the pattern: they remember some dates vividly, such as a first session or a milestone call. They admit to having forgotten many others, and sometimes correct names or dates in the discography. The segments share a format (reading a session list and reacting to it) more than a single story, and a couple of samples, such as the Bunn segment on kicking off tunes, do not fit at all.
threads: Interviewer reads the discography, musician can't recall the date
Hubert Laws's CTI and Creed Taylor sideman sessions
Liebman's early-1970s New York and Japan record dates
Correcting garbled names and dates in Tom Lord's discography
Milestone first sessions (Wes Montgomery, Mongo at the Village Gate)

communities.name: Working the New York clubs: Ryan's, the Vanguard, the Embers
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians recall landing and keeping club jobs in New York, mostly in the 1940s through the 1960s. The recurring rooms are Jimmy Ryan's and Nick's on 52nd Street, Condon's and the Village Vanguard in Greenwich Village, and the Embers and Hickory House uptown, with a few later stops such as Slugs and the Audubon. The stories are about how a gig came about: who hired whom, which leader or booker (Joe Glaser, Eddie Condon, Jimmy Ryan) opened the door, and how a trio or quartet grew out of one engagement. Several tellers stress long residencies, such as months at the Vanguard, 16 to 17 weeks at the Embers and five years at Ryan's. Many are traditional or swing players (Zutty Singleton, Art Hodes, Georg Brunis, Herman Autrey, Jonah Jones), while a few bop-era players like Roy Haynes and Ram Ramirez place their own groups in Harlem and the Village. The cluster is loose at the edges. A few samples are about forming a combo or leading bands in Boston and on 46th Street rather than about a specific New York room, and the period and venues vary widely.
threads: Jimmy Ryan's, Nick's and Condon's on 52nd Street and in the Village
Long residencies at the Vanguard and the Embers
Trios and quartets formed out of one club job
Bookers, agents and the union opening doors
Bandleaders running their own rooms and groups

communities.name: Juan Tizol's compositions and who got credit
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: In this cluster, mostly Juan Tizol (with a few other voices) talks about how his tunes for the Ellington band came to be. They are set in the 1930s and early 1940s, in Chicago, Los Angeles and New York. Tizol describes writing pieces such as Caravan, Moon Over Cuba, Moonlite Fiesta, Pyramid, Admiration and Conga Brava, often by noodling on the trombone or on request during the conga craze. He then played them for Duke Ellington and Irving Mills. His account is consistent: Duke arranged and recorded everything, while titles and lyric credits were left to Duke or Mills. Tizol is more hesitant about details, such as where Caravan was written or who played what on a session, and his wife Rose sometimes supplies the memory instead. Other interviewees (Gus Johnson on a tune he wrote at Chicago's Music Box that people assumed was Ellington's, Arthur Briggs on first playing Cole Porter's Night and Day) touch on related questions of authorship and first recordings. Most of the material comes from the Rutgers interviews with Tizol, so the cluster reads as one musician's account with a few loosely related echoes.
threads: Tizol tunes: Caravan, Moon Over Cuba, Moonlite Fiesta, Pyramid, Conga Brava
Duke arranged and recorded everything Tizol wrote
Titles and lyric credits left to Duke or Irving Mills
Disputed or vague credits and uncertain recollections
Other musicians' authorship and first-recording claims

communities.name: How I compose: process, ideas and commissions
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians across many generations describe how they write original music, and nearly all of it is the working method rather than any one event. Most tellers are living composers and arrangers, with a few older figures such as Mary Lou Williams, Percy Heath on John Lewis, and Juan Tizol among the frequent voices. They disagree on where a piece starts. Some begin at the piano or with score paper (Schneider, Rovatti, Rivello), some with a rhythm and bass line (Sheller), a melody that dictates the form (Murray), the changes (Lellis), a title (Frishberg), or the emotion to be conveyed (Scales). They agree that ideas arrive away from the instrument and that finishing is hard. Many also discuss commissions, which can force a piece or work against personal feeling, and several add the craft of titles, lyrics and poems (Spellman, Sidran). A few segments stray into specific tunes or sessions from earlier eras, such as 'Angry', 'A La Ba' and Lizzie Miles, and Baker's cantata. The whole cluster is set mostly in the late 20th and early 21st century, with little dated.
threads: Where a piece starts: piano, rhythm, melody, changes or emotion
Ideas that arrive away from the instrument, dry spells and finishing
Commissions versus writing from personal feeling
Titles, lyrics and poems as part of songwriting
Reusing sketches, form and the craft of revision
Origins of specific older tunes and who wrote them

communities.name: Talking about the latest or upcoming record date
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: Across 163 interviews from all four collections, musicians stop to talk about a particular album they have just made, are about to make, or are being asked about: who was on the date, which label or producer was behind it, where it was cut, and how it came out. The majority are set between the 1960s and the late 1990s, with a few earlier (1950s Girard session, 1959-62 jazz LPs) and a few later (Anat Cohen in 2021, Bucky Pizzarelli in 2003). Many are present-tense updates ("latest release", "coming out next month", "albums in the works") given in the middle of an interview, from sidemen and leaders alike. Producers and labels recur, including Norman Granz and Pablo, Concord, Jazzology and George Buck, Arbors and Laurel, and Japan and Tokyo come up repeatedly as a place to record or release. Tellers differ on how they judge the results: some are proud (Marshall Royal's first album as a featured artist), others dislike the outcome (Jackie McLean on patched solos, Helen Humes on a badly assembled session). The stories share a loose subject, the individual record project, rather than one event or shared narrative.
threads: Latest and upcoming albums mentioned in passing
Labels and producers: Concord, Pablo, Jazzology, Arbors
Recording in Japan and Tokyo sessions
Reissues and documenting overlooked musicians on record
Unhappy with the finished record: edited or badly assembled sessions
Early-career and archival sessions recalled (1950s-60s LPs)

communities.name: Record labels: signing, owning and running them
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection tell stories about their dealings with record labels: who signed them, why they moved, and what the deals paid. The most common story is the artist-run label. Marian McPartland founded Halcyon after a badly packaged Dot record, Carla Bley started WATT, Chick Corea started Stretch, Branford Marsalis started his own label, and Strata-East was built on musicians funding their own finished records. In New Orleans, Tommy Ridgley and Allen Toussaint tell of funding labels and production companies, and Ellis Marsalis recalls the AFO label. A second story is the career move between labels. Examples include Konitz from Atlantic to Verve and Norman Granz, DeJohnette to Blue Note, Abbey Lincoln signing with Verve, Charles Lloyd choosing ECM, and Ramsey Lewis moving to Narada. A third is the economics and control of a record date: pressing costs, which take is released, artistic freedom, and producers who held back or never released material. The tellers span 1950s R&B and Chess records through 1990s major-label retrenchment and small independent or Japanese and German labels. They broadly agree that independence brought control but often poor money, and they differ on whether majors or independents served jazz better. Some samples, such as the Corea and Burton duets or the Armstrong banter, are only loosely about labels.
threads: Founding and running a musician-owned label
Signing with or leaving a label (Verve, Blue Note, ECM, Concord)
Becoming a record producer
Money, pressing costs and contracts
Artistic control and unreleased or held-back sessions
New Orleans independent labels and R&B producers

communities.name: Small labels and the business of making records
communities.parent_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums
communities.narrative: These stories are set mostly between the 1920s and the 1950s. Musicians talk about the practical side of getting onto records: who ran the label, who acted as A&R man, and which company a band moved to after a falling-out. Tellers range from early New Orleans and Harlem-era players (the Spikes Brothers' Sunshine label and record shop, c. 1921) to bandleaders and singers of the 1940s and 50s. Machito lists the labels he recorded for after Decca, Charlie Barnet recalls recording for a short-lived independent after quarrelling with Decca, and Professor Longhair, Ernie Fields and Red Callender describe sessions for small regional or one-off labels. Others describe a bad date, a session abroad, or how an LP reissue was sorted out. The stories share a loose subject, the people and companies behind recording dates. They differ in what they remember: some name labels precisely, others cannot recall the label at all, and a few samples drift to home recordings, acetate playbacks or A&R personalities.
threads: Small independent labels and their owners
Switching labels after leaving Decca
A&R men and producers
Bad or unusual recording dates
Label artwork, acetates and early recording equipment
LP transition and reissues

communities.name: Making R&B records: labels, producers and session dates
communities.parent_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"
communities.narrative: This small cluster gathers stories about how 1940s-60s rhythm-and-blues and jazz records actually got made and released, but it does not share a single subject. Its center of gravity is Teddy McRae's account of 1955. At Henry Glover's urging he worked with Champion Jack Dupree and devised "Walking the Blues", a record where he walked on a board while Dupree played. The tape was dubbed with rhythm, sent to Sid Nathan at King, and released. RCA's new Groove label under Bob Rolontz then invited McRae to record as "Mr. Bear" with an all-star band that included Mickey Baker. McRae's 1964 listening session on the Sunsets and Enrica sides is a later addition to the same thread. Around this core sit unrelated single-teller recollections of the record business: Theodore Bunn on Jules Bihari and Modern Records, Percy Gabriel on the all-night Roy Brown sessions at J&M in New Orleans, Maxine Sullivan on an r&b arrangement of "Loch Lomond", and Red Callender identifying sidemen and titles on unissued or poorly documented sessions. What ties them is the mechanics of sessions, labels and producers rather than a shared event, and one interviewee, McRae, supplies most of the strongest material.
threads: Teddy McRae's "Walking the Blues" with Champion Jack Dupree (1955)
Bob Rolontz's Groove label and the Mr. Bear sides
Independent label owners and producers (Bihari, Sid Nathan, Glover)
New Orleans and West Coast session nights
Identifying sidemen and unissued sides in discographies

communities.name: Making records: sessions, studios and lost discs
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians from many eras recall the occasions on which they were recorded, and what became of the results. The stories run from Gennett sessions in Indiana in the early 1920s (the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, Rappolo and Chink Martin's unreleased guitar duet) and Black Patti and Melrose sessions, through 1930s Decca-supervised dates at the Roosevelt Hotel and wartime glass-disc home recordings, to 1950s Decca dates and a 2023 session with its takes and soloists. Tellers are mostly New Orleans players recorded by Tulane's archive, with Rutgers and Hamilton interviewees describing New York and California dates. The recurring concerns are who played, which takes were usable, whether anything was issued, and whether copies survive: some recordings were never released, some are lost, and some were reissued on collector labels. A few tellers say they made no records at all, or that their family never cared about them. The one thing holding it together is recording as an event, and the period (1920s to 2023) and the places are very varied.
threads: Gennett and other early 1920s sessions (Rappolo, NORK)
Unreleased, lost or hard-to-find records
Reissues and collector interest
Home and disc recordings made during the 1940s
Studio sessions: takes, sidemen and label dates
Players who never recorded or did not care

communities.name: Who wrote the book: bands and their arrangers
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians from many bands and cities describe who wrote the arrangements their bands played. Typical tellers are bandleaders, sidemen and pianist-arrangers recalling the 1920s through the 1950s, with a few set later. They name in-house arrangers (Cab Calloway's Andy Gibson and Buster Harding, Eckstine's Tadd Dameron and Budd Johnson, Hampton's Milton Buckner), outside freelancers hired or bought from by the chart (Don Redman, Reginald Forsythe, Zilner Randolph for Earl Hines), and stock arrangements that gave way to special charts. Many accounts are practical: how arrangers were paid, who wrote for whom, and how players like Harry Edison and Buck Clayton learned to arrange themselves. The tellers agree that arrangers shaped a band's sound and that the New York writers set the pace. They differ in setting, from New Orleans dance bands to Kansas City and territory bands, Harlem shows and Latin bands. A few segments drift away from the subject, such as an interview-day opener or a modern reworking of Basie charts, but most keep to arrangers and the band book.
threads: Naming the band's in-house arrangers
Freelance writers hired or paid by the chart
Stock arrangements giving way to special charts
Players learning to arrange and writing on the side
Arrangers for the big names: Basie, Hines, Lunceford, Calloway, Eckstine
Arrangers in regional, show and Latin bands

communities.name: Learning to arrange: self-taught and coached
communities.parent_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made
communities.narrative: Musicians across eras recall how they learned to write arrangements, usually with little or no formal schooling. The setting runs from 1920s New Orleans, Chicago and Harlem bands through the swing era to 1970s-90s studio and Latin work in New York and Hollywood. Many describe teaching themselves by trial and error. Benny Carter, Billy Taylor and Frank Foster studied stock arrangements, laying parts out on the floor or copying them from records. Artie Shaw used Forsyth's orchestration book, and others, including Anne Phillips and Jon Weber, learned from Henry Mancini's book. Others were coached by a colleague or bandleader, such as Charlie Johnson, Phil Moore, Moon Mullens or Nelson Riddle, who in turn learned voicings by asking the band to play pieces. Later players such as Fred Wesley, Alan Broadbent and Marty Sheller learned string and horn writing by asking players about ranges, studying scores and working in sessions. The tellers agree that learning by doing, and by listening to other arrangers' scores, mattered most. They differ on whether any formal teacher or school had a part. A few segments drift to related topics such as band service, head arrangements and a conservatory degree, but the arranging apprenticeship is the common thread.
threads: Teaching himself from stock arrangements and books
Coached by a bandleader, colleague or arranger
Learning voicings and ranges by asking players
Learning strings and horns in studio and session work
Head arrangements and band-built charts
Barriers and no formal training

communities.name: Musicians on politics, race and the state
communities.parent_name: Politics, race and the state of the country
communities.narrative: Musicians across eras are asked, or volunteer, what they made of politics: voting, parties, presidents, protest and race in America. The oldest strand is the 1930s to 1950s, when players such as Jimmie Crawford, Andrew Blakeney, Mary Lou Williams, Bud Freeman and Teddy Wilson describe leaning Democratic under Roosevelt, playing benefits and paid rallies, and deciding to stick to music. A sharper strand covers the Communist and McCarthy-era pressures on Artie Shaw, Art Hodes and John Collins, with Paul Robeson as a recurring figure. The 1960s civil rights movement, Martin Luther King and his assassination recur, and many tellers, including Slam Stewart and Luther Henderson, say they were insulated or too wrapped up in music. A late strand, from 2008 to 2020, covers reactions to Obama's election, the pandemic response and the protests after the Minneapolis killing, mostly in Hamilton and Smithsonian interviews. Tellers agree that race frames their view of politics but differ on whether music itself is political enough or whether musicians should organize and act. The cluster is a loose umbrella: some samples are unrelated fragments such as Nicki Parrott's citizenship, a New Orleans mayoral remark, and Eddie Palmieri and Alpha 66.
threads: Staying out of politics: voting, parties and Roosevelt-era leanings
Communist rallies, Paul Robeson and McCarthy-era blacklisting
Civil rights era and Martin Luther King, from inside or outside the movement
Obama's election and reflections on racism today
2020 pandemic, policing and protests
Race, suffering and why performers accommodated

communities.name: American jazz musicians working and touring in Europe
communities.parent_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan
communities.narrative: This is a large community of stories about American jazz musicians going to Europe, and sometimes Japan, to work. It runs from the 1920s through the 1970s, with some later tours, and is centered on Paris, London, Germany and Scandinavia. Tellers recall long residencies and band tours in the 1920s and 30s: Sam Wooding in Germany, Arthur Briggs moving between London, Brussels, Berlin and Paris, and Cab Calloway's and Teddy Hill's 1930s tours with the Palladium as a showpiece. Others describe postwar stays and festival dates, such as Kenny Clarke in Paris in 1948, Doc Cheatham substituting for Buck Clayton in 1950, and Duke Ellington's tours. Many contrast knowledgeable, respectful European audiences with American ones, describing fans who knew every record and crowds that mobbed arrivals. John W. Bubbles tells a harder version, stranded in Germany around 1949 on a one-way ticket, and Benny Carter describes a State Department tour of the Middle East. The samples agree on travel abroad as the setting but differ in era, motive and the musician's situation, so the cluster is broad and loosely bounded, and a few samples fit only weakly, such as personnel changes, teaching, or composition commissions.
threads: Interwar bands and residencies in Paris, London and Berlin
Postwar expatriates and festival dates in Paris
Big band and State Department tours abroad
European audiences versus American audiences
Stranded or staying on in Europe
Touring Japan and later-career European gigs

communities.name: Taking the band to Europe: tours abroad
communities.parent_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan
communities.narrative: Musicians recall going abroad to play, mostly to Europe, and what the trip was like on the ground. The core is the 1950s and early 1960s, when American big bands and soloists crossed the Atlantic. The stories centre on Count Basie's European tours, Woody Herman's 1959 trip, and above all Quincy Jones's 1959-60 "Free and Easy" tour. That show failed in Paris, and Quincy kept the 19-piece band working for months on his own money. Other tellers describe leaving for Europe and staying, as Slide Hampton did for eight years. Some describe Europe's clubs and unions, such as Ronnie Scott's, or the British jazz scene that grew around Ken Colyer and Chris Barber. The tellers agree that these tours were exciting but often badly managed and short of money. They differ in whether Europe was an adventure, an escape, or a stretch of hard travel. The edges drift to other trips: a 1985 tour with management trouble, a 2025 steelpan player whose instrument was lost in Latvia, and a 1930s missed overseas chance with Noble Sissle.
threads: The 1959-60 Quincy Jones Free and Easy tour and its collapse
Basie's European tours in the 1950s and 1960s
Woody Herman's band abroad and staying on in Europe
Bad management, money trouble and keeping a band together on the road
British and continental scenes met on arrival (Ronnie Scott's, Colyer and Barber)
Later travel mishaps (lost instruments, missing passports)

communities.name: Musicians on the news, technology and a worsening world
communities.parent_name: Politics, race and the state of the country
communities.narrative: In these digressions, musicians step outside music to give opinions on the state of the world: the media, politics, technology and social decline. Nat Hentoff compares the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal and talks about reading both sides. Laurence Juber describes society crashing into the Information Age and reading across the political spectrum. Cosimo Matassa defends NASA after the Challenger disaster, and Herbie Hancock describes a foundation meant to make technology serve humanity. Others take a darker view. James Moody says governments lie and divide people. Artie Shaw lists ocean debris, nuclear weapons and people who do not read. Eddie Sauter says life has been getting worse since World War I, with destructive tools and entrenched interests. Eddie Palmieri says poverty is the root problem and that his lyrics ask people to think. The tellers agree only loosely that they are commenting on society, and most of these segments are unanchored in time and place. They are tangents prompted by an interviewer's question, not a story about jazz.
threads: Newspapers, bias and reading both sides
Information overload and the Internet age
Technology, NASA and responsibility to humanity
Governments lying and social decline
Nuclear weapons, war and postwar disillusion
Poverty and music as social message

communities.name: Fish fries and lawn parties: neighborhood social gigs
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Most of the central stories describe the informal neighborhood social events where New Orleans musicians first played and where the community gathered: Friday and Saturday-night fish fries and Sunday-night lawn parties. They are mainly set in the 1910s and 1920s, with Kid Ory reaching back to the 1890s and a few accounts running into the 1950s. Tellers such as Paul Barbarin, Harold Dejan, Fess Manetta, Kid Howard and Joe Loyacano agree on the mechanics: a red lantern hung outside marked a fish fry, admission was a small charge, and drinks, sandwiches and supper were sold. Backyards, vacant lots and rented tarpaulins or canvas served as dance floors. They differ on whether a band was hired. Barbarin recalls singing and clapping with no band, while others describe hired bands or musicians sitting in. A smaller fringe drifts to related gatherings such as picnics, lakefront camps, quilting parties and a Christmas party job. These are told mostly by Tulane-archive musicians, and the fish-fry core is a clear, shared subject.
threads: Fish fries on Friday and Saturday nights, marked by a red lantern
Lawn parties in backyards and vacant lots: admission, drinks, who promoted them
Who hired bands, and musicians sitting in at house parties
Picnics and lakefront camps: food, beer kegs and hours
Other home gatherings: quilting parties, house parties, a Christmas yard job

communities.name: Who were the great drummers? Musicians rate their peers
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Across hundreds of interviews, musicians are asked, or volunteer, who the best drummers were, and they answer by naming names and sizing them up. The core of the cluster is early New Orleans: street bass drummers and brass-band men such as Red Happy Bolton, Black Benny, Henry Zeno, the Barbarin brothers, Louis Cottrell and Baby Dodds, remembered by the older players from the 1900s to the 1930s and often prompted by an interviewer (Russell, Dance) working through lists of names. Others carry the same conversation into territory bands and swing and modern jazz, praising Sid Catlett, Jo Jones, Cozy Cole, Buddy Rich, Gene Krupa, Mel Lewis, Louie Bellson, Freddie Waits and Bernard Purdie. The tellers agree on the qualities they prize: steady time, a drummer who blends under the soloist and shapes the backing to each player, and good press rolls, brushes and cymbal work. They differ on showy novelty effects, which some admire (sound effects for silent film, sleigh bells) and others treat as a failing. Many segments are brief name-dropping exchanges, and a few drift into band personnel or other instruments, so the shared subject is peer appraisal of drummers rather than any single event.
threads: Early New Orleans street and brass-band bass drummers
Favorite drummers named and compared by peers
Sid Catlett, Jo Jones and the swing-era greats
Time-keeping, blending with soloists and what makes a drummer good
Showy drummers, novelty effects and drumming for silent film
Territory-band and Chicago drummers remembered by sidemen

communities.name: What makes a good drummer: time, support, and solos
communities.parent_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why
communities.narrative: Across 110 interviews, musicians from New Orleans, swing and bebop circles share opinions about drumming itself: what a drummer is for and how it has changed. The core view is that a drummer keeps steady time, neither rushing nor lagging, supports the soloists and the band, and gives lift and a back beat. Freddie Green, Kenny Clarke, Theodore Saunders and Tommy Ridgley all say this, and Saunders calls the big band drummer the band's general. Older players, especially New Orleans men such as Pops Foster, Natty Dominique, Happy Goldston and Abby Foster, contrast the old drummers' rolls, sticks, bass drum, tuning and soft touch with modern drummers they hear as cymbal beaters or showoffs. Many date drum solos to the swing era (Krupa, Hampton, Cozy Cole, Buddy Rich) and say early bands rarely featured them. Bandleaders and sidemen such as Benny Carter, Slide Hampton and Holman say what they want from a drummer, including short solos and awareness of orchestration. A few segments drift into individual drummers (Baby Dodds, Zutty, Trepagnier) or other topics, but most share this one subject.
threads: Steady time and supporting the band: no rushing or lagging
Old New Orleans drummers versus modern drummers: rolls, tuning, bass drum
When drum solos arrived and whether they help or hurt
Favorite and influential drummers: Baby Dodds, Zutty, Krupa, Cozy Cole, Trepagnier
What bandleaders and arrangers want from a drummer
Show drumming versus jazz drumming and playing blues and breaks

communities.name: Working the New York clubs: rooms, bills and gigs
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: This small cluster gathers musicians' recollections of particular club engagements and the rooms they worked, mostly in New York, Harlem and Newark, with a few from Chicago, San Francisco and Louisiana. The tellers name specific venues such as the Half Note, Birdland, the Hickory House, Wells in Harlem, Jazz at Pearl's and the Iridium. They describe who they played with, how the bills were arranged, and what the room was like. The recurring experiences are being booked into a room that did not suit the music (show tunes in a steak house), a noisy or unfriendly setting (a disco upstairs drowning out a trio), and the satisfaction of finding a good room after years of hard ones. Stories are set mainly from the 1950s through the 2000s, and the tellers include bandleaders, sidemen, a pianist and singer, and even recording engineer Rudy Van Gelder hauling gear to club dates. The shared subject is only loosely 'a gig at a named club'. The samples differ widely in era and place, so the cluster is a loose grouping rather than one story that musicians tell in common.
threads: Booked into a room that did not fit the music
Long runs and weekly residencies at a club
Harlem and Newark rooms and their bandleaders
Who shared the bill: opening acts and snubs
Recording live at the clubs
Finding a good room after years of hard ones

communities.name: Musicians on politics, power and the state of the world
communities.parent_name: Politics, race and the state of the country
communities.narrative: These segments gather musicians stepping outside music to comment on politics, society and world affairs, mostly in interviews from the 2000s to 2020. Tellers weigh in on elections and presidents (Trump, Obama, the 2008 race), on terrorism after the 2001 attacks, on who really controls the system (Buffett, Soros, Halliburton, prison and war corporations), and on whether lasting peace is possible. Others turn to history and conscience, such as Hitler's regime and what one would have done, or to money in medicine and drug prices. There are also personal statements of social purpose: a concert speech urging people to vote, AIDS advocacy, and teaching as a way of leaving the world better. Mingus's 1978 wish to start the world over with more love is the earliest voice. The tellers share a worried, often cynical view of institutions and a belief in love, service or music as the remedy, but they do not tell one single story. The cluster is a loose set of reflective opinion pieces rather than a shared event, and it draws on a wide spread of musicians from the Smithsonian, Hamilton and Rutgers collections.
threads: Elections, presidents and a corrupt country
Terrorism, war and the prospects for peace
Who really controls the system: money and corporations
Conscience and history: Hitler's regime
Music, voting and service as a force for good
Social causes: AIDS work and healthcare costs

communities.name: Asked about the state of the country
communities.parent_name: Politics, race and the state of the country
communities.narrative: In late-career interviews, mostly from the Hamilton College (Fillius) collection and mostly recorded between 2000 and 2024, musicians are asked a closing question about the state of America and answer with their politics. The answers follow the presidents of the day: Clinton and Bush and the Iraq war, Obama and obstruction, Trump's two terms, the pandemic, January 6 and Biden. Most tellers are worried or angry. They cite polarization, racism, inequality, police stops, health care and the cutting of arts education. A few stay cautiously hopeful, citing good people outlasting bad and the system's safeguards. Many say music is their refuge or the thing to focus on, and some are cautious about airing political views at all. Expatriates and visitors, including Canadians, Britons and Europeans, compare the US with home, while a few segments drift to Covid or to related items such as a goodwill ensemble and a new dystopic record. The interviewer, Monk Rowe, often chimes in. The tellers agree that the mood is dark but differ on whether things are really worse or only more visible.
threads: Trump years, January 6 and the 2024 election
Bush, Iraq, the Patriot Act and civil liberties
Obama, obstruction and the unchanging system
Racism, inequality and policing
Pandemic and Covid politics
America seen from abroad: Canada, Britain, Europe
Music as refuge and fears for the arts

communities.name: Working the New York clubs: 52nd Street and Birdland
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: These are stories of playing and hearing music in the New York club scene, centered on 52nd Street in the 1940s and Birdland in the 1950s, with a few later echoes up to Birdland's 60th anniversary in 2009. Tellers describe the rooms (the Three Deuces, Kelly's Stable, the Onyx Club, the Downbeat on 54th Street, the Metropole, the Apollo) and the groups they led or sat in with there. Some stress learning from the legends who came in to listen, such as Hawkins, Byas, Lester Young and Eckstine. Others give working detail: who was in the band, who booked it, how long the engagement ran, and Morris Levy's role at Birdland. The tellers are mostly working instrumentalists and bandleaders, with a few pianists and Latin-band leaders, and they agree on the clubs as the center of the music. They differ on which era and which scene they are describing, and the shared subject is loose: the cluster is small, spans 63 interviews and runs from the 1940s to 2009. Several samples are only tangential, such as dating a gig from a reference book or club dates in Brooklyn.
threads: Leading a group on 52nd Street
Playing and hearing music at Birdland under Morris Levy
Learning from the older masters who came to listen
Midtown rooms and sitting in: Metropole, Downbeat, Hickory House
Pinning down dates and personnel of club engagements

communities.name: Swing Street and Harlem: New York's jazz clubs and hangouts
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations and all four archives recall the New York clubs and musicians' hangouts where they heard, sat in and worked. The core is Harlem's Seventh Avenue and its side streets (the Rhythm Club on 132nd Street, the Nest Club and Tillie's on 133rd, Smalls Paradise, Greasy's, the Victoria Bar) and 52nd Street (the Onyx, Famous Door, Three Deuces). Most stories are set between the late 1920s and the 1950s. Tellers agree that these rooms were a social world as much as a workplace: places to eat, play pool, jam, get cut by a rival, and see Hawkins, Tatum, Eldridge or Billie Holiday. Older Harlem players stress jam-session tests and juice joints. 52nd Street players and later arrivals describe sitting in at the Onyx and the Street's decline into strip shows around 1949-50, when Birdland and the Royal Roost took over. Some samples drift to Greenwich Village rooms, Chicago and Boston Road, and many are very short, list-like mentions of club names.
threads: The Rhythm Club and Harlem hangouts: jam sessions, cutting contests
Seventh Avenue and 133rd Street juice joints, the Nest Club and Tillie's
52nd Street: the Onyx, sitting in, and the Street's end in 1949-50
Bebop-era rooms: Birdland, Royal Roost, Minton's
Village and midtown clubs: Nick's, Condon's, Metropole, Half Note
Lists of clubs and who played where

communities.name: First nights in New York and 52nd Street
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians from across the country, and a few from abroad, recall arriving in New York for the first time and going straight to the clubs. The commonest version is the 1940s trip to 52nd Street, where young players such as Ray Brown, Roy Haynes, Phil Woods, Lee Konitz and George Wein heard Dizzy Gillespie, Coleman Hawkins, Art Tatum, Don Byas and Charlie Parker at the Three Deuces, the Onyx Club and Kelly's Stable. Others tell the same story from different decades: soldiers hearing a New Orleans band at Rector's in 1918, the Original Dixieland Jazz Band becoming a sensation at Reisenweber's in 1917, Big Nick Nicholas living over Minton's, and later arrivals at Birdland, the Village Vanguard, the 34th Street loft and Small's, running into the 1990s. Tellers agree that the city was overwhelming and the music was the main reason for going, and several say they were quickly accepted. They differ in what they found: some were thrilled, John Levy was disappointed by the Onyx, and Marian McPartland avoided Harlem altogether. A few samples drift away from the arrival theme, for example the 1960s downtown arts scene and the late-1990s neo-soul wave, but most share one subject.
threads: First trip to 52nd Street in the 1940s, hearing Hawkins, Tatum, Gillespie and Byas
Arriving in the city: buses, hotels, relatives and first impressions
First jam sessions, lofts and getting accepted on the scene
Harlem and Minton's versus midtown clubs
Earlier and later arrivals, from the 1917 Dixieland sensation to the 1990s

communities.name: Arriving in New York: finding a room and a break
communities.parent_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene
communities.narrative: Musicians from across the country, and from Cuba, Britain and abroad, tell of coming to New York to make it, mostly in the late 1920s through the 1940s with a later run into the 1950s and 1960s. The arrival story usually starts with a decision, often prompted by a friend, a bandleader or a record-company argument that serious players have to be in New York. It then turns to the practical problem of where to sleep. Tellers describe landladies, an aunt's or uncle's flat, rooming houses, a shared apartment in Harlem (Lenox Avenue, Edgecombe, 126th Street, 111th Street), a hotel near Birdland, or in one case a pickup truck. Money is thin: dime rolls and coffee, fifty-cent rehearsals in an unheated hall, union transfer rules that limited early work. Established players such as Chick Webb, Booker Little, Ben Webster and Duke Ellington appear as the people who took newcomers in, and a few tellers, like Buster Smith, say the New York stamp brought them no work. The earlier tellers are mostly Black bandsmen settling in Harlem, and the later ones are younger players, including women and non-American musicians, arriving in the 1950s through the 1990s. The edges of the cluster drift into general New York life, such as the Polo Grounds, teaching in Philadelphia while commuting, and job offers elsewhere, so the core arrival-and-lodging story is clear but the outer samples are looser.
threads: Deciding to go: the pull of New York and who urged them
Getting there: buses, boats, trains and a car with two dogs
Where they slept: Harlem rooms, relatives, landladies and roommates
Broke and hungry: scraping by before the first steady job
Being taken in by an established player
Later arrivals: 1950s to 1990s newcomers finding a place

communities.name: What "free jazz" means: structure within freedom
communities.parent_name: Playing with and hearing Coltrane
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations are asked about free jazz and free improvisation, and they mostly answer by resisting the label. Rashied Ali says the new music was not planned and arose spontaneously on the bandstand as an evolution from bebop. Joseph Daley rejects "avant-garde" and "free jazz" as labels and describes spontaneous composition with Sam Rivers, in which structure emerges and tradition and the standards are never abandoned. Karolina Strassmayer and Tom Varner, both younger players, say they cannot define free music and keep returning to structure, self-imposed guidelines and serious ideas, often reacting to remarks by Karl Berger, Roscoe Mitchell or Braxton. Older players tell it from experience. Lee Konitz recalls the free pieces recorded in 1949 for Capitol, Ellis Marsalis a fully free concert and a partly free duo with Eddie Harris, and Doc Cheatham a 1970s record date with Beaver Harris where free playing meant forgetting conventional changes. The tellers agree that freedom was never formless, but they disagree about how much to call it a break with bebop and how much a continuation of it. The samples are set between 1949 and the late 1980s, and most come from the Hamilton and Smithsonian interviews.
threads: Rejecting the labels: avant-garde and free jazz
Free playing grew out of bebop, not a plan
Structure, tradition and standards inside free improvisation
Playing with Sam Rivers, Karl Berger and other free-music figures
Free sessions and records: Konitz's Intuition, Marsalis with Harris, Cheatham with Beaver Harris
How time and form work without changes

communities.name: Society halls: Monday banquets and dances
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the neighborhood dance halls and benevolent-society events of early New Orleans, mostly from about 1900 to the early 1920s, with some tellers carrying it into the 1930s. The central picture is the society banquet, usually a Monday afternoon anniversary affair at halls such as Economy, Perseverance and Artesian. A band was hired, the society paid for free food, beer or wine, and musicians were paid a few dollars. Alongside it sit the ticketed dances, with admission, deposits for the band, soft drinks or wine, and respectable manners. Several tellers also describe lawn parties and small neighborhood halls tied to a grocery or church, and a few place similar halls outside the city, in Mandeville and Thibodaux. Tellers agree on the rhythm of Sunday dances and Monday banquets and on the food and drink. They differ in which hall or ward they place the events, and a few mention Prohibition-era near-beer. Almost all are New Orleans players interviewed for the Hogan Jazz Archive.
threads: Monday afternoon society anniversary banquets with free food and drink
Economy, Perseverance and Artesian Hall dances
Lawn parties and small neighborhood halls by ward
How bands were hired and paid for hall jobs
Dance halls outside the city (Mandeville, Thibodaux)

communities.name: Remembering the old dance halls of New Orleans
communities.parent_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the dance halls where jazz was played in New Orleans, mostly in the 1890s to 1920s. They name the halls, say where each stood (downtown, uptown, Algiers, Canal Street), and describe how they were built. Economy Hall, Globe Hall, Artesian Hall, Perseverance Hall, Masonic Hall and Funky Butt Hall come up most often. Many tellers are asked about this by interviewers such as Bill Russell, who sort out locations and, in some cases, hope to photograph surviving buildings. Details include high bandstands, balconies, upstairs rooms, and halls now turned into churches or torn down. Tellers also separate the halls by social stratum, by uptown versus downtown, and by Black, white or Creole clientele. A smaller strand covers related dance venues such as jitney (taxi) dance halls, roof gardens, rifle clubs, society dance sites and Bourbon Street rooms. These venues sit at the edges of the main subject and are the weaker part of the cluster. The tellers are mostly Tulane archive interviewees, with a share from Rutgers.
threads: Where specific halls stood and what they looked like
Halls turned churches, burned, rebuilt or torn down
Downtown versus uptown halls and who they served
Algiers and across-the-river halls
Jitney dance halls, roof gardens and club rooms
Halls where musicians played and with which bands

communities.name: In the studio versus on the bandstand: how records get made
communities.parent_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology
communities.narrative: Musicians from every era and collection talk about what it is like to make a record, usually by contrasting it with playing live. The earliest tellers, working in the 1920s, describe acoustic recording: playing into horns in Berlin or Cincinnati, drums and bass left out or reduced to woodblock and cymbal, a few rehearsals and the occasional remake on the Morton dates. Later players recall the swing and bop era studios (Liederkranz Hall, Columbia's 30th Street, Rudy Van Gelder's) and the Blue Note rule of about three takes. Then come the multitrack, overdubbing, splicing and click-track years, up to virtual recording in 2020. The tellers broadly agree that the first or second take is usually best and that live feel matters, and many distrust editing, isolation booths and studio gimmicks. They differ on technology: Mingus, Jon Hendricks and George Lewis favor live or close-together playing, while engineers and producers such as Charles Calello and Joel Dorn explain what tracking and overdubbing add. A few segments only share the loose recording setting, such as session personnel, photographs taken at sessions, or how bandmates learn parts.
threads: Acoustic-era recording in the 1920s
First takes, retakes and the three-take rule
Live recording versus studio polish and editing
Multitrack, overdubbing, splicing and click tracks
Studios, engineers and room sound (Van Gelder, Columbia)
Preparing charts and rehearsing for sessions

communities.name: Benny Goodman and breaking the color line
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Musicians and observers recall how Benny Goodman put Black players on the bandstand in the mid-1930s, first Teddy Wilson in the trio (1935-36), then Lionel Hampton in the quartet and Charlie Christian in the sextet and orchestra. Most tellers credit Goodman himself, and many add John Hammond and Helen Oakley Dance for pushing him to do it. Players such as Wilson, Hampton, Jimmy Maxwell and Sonny Greer describe audiences that liked the mixed groups and Goodman standing up to hotel managers, while Harry Edison notes that hotels still would not hire Black bands. Others complicate the picture: Pelote describes Wilson and Hampton as a side act, Bobby Shew recalls Goodman's racist treatment of Buddy Tate, and Cliff Leeman notes that Dorsey hired a Black player years later. Set mostly in Chicago, New York and Harlem between about 1928 and 1960, the stories are told by Black and white sidemen, producers and later players who judge Goodman's legacy. A few side stories cover earlier hidden mixed jamming and mixed recordings, and Sicilian and Chicago experiences of prejudice.
threads: Teddy Wilson joins the trio, with John Hammond and Helen Oakley Dance pushing
Hampton and Christian join: the quartet, mixed audiences and hotels
Hotel managers and unions resisting mixed bands
Comparisons with Dorsey, Shaw and Basie's band
Later judgments of Goodman's legacy and his treatment of Black players
Earlier hidden mixed jamming and recording

communities.name: Synthesizers and machines taking musicians' work
communities.parent_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1920s through the 1990s describe new technology eliminating paid playing jobs. Teddy Wilson and Skitch Henderson recall sound movies ending theater pit orchestras; later tellers such as Tom Porrello, Dick Hyman, Lou Marini and Pete Levin describe synthesizers and samplers displacing string sections, pit and film orchestras and staff work in the 1970s to 1990s. Drum machines and backing tracks are said to be cheaper than drummers, and Ronnie Zito mentions laptops and tracks replacing live bands at a casino. The tellers disagree on how bad it is. Jerry Hey and Michael Abene see synthesizers as a legitimate instrument or a useful tool, while Wilson accepts progress but says electronics should not replace instruments that express the soul. Greg Caputo thinks the electronic drum era has passed because studios still want real drummers. The tellers are mostly working studio, pit and big-band players and arrangers, with one off-topic sample (Jimmy Maxwell blaming publicity and the union) outside the core theme.
threads: Sound movies ending pit orchestras
Synthesizers and samplers replacing strings and horns
Drum machines cheaper than drummers
Backing tracks and computers replacing live bands
Human soul versus electronic sound

communities.name: Do you remember making records?
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Across 149 interviews, mostly Tulane and Rutgers with some Smithsonian and Hamilton, interviewers ask musicians what they recorded, and the musicians try to remember. Most of the sampled stories are set in the 1920s through the 1950s. The recurring pattern is the interviewer's discography question: which sessions, which labels, which sidemen, which titles. Answers are often hazy. Some players recall one session, such as Narvin Kimball with Celestin. Others say they never recorded, like Mitchel McAllister and Bella Cornish. Others only learn years later that they are on a record, like Darnell Howard on Tiny Parham's Frogtown Blues or Vic Dickenson on a Blanche Calloway side. New Orleans is the strongest cluster of sessions, especially Papa Celestin's recordings, Richard M. Jones's dates and the question of which local bands were recorded at all. Chicago, New York and California dates appear too, and a few later outliers, such as a 2005 Thad Jones tribute, a 1976 India recording and a 1980 direct-to-disc session, only share the word recording. The samples agree on the topic of recording sessions but not on a single story, so this is better read as a discography-recall pattern than one shared event.
threads: Celestin and other New Orleans band recordings of the 1920s
Richard M. Jones, Chicago and other 1920s race-record dates
Vague memory: cannot recall titles, labels or dates
Never recorded, or unsure whether the band did
Learning years later that they are on a record
Later-era sessions: V-Discs, tributes, direct-to-disc, tours

communities.name: Recording dates of the 1920s: personnel and discography checks
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians are asked to recall specific 1920s record sessions, usually while an interviewer such as Schaap, Albertson or Willard reads from a discography. The core is King Oliver's New York and Victor dates of 1926-32, along with the Clarence Williams sessions that Oliver and others were hired for. Benny Waters, Barney Bigard, J. C. Higginbotham and Charlie Holmes sort out who was on which date, and Waters distrusts the discographies. Around that core sit similar identification exchanges: Alberta Hunter on her Black Swan, Vocalion and Victor sides, Ory on the Spikes Brothers session, and Hazel on the New Orleans Rhythm Kings records. Others recall how recording worked, with megaphone and wax, a padded studio, and portable equipment in a Dallas furniture store. The tellers agree that memory of titles, personnel and dates is patchy and the printed record often wrong. The settings are mainly New York and Chicago, with a few in New Orleans, between about 1921 and 1932. The samples do not all concern Oliver, so the shared subject is the recording session as something to be reconstructed, not one event.
threads: King Oliver's late-1920s recording dates and who played
Clarence Williams hiring sidemen and running sessions
Interviewers checking discographies and correcting errors
Alberta Hunter's Black Swan, Vocalion and Victor sides
Early recording methods and studios
Other 1920s sessions: Spikes, Keppard, Ma Rainey, Sam Morgan

communities.name: Making my first record
communities.parent_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography
communities.narrative: Musicians across the archives recall their first recording date, or their first session as a leader, and how it came about. The stories run from the 1920s (Doc Cheatham with Ma Rainey, Buddy Burns in Chicago with Richard M. Jones, Punch Miller in New Orleans, Benny Waters in Philadelphia and New York) through the 1940s (Etta Jones with Leonard Feather, Billy Taylor, Melba Liston with Dexter Gordon, Terry Gibbs and Marty Napoleon under Teddy Reig) and the 1950s and 60s (Jackie McLean, Yusef Lateef, Hubert Laws, Ron Carter, George Benson), and a few reach the 1980s. Most are set in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles or New Orleans, and many name the label, the personnel and the pay. Tellers agree that the date was memorable, and several admit it was nerve-racking, as when Dave Frishberg read every written-out triplet. They differ in what they stress: some are sorting out which record was really first, often with an interviewer reading from a discography, while others tell anecdotes about producers, engineers or record strikes. The tellers are sidemen, singers and leaders, plus a few producers and engineers such as Rudy Van Gelder and Ed Kirkeby.
threads: First record date as a sideman with a bandleader
First album or session as a leader
Sorting out which record was first against the discography
Labels, producers and engineers on early sessions
Nerves, mistakes and anecdotes from the studio
Early race-record and 78 era sessions in the 1920s and 30s

communities.name: Roped-off dances: playing for segregated audiences
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Musicians recall dance halls, theaters and clubs where race decided who sat, danced and entered, set mostly from the 1920s to the early 1950s and across the South, Oakland, St. Louis and Memphis. The most central and most repeated image is the rope down the middle of the hall, dividing white and Black dancers or placing white spectators at Black dances. Tellers such as Buster Smith, Jay McShann, Keter Betts, Ruth Brown and Erskine Hawkins add that dancing or young people often knocked the rope down. Others describe separate nights for white and Black patrons (Sweet's Ballroom in Oakland), Black audiences confined to balconies, and bands entering by the back door. A looser strand covers firsts and exceptions: a Black band at a white hall, mixed benefit bands, integrated groups, and Machito mixing audiences at the Palladium. Tellers include big-band sidemen, bandleaders and singers from every collection, and they agree on the practice while differing on how rigid it was. The sample edges drift into related race stories (Detroit, Native American audiences, Latin bands).
threads: The rope across the dance floor
Separate white and Black nights at ballrooms
Balconies, back doors and Jim Crow seating in theaters and clubs
Rope torn down: dancers and crowds defying segregation
First Black or mixed bands in white halls
Playing white fraternity and society dances

communities.name: Drunks, guns and racist threats on the bandstand
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Black musicians recall playing jobs where drunk, armed or racist white patrons turned the night dangerous. The stories are set mostly between the 1920s and the 1940s, with a few reaching the 1960s, and they cluster in Texas and the Southwest, the South and on the road. Typical scenes are a drunk with a pistol forcing someone to dance, cowboys demanding the band keep playing, a sheriff who wants only one tune all night, bottles thrown at a drummer or at Cab Calloway, hecklers pushing corn whiskey, and a radio announcer introducing a band with a slur. Tellers such as Buster Smith, Buck Clayton, Punch Miller, Doc Cheatham and Snub Mosley mostly describe how the band got through it.
