They sit at the door with booking agents, stay armed, shrug it off as ignorance, fight back, or rely on a police chief or sheriff for protection. They differ on whether the danger came from ordinary drunks, from organized racism or from the police themselves. The late outliers, such as a state trooper throwing a trombone off the Turnpike, extend the same theme of racial menace on the job into the 1960s.
threads: Drunk white patrons, pistols and forced requests at dances
Bottles, brawls and fights breaking out mid-set
Racist insults and slurs aimed at bands, on the air and at the door
Protection from sheriffs, police chiefs and armed bandmates
Playing white West Texas dances and Southern whites-only venues
Police harassment on the road, as in the trombone and the Turnpike

communities.name: Being a woman (or Latino) in jazz: stereotypes and tokenism
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Musicians describe what it means to be treated as an exception in jazz because of who they are. Most of the tellers are women instrumentalists and bandleaders, from Marian McPartland and Mary Lou Williams (as recalled by Carol Bash) in the 1930s-50s to Karolina Strassmayer, Christine Jensen, Jane Ira Bloom, Ellen Rowe and Ada Rovatti in recent decades. They talk about being labeled a "girl pianist" or told they play like a man, about tokenism, about a male-dominated "boy's club", and about the media fuss when Strassmayer became the first woman in the WDR Big Band. They differ in how much it affected them: McPartland says it was never an uphill struggle, while later players describe persistent barriers, mixed feelings about Me Too, and slow gains such as women's festivals and record Sisters in Jazz applications. Two Latino musicians, Ignacio Berroa and Arturo Sandoval, tell a parallel story of being typecast by origin and overlooked in polls. Sherrie Maricle adds the bandleader's view, admitting she once never thought of hiring women. The theme is shared, but the Latino segments and the period range (1930s to 2020s) make the cluster slightly looser.
threads: Being a woman instrumentalist: labels like 'girl pianist' and 'plays like a man'
Tokenism and the boy's club in bands and programming
Firsts and media attention, such as the first woman in the WDR Big Band
Is the situation improving: festivals, Sisters in Jazz, Me Too
Latino musicians typecast as percussionists and left off polls

venues: Sisters in Jazz Collegiate Combo Competition

communities.name: Race, color lines and who owns jazz
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives reflect on race in jazz, mostly in the first person and mostly in the later decades, though the stories range from the 1920s to the 1990s and beyond. The largest group is white players, such as Ed Shaughnessy, Hal Smith, Adam Nussbaum, Johnny Varro and Peter Appleyard. They describe being the only white player in a Black band and being accepted because they could play. They also ask why traditional and mainstream jazz audiences and players are now mostly white, and why few young Black players take it up. Black and mixed-race voices (Benny Powell, Jo Jones, Billy Taylor, Harry Edison, James Moody, Vincent Pelote) talk about segregation. They say it kept musicians from playing together, pushed Ellington and Basie into the Black community, and denied Black creators credit for the music. Older stories recall color and class distinctions inside bands and clubs, light-skinned preferences, separate unions with unequal pay, and La Rocca's claims that Black bands copied Dixieland records. Many tellers agree that listening matters more than looking, while disagreeing on whether jazz is a Black music, whether race is an illusion, and how much polarization remains today. The cluster is large and loosely bounded: a few segments drift into gender, campus politics or unrelated career detail.
threads: White players accepted in Black bands: the music as the badge of acceptance
Why trad and mainstream jazz are mostly white, and few young Black players
Segregation, separate unions and unequal pay in the bands
Color and caste: light-skinned preferences and Creole clubs
Who gets credit: Black creation of jazz and debates over ownership
Race on the scene then and now: festivals, booking and polarization

communities.name: Playing with strangers: calling and not knowing tunes
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians describe the everyday problem of walking onto a bandstand with players they have never met, with no rehearsal and no charts, and having to make music anyway. The setting is mostly jazz parties and festivals from the 1990s into the 2010s, with some stories from jam sessions, tours abroad (Australia, Sydney) and Preservation Hall. The central worry is the unfamiliar tune. Players such as Allan Vaché, Norris Turney, David Finck and Bobby Gordon admit when they do not know a song, ask for the chords, or let someone else take it. Leaders such as Joe Wilder, Jerry Bergonzi and Jon-Erik Kellso call tunes, and the trumpeter is expected to know and lead the melody. The tellers agree that a wide shared repertoire of standards and a common musical language make pickup bands work, and that musicians help each other through it. They differ on tactics: some send tunes ahead or refresh unfamiliar ones beforehand, while others keep endings simple or size up the pianist on the spot. A few samples drift off this subject, such as a Christian Sands trio performance and a note about vocalizing while playing, but most share the same situation.
threads: Admitting you don't know the tune and getting help
Calling tunes on the stand at jazz parties
Shared repertoire and a common musical language
Sizing up unfamiliar rhythm sections abroad and on tour
Preparing ahead: sending tunes and refreshing material
Unrehearsed festival and jam-session etiquette

communities.name: What is New Orleans, Chicago, and Dixieland style?
communities.parent_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels
communities.narrative: Musicians from many regions are asked, or volunteer, to define regional and period jazz styles and say how they differ. The dominant question is what distinguishes New Orleans style from Chicago, Texas and Midwest, Kansas City, Jacksonville, Mobile and Florida playing. Tellers such as Quinn Wilson, Jimmy McPartland, Ed Garland and Amos White offer concrete descriptions: Chicago as faster, harder and more competitive, Dixieland as four beats to the bar with ensemble playing and passed-down solos and breaks, Texas bands as more arranged and swinging, and out-of-town bands as playing strictly by the note. Others, like George Lewis on uptown versus downtown, Ed Polcer on critics' labels, and Quinn Wilson on Chicago, say the differences are small or the labels mislead. A second strand concerns the word Dixieland itself, its link to the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, and the split between trad, revival and traditional New Orleans playing, discussed by revivalists like Evan Christopher, David Torkanowsky, Bob Schulz and Dave Robinson and by Vic Dickenson on tailgate style. Most stories are set from the 1900s to the 1970s, with revival-era retellings reaching the 1990s. A few samples drift to other subjects, such as Machito on Arsenio's Cuban style, Professor Longhair on having no name for his music, and a band-photo identification.
threads: Defining New Orleans style versus Chicago style
Regional comparisons: Texas, Kansas City, Mobile, Jacksonville and Florida
Why the word Dixieland is contested
Trad, revival and traditional New Orleans playing
Uptown versus downtown and 'no real difference' answers
Tailgate trombone and instrument roles such as tuba versus string bass

communities.name: What is jazz? Defining the word and its origins
communities.parent_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels
communities.narrative: Musicians across many interviews stop to define jazz itself: where the word came from, what it replaced, and what counts as the real thing. Older New Orleans and Chicago players such as Monk Hazel, Johnny DeDroit, Ed Garland and Reb Spikes recall the music being called ragtime before "jass" or "jazz" arrived in the 1910s, and they offer competing explanations of the word, including jasmine oil, red-light slang, a French derivation and the Fisher card of 1911. Others, such as Danny Barker, Allan Vaché, Johnny Wiggs and Gerald Wilson, argue about origins: Jelly Roll Morton's claim to have invented jazz, New Orleans versus Memphis, Congo Square, and the blues and spirituals as the base. Later and younger musicians (Jon Hendricks, Nancy Wilson, Eddie Palmieri, Paquito D'Rivera, Robert Glasper) shift to the boundaries of the label, asking who is a true jazz singer, how Latin jazz differs from Jazz Latin, and how swing, bop, trad and classic jazz divide the music. The tellers agree that labels are unstable and that the word arrived late, but they disagree on its origin, on who deserves credit and on whether the question matters at all, as Benny Carter says it does not. The cluster is mostly one subject, with a few segments (R&B, a Welk contrast, batá rhythms) at the edges.
threads: Where the word jazz came from, and ragtime before it
Origin claims: Jelly Roll Morton, New Orleans versus Memphis, Congo Square, the blues
Terminology wars: swing, bop, trad, classic, Dixieland
Latin jazz, vocalese and other contested labels
What jazz is: a language, the human voice, life itself

communities.name: Where jazz came from: Africa, slavery and the Americas
communities.parent_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels
communities.narrative: Musicians and interviewers across 25 interviews offer their own theories of where jazz comes from. The dominant answer is Africa: rhythm carried across the Atlantic by enslaved people, surviving in rumba, the griot tradition, church revival beats and communal singing. Several tellers, including Jimmy McPartland, describe jazz as African rhythm joined to European melody and harmony, while Eddie Palmieri, Machito and Mario Bauza trace the same roots through Cuba, the Caribbean and Latin music. Others stress jazz as black folk music born of frustration, denial and the search for freedom, as Marshall Royal, Frank Wess and Wendy Oxenhorn put it. A few add other lineages, such as Native American influence, Scottish and Irish thigh slapping, and reggae heard in early Fats Domino. Most of these are origin-of-jazz reflections prompted by interviewers' questions rather than memories of events, and no particular period is tied to them. The cluster's edge drifts into national identity and "America's only art form" questions, with Australian music as an outlier.
threads: African roots and rhythm carried across the Atlantic
Afro-Cuban rumba, salsa and Caribbean connections
Jazz as black folk music born of slavery, frustration and freedom
African rhythm meeting European harmony
Other claimed influences: Native American, Celtic, church revival, reggae
Is jazz America's original art form?

communities.name: Violence and arrest on Southern tours
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Touring musicians recall the physical danger and humiliation of Jim Crow travel, mostly in the 1930s and 1940s with some stories reaching back to the late 1920s and forward to the 1950s. The stories are set on the road in the South, especially Florida, Georgia, Texas and Mississippi, and in northern towns with their own color lines such as Kankakee, Whiting and Pittsburgh. They describe police arrests at train stations, fines and jailings, bands run out of town, beatings of bandmates and drivers, refused meals and rooms, and flashpoints around white women and the bandstand. Ernie Fields supplies a long run of linked episodes, and Harry Edison, Budd Johnson, John Simmons, Eddie Barefield and others add their own. Several, including Edison and Budd Johnson, say the bands carried guns, while J. C. Higginbotham says no one did, and JJ Johnson remembers mostly psychological rather than physical violence. Big-band sidemen, leaders and singers all tell it, and a few say it taught them to avoid the South or leave the road.
threads: Arrested or fined by police at stations and in small towns
Beatings of musicians, drivers and bystanders
Ordered out of town and refused food, rooms or restrooms
White women, the bandstand and mixed-audience danger
Carrying guns for protection (and denials)
Ernie Fields's run of road incidents in Florida and Oklahoma

communities.name: Jim Crow on the road: touring the segregated South
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Musicians from big bands, small groups and package tours recall running into segregation while travelling, mostly between the late 1930s and about 1960. The stories are set in Southern towns and states (Alabama, Mississippi, Texas, Virginia, the Carolinas, Florida) and also in Northern and Western places such as Michigan, Worcester, Santa Barbara, Salt Lake City and Harrisburg. They cover being refused hotel rooms, restaurants, restrooms and waiting rooms, eating in kitchens, staying in Black hotels or rooming houses, roped-off or balcony-segregated audiences, and bandleaders (Shaw, Barnet, Basie, Kenton, Granz) who insisted on mixed bands, cancelled dates or negotiated around the rules. Black and white sidemen both tell it, and some white players describe being sent to the colored restroom or refused service alongside their bandmates. The tellers differ in tone. Many describe humiliation or danger, while a few (Jillean Williams, Helen Humes, Tommy Ridgley, Machito, Punch Miller) say they had little trouble or were treated well. Others say the North could be as bad as the South. Interviewers often prompt the topic directly with questions about segregation on tour.
threads: Refused hotel rooms and restaurants on tour
Mixed bands and bandleaders who resisted the color line
Segregated halls, roped-off dances and balcony audiences
Billie Holiday and Black soloists with white bands in the South
Package tours, buses and passing as Haitian or Cuban
Musicians who report little trouble or kind hosts
Northern and Western prejudice, not only the South

communities.name: Rooms, meals and Jim Crow on the road
communities.parent_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand
communities.narrative: Black bandsmen of the 1930s and 1940s, with some stories running into the 1950s and 1960s, describe the daily mechanics of touring a segregated country. Hotels refused them or charged double, restaurants served them only at the back door or not at all, and toilets and facilities were off limits in small Southern towns. Bands coped by staying in rooming houses and private homes, often across the railroad tracks or in Black-owned hotels, and by eating home cooking, buying groceries or sending a white road manager for food. Some travelled with their own Pullman car, as Ellington's band did, or cooked in the baggage car or on the bus. Tellers include big-band sidemen such as Vic Dickenson, Harry Edison, Trummy Young, Teddy McRae and Barney Bigard, and later bebop and R&B musicians such as James Moody and Ruth Brown. They agree on the humiliation and the lodging networks of hosts in many towns. They differ in tone: Doc Cheatham says he was not bitter, Teddy McRae recalls being welcomed everywhere, and JJ Johnson and Frank Foster note that conditions eased in the mid-1940s and early 1960s. A few samples drift off the theme, such as a western tour in 1940 and a tour of Asia in 1958-59, a late arrival on an Ella Fitzgerald tour, and a Las Vegas hotel stay.
threads: Rooming houses, private homes and Black hotels as lodging
Back-door service and finding food in segregated towns
Bus, Pullman and baggage-car travel on one-nighters
Danger and humiliation in the South: sheriffs, arrests, refused facilities
Easing of conditions and dissenting views, from bandstand relief to being welcomed

communities.name: Playing for the audience: rapport, presence and explaining the music
communities.parent_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand
communities.narrative: Across decades, from 1940s New Orleans players to 2000s working musicians, these tellers talk about the performer's duty to the listener: reading the room, winning it over, and making the music understandable and enjoyable. Many describe talking to the crowd, explaining tunes, crediting composers and telling stories, and they hold up models such as Cannonball and Nat Adderley, Clark Terry, Bobby Short, Dizzy Gillespie and Bunk Johnson. Older New Orleans and swing-era players frame it as pleasing the public and playing pretty or melodic, even taking requests. Younger and jazz-school-era players stress communication, stage presence and engaging the audience, and some (Rowe's interviewees, Greg Thomas) say schools do not teach it. Branford Marsalis and Artie Shaw show the tension: audiences are needed, sometimes a necessary evil, and melody is what keeps bands working. A few tangents sit at the edges: selling records and bands, studio comfort, and gig preparation, so the fit is strong at the centre and loose at the margins.
threads: Talking to the audience and explaining the tunes
Reading the room and winning over a skeptical crowd
Pleasing the public with melody and requests
Stage presence, warmth and humour (Cannonball, Clark Terry)
Intimate venues, house concerts and clubs versus concerts
Teaching young players to entertain

communities.name: Musicians on critics, reviews and polls
communities.parent_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press
communities.narrative: Across about 99 interviews from all four archives, musicians talk about the jazz press and how it shaped, ignored or damaged their careers. The stories run from the 1930s and 1940s (George Frazier's Down Beat reviews of Buddy Tate and Jimmy McPartland, Teddy Wilson on critics as parasites) through the 1970s and 1980s (John Collins ignored by writers, Lou Donaldson and Toshiko Akiyoshi on being overlooked or doubted) to the 1990s and 2000s (Michael Moore and the Balliett quote, Branford Marsalis and Cecil Taylor, Howard Mandel on why musicians dislike critics). The most concentrated thread is Art Hodes's account of the 1940s "jazz war" with Leonard Feather and Barry Ulanov, including his defamation suit. Tellers largely agree that critics wield real power over bookings, awards and reputations, and that many are under-prepared. They differ on whether critics are allies or enemies: Marian McPartland and JJ Johnson are balanced, while Hodes, Wess and Mingus are bitter or wary. Polls and awards such as Down Beat, Metronome and Esquire appear as a related, more skeptical strand. Speakers include veteran players, younger bandleaders and a few critics and interviewers.
threads: Art Hodes and the Leonard Feather jazz war and lawsuit
George Frazier and 1930s-40s Down Beat reviews
Being ignored or underrated by critics
What critics should be: preparation, fairness, press inaccuracies
Polls, awards and their politics
Reviews of books and records, and the controversies they caused

venues: The Tonight Show with Jay Leno

communities.name: Critics, criticism and what musicians make of them
communities.parent_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press
communities.narrative: Most of the samples return to one loose subject: jazz criticism and how musicians and writers regard it. James Moody (three consecutive segments) says non-players can still judge a performance but should explain why, that critics must remember musicians have the ears, and that many critics follow reputation rather than listen. Lonnie Liston Smith recalls critics who said he was banging or putting people to sleep, while he held that his stretched-out sections were pure sound modeled on nature. From the writers' side, Howard Mandel describes the critic as a consumer guide and mediator between musician and reader, and Scott Yanow argues that critics need not be players and should use plain language rather than jargon. Two further strands sit at the edges. Nick La Rocca's segments are a reader reading out 1918 Times-Picayune editorials and letters for and against jazz, which is early press hostility rather than later criticism. The Konitz segment on Lennie Tristano and Gioia's writing concerns jazz historiography. The set is small, mostly set in no stated period, and spread across 68 interviews, so the common thread is loose and the boundary cases are real.
threads: Musicians on what makes criticism valid (Moody)
Critics misreading an artist's music (Lonnie Liston Smith)
The critic's role: mediator, plain language, need not be a player (Mandel, Yanow)
1918 New Orleans press fight over jazz (La Rocca)
Jazz writers and history: Gioia, Balliett and Tristano's influence

communities.name: Creole language, French at home, and Eh La Bas
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Most of these stories are about the Creole and French languages in New Orleans families, told mainly by Tulane interviewees born between about 1860 and the 1940s. Musicians and relatives say what they spoke at home: Creole or French as a first language, with English learned at school. Some call themselves Creole but admit they cannot speak it. Several trace language and songs to grandmothers and great-grandmothers, including Alice Zeno's Senegalese forebears and a song about the Haitian revolution. Two linked groups form a sub-core. De De Pierce works through Creole word lists with interviewers, and a group of tellers recall where the song "Eh La Bas" came from and who made it up. Their accounts differ: Pierce is credited with the jazz version, while others say it is older or that they learned it from Creole-speaking elders. A smaller set drifts away from language to family background, the Bahamas and Mobile songs, and club social events. The common thread is looser than a single event, so the cluster is only moderately tight.
threads: Speaking Creole and French at home, English at school
Creole identity: claiming it without the language
Grandmothers and ancestors from Senegal and Haiti, and the songs they passed down
De De Pierce's Creole word lists and translations
Where Eh La Bas came from and who made it
Alice Zeno's French and language lessons in the King household

communities.name: Will jazz survive? Schools, young audiences, lost clubs
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: Musicians and industry figures from the 1950s through about 2010 reflect on the future of jazz, mostly in the 1970s to 2000s. Most weigh the same question: where the next generation of players and listeners will come from. Many point to schools, college campuses, student subscriptions, Monk Institute competitions and kids' programs as proof the music is thriving, and to Kind of Blue and Brubeck concerts as gateways for young listeners. Others, including Art Hodes, Bob Haggart, Allan Vaché and Jackie Williams, lament the loss of small clubs, dances and other working venues where earlier players learned by sink-or-swim experience. George Wein disagrees with the school-centered view and expects the future audience to come from the pop generation and older fans. Mike Wofford's account of San Diego's scene and Ira Gitler's remarks on the Marsalis revival and jazz's separation from black culture are looser fits. Most are optimistic but wary, and the tellers are veteran players, educators, a Down Beat executive and critics.
threads: Jazz education and young audiences in schools and colleges
Lost small clubs as the training ground for young players
Optimism versus worry about the future of jazz
Where the future audience will come from (students versus pop fans)
The Marsalis-era revival and jazz's ties to black culture
Local scenes in decline, such as San Diego

bands: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

communities.name: Finding your own sound, not copying
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians from many eras and regions tell the same lesson: a jazz player should learn from idols and predecessors but must eventually stop imitating and develop a personal sound. Most tellers speak in general advice, often to younger players, and only a few give a dated setting (Mose Allison in 1949-58, Harry Edison in the 1990s). Most tellers agree that imitation is a legitimate first stage. Red Holloway compares it to learning to drive before driving your own way. Pepper Adams, as Jerry Dodgion recalls him, says copying one person is plagiarism but copying everybody is research. Clark Terry's imitation-assimilation-creation sequence is also cited. They differ on emphasis. Harry Edison, Joe Muranyi and Wilbert Tillman stress originality and the failure of copyists. Jimmy Maxwell and Hank Jones add that players must know their heritage and are the sum of their experiences. Teddy Wilson, Emile Barnes, Punch Miller and Jim Cullum offer their own sounds, or Armstrong's and Bix's limitations, as examples of individuality. Many tellers complain that players today sound alike. Parker, Armstrong, Miles Davis and Cannonball Adderley recur as models to learn from and move beyond.
threads: Copy first, then move beyond your idols
Don't be a copycat: be an originator
Pepper Adams's 'plagiarism versus research' and Clark Terry's three stages
Today's players all sound alike
Style as the sum of influences and experience
Limitations and individuality as part of expression

communities.name: Going to school: conservatories, NYU and the Schillinger system
communities.parent_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1920s through the 1980s describe their formal music study: enrolling at Juilliard, NYU, Berklee, Boston Conservatory, the Kansas City Conservatory and Wesleyan, often alongside or after working as professionals. The strongest recurring thread is the Schillinger system, a mathematical approach to rhythm and composition that several tellers studied at NYU or with private teachers. It was a fad among Fletcher Henderson's men, and Eddie Barefield, Bill Challis (with Eubie Blake as a classmate) and Luther Henderson all took it, some under the GI bill after the war. Others tell of choosing a school on a mentor's advice, such as John Lamb being steered from Berklee toward a teaching degree by Dean Earl. Some take courses while on the road, as Jimmy Jones did with Sarah Vaughan. Tellers differ on how much school gave them. Branford Marsalis says he learned mostly from friends at Berklee, and Horace Henderson enrolled in theory but did not stay. Toshiko Akiyoshi says theory follows music. A few samples drift to teachers (Bill Barron at Wesleyan) and studio teaching, so the shared subject is clear but not tight.
threads: Studying the Schillinger system at NYU and with private teachers
Juilliard, Berklee and conservatory enrolment
GI bill and postwar schooling
Mentors steering school choices
Studying while working on the road
Doubts about what formal training adds

communities.name: The decline of live jazz work and clubs
communities.parent_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship
communities.narrative: Across about eighty interviews, musicians, a few producers and a record-store owner explain why steady jazz work has dried up. Most stories are set between the 1950s and the 2000s, with New York as the main scene and New Orleans, England and Philadelphia appearing less often. The tellers agree on the symptoms: fewer clubs and weeklong engagements, hotel and pub jobs lost, shrinking bands, fewer recording sessions and studios, and festivals and jazz parties standing in for nightclubs. They differ on the causes. Some blame rents, urban safety, TV and rock taking over the colleges. Others point to jukeboxes, DJs, synthesizers, downloading or cheap part-time players. Veterans such as Ray Brown, Wild Bill Davison and Ram Ramirez contrast a busier past with today. Younger players such as Winard Harper, Michael Weiss and Ray Vega describe how hard gigs are to sustain now. A few segments drift to related loss, such as the end of New Orleans funerals and society clubs, a record store sold in 1989, or the fall of Harlem entertainment in the 1920s-30s. One outlier, on the number of Mardi Gras tribes, does not belong.
threads: Clubs closing and festivals replacing them
New York gig scene then and now
Causes: rents, TV, jukeboxes, DJs, downloading
Shrinking bands and vanishing hotel, pub and studio work
Fewer places for young players to develop
Decline of traditional jazz in New Orleans and England

communities.name: How the record business changed: labels, lawyers and downloads
communities.parent_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations reflect on how the jazz record business has changed, mostly from a 1990s-2000s vantage point, looking back at an earlier era. The older view is that record companies were once run by musicians and music people, and that lawyers, accountants and marketers now run them. Labels are said to box artists into molds, chase very young, unseasoned acts, skip artist development, and push musicians toward commercial work (Sam Jones on the 1970s, Wendell Brunious, Jon Hendricks, John Levy, Robert Glasper). A second strand is technology. Cheap CD production, home studios, Napster and downloading, streaming, YouTube and social media have produced a flood of releases, made music feel less important, and shortened the window artists get. Tellers disagree on whether this is liberating (artists finding their own audience, independent labels) or damaging (sameness, lost albums, tangled rights). A few older tellers add a contrast with the Brill Building song business and earlier labels and talent scouts. Most tellers are working players and writers commenting on the present as they see it, and the cluster is small and spread across many interviews and archives.
threads: Labels run by lawyers and accountants, not musicians
Labels favoring the young and boxing artists into molds
Downloading, Napster, streaming and the end of CDs
Home recording and the flood of independent releases
Social media, singles and the lost art of the album
Older song and record business: Brill Building, Hammond, Prestige

bands: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

communities.name: Jazz on the radio: programming, formats and neglect
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: Musicians across several decades, mostly speaking in the 1970s through the early 2000s, complain about what radio does and does not play. The common grievance is that stations offer too little real jazz: programmers repeat one kind of music (Vic Dickenson wants variety), rock and fusion crowd out jazz (Wilbur Ware), smooth jazz replaces swing (Allan Vaché, Don Alias), and corporate chains dominate (Nat Hentoff on Clear Channel). Some tellers add that this turns young listeners away from jazz (Chico Hamilton, Eiji Kitamura on Japan). Others praise public and community stations such as WUCF, or recall call-in jazz shows (Theodore Saunders). A few drift to related media: Flip Phillips on television hurting jazz, Bela Fleck on the Internet and file trading, and Hank Cicalo on mixing for car radio speakers. The tellers largely agree that radio is a poor outlet for jazz, and differ mainly on who is to blame: record companies, promoters, corporate owners or listener taste.
threads: Radio plays too little real jazz
Smooth jazz, rock and fusion crowding out swing
Corporate radio, promoters and record companies
Public and community stations as refuges
Television, the Internet and other media hurting jazz
Young listeners and the lack of exposure

communities.name: What's next for jazz graduates: versatility and work
communities.parent_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories
communities.narrative: Musicians and educators, mostly interviewed for the Hamilton (Fillius) archive, reflect on what awaits young players who finish jazz programs. The setting is the college and conservatory world (USC Thornton, Eastman, North Texas, Berklee, York University), told largely from the 1990s through the 2020s. The tellers agree that opportunities are scarce and that only a tiny fraction become stars; Shelly Berg cites Joshua Redman as a rare exception who lives on jazz alone. Their usual advice is to be versatile: play many styles, write, teach, and take weddings, pop tours and other gigs, as Jimmy Heath says of his student Tia Fuller working with Beyonce. They differ on tone. Dave Rivello is blunt that prospects are poor but offers passion and entrepreneurial training as help. Oscar Peterson blames money and agents for distracting students. Newsom and Tompkins point to growth in college jazz teaching and strong service bands. A few segments drift to related points, such as Alicia Olatuja on opera versus jazz and Jimmy Maxwell on urging students into the Navy, and these fit only loosely.
threads: Prospects are poor and only a few become stars
Be versatile: many styles, writing, weddings and pop tours
Most jazz players end up teaching
Advice to students: listen, stay passionate, be entrepreneurial
Money, agents and too many schools hurting young players

venues: Thornton School of Music, University of Southern California

communities.name: Teaching jazz: ear, tunes, scales and transcription
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about how jazz is learned and taught, mostly in their own advice to students. The most common message is to learn by ear: learn tunes from the record or the original melody, transcribe and memorize solos, and listen widely, from Lester Young and Parker to Rollins and even Bach. Others stress the grounding: scales, chords, modes and building a reusable vocabulary, with teachers such as David Baker, Maria Schneider, Pat LaBarbera and Eric Alexander describing their classroom methods and assignments. Tellers differ on theory. Fred Wesley, Clark Terry and Pizzarelli lean on hearing and experience over theory, while Howie Shear and Carmen Caramanica want it taught simply and analytically. Paul Smith argues that improvising cannot be taught at all, and Walter Thomas believes it can. The tellers are mostly working players who also teach, speaking in the 1930s-2020s span with no single dominant era. A few samples drift off the subject, such as Chick Corea on what Stan Getz taught him, Derek Brown's banter, and Walter Thomas's spiritual principle.
threads: Advice to young players: learn tunes and solos by ear
Transcribing, memorizing and practicing solos
Scales, chords and modes as the foundation
Teacher methods, assignments and clinic exercises
Can improvisation be taught? Theory versus gift and experience
What was learned from mentors and records

communities.name: Hype, youth marketing and the businessmen's music industry
communities.parent_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship
communities.narrative: Musicians from every generation complain that the music business has moved from artists to marketers. The stories run from Teddy Wilson in the 1970s, who says businessmen and advertising planners now shape taste where John Hammond once backed artists, to players interviewed around 2001 (Abercrombie, Reeves, Owens, Sandke, Hendricks). The recent tellers focus on the "young lions" era after Wynton Marsalis. They say labels sign inexperienced young players on looks and publicity, skip the apprenticeship with elders, and neglect mid-career masters. Jimmy Owens calls this "jazz in the middle ages", and Evan Christopher describes the market's missing middle. A second strand covers crossover, fads and novelty hits, such as disco, rock emphasis at Berklee, Kenny G's Latin album, Macarena and Tiny Tim. Wilson, Percy Heath and Wilbur Ware say these flare up and vanish while real jazz endures. The tellers agree that hype and accountants cheapen the music. They differ on the target, which is age, genre-crossing or tribute and centennial projects. A few outliers, such as Albert Murray's cars-and-quality analogy and Harry Edison on Erskine Hawkins, only loosely fit.
threads: Young lions: labels signing youth without apprenticeship
Neglected middle-generation and older players
Businessmen, accountants and lawyers taking over the record industry
Crossover, rock and novelty fads versus lasting jazz
Tribute albums, centennials and the market's missing middle
Quality and workmanship versus hype

bands: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven

communities.name: How the music business has changed: streaming, CDs and lost work
communities.parent_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations step back from their own careers to say that the music business is not what it was. The stories are mostly set from the 1990s through the early 2020s, with a few looking back to the 1960s and 1980s. Most tellers date the break to the collapse of CD sales, Napster, downloads and then streaming. They say royalties are tiny, studio and session work has dried up, records are now made by trading files instead of playing together, and there are more players than paying work. Many add that labels no longer fund artist development, agents and managers block direct contact, and publicity and follower counts now count for more than the music. Older players such as Liebman, Slide Hampton and Hentoff compare this with the apprenticeship system, bandleaders who owned their sidemen, and the long-gone major jazz labels. Younger and mid-career players describe building audiences online or creating their own mentoring spaces. A few add pandemic-era worries about latency and the survival of clubs. The tone is mostly lament, though some such as LaBarbera and Stripling stay hopeful or practical. About 20 of the 29 central samples share this subject, and a few drift to print journalism and magazine editing.
threads: Streaming, downloads and the CD collapse
Studio and session work disappearing
No more label artist development or apprenticeship
Agents, publicity and followers over music
Covid, latency and the return of live gigs
Veterans scrambling and ageism

communities.name: Music school versus learning on the bandstand
communities.parent_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1910s through the 1990s recall their formal music education: conservatories, college theory classes, high-school harmony teachers and private lessons. They set it against what they learned on gigs, in jam sessions and in New York. The tellers are mostly jazz players who studied harmony, theory or arranging at places like Chicago Musical College, Berklee, Wayne State, Indiana University, the Sydney Conservatorium or Dunbar High School. Several credit a single teacher or class for a foundation, such as Dyett's four-part hymns, Pomeroy's arranging workshops or Gaber's lesson on touch. Others, including Horace Henderson, Neal Caine and Ruthie Foster, say school gave a base but their real education came from working musicians, or that jazz school can erode individuality. Woody Herman notes that music schools began supplying technically strong players in the 1960s and 70s. The cluster is only loosely coherent. Most samples are about studying harmony and theory, but a few drift to self-teaching, WPA band training, or one interviewee's lack of knowledge of Jelly Roll Morton's schooling.
threads: Studying harmony and theory at conservatories and colleges
High-school and early teachers who taught harmony
Private lessons with a particular mentor or teacher
School versus gig experience and learning from veterans
Self-taught musicians who also had some schooling
Music schools supplying trained players to big bands

communities.name: Solo length and never playing the same solo twice
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, swing, bebop and modern jazz talk about how long a solo should be and whether it should ever be repeated. Players from the early bands of the 1900s to 1920s (Tom Albert, Alfred Williams, Eddie Dawson, Ridgley, Earl Humphrey) describe a time when ensemble playing dominated, solos were short or rare, and everyone laid out or backed the soloist. Swing-era players (Vic Dickenson, Count Basie, Buddy Tate, Slam Stewart, Artie Shaw, Jerry Jerome, George Masso, Sonny Greer) debate whether to replay a hit record solo note for note. Miller wanted the record solo played live, while Goodman and Basie's men preferred fresh invention, and Lester Young would not repeat himself except on records. Later musicians (Gil Evans, Percy Heath, Branford Marsalis, Tim Ries, Dave Rivello) talk about letting soloists stretch out, knowing when to quit, and treating a solo as a compositional continuance. The tellers broadly agree that a solo should be a story, a chorus or two with a shape, and that fixed solos are the exception. They differ on whether the public and bandleaders want the recorded version or something new. The cluster is loose at the edges, with a few segments about specific lineups or a playback session.
threads: How long a solo should run: a chorus is a story
Repeating a hit record solo versus improvising anew
Early New Orleans bands: ensemble playing, few solos, laying out behind a soloist
Bandleaders giving soloists room, cues and guidelines
Knowing when to stop and building a solo through the choruses

communities.name: What goes through your mind when improvising
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four collections reflect on the inner life of improvisation: what they think about while soloing, and whether they should think at all. Most are post-1960s players and educators (Dobbins, Charlap, Harris, Soskin, Bergonzi, Zeitlin, Aebersold-circle teachers) speaking in interviews, often in answer to a stock question, and they set the stories in no particular year. They broadly agree that the best playing happens when conscious thinking recedes: technique and theory should sink into the subconscious, leaving room for listening, flow and being in the moment. Many compare improvising to speaking a language or telling a story, with accents, concision and no filler, and cite Parker, Rollins, Coltrane, Miles and Chet Baker as models. A large recurring subtopic is the "wrong note": most say there is none if you commit, resolve it or make it convincing, and they distinguish wrong notes from tension notes. They differ on how much to analyze, since some defend transcription and theory while others warn that over-analyzing solos or being overly mathematical kills expression. A few older players, such as Mike De Lay on learning the chord numbering system, Benny Carter on technique and Percy Heath on mistakes, give period variations on the same questions.
threads: Thinking versus not thinking while soloing: flow and the subconscious
What makes a wrong note, and turning mistakes into music
Improvising as speaking a language or telling a story
Theory, technique and transcription: how much is too much
Psychological obstacles and being in the zone
Learning by ear, chord numbers and the Parker, Rollins, Coltrane models

communities.name: Older players on the promising young generation
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: In this cluster, veteran musicians stop to comment on the younger players coming up behind them. The tellers name specific rising artists. Roy Hargrove, Nicholas Payton, Jason Moran, Danilo Perez, Benny Green, Geoff Keezer, Terence Blanchard, Antonio Hart, David Sanchez, Warren Vache and Jon Faddis all come up, and the samples run from the 1970s to about 2011. The remarks are mostly short, generous assessments: who is worth watching, who sits in with older players, who has the will to reach the top. Some tellers add caveats, such as Ramsey Lewis saying younger pianists still need polish and experience. Others compare the younger generation with their own self-made routes, or say today's players stand on earlier musicians' shoulders. Trumpeters and pianists dominate, and the speakers include Doc Cheatham, Clark Terry, Snooky Young, Marian McPartland, James Moody and Big Nick Nicholas. A few segments drift away from the theme. One is a closing remembrance, another is an aside about how a recommendation travelled, and another is about a jazz camp's alumni. Because of these, the cluster is a loose commentary genre and not one tightly bounded story.
threads: Praise for young trumpeters, especially Roy Hargrove
Naming promising young pianists
Veterans praising young sidemen they have heard or played with
Today's players versus the old self-taught path
Jazz education and camps as a route for the young
Wishing to hear the departed greats

bands: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

communities.name: Will the music last? Old masters on young players
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: In this cluster, musicians from many collections step back from their own careers to judge the state of the music and the generation coming up. The tellers range from the blues fiddler Butch Cage to the saxophonists, drummers, producers and critics of the jazz world: Abbey Lincoln, Jimmy Cobb, Melba Liston, Randy Weston, Nat Hentoff, Randy Sandke and Rudy Van Gelder, among others. The strongest agreement is that older players paid dues and cared more. Lawrence Marrero says the music is going backward, Wendell Brunious says publicists and licks have replaced the blues, and John W. Bubbles says vaudeville performers had to be cleverer than today's. Several doubt that young players have the seasoning or individuality of the past, though a few name hopeful exceptions such as Esperanza Spalding and Aaron Weinstein. They differ on whether jazz will survive. Hentoff and Cobb say it will last, while Sandke fears it is becoming a museum piece. Some of the stories turn to technology and media, with Van Gelder blaming multi-track fixes for lost spontaneity and Bill Dobbins saying media flatten speech and music. Few of the stories are tied to a particular year, so the cluster reads as a set of general reflections more than shared events. The segments are loosely held together, and a couple are interview logistics or small talk.
threads: Older players paid dues, today's learn for free
Do young players have the individuality and seasoning?
Will jazz survive or become a museum piece?
Technology, media and recording flattening spontaneity
Hopeful young names: Spalding, Weinstein and others
Old-time folk and vaudeville traditions fading

communities.name: Judging the young players coming up
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: Musicians from every generation and all four collections comment on the younger players coming up behind them, mostly from the 1960s to 2011. Most of the tellers are older instrumentalists, with some producers and educators, and they are asked about the state or future of jazz. Many are warmly encouraging. Vic Dickenson predicts a not-yet-20 Warren Vache will be a good one. George Benson praises the guitarists he mentored. Woody Herman finds no deficits in the current generation, and Harry Edison says he does not resent youngsters being signed. Others are more critical. Art Farmer, Jimmy Owens and Rufus Reid say technique has to serve expression and lived experience. Horace Henderson, Howard Scott and Alvin Queen complain that young players cannot read, lack big-band or road experience, or imitate rather than create. Louis Armstrong says younger street bands want volume without feeling. A few segments drift to related topics such as the future of New Orleans jazz, jazz education and releasing music online. The shared subject is the speaker's verdict on younger musicians, but some segments are only loosely tied to it.
threads: Praise and encouragement for named young players
Young players can't read or lack road and big-band experience
Technique versus feeling, experience and individuality
Creators versus imitators
Future of jazz, jazz education and young brass bands
Young lions, hype and recording young musicians

communities.name: Homemade instruments and boyhood street bands
communities.parent_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught
communities.narrative: Musicians recall building their first instruments as boys out of whatever was at hand, then playing in neighborhood groups before they owned or could afford real ones. The stories are set mostly between the 1890s and the 1920s, and Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive interviews supply most of them, with a few from Hamilton and Rutgers. Tellers describe wash-tub and soapbox basses, cigar-box guitars and fiddles, bucket banjos, cane or fishing-pole kazoos, and drums improvised from scraps. Kid Ory, who tells the most of these, describes burning f-holes into cigar boxes and stringing a banjo with thread and fishing line, and he names the Woodland Band. Others recall serenading neighbors at night, penny parties and street groups of guitar, tub and washboard. Most tellers treat this as play and a first step toward real bass, banjo or brass playing. Eddie Durham's frontier fiddle-making, with gut strings, cedar necks and rattlesnake rattles, is a western variant of the same craft. The cluster is small and a few samples drift toward other first-instrument memories, but most share the one subject.
threads: Cigar-box guitars, fiddles and banjos
Soapbox and wash-tub basses
Kazoos, fences and household-object percussion
Boys' serenading groups and penny parties
Frontier fiddle-making in the West
Kid Ory's Woodland Band

communities.name: Teaching myself guitar and banjo, no teacher
communities.parent_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they got their first stringed instrument, usually a guitar, banjo or ukulele, and how they learned it with little or no formal instruction. The stories are set mostly between about 1900 and the mid-1940s, though a few reach the 1950s and 1960s. Most are New Orleans players, and others come from Memphis, Chicago, Detroit and elsewhere. The instrument often arrives cheaply or by chance: a one-dollar guitar from a mother, a ukulele brought back from Honolulu, a pawnshop guitar, a cigar-box guitar, a loaned instrument, or a grandfather's banjo. Tellers agree that they worked it out by ear or from a chord book, a tuning fork or a diagram book. Many say no teacher was available, and they picked up chords by watching older players or from a friend, relative or visiting musician. Some had a few paid lessons that did not stick. Ukulele, banjo and guitar are often linked, with ukulele or banjo chords carried over to guitar. Some tellers moved between guitar, banjo, piano, violin and cornet, and a few stories drift into band personnel or gigs. They are told by guitarists, banjoists and bandleaders across the collections, and a few pianists and a drummer appear too.
threads: Self-taught from chord books, tuning forks and records
Cheap, borrowed or homemade first instruments
Ukulele and banjo as stepping stones to guitar
Picking up chords by watching older players or relatives
A few failed or brief formal lessons
Switching between guitar, banjo, piano and violin

communities.name: Advice to young musicians: only if you must
communities.parent_name: Advice to young musicians starting out
communities.narrative: Across interviews from Hamilton's Fillius archive (the large majority), the Smithsonian, Rutgers and Tulane, musicians are asked, usually near the end, what they would tell a young person who wants a life in music. The dominant answer is passion: play only if you love it enough to give up everything, or, in Phil Woods's often-quoted line repeated by Ellis Marsalis, Ellen Rowe, Longineu Parsons and others, only if you have no choice. Many pair that with hard-headed practicalities: be versatile (arranging, composing, teaching, Pro Tools, sight reading), learn the business, get a lawyer, avoid drugs, and do not treat teaching as a safety net, though a few, like Howie Shear, recommend diversifying. Others stress craft and heritage: practice, listen to earlier recordings, play with better players, and take time to develop a sound. Most tellers are working players and educators speaking in recent decades, and the samples carry almost no specific dates. They disagree mainly on how much to warn against the career versus encourage it. A few segments are only incidentally here, such as interview openings, closings and reel changes.
threads: Only do it if you have to: passion over career
Be versatile: teaching, arranging, technology, income lanes
Learn the business, get a lawyer, protect yourself
Practice, listen to the heritage, play with better players
Discipline, staying clean and cherishing friends
Closing words and offers to help the young

communities.name: Advice to young musicians
communities.parent_name: Advice to young musicians starting out
communities.narrative: Across 34 interviews from all four archives, musicians are asked, or volunteer, what they would tell the next generation, and they answer in the same terms. The stories are mostly undated and come from players of many instruments and eras, including a 1924-25 anecdote from Sam Wooding and 1970s interviews with Quentin Jackson and Theodore Saunders. The most common advice is to learn the fundamentals: technique, theory, reading and the whole craft, including related instruments. Next comes listening widely, to the best players and even the bad bands, and transcribing and researching a chosen hero. Others urge self-respect, humility, honesty and being believable, and some add practical points such as arriving early, supporting the band and getting out to play for people rather than relying on schooling. A smaller strand is about mentoring itself, with Clark Terry and Gary Burton explaining why they teach and how. The tellers agree on study and listening and differ mainly in how much they stress formal schooling versus learning in the world. A few samples, such as the Timothy lesson on repetition and the interview closing, only loosely fit.
threads: Study technique, theory and the whole craft
Listen widely, transcribe and research a hero
Humility, self-respect and being believable
Practical habits: arrive early, read, support the band
Why and how veterans mentor younger players
Learn Black music history and respect every genre

communities.name: Advice to young players: study, listen, play
communities.parent_name: Advice to young musicians starting out
communities.narrative: In this cluster, musicians from many generations and regions step out of their own biographies to address the next generation directly. The advice has little to do with a particular time or place: only a few segments carry a decade (the 1920s New Orleans recollection of Albert Glenny's rule), and most are undated reflections given late in a career. The dominant counsel is to build a foundation by studying the fundamentals: harmony, scales, reading and sight reading, and learning the instrument properly (Jeanette Kimball, George Mitchell, Benny Waters). A second strand says to learn by listening widely rather than copying one player, to learn solos, and to play live with better musicians instead of only with records or alone (Cootie Williams, Jon-Erik Kellso, Jane Ira Bloom, Bill Berry). A third stresses humility, treating others as better than yourself, and playing what you can sing (Benny Golson, Herb Ellis). Tellers differ mainly in emphasis, formal study against learning on the bandstand, and in attitude, such as Mitchell's distaste for bop's complexity. The speakers come from New Orleans veterans, swing and bebop players, and later instrumentalists across all four collections.
threads: Study the fundamentals: harmony, scales, reading
Listen to everyone and find your own voice
Play with better players, live, as much as possible
Humility and learning from everyone
Play what you can sing
Ask someone who knows (Glenny's rule)

bands: Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers

communities.name: Why young Black musicians don't play jazz
communities.parent_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories
communities.narrative: Older musicians, producers and educators, speaking mostly from the 1970s to the 1990s, ask why so few young Black Americans play or know classic jazz. Tommy Ridgley says that in 1986 young New Orleans players can neither play blues nor read, so he hires white musicians. George Avakian says they lack the foundation, with Nicholas Payton the exception. Billy Taylor, Chuck Mancuso and Pug Horton blame education: schools and Black universities neglect jazz, and students treat music courses as fluff. Jimmy Maxwell, in a 1979 conversation with Milt Hinton, adds that young players don't know Armstrong, Morton or Ben Webster and that economics, not indifference, leaves them no time for history. Joey Morant is more blunt and says today's players assume they already have it. The tellers mostly agree that the cause is missing education and opportunity rather than race or talent. They differ on whether to blame the young musicians, the teachers or the money.
threads: Young players lacking blues and reading skills
Schools and Black colleges neglecting jazz education
Young players not knowing Armstrong, Morton and Webster
Economics and opportunity versus indifference
Exceptions and role models like Payton and Marsalis
White players reviving older jazz while Black stars don't

communities.name: The state of jazz: dying, aging, or here to stay?
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: Across 140 interviews, mostly from the Hamilton collection and recorded from the 1970s to the 2010s, musicians are asked to take stock of jazz as a whole. They ask whether it is healthy, dying, or becoming "museum music". Many worry about an aging audience, especially at jazz parties and for traditional or Dixieland jazz, whose WWII-generation fans are dying off, and about too few young listeners. Others point to a resurgence at colleges, teens playing at NJPAC, and festivals with younger crowds. They largely agree that jazz will always exist but stay a small share of the market, perhaps one percent. They differ on whether exposure, publicity, media such as Ken Burns, and institutions like Lincoln Center help or only breed tribute acts. Players also argue over whether jazz should engage hip hop and rap. A few earlier tellers from 1959 and 1976 ask the same question about New Orleans style and brass bands surviving. A handful of segments drift into related topics such as jazz magazines, local scenes, and the alto saxophone.
threads: Jazz is dead? Resurgence vs. decline
Aging audiences and winning young listeners
Small market share: jazz as esoteric or folk music
Institutions, tributes and repertory: help or museum music
Will traditional, Dixieland and brass band styles survive
Jazz meets rap, hip hop and DJs

communities.name: Complaints about today's pop, rock and rap
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: Across 167 interviews and all four collections, older and mid-career musicians are asked what they think of music today and answer with criticism. The target changes with the teller's era. Early players such as Punch Miller, Emile Barnes and Jack Teagarden, and swing figures such as Sonny Greer and Teddy Wilson, dismiss rock and roll as noise or commercial exploitation. Later interviewees (Harry Edison, Eddie Marshall, David Finck, Art Farmer, Branford Marsalis, David Murray) aim at rap, hip-hop, sampling and loop-based pop. The recurring charges are the loss of melody, chords, song form and finesse, singers who shout instead of sing, and an industry that sells skimpy images of young women singers (Abbey Lincoln, Horn Shirley). A minority soften this: Joe Wilder came to respect The Beatles, Mike Wofford wants to stay open to new music, and Procope and Francis expect jazz or rhythm fundamentals to return. The period runs from the 1970s to the 2000s, but the stories look back from the speaker's present. The cluster is almost entirely reflective commentary, not anecdote. A few samples (Latin music, disco requests, jazz as an art form) are loose fits.
threads: Rock and roll as noise that will pass
Rap, hip-hop and sampling versus melody and song form
How women singers are packaged and marketed
Will jazz come back, and do Americans value it
Generational taste: parents' view of The Beatles then and rap now
Staying open to what young musicians do

communities.name: Rock and roll arrives and jazz work dries up
communities.parent_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future
communities.narrative: In the stories of this cluster, musicians recall the 1950s and early 1960s, when rock and roll and rhythm and blues pushed jazz and Dixieland aside. The tellers describe clubs, theaters and dances changing their bills. Examples are the Apollo house band, the Metropole and the Colonial Inn, where go-go girls and flashing lights replaced jazz rooms. Alan Freed, Bill Haley, Elvis, Fats Domino and later the Beatles recur as markers of the shift. Many say the young audience, with money to spend, followed rock, and that bebop was not danceable. Players split on how to respond. Some switched to club dates, rock or R&B when they were paid, such as Carmen Leggio, Ed Allen and Fred Staton. Others, like Eddie Alley and Alex Bigard, refused or disliked it. A few, like Jon Hendricks, Ed Polcer and Dick Spottswood, trace rock back to jazz, blues and swing. Later tellers, such as Gary Burton and Jackie Cain, describe deliberately combining rock and jazz in the 1960s. Tellers range across New Orleans traditionalists, New York swing and bebop players, and singers. A few samples (for example Jon Jang on Chinese rock) drift off the theme.
threads: Rock and roll taking over clubs and theaters
Alan Freed, Bill Haley and Elvis as turning points
Adapting: club dates, R&B and go-go versus refusing to play rock
Dixieland and bebop losing the dancing public
Where rock came from: roots in jazz, blues and R&B
Jazz-rock crossover and the Beatles in the 1960s

communities.name: Teaching improvisation: ear, melody and fear
communities.parent_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about what happens when they teach, especially how to teach improvisation and how to get students past fear and reliance on the page. The tellers are mostly jazz educators and working players, with a notable run of Hamilton College interviews and some Smithsonian and Rutgers ones. They largely agree that students should learn the original melody, develop their ears and play what they hear, and that children and beginners are naturally creative. Several describe methods: Jamey Aebersold's sing-then-play exercise, Sheila Jordan's cure for the 'scat virus', Nick Mondello's two-note start, Jackie McLean playing students the records that woke him, and Bob Wilber's lesson with Bechet to tell a story with the melody. They differ on whether improvisation can be taught at all (Norris Turney doubts it, Pat LaBarbera says everyone can improvise), and on theory versus intuition. Singers add practical points about working with instrumentalists: keys, counting off, endings. The stories range from the 1940s to the 2020s and are loosely anchored in workshops, schools and camps, with some drift into unrelated asides.
threads: Can improvisation be taught? Ear versus theory
Starting beginners and children without fear
Learn the melody first: Bechet, Jordan and storytelling
Teaching scat and what singers must know
Workshops, camps and school clinics (Aebersold, Skidmore)
Playing students the records that shaped you

communities.name: Teaching jazz: building programs, clinics and classrooms
communities.parent_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about becoming teachers and about how jazz is taught, mostly from the 1960s through the 2010s, with a few set in 2020. The stories are about founding or joining university jazz programs: David Baker hired at Indiana in 1966, Kenny Burrell building the UCLA faculty and the first Ellington course, Chico Hamilton at Parsons, and Benny Carter and George Russell as visiting or part-time teachers. Others describe camps, clinics, workshops and master classes, such as Clark Terry's camps and institute, Jimmy Cobb's Italian clinics, and Cedar Walton's visit to Juilliard. A third strand is reflection on teaching itself. Tellers describe their own methods, learning from students, jazz education versus the old trial-and-error route, big bands versus combos, competitions, and teaching online. Most tellers are established players and bandleaders who became educators, and the tone is generally supportive, with some criticism of competitions, the IAJE and abusive teachers. The cluster is broad. It draws on hundreds of interviews and spans many institutions, including Berklee, Juilliard, Eastman and Rutgers, and the stories come from New York, New Orleans and California. A few samples are tangential, such as a one-line note about a cartoonist student.
threads: Founding and joining university jazz programs
Camps, clinics, workshops and master classes
Personal teaching methods and learning from students
State of jazz education: competitions, big bands vs combos, school vs trial and error
Passing it on to youth and mentoring

communities.name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters, Grammys and other awards
communities.parent_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about receiving awards and honors late in their careers, above all the NEA Jazz Masters fellowship, mostly in interviews recorded between the 1970s and 2014. The core story is the phone call or letter announcing the award, the surprise and sense of shock, and then what the honor means: peer recognition, belated acknowledgement of a lifetime of work, a sense of responsibility, or in some cases a modest payback. Several tellers describe the ceremony in New York or Washington and the company of fellow honorees. Others widen the frame to Grammy nominations, honorary doctorates, keys to the city, named days, society plaques and NEA grants. Tellers differ in tone: some are humbled or thrilled, others like Lou Donaldson say it was long overdue or means little at their age, and Jason Marsalis discusses controversy over whether he deserved it. A few samples drift to loosely related recognition stories, such as an asteroid named for Jane Ira Bloom, Woody Herman's best compliments, and Eddie Palmieri's campaign for a Latin Jazz Grammy category.
threads: Getting the call: learning of an NEA Jazz Master award
What the Jazz Master honor means: peer recognition and responsibility
The award ceremony and fellow honorees
Grammy nominations and who wins
Honorary doctorates, keys to the city and named days
Feeling overlooked or the award coming late

communities.name: Old New Orleans picnic parks and amusement grounds
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians and other old-timers recall the picnic parks and amusement grounds of New Orleans around 1890 to 1915: Lincoln Park, White City, Southern Park, Crescent Pleasure Park, Commercial Park and the lakefront gardens at Milneburg and Lake Pontchartrain. The stories are mostly about places, not music. Tellers locate each park by street or bayou, and describe what drew crowds: Sunday dances in big halls, flying horses and ferris wheels, boxing, skating rinks, and the balloon ascents and parachute jumps that Stecklet, Thompson, Ory and Tillman all remember. They also recall getting there on the Smokey Mary or the steam train to the lake, which took half an hour and cost fifteen cents round trip, with bands playing on Sundays. Clementin traces Lincoln Park to a former vegetable garden, and La Rocca describes burning-city shows and opera bands at White City. The tellers agree on the picture of a festive Sunday scene but differ in what they know first-hand. Stecklet admits he only guesses the locations of some parks, and a few samples drift off the theme, such as a flag-raising shooting contest at Razo and a ballpark band job.
threads: Locating the old parks: Lincoln, Southern, Commercial, White City
Sunday amusements: dance halls, flying horses, boxing, skating
Balloon ascents and parachute jumps
The Smokey Mary and steam trains to the lakefront
White City shows, drinks and opera bands
Gardens and picnics, such as the gardeners' picnic

communities.name: Faith, karma and the philosophy of a life in music
communities.parent_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live
communities.narrative: In these segments musicians step back from the music and talk about how they understand life: what guides them, why bad things happen, and how they stay kind and steady. Most tellers speak in the language of belief. Jon Hendricks and Harold Ousley talk about karma, Wayne Shorter and Terri Lyne Carrington about Buddhist practice, and Yusef Lateef, Hubert Laws, Earl May and Red Callender about the Creator or Christian faith. Others put it in secular or personal terms, such as optimism, positive thinking, humility, anger at injustice, or a belief that everyone is connected. Common ideas are a larger plan or guiding spirit (Von Freeman, George Russell), turning hardship into strength, and being a role model. The tellers are mostly from the Smithsonian, Hamilton and Rutgers interviews, and many of the segments answer a closing, reflective question from the interviewer. A few samples drift off this subject: Corea on music as communication, Heard on sculpting, Tinney on a good woman, and Purdie on friends versus associates. They sit near the cluster only because they are also reflective, values-driven talk.
threads: Karma, Buddhism and Nichiren-style practice (Hendricks, Shorter, Carrington)
Christian faith and a Creator as the source of music and character
A larger plan or guiding spirit through hardship
Anger, injustice, optimism and choosing a loving stance
Being a role model and what music can and cannot do for morals
Closing reflections and what matters most in life

communities.name: Music over money: what making it means
communities.parent_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant
communities.narrative: Musicians from all four collections reflect, usually late in an interview and without a fixed period, on what a career in jazz is for and what counts as success. The dominant answer is that money should not be the measure. Cosimo Matassa says he never exploited his publishing position and took satisfaction from the music. Arnett Cobb wants only enough to live on. Wild Bill Davison says happiness mattered more than pay, and Marshall Allen calls music a product made from the heart. Jon Hendricks sees his work as a ministry, and Bill Easley recalls Billy Mitchell's idea that music is a calling. A second strand is more pragmatic. Reggie Watkins defines making it as doing what you want and getting paid, accepting compromises. Tom Malone, David Albert Francis and Jon-Erik Kellso openly say they want more money, and Marian McPartland gripes about the business. Doug Carn defends playing weddings and rejects the idea that musicians must suffer, while Charles Lloyd and Adrian Cunningham weigh the hardship against what music has given them. A few samples drift to other topics, such as Warne Marsh and the Tristano circle, or Davison's dislike of territory-band mute effects.
threads: Not about the money: satisfaction over pay
Music as a calling or ministry
What making it means: getting paid and doing what you want
Wanting more money and gripes about the business
The artist's struggle and the rewards of the life
Career goals and plans for the future

communities.name: Looking back: luck, legacy and what music means
communities.parent_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant
communities.narrative: These are closing-reflection stories in which musicians, usually near the end of an interview, step back and assess their lives in music. They are not set in one period or place; the years run from the 1930s to 2011 and the tellers come from all four collections. Many credit luck, being in the right place at the right time, and being prepared when opportunity came (Cozy Cole, Benny Golson, Bucky Pizzarelli, Jimmy Cobb, Jimmy Jones). Others say what they hope to be remembered for (David Baker, Lee Konitz, Abbey Lincoln, Earl Turbinton on the New Orleans Jazz Workshop) or what music has given them: joy, escape from pain, security, a purpose. A few reflect on success, recognition and reputation (Nancy Wilson, Candido Camero, Buddy Tate, Tuts Washington). The tellers differ in tone: some are modest and deny any special status, while others take pride in their standing. Because the samples share a general mood of retrospection and not one subject, the cluster is loosely held together, and a few segments about oral history, journalism or specific events (the WPA photograph, Bluesette with Stevie Wonder, honoring Jaco) fit only weakly.
threads: Luck, right place and right time, being ready
How I want to be remembered: legacy and contributions
What music means: joy, escape, and a way of life
Success, recognition and modesty about reputation
Oral history and the value of telling the story

bands: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

communities.name: Looking back: no regrets, and would I do it again
communities.parent_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant
communities.narrative: These are the closing questions of jazz oral-history interviews, where the interviewer asks the musician to sum up a life in music. Tellers from the 1920s to the 2010s, from New Orleans traditionalists such as Ridgley, Desvigne and Jim Robinson to bandleaders and modernists such as Woody Herman, Mary Lou Williams, Benny Golson, Sonny Rollins and Joanne Brackeen, give strikingly similar answers. Most say they have no regrets and would choose music again, and they cite the music itself, the travel, the people and the privilege of being paid for something they loved. A few name specific regrets, such as Hodes missing Joe Oliver, Buster Smith leaving electrical work, or Carter's missed opportunities. Some are asked whether they wish they had lived in another era and mostly say the present suits them. Others reflect on success, legacy and the interview itself. The samples come from many collections and interviewers, and about half are explicit closing exchanges. The rest drift into related reflection or segment-specific detail, so the subject is shared but loosely bounded.
threads: No regrets: would do it all again
Specific regrets and roads not taken
Which era would I have lived in
Gratitude and the privilege of making a living from music
Legacy, success and how to be remembered
Closing remarks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

communities.name: Learning drums: teachers, method books and rudiments
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Drummers, and a few other instrumentalists, tell how they were taught: who gave them their first lessons, what book they worked from, and what the teacher drilled into them. The core is New Orleans in the 1910s-20s. Alex Bigard, Albert Francis, Bill Matthews, Joseph "Red" Clark and Milford Dolliole recall strict teachers such as Lloyd Cantrell, Louis Cottrell, Vic Gaspard and Dave Perkins. Lessons cost about fifty cents, students spent months on the practice pad working on rolls, and the Imperial, Langley and Carl Fischer method books taught reading and keeping time with the foot. Later tellers describe the same routine in other places: Cozy Cole's rudiment drills at the Krupa-Cole school in New York, Jake Hanna on grip and tuning, and Jason Marsalis starting with James Black and Stick Control and then taking a lesson with Alan Dawson in Boston. Several tellers say they were largely self-taught, picking things up from pit drummers or practicing alone, and add a lesson or two for reading or tuning. The tellers agree that reading and rudiments came first, but the older ones stress the teacher's strictness while the younger ones name books and famous teachers. A few samples drift to other subjects, such as Cascadu's spiritual teacher, Karl Berger's teaching at Creative Music Studio, and Phil Schaap being taught to listen.
threads: Strict New Orleans teachers and their fifty-cent lessons (Cantrell, Cottrell, Gaspard, Perkins)
Method books and rudiments: Imperial, Stick Control, Harr, Wilcoxon, Ted Reed
Alan Dawson and the Boston lesson, passed on to Tony Williams and Jason Marsalis
Cozy Cole, Jake Hanna and other big-name drum teachers
Self-taught drummers: tubs, pit drummers and learning to read alone
Learning tuning, brushes and technique from older drummers

communities.name: Faith, spirituality and what musicians believe
communities.parent_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection and many generations reflect on religion and spirituality and how it bears on their lives and playing. Most of the samples are direct statements of belief: Fred Wesley belongs to no religion but credits God for his ability, Ramsey Lewis calls religion something many people do only on Sunday, Charles Lloyd follows Vedanta, Doug Carn converted to Islam, and Jamey Aebersold moved from Methodism to Unity. Others tell personal episodes of faith at work. Arnett Cobb was turned around in the hospital by a newspaper prayer around 1948, and Sonny Rollins remembers praying as a boy. Walter P. Thomas describes Christian Science and Lionel Hampton's practice of it in the 1940s, and Joe Williams also invokes Christian Science. The tellers differ widely in creed, from Christian Science, Methodism and gospel-rooted faith to Vedanta, Islam and unaffiliated belief in God. They agree that spirit and belief shape character and music. The stories are mostly told in later life and are rarely tied to a specific date or place. A few outliers, such as a psychic's prediction and Sammy Price's Jerusalem and Bethlehem in heaven, are about the unseen rather than organised religion.
threads: Personal belief and God without a church
Conversion and other faiths: Vedanta, Islam, Christian Science
Prayer and faith as a turning point or healing
Spirituality in the playing itself
Church, Sunday religion and its limits
Fate, past lives and unseen realities

communities.name: Work songs: railroad, field and prison gangs
communities.parent_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
