communities.narrative: Musicians and other interviewees describe the songs sung to ease and pace manual labor in the early twentieth century South. The settings are railroad track gangs (tamping, laying steel to the hammer song, with axes beating a log for rhythm), sugar cane and cotton fields, cement and wood crews, and penal farms such as Parchman and Angola, where Robert Welch served time alongside Lead Belly at Camp A. Tellers agree that songs fit the task, that a lead singer calls and the gang answers, and that the same work songs were sung in every penitentiary. Several, such as Punch Miller and Jim Robinson, recall singing in the fields as children and say none of it was worked into jazz tunes. Lemon Nash adds a few songs of his own, one about a raid and another about a railroad singer and a chain gang. The tellers are mostly blues and folk singers and older New Orleans players, recorded by Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, with the stories set mainly between 1900 and 1960.
threads: Railroad track gang and hammer songs
Prison farm singing at Parchman and Angola
Lead Belly and the lead singer's role
Field and cane work singing in childhood
Lemon Nash's own songs about raids and chain gangs

communities.name: Talking about their children and grandchildren
communities.parent_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren
communities.narrative: In these segments musicians, mostly late in life and speaking in interviews from the 1960s through the 2010s, step away from the career story to talk about their own families: their children, grandchildren and sometimes stepchildren. The tellers give names and occupations, and many report whether the next generation went into music. Some did: Gerald Wilson's son tours with Diana Krall, Jay Leonhart's son is a trumpeter, Jimmy Rowles played with his daughter Stacy, and Kidd Jordan trained his children on their instruments. Others went elsewhere, as with Nat Hentoff's circus-director and lawyer children, Snooky Young's horticulturist son, and Steve Gilmore's and Lawrence Marrero's children, who took no interest after seeing the struggle. Several tellers say their children were polite but unimpressed by their fame, or simply saw Dad going off to work. The warm tone and domestic detail (photos, Christmas, kids meeting Zoot Sims at the house) is shared across New Orleans, New York and California players, and across all four archives. A couple of samples drift to other family topics, such as Buddy Bolden's children and a band's family lineage.
threads: Children who followed their parent into music
Children who chose other careers or lost interest
Kids' indifference to or view of their parent's work
Grandchildren and family snapshots
Performing or recording with a son or daughter
Raising kids around music at home

communities.name: Wives, children and family trees
communities.parent_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Musicians and the people who knew them set out who their families were: spouses, children, grandchildren, and sometimes the names and addresses needed to reach a relative. Most of the stories are family rosters. Al Hall and Jimmy Maxwell go through their children's careers and the naming of grandsons. Percy Heath lists Connie Kay's real name, wives and sons. Clarence Vincent counts the babies he lost and the children he never saw while on the road. Others tell it as a household history: Mose Allison on moving to Jackson Heights and Smithtown while his wife worked in advertising and then taught, Ron Carter on young sons and 3:30 AM dinners, and Leslie Johnson on a family that all worked for The Rag. Two sub-stories stand apart. David Albert Francis tells of tracing his lost daughters through phone books and a chain of contacts in Montreal, Detroit and the Bronx. Interviewers in New Orleans collect remarriage and kinship details, such as Mother Richards' second marriage and the Zeno family's address. The set spans roughly the 1920s to the 1970s and draws mostly on Rutgers interviews, with Tulane, Hamilton and Smithsonian interviews also contributing. It is a loosely bounded cluster, because the family-tree detail is shared but the tone ranges from biographical fact-gathering to personal and emotional accounts.
threads: Listing children, grandchildren and their names
Wives, remarriages and separations
Raising young kids while on the road or at night work
Tracing and reuniting with lost children
Documenting a musician's kin for the archive
Family members who also work in the music

communities.name: Fighting to survive tough streets as a Black boy
communities.parent_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
communities.narrative: Musicians recall childhood and adolescence shaped by street violence, bullying and racial hostility, mostly in the 1910s through the 1950s. The most vivid tellings come from John W. Bubbles, who describes c. 1912-14 Indianapolis: boxing the newsboys, stoning fights with white schoolchildren, a park-swing standoff, cutting a boy with a pocket knife while fleeing a mob, and the Detention Home decision that took him away from a life of violence. George Benson tells a later version from 1950s Pittsburgh, with tough cousins, a cousin killed in a gang fight, and a muscular friend who earned the group respect. Kenny Burrell and Charles Thompson describe how music, or a father's advice, kept them out of fights and gangs. Several other samples drift to neighborhood life more broadly, such as Sammy Price freeing Black kids from Dallas jails, Ram Ramirez's 63rd Street neighbors, and the integrated or outsider neighborhoods of Elvin Jones, Shirley Horn and Nat Hentoff. The tellers agree that physical toughness was a childhood necessity, but they differ on whether race or neighborhood was the main source of danger.
threads: Bubbles's boyhood fights in Indianapolis
Gang fights and street reputations in the 1950s
Music as protection from gangs and bullies
Racial hostility and mob violence toward Black children
Growing up in mixed or working-class neighborhoods
Boxing and fighters in the community

communities.name: Growing up with segregated and mixed schools
communities.parent_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
communities.narrative: Musicians from many cities describe how race shaped their childhood neighborhoods and schools, mostly in the 1920s through the 1940s, with a few earlier and later cases. The tellers disagree about what they found. Some, such as David Baker and JJ Johnson in Indianapolis, Frank Foster in Cincinnati, Percy Heath in Philadelphia and Art Farmer in Phoenix, recall formally segregated schools, theaters, ballparks and Jim Crow travel. Others, including Gerald Wilson in Detroit, Milton Batiste in New Orleans, Marshall Royal and Reb Spikes in Los Angeles, and Eddie Alley in San Francisco, remember mixed neighborhoods and little early awareness of segregation. Many accounts fall in between: integrated schools in a segregated town, as in Columbus, Newark and Kansas, or Detroit formally integrated but segregated in practice. Smaller episodes cover learning about prejudice from a parent or mentor, shared neighborhoods with Italian, Polish and Jewish children, and one Japanese schooling story. Tellers include Black and white musicians from every collection, and most are describing where they grew up rather than their careers.
threads: Segregated schools and the feeder-school system
Mixed neighborhoods and integrated schools in the North and West
Integrated schools in a segregated town: theaters, ballparks, stores
Learning about prejudice and slurs from parents and mentors
Growing up among immigrant groups in multi-ethnic neighborhoods
Self-contained Black communities that cushioned childhood

communities.name: Growing up Black in mixed neighborhoods and schools
communities.parent_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
communities.narrative: Musicians recall childhoods spent in racially and ethnically mixed neighborhoods and schools, mostly between the 1900s and the 1940s, with a few later accounts. The settings range from Boston, Pittsburgh and Everett to Colorado Springs, Texas, Missouri and rural and urban Louisiana. Many describe schools and streets shared with Polish, Lithuanian, Jewish, Irish, French-Canadian and white Southern neighbors, and several say segregation was absent or only subtle. Others describe its edges: racial slurs, fights with classmates, biased teachers, gangs harassing children, and in one case a segregated school in a prejudiced town. Several tellers, including Jon Hendricks and Branford Marsalis, add what their fathers taught them about not letting insults define them. The tellers come from every collection, New Orleans Creole elders alongside northern jazz players, and they agree that mixing was common but disagree on how comfortable it was. The cluster is smaller and looser than a full community, because a few segments drift into family anecdotes unrelated to schooling or neighborhoods.
threads: Mixed neighborhoods and integrated schools
Slurs, fights and biased teachers
Fathers' lessons about not being defined by others
Subtle or absent segregation in early childhood
Migration and ethnic mix in mill and industrial towns

communities.name: Church and faith in a musician's upbringing
communities.parent_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection recall the church and religion of their childhood homes and how they did or did not shape their music. The settings are mostly 1905 to 1970. New Orleans is most common, with Chicago, New York and the Mississippi and Texas South also appearing. Many tell of Baptist, Methodist, Catholic, Pentecostal or AME congregations. They describe Sunday school, choirs, mothers who sang, deacon fathers, and chores like ringing the bell. Several, including Jackie McLean, Hubert Laws and Elvin Jones, say gospel and church rhythm are roots of their musical sense. Others, like Lawrence Cotton and Melba Liston, say church did not influence them, or they left it. A smaller group tells of adult conversions and other faiths (Jehovah's Witnesses, Islam, Baha'i, Christian Science). A few segments concern jazz inside churches, such as Jazz Vespers at St. Peter's, a jazz mass, or Lent shutting down dancing. The tellers differ on whether faith fed the music or stayed apart from it. The cluster is held together by religion, though it covers a lot of ground.
threads: Growing up in the Baptist, Methodist, Catholic and Pentecostal church
Church choirs, hymns and gospel as the root of musical sense
Rejecting or leaving the church of childhood
Conversion to Islam, Baha'i, Jehovah's Witnesses and other faiths
Jazz in the church: Jazz Vespers, jazz masses, Easter spirituals

communities.name: Wives, marriages and family life
communities.parent_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections talk about their spouses, weddings and households rather than their music. Louie Bellson describes adopting children with Pearl Bailey, her earlier unhappy marriages and her Georgetown degree, and later meeting Francine on a Duke Ellington cruise. Jo Jones recalls marrying Lorraine and becoming a father and grandfather on the same day. Nat Hentoff lists his three wives and Lorraine Gordon describes life among the Blue Angel crowd after marrying Max. Don Albert tells of a double anniversary and his daughter's wedding in the 1970s. The older New Orleans and Chicago tellers (Natty Dominique, Frog Joseph, Roger Mitchell, Bernard Steinau) place marriage in the early 1900s through the 1950s. They talk about a school friend's husband, a wife's musical family, wedding photographs, and the custom of keeping an outside wife. The stories share the theme of private family life. They differ in period and tone, ranging from affectionate portraits of one marriage to frank remarks about infidelity. Only some of the ten core samples are about the interviewee's own marriage, and a few concern other people's.
threads: Bellson and Pearl Bailey: adoption and her earlier marriages
Multiple marriages and second wives (Hentoff, Jo Jones)
Weddings, anniversaries and wedding photographs
Wives from musical families and married women of the scene
Outside wives and musicians as ladies' men

communities.name: Marriage and the musician's wife
communities.parent_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection, in about a hundred interviews, talk about their spouses and what it takes to stay married while working in music. The stories range from the 1930s, when Billie Pierce and her husband decided to marry after three weeks, to the 2010s, when Wayne Shorter reflected on musicians' wives putting ego aside. Tellers praise a wife's patience and support through lean years and long road trips. Chico Hamilton credits sixty years of marriage to Helen, and Ernie Fields says Bernice never worried while he travelled. Several wives are described as working partners: Red Callender's wife heads his publishing company, Bucky Pizzarelli's handles business and mail, and Ramsey Lewis's Jan advises on his pieces. Others say love is the secret of a long marriage, or stress putting family before music, as Vince DiMartino does. Toots Thielemans admits musicians are hard to live with, and Milt Hinton calls it lucky to keep one wife over decades. The tellers are mostly established, older musicians looking back, and they largely agree that marriage lasted because of the spouse's tolerance and shared love of music. The differences are in whether the wife is a muse, a business manager or a quiet anchor.
threads: Decades-long marriages and their secret
Wives as business partners and managers
Spousal support during life on the road
Spouse as muse and musical partner
Family before music
Remarriage and being widowed

communities.name: Boyhood games, school days and growing up
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers musicians' scattered recollections of ordinary childhood before music takes over: what they did as kids, how they were raised, and where they went to school. The settings range across the 1910s to the 1960s and across many places, including Pontiac, Greensboro, Memphis, Kalamazoo, Five Points, Georgia and New Orleans. Recurring episodes include Boy Scout troops (sometimes used as cover to slip off to a party), swimming holes, ice skating, boxing lessons from a neighborhood champion, baseball and football on the green, and earning small money shining shoes or renting bicycles. Others describe early schooling, such as a brewery kindergarten that taught German, a skipped kindergarten recess, and classroom mishaps. Several tellers, such as Marshall Royal and Roger Mitchell, contrast the discipline, chores and neighborhood respect of their youth with today's looser upbringing. A few segments drift into adolescent family circumstances, including a mother moving the family for a segregated high school, a barber shop as a place of learning, and a family settling in Las Vegas. The tellers agree that childhood was communal and structured by neighborhood and school, but there is no single event, and a few samples are only loosely related to the rest.
threads: Boy Scouts and neighborhood clubs
Childhood games, sports and swimming
Early schooling and kindergarten mishaps
Chores, discipline and community values then versus now
Teenage family moves and growing up in the neighborhood

communities.name: Going to school: Black education in the early South
communities.parent_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians recall their schooling in the 1900s to early 1930s, mostly in Black schools across Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and the Midwest. The recurring thread is Tuskegee Institute: Teddy Wilson describes growing up there under Principal Moton and defends Booker T. Washington's trade-school philosophy, Ernie Fields remembers registering there, and Leonidas Young's father graduated from it. Others tell of ordinary school days: Gus Johnson's moves between Tyler, Beaumont, Houston and Dallas, Frank Amacker's Fifth School and its teachers, John Levy's teachers and early ambitions, and Walter Thomas's high school in Topeka. A few segments cover other things, such as shop classes, a Catholic military school, a scrapbook of a 1906 graduation, and an unintelligible remark about Piney Woods. The tellers agree that school was where they first met discipline, teachers and ambition, and they differ mainly in how closely their schooling was tied to Washington's Tuskegee model or to a local neighborhood school. Tellers include both Rutgers and Tulane interviewees, and most are men who went on to become professional players.
threads: Tuskegee Institute and Booker T. Washington's legacy
Elementary and grammar schools in Texas towns
Teachers and principals who shaped them
Black colleges and schools in Louisiana and Mississippi
Shop, math and other school subjects
Family moves that changed schools

communities.name: Wives, marriages and family life
communities.parent_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections, nearly all different interviewees, talk about their spouses and marriages. Most of these are short personal asides rather than stories about music. Johnny DeDroit recalls meeting his wife at 14 and her poise at Biloxi dances. Lawrence Cotton describes a 1946 wartime-leave marriage, fifty years together and his wife's later stroke. Santo Pecora, Eddie Durham and Art Farmer count several marriages and the children who came from them. Avakian George says he proposed to only one woman, the violinist Anahid. John W. Bubbles tells of a girl who married someone else. Dave Brubeck and Vince Lateano mention partners who are also sounding boards or fellow singers. Percy Heath follows Kenny Clarke's marriage to Annie Ross and their son. The tellers agree that marriage was part of a working musician's life. They differ in tone, from devoted long marriages and caregiving to serial marriages and lost love. A few segments drift to related topics, such as Jules Cahn on women sewing Mardi Gras Indian costumes. The period runs from about 1910 to 1955, though many segments have no date.
threads: Meeting and courting a future wife
Multiple marriages and raising children
Long marriages, illness and caregiving
Spouses as musical partners and sounding boards
Marriages of fellow musicians (Kenny Clarke, Annie Ross)
Women's roles around the music (costume sewing)

communities.name: Meeting and marrying my wife
communities.parent_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives
communities.narrative: Musicians and a few of their spouses tell how they met the person they married, and how courtship and wedding fit around life on the bandstand. The stories run from the 1920s to the 2000s, with most set between the 1930s and the 1950s. Meetings happen at dances and clubs (Birdland, the Savoy, a Chicken and Waffle restaurant), at funerals and movie theaters, on tour (a Swedish train station), and through friends or a band's dancers. Many tellers give the wedding date, the church, the children, and sometimes a first marriage that did not last. Some tellers are reluctant or terse, such as Lee Konitz and Helen Humes. Others turn it into a long love story, such as Hank and Teddie Jones, and Dave Brubeck and Iola. A few spouses, including Alice Russell, Teddie Jones and Anita Evans, tell the story themselves. Differences show up in era and setting: 1930s bandleaders preferred married men, and later stories involve marriages across racial lines, international romances and second marriages. The category tags are mostly health_personal, but the subject is courtship and marriage, not health.
threads: How we met: dances, clubs, tours and funerals
Courtship and the wedding itself, with dates and churches
Wives and children raised around a musician's career
Brief, failed or multiple marriages
Spouses telling their side of the story
Marriage and band life: bandleaders' rules, the road and being away

communities.name: After Katrina: displacement, return and rebuilding New Orleans
communities.parent_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow
communities.narrative: Most of the central stories are New Orleans musicians recalling Hurricane Katrina and its aftermath, set mainly in 2005-2010. Tellers describe evacuating to places like Baton Rouge, Jackson, Florida, Georgia and New York, finding houses flooded, damaged or surprisingly intact, and returning months later. Others focus on the wider recovery: the uneven rebuilding of the Lower Ninth Ward, the Musicians' Village and Ellis Marsalis Center, Snug Harbor reopening, housing aid for scattered musicians, and WWOZ helping locate people. Several, including Jason Marsalis, Ellis Marsalis and Germaine Bazzle, argue that the musical tradition and the city's spirit survived even though livelihoods, neighborhoods and musicians' presence suffered, while David Torkanowsky laments gentrification. Tellers include native musicians, educators and the aid worker Wendy Oxenhorn. Toward the edges the cluster drifts into loosely related material (musical families, what defines New Orleans music, Ellis Marsalis in Cajun country, Anat Cohen on Israel and the pandemic) that is not about the storm.
threads: Evacuation and flooded or surviving houses
Musicians scattered and tracked down (WWOZ, housing aid)
Rebuilding: Musicians' Village, Snug Harbor, Lower Ninth Ward
Did the music and the city's spirit survive?
Gentrification and loss of New Orleans culture
Loosely related asides on New Orleans musical identity

communities.name: Odd jobs, side hustles and everyday life
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: This cluster is a loose collection of everyday-life recollections told by New Orleans musicians and their relatives, mostly in the Tulane (Hogan) interviews. They are set between the 1920s and the early 1970s, and the tellers are mostly not talking about music. Some stories are about making a living outside the bandstand: peddling vegetables and Christmas trees after leaving the post office, hanging paper ceilings, running a hauling job to Philadelphia, killing chickens at a restaurant, and cutting hair. Others are household and neighborhood life: fish fries in Prohibition days, scrubbing steps with red brick, burial insurance, playing lottery numbers in the Depression, keeping meat before refrigerators, and feeding the dog. A few are anecdotes such as winning $100 in a gas-station game, a friendship with a baseball team owner, and amateur baseball in Algiers. The stories do not agree on one subject, and the common thread is only that they are small, practical, non-musical details of how ordinary people got by.
threads: Peddling, hauling and other side jobs
Trades and household chores: paper hanging, scrubbing, chickens
Burial insurance, lottery numbers and Depression-era money
Food, markets and fish fries before refrigeration
Pets and home life in interviews
Sports and chance windfalls: baseball, prize games

communities.name: Growing up in a musical family, father's instruments and early violin
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the household that first put an instrument in their hands: a father (sometimes a mother, uncle, grandparent or brother) who played in a brass band, taught lessons, or filled the house with strings and horns. Set mostly between the 1890s and the 1930s, in New Orleans but also Chicago, Louisville, Des Moines and the West, the stories repeatedly begin with violin lessons at age five to ten, often on a parent's own violin, and with family string groups, musical evenings and Cajun dances. The tellers broadly agree that music was simply what the family did, and several say they were handed or pushed into it, as Lee Young was by his father who kept supplying instruments. They differ on parental attitude: some fathers or mothers encouraged and taught, while others (Blanchin's father, Buddy Burton's father, the Humphrey-type religious grandparents, Lanny Morgan's mother, Eddie Bert's baseball-minded father) disapproved of jazz or horns. New Orleans Creole and brass-band players dominate, but the pattern also appears among later swing and bebop players such as Conte Candoli and Eddie Bert. A few samples drift to adjacent topics such as a father booking bands or a cousin who taught, but the shared core is the musical home and first instruments.
threads: Father as the first teacher or bandleader
First violin lessons at five to ten
Family string groups and musical evenings at home
Parents or grandparents who disapproved of jazz
Reluctant starters and the instruments handed to them
Siblings and relatives who taught or played alongside

communities.name: Early music lessons and the teachers who shaped them
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from every collection recall their first formal instruction: who taught them, what they were made to practice, and how strict or limiting the teacher was. The stories are set mostly between the 1910s and the early 1950s, in New Orleans, Chicago, Boston, Washington and New York, with a few later cases such as Loren Schoenberg's lessons in the 1970s. Tellers name local professors, school music teachers, church or community programs, parents and relatives, and sometimes conservatory or concert-hall teachers. They agree that classical technique (scales, Bach, Hanon, Arban, sight reading) was the common foundation. They differ on whether it helped or held them back. Some teachers forbade jazz and rapped fingers, others added chord symbols or a jazz crash course, and a few musicians such as Arnett Cobb say there were no teachers at all and they taught themselves. Tellers include New Orleans players, big-band sidemen, pianists and drummers who went on to bebop and later jazz careers.
threads: Naming the first teacher and lessons from age eight to thirteen
Classical grounding: scales, Bach, Arban and sight reading
Teachers who forbade or discouraged jazz
Jazz taught on the side or by a later specialist
Conservatories, school systems and community programs
Going without teachers and learning on your own

bands: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band

communities.name: Taking up drums: homemade kits, first sets, few lessons
communities.parent_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons
communities.narrative: Drummers recall how they first came to the drums, mostly in New Orleans and mostly between about 1900 and the early 1940s. The stories start with improvised instruments: tubs, cheese boxes, lard buckets, tin cans, pots and pans, and chair rounds beaten on steps. Then comes the first real set, bought secondhand from a music store or pawnshop, built by a friend, or handed down by a brother. Most tellers say they were self-taught or had no formal lessons. Some name a brother, a local drummer, a school teacher or a delivery-truck driver as a model or informal teacher. A few have one or two paid lessons, and some mention the burden of carrying drums around. Others, such as Papa Jack Laine in the 1880s and Butch Miles and Greg Caputo in the 1950s-60s, tell it from outside the core period. Many of these drummers go on to a first job in a local band, but that part is secondary. The pack is dominated by New Orleans players from the Tulane collection, with a scattering from Rutgers, Hamilton and the Smithsonian.
threads: Homemade first drums: tubs, cheese boxes, cans, pots and pans
Buying or being given the first drum set
Self-taught, with no formal lessons
Learning from a brother or local drummer
First jobs in neighborhood and brass bands
Drums as a burden to carry, or a switch to another instrument

communities.name: Studying with teachers: lessons, schooling and learning by experience
communities.parent_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees
communities.narrative: Musicians across New Orleans, New York, Hollywood and the conservatories recall the individual teachers who shaped them and weigh what formal instruction was worth. The stories range from the 1920s (Zilner Randolph's four years of lessons with Eddie Hudson, Narvin Kimball's schoolmate-teacher Valmo Victor) through the 1930s-50s (Schillinger's mathematical method with Bill Challis and Walter Thomas's teacher, Copland with George Handy, Wolpe and Tremblay with Johnny Mandel) to later conservatory and college settings (Billy Taylor and Undine Smith Moore, Charles Lloyd and Halsey Stevens, Carmen Lundy and Brewster). Many tellers describe a particular lesson method or what a teacher gave them, such as counterpoint, atonal writing or strict habits. Others are openly ambivalent: Eddie Sauter calls teachers a crutch and an intellectual force, and Wilbur DeParis and Mandel say they learned mostly from experience. Several recall teachers who tolerated or encouraged jazz against institutional rules, while some jazz players found their classical teachers did not know jazz. A few segments drift toward portraits of a teacher or to local history, such as Jim Humphrey teaching at a plantation, but the common thread is who taught them and how.
threads: Classical and modernist composition teachers (Copland, Schoenberg circle, Wolpe, Schillinger)
Early local teachers and schoolmates in New Orleans and the South
College and conservatory teachers who allowed or resisted jazz
Lesson methods and what a teacher actually taught
Teachers versus learning from experience
Teacher-student relationships and quitting lessons

communities.name: Learning chords by ear, without schooling
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Musicians across many eras describe picking up jazz harmony outside any school, because jazz was not taught formally. They learned by listening to records, copying 78s, sitting in at sessions, and getting chords shown to them by a bandmate, an older player or a book. Settings run from 1910s-20s New Orleans and string-band players, through the 1940s-50s (James Moody learning chords from Tom McIntosh on a tour bus, Phil Woods with LaRose, Bud Freeman with the McPartlands), to 1960s-2000s players such as Abercrombie, Bennett and Bunnett. Many tellers say they knew a chord by sound before they knew its name. Others, such as Marty Grosz and Johnny Varro, found chord symbols in books. A minority, such as Jamey Aebersold at Indiana University, recall a more formal ear-training route. Tellers also note that older players guarded their knowledge, that well-known self-taught figures like Erroll Garner could not read music, and that reading was sometimes seen as overrated. A few samples drift to adjacent topics, such as Mary Lou Williams on left-hand technique and Eddie Palmieri on finger independence, but the core is a shared account of learning harmony by ear.
threads: Learning chords from records by ear
A bandmate or older player shows you the chords
Self-taught players who could not read
Chord books, fake books and informal lessons
Jazz not taught in school, and players who would not share
Hearing intervals and ear training

communities.name: Family music and the first instrument
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how music entered their lives at home as children, usually through a parent or relative. A father, uncle or cousin hands over, buys or barters for a first trumpet, clarinet, drum, guitar or piano. Others describe growing up in houses full of records, a Steinway, vaudeville brass or a jazz-guitarist father. The stories are set mostly between about 1912 and 1964, in places such as Chicago, New York and Detroit, and they come from all four collections. Many start on the wrong instrument, such as violin or piano, and switch to drums or trumpet, or they combine family-led playing with later formal or classical lessons. Some tellers describe a moment of deciding at about eleven that music would be their life. The tellers differ on whether the family encouraged them or resisted, as with Marty Grosz's mother objecting once he got serious. The tellers are mostly instrumentalists, with a few women among them, and the stories run from the earliest decades of the century into the 1960s.
threads: A father or uncle hands down or buys the first instrument
Growing up with parents' records, piano and music in the house
Starting on violin or piano, then switching to drums or trumpet
Family lessons before classical or formal training
Deciding around age eleven to become a musician
Parents supporting or resisting a serious commitment

communities.name: Rural Louisiana childhood: plantations, floods and household chores
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: These stories are loosely held together by musicians and relatives recalling everyday life in rural and riverside Louisiana, mostly in the 1890s to 1920s, before the city scene enters the picture. The tellers describe domestic labor and household routines (washing and drying sea-hair mattresses, scrubbing floors and pots with brick), bedtime and fireside tales such as Brer Rabbit and the syrup barrel, and the physical setting of plantations and sugar refineries along the river, such as McCall. Several tellers recall moving between places like Belle Chasse, Sox's Lane and Dubin, and living with floods and crevasses. Others recall early jobs and family kindness, including a first job in the city around a September storm, a neighbor who gave bread and clothes, and gifts from a relative who was a musician. A few segments touch music, such as a country band that played at a plantation while city bands never came, but music is incidental. A couple of segments are outliers, notably a family china-and-glassware rental business. The samples share a time and a region more than a single event, so this is a mood of remembered rural and working-class life, told mostly by Tulane interviewees, including women relatives, rather than one shared story.
threads: Household chores and domestic work (mattresses, scrubbing floors)
Plantation and sugar-refinery settings along the river
Floods, crevasses, storms and moving house
Fireside stories and family memories
First jobs and kindness from neighbors and relatives
Country bands and why city bands did not visit

communities.name: Learning an instrument in the school band
communities.parent_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they first took up an instrument through a school band, orchestra or music class, usually before they turned professional. Most stories are set between the late 1910s and the 1950s, with a few from the 1960s and 70s. They span Black boarding and vocational schools such as Biddle, Calhoun, Bordentown, St. Emma's and the Kansas Vocational Institute, and big-city public programs such as Philadelphia's Mastbaum School and Dunbar High School. Tellers often name the director or teacher who handed them the horn, switched them to another instrument (trumpet to baritone horn, trombone to tuba, cello to viola) or taught them fingering. The repertoire was marches, overtures and classical pieces, with Sousa as a recurring name. Several, including Doc Cheatham and Trummy Young, say jazz was discouraged or banned in school bands. Others praise required school music, especially in Philadelphia, as the foundation for their later careers. The cluster is loosely held together: a few samples are mainly about other things, such as Willcox's whole early career, Jo Jones with a medicine show, or a comment about the Goodman band.
threads: Being handed or switched to an instrument by a band director
Marches, Sousa and classical repertoire, with jazz discouraged
Black boarding and vocational school bands (Biddle, Calhoun, Bordentown)
Philadelphia and big-city school music programs (Mastbaum, Dunbar)
Classmates who later became professionals
Youth orchestras and school-to-college band pathways

communities.name: Going to school: schooling and formal music training
communities.parent_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four collections recount their formal education: the schools they attended, the teachers who shaped them, and whether and where they studied music. The great majority of the stories are about schooling itself, set mostly between the 1910s and the 1970s, with a few later ones from the 1980s and 1990s. Some are plain school lists. Others are about particular high school music programs, such as Major N. Clark Smith's in Chicago, Lanier High and the Wilberforce Collegians. A large group are about conservatory and college choices: Berklee, Juilliard, Manhattan School, USC, Eastman and Virginia State. Tellers differ on whether school helped or hindered. Some got scholarships or ambitious training. Others met a curriculum with no place for jazz, left, or skipped formal study to be on the gig. A few say they had no music training at all before the service or before professional work. The cluster is broad and includes a few off-topic segments, but the shared subject of education runs through most of the samples.
threads: Lists of schools attended and early teachers
High school music programs and band directors
Choosing and entering conservatories and colleges (Berklee, Juilliard, Manhattan School)
Jazz excluded from the curriculum and conflicts with teachers
Skipping or leaving formal study for the gig
Scholarships, parents' wishes and non-music majors

communities.name: Starting on the violin as a child
communities.parent_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, Boston, Houston, Flint, Harlem and elsewhere recall that their first instrument was the violin, usually begun between about six and twelve in the years from the 1890s to the early 1930s. The push often came from a parent, such as a mother who wanted violin rather than piano or drums, or from a school, a nun, or a door-to-door lesson deal that came with a free violin. Teachers range from opera conductors and symphony players to poor or money-minded instructors, and the tellers disagree on quality, with some getting a rigorous classical grounding and others a bad start. Most eventually gave the violin up, either because it was too hard to master, because they disliked it, or because a Black violinist faced limited prospects, and they moved to piano, bass, drums, trombone or saxophone. The stories come from Tulane, Rutgers, Smithsonian and Hamilton interviews and are told by many different players, with only a few appearing twice, so the pattern is widespread rather than the experience of one scene.
threads: Parents and nuns steering a child to violin
Cheap or free lessons and mail-order deals
Classical teachers and school orchestras
Bad teachers and losing interest
Giving up violin for piano, bass or another instrument
Violin seen as limited for a Black musician

communities.name: Boyhood hustles: odd jobs before the music
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the small jobs they worked as children and young teens to earn money and help their families, long before music became a livelihood. The stories span roughly 1900 to 1940, with a few later outliers, and are set in New Orleans, Los Angeles, Tulsa and Muskogee, Charleston, Kansas City and elsewhere. The recurring jobs are selling newspapers, shining shoes, water-boy and delivery work, dishwashing, running errands, hauling junk, picking crops, and factory or grocery chores. Tellers agree that work was expected and the pay tiny: pennies per paper, a dollar a day, a few dollars a week. Some tie the money to a goal such as tuition or Tuskegee, others to family poverty, and a few jobs end in comic or tragic mishaps, like a deducted bicycle or a lost pair of legs. The accounts differ mainly in region and decade, and in whether the work was a stepping stone toward music or simply the texture of a hard childhood. Most tellers are Black musicians from working families, drawn from all four archives.
threads: Selling newspapers and shining shoes
Water boys, delivery boys and errand running
Dishwashing, cafe and factory jobs
Junk hauling, horse-and-wagon hustles and farm picking
Working to pay tuition or support the family

communities.name: Could you read music? Ear versus the page
communities.parent_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear
communities.narrative: Musicians across all four archives talk about whether they, their bandmates and their heroes could read music, and what it cost or gained them. Most stories are set in New Orleans and Chicago from the 1900s to the 1940s. Tellers such as Peter LaCaze, Preston Jackson and Ricard Alexis dispute the idea that uptown players could not read, and say hiring often turned on reading ability. Others, including Bigard, Bauduc and Jimmy McPartland, describe bands that worked by ear: the Wolverines, Johnny Dodds, Buddy Petit. Many tell how they learned to read: in army and brass bands, from method books and teachers, in study circles, or on the job (Punch Miller, Slide Hampton, Tiny Grimes, Nick Brignola). Some regret never learning, like Marian McPartland and Jay McShann, and some admire others who taught themselves, like Trumbauer. The tellers agree that reading and ear both matter. They differ on whether reading was common in early jazz and on whether it helped or hurt a player's feel. Newer interviewees, such as Stefon Harris and Sheryl Bailey, carry the same debate into later decades.
threads: Disputing whether early New Orleans musicians could read
Bands and stars who played by ear (Wolverines, Dodds, Petit)
How musicians learned to read: teachers, method books, army and brass bands
Reading as a hiring test and job skill
Regret at not reading, and self-taught versus trained players
Reading numbered parts and orchestrations on the bandstand

communities.name: Getting a first horn and learning trombone or trumpet
communities.parent_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they came to their first brass instrument: where it came from, who steered them to it, and who taught them. The instrument is usually a cheap, second-hand or improvised acquisition: a $1.50 junk-store cornet, a $6.95 Sears catalog cornet, a $5 neighbour's cornet, a pawn-shop trumpet or trombone, a horn bought by a parent or the band, or a defective instrument handed down by a neighbour. Many describe drifting through other instruments first (violin, drums, cornet, alto horn, ukulele) before settling on trombone or trumpet, often at the urging of a teacher, relative or older player such as Jim Humphrey, Joe Oliver or an uncle. Most are set in the 1900s-1930s, mainly in New Orleans, with others in Chicago, Washington, Texas, New York and Puerto Rico, and a few later stories from the 1950s onward. Tellers agree that family money or musical background was thin and that learning was by ear, from an instruction book, from school or boys' bands, or from a local teacher. They differ in whether the route was formal (school orchestras, lessons, the union) or self-taught. Trombonists are especially prominent, but the theme covers trumpet and cornet players too, so it is a broad starting-out story rather than a single episode.
threads: Buying a cheap or second-hand first cornet, trumpet or trombone
Being steered to trombone or trumpet by a teacher, relative or bandleader
Trying violin, drums or cornet before the final instrument
Learning in school bands, boys' bands and from local teachers
Self-taught by ear or from an instruction book
Early jobs and joining the union after starting

communities.name: Getting a first clarinet or saxophone
communities.parent_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1890s through the 1960s tell how they came to their first reed instrument, usually clarinet and often the saxophone soon after. The instrument arrives through a family or community route: an uncle's or father's old horn, a mother's surprise purchase (Benny Golson's Martin), a $13 pawn-shop C-melody (Von Freeman), a school bandmaster's aptitude test or lodge band, or a newspaper ad for Wurlitzer or Conn. Many tellers started on piano or violin and moved to reed instruments, sometimes to escape piano lessons (Lou Donaldson, Branford Marsalis). Others say a record or a live performance made them want a saxophone: Benny Goodman, Hawkins's Body and Soul, Lionel Hampton and Arnett Cobb, Tab Smith, Coltrane. Teachers appear briefly, whether a neighbor, a band director or a clarinetist, and several people (Donaldson, Brignola, Hubert Laws) taught themselves. The earliest New Orleans and Midwestern players describe small local arrangements. Later bebop and postwar musicians describe buying instruments with scarce money or paper-route savings. The common thread is acquiring the instrument and the first lessons, not the later career.
threads: Hand-me-down and gift horns from uncles, fathers and mothers
Buying a cheap used saxophone or C-melody at a pawn shop or from an ad
Clarinet first, then switching to tenor or alto after hearing Goodman or Hawkins
Escaping piano or violin lessons for a reed instrument
School bands, aptitude tests and first teachers
Teaching oneself from a book or by ear

communities.name: Learning the reed horn: early teachers and self-teaching
communities.parent_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, Little Rock, New York and later generations describe how they first learned clarinet and saxophone: who taught them, what those teachers stressed, and what they had to work out alone. The core stories are set mostly in the 1910s and 1920s. Benny Carter names Eugene Mikell, Rudy Powell and Arthur Reeves, and says Reeves shaped his tone, sound and intonation. Creole-tradition players such as Isidore Barbarin, Joe Darensbourg, Wilbert Tillman and Luke Schiro recall lessons with Charles Sio, Picou, Lorenzo Tio and Dan Sanderson. Hayes Pillars supplies a sharply different account. A white teacher refuses him because he is Black, and another tries to swap horns with him, so he learns fingering, embouchure and reading from an instruction book on his own. Later players such as Anat Cohen and Ray Ricker describe classical teachers who supported or were kept separate from their jazz playing. The tellers agree that early instruction shaped their sound. They differ on whether it came from formal teachers or from solitary effort, and on how race limited access to lessons.
threads: Named early teachers and what they stressed (tone, intonation, breath control)
New Orleans clarinet lineage: Tio, Picou, Sio, Sanderson
Self-taught fingering, embouchure and reading from instruction books
Being refused or exploited by white teachers
Classical training alongside or apart from jazz

communities.name: Early clarinet lessons with local teachers
communities.parent_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they first learned to read and play, mostly on clarinet, from neighborhood and professional teachers in the 1910s and 1920s. New Orleans tellers name Lorenzo Tio as the central figure: Harold Dejan, Don Albert and Albert Nicholas all studied with or alongside him, and Nicholas lists his best-known pupils (Jimmy Noone, Barney Bigard, Omer Simeon). Others describe less famous teachers, such as Santo Giuffre with his strict solfege and Klose method, Manuel Roque the bricklayer, Isadore Fritz giving free lessons, and a cheap two-bit teacher who made pupils hum notes before touching the horn. Some, like Paul Barnes, were largely self-taught or learned from a brother. The tellers agree on strict fundamentals and modest cost. The later outliers, Sol Yaged studying with Simeon Bellison in 1946 and Robert Lewis taking a first lesson from Sidney Bechet in 1947, extend the theme into the 1940s, and Louis Keppard's cornet lessons from Mal Perez and Hippolyte Charles reach back to c. 1900-1910.
threads: Lorenzo Tio and his pupils
Strict fundamentals: solfege, Klose method, theory before the horn
Cheap or free lessons from neighborhood teachers
Self-taught or taught by a brother
Later teachers: Bellison and Bechet in the 1940s

communities.name: Taking lessons: teachers, method books and fees
communities.parent_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations recall how they first learned their instruments through private lessons. The stories are set mostly between 1900 and 1950, chiefly in New Orleans, with others in St. Louis, Chicago and New York. The tellers name their teachers: Papa Tio, Jim Humphrey, Paul Chaligny, Manuel Perez, Manuel Manetta and Dave Perkins in New Orleans, and bandmasters or symphony players elsewhere. They describe the method books (Klose, Arban, Otto, Clodomir), the strict insistence on counting, solfege and reading notes before playing, and the price of a lesson, typically 25 cents to a dollar. Many were already playing by ear and were pushed to learn to read. A few later accounts (Joe Morello, Dave Holland, David Baker, Jaroslav Cimera in Chicago) carry the same subject into the 1930s through the 1980s. The cluster is fairly coherent around lessons, though some samples drift into tangents about bands and early careers.
threads: Papa Tio and Creole teachers in New Orleans
Jim Humphrey, Chaligny and neighborhood professors
Method books and solfege
Lesson fees and strict teaching manner
Learning to read after playing by ear
Later conservatory and private study outside New Orleans

communities.name: Poor boyhood: welfare, odd jobs and early work
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall growing up poor in the 1920s through early 1940s, much of it in the Depression, and the small jobs and family arrangements that kept households going. Robert Pete Williams describes the welfare office, a $12 monthly job and raising his siblings without a father. Benny Golson recalls welfare, government food and hand-me-down clothes, then taking in roomers on Page Street. Jimmy Cobb talks about his parents separating and his mother's domestic work, while he shined shoes, delivered papers and hauled ice. Monk Montgomery quit school at 14 to work a coal and ice shed, then worked with his father unloading produce boxcars, then in an Indianapolis foundry. Others, such as Harry Edison, Tiny Grimes, Budd Johnson and John W. Bubbles, describe farm chores, packing-house, plant and cleaning-shop work. Kenny Davern's nine foster homes extend the theme of unstable homes. The tellers agree on hardship and early wage work, and differ in whether the family stayed together or the father held a job. Music appears only in passing, as a saxophone or records from a neighbor.
threads: Welfare, relief and absent fathers
Mothers' domestic work and raising siblings
Boyhood hustles: shoeshine, papers, ice and coal
Quitting school for wage work in the Depression
Farm, factory and packing-house jobs as teenagers
Foster homes and unstable households

communities.name: Childhood beginnings: first lessons and picking an instrument
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the small, often accidental moments in childhood and adolescence when music first took hold. The stories range from the 1940s to the 1990s and are set in places such as Chicago, Detroit, a small Washington State town, Cuba and Japan. Several tellers grew up in musical households. Gardner had musician parents and insisted on trumpet at nine, Brown's parents played and he picked the saxophone on fifth-grade band day, and Conte watched his father's friend Compay Segundo play at house parties. Others describe a single spark: a kindergarten teacher's praise for Olatuja, Ron Carter hearing a cellist play Dvorak with the Detroit Symphony at fourteen, and Akiyoshi hearing a collector's Teddy Wilson record. Piano, guitar, flute and cello lessons recur, and tellers disagree on whether the path felt planned or chosen for them (Conte "never planned" a music career, while Alexander says the music chooses you). The samples share the early-life origin theme but not one specific event, so this is a loose grouping.
threads: Growing up in a musical family
Choosing an instrument and starting lessons
A single moment that sparked it: a teacher's words, a concert, a record
Discovering jazz as a young listener
Feeling like a late or unplanned starter

bands: University of Michigan Men's Glee Club

communities.name: Musical families: fathers, brothers and relatives who played
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews, mostly in the Tulane collection, mention the relatives who played before them or beside them. The setting is largely New Orleans and its neighbors, in the 1890s to 1930s, with side trips to Chicago, New York and Philadelphia. The most common figure is a father who played cornet, brass band, bass or accordion. Some of those fathers died young, as in Bill Phillips's account around 1906-07, and some played into old age, as in Joe Wilder's account of a father still playing at 88. Others describe brothers, cousins, uncles and aunts: the Santiago siblings teaching one another piano, Picou's younger brother the Creole songwriter, Tommy Ridgley's singing aunts, the Frasier piano family. Many of these are brief family-background asides, often with an interviewer asking for a photograph or an address, so the segments share a theme of kin and music rather than one event. The tellers agree that music ran in families and was learned informally at home, and they differ mainly in which relative they emphasise and how much they remember about that person.
threads: Fathers who played cornet or brass band
Siblings teaching each other instruments
Cousins and brothers in bands in Chicago and New York
Singing aunts, uncles and Creole song traditions
Relatives who died young or never recorded
Interviewers asking for photographs and addresses of kin

communities.name: Neighborhood memories: streets, districts and local lore
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians, mostly New Orleans-born and interviewed for Tulane's Hogan archive, talk about the neighborhood they grew up in or knew: where it was, what it was called, and what it used to be. The stories are set mainly between about 1900 and the 1940s. They cover uptown districts such as Gert Town, Carrollton and Zion City, the French Quarter's changing mix of Mexican, Spanish and Italian residents, Frenchman Street and Washington Square, the filled-in Old Basin on Lafitte Street, and the back-of-town lake districts like Pilot Land. Some tellers add small pieces of lore, such as how a place got its name, streetcar rides to Spanish Fort, or what "the city" meant. The tellers agree only on place-talk and differ in which neighborhood they describe, so this is a loose family of geography and residence recollections. A few samples are fragments or small talk, such as a post-tape remark about where someone lived or the Baton Rouge food and "the city" segment, and they only loosely belong.
threads: Uptown districts: Gert Town, Carrollton, Zion City
French Quarter ethnic neighborhoods and street lore
Vanished geography: the Old Basin, Pilot Land and back-of-town lakes
Streetcar lines and amusements like Spanish Fort
Where I lived: addresses and neighbors

communities.name: Where I grew up: childhood homes and neighborhoods
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from many cities describe the house and neighborhood of their childhood, usually with concrete, almost mapped detail: street names, which houses the family lived in, the nearby school, church or store, and who lived around them. The strongest strand is the old-fashioned household, set in the 1910s to 1930s, with no electricity or gas, a wood stove, lamps, an outhouse or tub baths, and wood to fetch (Curtis Mitchell, John Levy). Others fix a birthplace or move, such as the Irish Channel, Gert Town and the shift out to rural Jefferson Parish, Central Los Angeles, Pontiac, Milwaukee, and Gilmore Alley in Pittsburgh. A few segments are really about a relative or a neighbor: a cabinet-maker uncle, a stepfather, a famous neighbor's family on Elmira Street. The tellers agree on the practice of locating themselves precisely, and differ in setting, from New Orleans, where most of the facets point, to Midwestern and West Coast cities, and in whether the home was poor, middle-class or just plain. Little music appears; the stories are about place and household rather than about playing. Tellers come from all four collections and are mostly New Orleans-born or American-born players of the 1910s to 1950s.
threads: Houses without electricity: wood stoves, lamps, outhouses
Pinning down the birthplace and street

communities.name: Where I was born and grew up in New Orleans
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians, mostly interviewed by Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive, answer the interviewer's opening biographical question: where were you born, which street did you live on, and which neighborhood did you grow up in. The answers are short and address-heavy, naming streets such as Liberty, Tulane Avenue, Magazine, Charter, Touro and Columbus, and wards and districts such as the Seventh Ward, Tremé, the Irish Channel, Algiers, the Garden District and the French Quarter. Most are set between the 1880s and the 1930s. Tellers often add which musicians lived nearby, so the neighborhood doubles as a map of who played where: Buddy Bolden's First Street, the Tios, Picou and Big Eye Louis in the Seventh Ward, and George Lewis in McDonoghville. Some tellers mention family origins, moves after marriage, or how a street was renamed. A few samples drift to other places or topics, including San Francisco's changes, Baton Rouge geography, Cosimo Matassa's studio move, and a general comment on how the city has changed. The tellers agree that childhood places were close-knit and musical, and differ mainly in uptown versus downtown and Creole versus Anglo neighborhoods.

communities.name: Records at home: how childhood listening started
communities.parent_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening
communities.narrative: Musicians describe how jazz first reached them as children, usually through a parent's or sibling's record collection, the radio, or television. The records range from 78s of Armstrong, Ellington and Basie to Brubeck, Monk and Charlie Parker LPs. The tellers are mostly postwar-born players who grew up in the 1950s to 1970s, with a few earlier voices from the 1920s to 1940s, such as Red Norvo's Edison records and Norman Simmons's player piano. Parents and older siblings appear as the gatekeepers: some were amateur singers or musicians, others simply loved big bands. Several tellers tie that early listening to a first instrument or to the moment they decided to be a musician, while others (Ted Piltzecker, Sherrie Maricle) say there was no single aha moment. A few samples drift to adjacent stories, such as Mickey Roker's Army drumming, Dan Morgenstern's escape from Austria, and Marty Morell's rock and roll revue. The core is consistent, but the edges are loose, and the large Hamilton share suggests an interview prompt about early influences.

Radio and TV discoveries of jazz and big bands

communities.name: First jazz records and the albums that hooked us
communities.parent_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening
communities.narrative: Musicians from many generations recall the first jazz they actually heard or bought, and how a particular record or live encounter turned a passing interest into a calling. The most common object is the record itself: Kind of Blue (via a Columbia Record Club freebie, a friend's dumped cassette, or a seventh-grade teacher), Horace Silver and Milt Jackson sides, Brubeck's Time Out, the Mulligan tentet, and Sweets Edison's album bought for the cover. Earlier tellers such as William Russell and Geoff Bull describe 78s, cheap Paramounts, reissues and early discographies, while later ones (Michi Fuji, Derek Brown, Orrin Evans) start from CDs, Kenny G or show tunes. Miles Davis, Coltrane, Parker and Brubeck recur as the figures who made the connection. Tellers agree on the sudden, formative impact and on borrowed or cheap sources like neighbors, uncles, record clubs and village stores, and differ mainly by era and format. A minority of samples drift to pop and rock listening, live shows, or Latin jazz, so the cluster is only loosely unified.

Record clubs, cheap 78s and borrowed LPs
Hearing Miles, Coltrane or Brubeck for the first time

communities.name: Growing up on the radio and records
communities.parent_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they first came to jazz as children and teenagers: through the radio, a family record collection, or an older relative's 78s, rather than through formal teaching. Most stories are set in the 1930s and 1940s, when big-band remotes from Chicago's Grand Terrace and New York hotels, disc jockeys and network broadcasts of Ellington, Basie, Goodman and Hines were the main source. Tellers like Jimmy Jones, Dorothy Donegan, Wilbur Ware, Clark Terry and Billy Taylor describe staying up late, hiding a radio, or building a crystal set. Others hear it elsewhere: Candido Camero on Cuban radio, Jim Galloway on AFN and Voice of America, Gunther Schuller after arriving from Germany. Later-born players (Kirchner, LaBarbera, Liebman, Caputo, Smulyan) found jazz through 1950s-60s TV scores, 45s, rock and roll and AM radio. Most households were not musical, and a parent, uncle, brother or friend's records often opened the door. A few samples drift into school bands, record production anecdotes or unrelated asides.

Family record collections and relatives' 78s

communities.name: Deciding on music and what the family said
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the moment they chose music over another path, and how their parents and relatives reacted. The settings run from the 1920s to about 1971, and the tellers include New Orleans players, swing-era horn men, bandleaders, and later jazz and academy-trained musicians. The family trades on offer are plastering, a ranch, electrical work, engineering, medicine, law and a math scholarship. Some families were supportive or left the choice to the child (Alden, Morell, Barnet, Chico Freeman's father). Others objected or doubted it (Chico Freeman's mother, Vi Redd's father, Cobb's mother, the mothers who warned girls away from Wild Bill Davison). A few tellers drifted into music because older brothers or a lucky accident pointed the way (Urbie Green, Vic Dickenson). The shared thread is the career decision and the family's attitude, but the stories do not all concern one event, so the cluster is only loosely unified. A couple of samples, such as Lorraine Gordon wanting art school and Monk Montgomery's reflection, are only tangentially related.

communities.name: Growing up in a musical family
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall the household they grew up in and how music first entered it: a father's weekend or wedding-party band, a grandmother who taught piano, an uncle at the keyboard at Sunday dinners, a godfather's band, records and a record player. Most are set between the 1930s and the 1960s, in many places, and a strong share tell of Italian, Slovak or Austro-Hungarian immigrant families, where feast bands, polka bands, opera and folk songs were the first music they heard. The tellers agree that music was simply in the house and often led directly to a first instrument, such as drums at four or eight, trumpet like Dad, or a borrowed trombone. They differ on how the family felt about it. Some parents nurtured it, some tried to steer the child away from music or saw jazz as youth rebellion, and a few came from families that were not musical at all, with only a neighbor's bells or a bombed piano as the spark. Tellers range from New Orleans and swing-era players to rock-jazz and contemporary musicians, so the pattern holds across generations.

communities.name: My father's work and growing up in the household
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from many collections and regions recall their fathers' livelihoods and the family conditions they grew up in. The fathers' jobs run from pie-wagon selling in the 1890s riverfront, fur buying and a gambling house in Mobile, hotel and club waiting, and a music store in Moline, to society-party playing in Los Angeles and farming 365 acres. Tellers describe whether the family was poor or comfortable, with Chico Hamilton and Stuart Bergen at opposite ends of that range. They mix in household and neighborhood details such as chores, food, aunts and uncles, nicknames and summers with grandparents. The stories are set mostly between 1900 and 1940, in places from Havana to Peoria to the Mississippi riverfront. What they share is a childhood seen through the father's occupation and the family's circumstances, but there is no single event or place that unites them, so the cluster is loose.

communities.name: Birth dates, ages and missing records
communities.parent_name: Opening the tape: name, birth date and birthplace
communities.narrative: These are mostly short, factual stretches at the start of interviews (and some interviews with widows or relatives) where the speaker, or a family member speaking for a late musician, pins down a birth date, an age at death, or a spouse's or parent's dates. They are mostly set between the 1880s and the 1930s, and almost all come from Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive. The tellers agree that the official date is often unreliable. Birth certificates burned in a courthouse fire, a family Bible was lost in a flood, a christening came years after the birth, and a census clerk assigned the wrong year. They differ in what is at stake: a union card, Social Security proof, or simply getting the interview's biographical record straight. A few segments are plain intake details (name, pronunciation, birthplace, a later arrival in America) with no dispute at all. This is more a recurring interview ritual than a single story, so the shared subject is loose and the cluster is only moderately coherent.

communities.name: The family piano and a musical home
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from all four collections recall the household where they first met music: a piano or pump organ in the parlor, a mother or grandmother who played hymns or taught lessons, and a family that sang, played by ear or filled the house with visiting players. Most stories are set between about 1905 and 1940, in Black and white homes from Georgia and Baltimore to New Orleans, Pittsburgh and Texas. Mothers are the central figure for many tellers (Mary Lou Williams, Kenny Clarke, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, Benny Waters, Sam Wooding), while others stress fathers, siblings or uncles (Horace Henderson, Malachi, Carla Bley). Players and tellers differ on how the instrument arrived: a gift or purchase, a player piano with rolls, or a broken upright. They also differ on whether the family encouraged a career or discouraged it, as Basie's and Collins's mothers did. A few samples drift to other topics, such as music school, a first band, dance lessons or later-life reflections, but the shared core is the instrument and the family at home in early childhood.

communities.name: First piano lessons: teachers, rulers and playing by ear
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from all four collections tell how they first came to the piano, mostly as children between about 1905 and 1940. The usual story is a modest start: a neighbor's or grandmother's piano, a mother's organ, a house-call teacher charging fifty cents, a nun, a school principal or a local "professor". The tellers differ on whether the lessons helped. Some praise a teacher or a method book (Czerny, Hanon, Matthews). Many remember harshness, such as a ruler or slap on the hands or a mother's miserable teaching, and they quit or resent teachers afterward. Others had little or no formal training and taught themselves by ear, from records, player pianos, siblings or other musicians, often because the family could not pay. For several of them, including drummers, bassists and horn players, piano was only a first or secondary instrument. A few later samples (Herbie Hancock, Cedar Walton, Tom Varner) move into the 1940s to 1970s. The cluster also holds a few loosely related segments, such as sandlot baseball, terrible Memphis pianos, an interview opening and a piano-for-theory story.

communities.name: Childhood piano lessons at home and church
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how they first came to the piano as children, mostly in the 1910s through the 1940s, with a few later or earlier outliers (Sippie Wallace around 1905, Jack DeJohnette and Bobby Hutcherson in the late 1940s). The usual setting is the family home or church: a mother who sang in the choir or played at home, a piano or pump organ in the house, and lessons arranged by a parent, grandmother, aunt or visiting teacher. Tellers like Hank Jones, JJ Johnson, Urbie Green and Mose Allison describe lessons, their cost and the daily practice parents insisted on. Others, such as Tiny Grimes, Sugarboy Crawford, Harry Edison and Kenny Clarke, learned by ear or taught themselves, and some resisted or were denied formal study. Harsh or eccentric teachers (Sheila Jordan's great aunt, DeJohnette's first teacher, Bobby Hutcherson's aunt) and church-versus-secular tension recur. A few segments drift to other instruments, such as Louie Bellson's drums, Hubert Laws's mellophone and Jack Teagarden's dislike of the piano, so the cluster is clear in its core but loose at the edges.

communities.name: Parents' reaction to a music career
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians recall how their parents responded when it became clear that music was to be a living rather than a hobby. The stories run from the 1930s to the 1990s and come from a wide mix of players, including big-band veterans, bebop-era figures, and later women instrumentalists and singers. Most parents begin with a safer ambition: a doctor, lawyer, farmer, minister, or a steady trade. They worry about insecurity, the road, and dance halls or jazz clubs, and fathers are often the stronger objectors while mothers more often support, persuade, or drive. Many tellers describe a turning point that won the family over: joining the union and earning money, a first road job, a Broadway sub gig, or a parent seeing them play. A few families were supportive from the start, and some parents never fully accepted a choice such as leaving college. Women tellers add a gendered note, with fathers appalled at a daughter playing in dance halls or jazz.

communities.name: A musical family: who played what at home
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians asked about their family backgrounds list the relatives who played music, usually in the first decades of the twentieth century and often in New Orleans. The stories are mostly inventories: a father on guitar, violin or banjo, a grandfather on violin or cello, uncles and brothers on reeds, brass or drums, and a mother or aunts who sang or played piano or guitar. Several tellers describe whole family bands, such as the Christophe string band, the Durham Brothers and Dixie Ramblers, Montgomery's family band, and a brass band led by a father or father-in-law. Some say the family was not musical at all, or that only one relative played. Others, such as Lanoix and Fontenet, mention only a guitar-playing parent or a relative who bought a first instrument. The tellers come from every collection, but most are New Orleans players from the Tulane interviews. Rutgers interviewees, including swing-era and Midwestern players, tell the same kind of story. A few segments drift into the family tree itself, with the interviewer straightening out the Catos, or into later anecdotes such as Jay McShann visiting.

communities.name: Musical fathers, brothers and relatives at home
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians asked about their families answer by listing who played what at home. The stories are mostly set in early twentieth-century New Orleans, from about 1900 to the 1950s, with a few later outliers. The usual cast is a father who played an instrument (guitar, clarinet, trumpet, homemade flute, alto horn in a reserve brass band), an older brother who played drums, sousaphone or piano, and uncles or cousins who played music. Several tellers, among them Kid Thomas Valentine, Lawrence Marrero, Cie Frazier and Slow Drag Pavageau, trace their own start in brass bands or jazz to these relatives. Some tellers stress that the household was full of music. Others say music was only a sideline: Albert Burbank's father painted, and Don Albert's father was a cigar maker with a fine voice. Sonny Rollins goes further and argues that musical talent is genetic rather than learned. Benny Golson and Wendell Brunious talk about younger families, such as the Bryant brothers and Wendell's trumpet-playing brother John. The segments are brief genealogical answers to family-background questions, not a single event, so the story is a recurring answer more than a narrative.

communities.name: Growing up with parents and family music
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from many interviews describe their parents and home life as the starting point of their musical lives. The dominant version is a musical household: a songwriter father (Bill Charlap), a playwright father and opera-singer mother with home cabarets (Orrin Evans), a father who air-conducted the Vienna Philharmonic (Karolina Strassmayer), and a father who made home movies and practiced piano (Catherine Russell). A second strand stresses the opposite: families with no professional musicians, such as a ballet-teacher mother (Gary Smulyan), parents who were not in show business (Nancy Wilson), or a non-musician father who could comp chords (Gary Burton). Others describe family pressure to practice (Branford Marsalis), a mother who could not understand jazz (Nat Hentoff), or extended New Orleans families (Kent Jordan). Most of the stories are set between the 1930s and 1970s, mostly in New York and Louisiana, and are told mainly by musicians interviewed at Hamilton and the Smithsonian. A few samples drift into other territory, such as Dan Morgenstern's travels to Denmark and Vienna and a mother's account of her daughter's band, so the cluster is a loose family-background theme and not a single tightly bounded story.
threads: Artistic or musical parents and home performances
Non-musical families and parents who were not in the business

communities.name: Music in the family: parents, uncles and the home parlor
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Asked early in their interviews about family background, musicians describe who in their households played and what music filled the home. Most stories are set between roughly 1889 and 1930, mainly in New Orleans but also in Detroit, Michigan and elsewhere. Fathers, uncles and grandparents turn up as brass-band trumpeters, tuba players, fiddlers, flutists and violinists. Mothers and sisters appear as guitarists, pianists, singers and vocal teachers, and homes held pump organs, zithers, washboards and family quartets. The tellers differ on whether music ran in the family. La Rocca, Barker, Marrero and Bushell name musical relatives who gave them instruments, while Wilbert Tillman and Howard Johnson say there were no real musicians at home. Some tellers add details of family origins, such as Mooney Martin's uncle born in slavery or Tillman's account of uptown Carrollton. The stories come from New Orleans players and from musicians of the swing and later generations in the Rutgers and Hamilton collections.

communities.name: Music in the childhood home: parents and siblings
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from many backgrounds describe the household they grew up in and the music that was already there before they played professionally. Fathers who played a little trumpet, led a band, sang on amateur nights or sold pianos appear again and again. Mothers play piano, sing duets, love dancing or play folk guitar, and siblings sing, dance or become musicians' first company. Some homes are explicitly musical, with parents in vaudeville or show business, a family band, or an upright piano hauled through the window. Others offer only a mixed musical diet of opera broadcasts, Broadway tunes, radio and church, or divided family backgrounds, as with Bela Fleck and Roscoe Mitchell. The tellers broadly agree that home was where music first became ordinary and expected. They differ in whether the family was trained and professional or merely musical in an informal way. A few segments drift into adjacent material, such as early gigs, the Army or New Orleans theaters, so the cluster is anchored by childhood family life rather than a single event. Tellers come from every collection and decade, but the New Orleans and 1910s-1920s accounts are most tied to local bands and venues.
