communities.name: Where and when I was born
communities.parent_name: Opening the tape: name, birth date and birthplace
communities.narrative: These are the opening biographical answers of interviews: musicians stating their birth date, birthplace and sometimes the street or house, their parents, and the neighborhood they grew up in. Most are New Orleans musicians born between about 1893 and 1912, and they locate themselves precisely, for example Palmyra and Roman Streets, the French Quarter, Barracks and St. Claude, Carrollton, or the plantations downriver such as Deer Range and Magnolia. A few were born elsewhere (Versailles, Kentucky; Baton Rouge; Charleston; St. Bernard Parish) and then describe moving to New Orleans or Chicago. Several tie the birth account to first musical surroundings: brass bands, dance halls, funeral parades, church, or neighbors who played. Details vary: some give family facts such as a midwife grandmother, French-speaking parents or a spouse, while others move quickly into early music-making. The tellers are mostly Tulane interviewees answering the standard first question, so the cluster is shaped by interview structure as much as by a shared event. Coherence is moderate because the samples share the birth-statement form rather than one story.

communities.name: Family, origins and growing up before jazz
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers early-life recollections from musicians born roughly between 1900 and 1930, told before their music careers begin. The tellers describe parents, grandparents and stepparents, what those relatives did for work (railroad porter, longshoreman, cobbler, Sanitary Department clerk, farmer, preacher), and where the family came from. Small-town and rural settings recur: Mount Sterling, Kentucky; Beardstown and its river floods; Mississippi; a ranch with oil struck on it. Some tellers go back a generation to slavery, Cherokee ancestry, or an orphaned father with obscure origins. Others tell of family breakups, adoption, being raised by grandparents, or leaving the farm. A few segments are personal asides, such as Jimmy Scott's Kallmann Syndrome and Eddie Durham's rattlesnake hunting. The tellers share the genre of childhood and family background but not one event, so it works as a loose grouping rather than a single story.

communities.name: What my parents thought of my becoming a musician
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from the 1910s to the 1990s recall how their families reacted when they chose jazz as a career. The most common older version is religious and moral. Churchgoing parents, deacons and grandmothers called jazz the devil's music, and fathers feared musicians were drunkards or dope fiends. Doc Cheatham, Hubert Laws, Carter Benny, Danny Barker and Red Norvo tell it this way. Fathers often wanted a respectable profession instead, such as doctor, minister, theologian, violinist or university graduate. Many of these stories end in acceptance, which usually came once the musician earned money, sent some home or proved steady. Bill Mays's father decided his son had become a minister through music, and Laws's father cried at Amazing Grace. Other tellers, including Frank Foster, Ralph Humphrey and Jane Ira Bloom, describe parents who simply supported them or found the path a mystery. Mothers are often the supporters and fathers the doubters. Later, younger players describe indifference or a fallback-career condition rather than moral condemnation. Nearly all the tellers are different people (66 interviews across all four collections), so this is a widely shared experience rather than one person's anecdote.

communities.name: Musical families: brothers, cousins and in-laws
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians asked about their kin, usually by an interviewer working through a family tree, name the relatives who also played and what instruments they took up. The stories are mostly set in New Orleans between about 1900 and 1950, with spillover to Chicago, Texas, California and New York. Tellers list brothers, sisters, uncles, cousins, nephews, half brothers and in-laws, and often untangle how interlinked families such as the Barbarins, Marreros, Fraziers, Santiagos and Millers are related. Some tellers have a large web of musical relatives, as Danny Barker, Emile Barnes and Cie Frazier do. Others, like Joseph Ralph Robinson, Lizzie Miles and Milton Batiste, say that few or none of their family played, or that they are unrelated to musicians who share their surname. The segments are short genealogical exchanges rather than anecdotes. They come from Tulane's Hogan archive and the other collections, and from New Orleans players of several generations. A few segments drift to related questions such as other musicians in the neighborhood, a family bathhouse, or interview contact details.

communities.name: Brothers in the band: kinship and quarrels
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians talk about siblings, and occasionally sons and cousins, who played music alongside them or in the same circles. The stories range across roughly the 1910s to the 1990s and span New Orleans, New York, Los Angeles and the big-band world. Some tellers simply trace a family tree, as Leonard Bocage does with his brother's clarinet, his nephews and a cousin's son, and as Horace White does with the Matthews brothers of the parade bands. Many others dwell on friction: the Lindsay brothers who could not get along, Wilbur and Sidney De Paris airing old grievances at a Savoy rehearsal, Happy Caldwell's list of quarrelling band brothers, Arnett Cobb's account of Illinois Jacquet mistreating Russell, and Horace Henderson denying any resentment toward Fletcher. Against these, Al Gallodoro says his brothers respected each other and Abe Most describes reconciling with Sam after years apart. The tellers are mostly sidemen and bandleaders talking about other musicians' families, with one outlier about a famous father's pressure on the Brubeck sons. They agree that blood ties both brought musicians into bands and strained them once money, leadership or credit was at stake.

communities.name: Parents and family: who raised me
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians describe the parents, stepparents, siblings and grandparents who shaped them before they turned professional. The portraits are mostly of mothers and fathers: a mother who was gentle, hard-working and proud, or a father who was a carpenter, a mechanic, an instrument seller or a weekend clarinetist in the Elks band. Most are set between the 1910s and the 1940s, in places such as Chicago, Cleveland, Pittsburgh, Philadelphia and Havana. The tellers agree on the basic move of naming the family and saying what each parent did and was like. They differ in how music enters the story. For some it runs through the family, as with a conductor father and flamenco mother, or a grandfather who played with James Reese Europe. For others the parents had no musical role, or never heard the player live. Some tellers also bring in a protector or a lost sibling, such as Mary Lou Williams's gambler stepfather or Alberta Hunter's sister who died young. The segments come from all four archives and from 61 different interviews, so this is a standard early-life opening more than a single event. Because the samples are short family sketches that do not tell one shared incident, the grouping is real but loose.
threads: Portraits of mothers: kindness, hard work and pride
Fathers' trades and side-gigs: mechanic, carpenter, instrument seller
Musical families and relatives who played with famous bandleaders
Stepparents, siblings and grandparents who shaped them
Parents who never heard them play, or did not object to show business

communities.name: Growing up: my parents' work and our household
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Across nearly two hundred interviews, musicians describe the family they grew up in before music took over, mostly in the 1910s through the 1930s. The dominant subject is the parents' livelihood and character: fathers who were lumber inspectors, Studebaker mechanics, county agents, drayers, haulers, railroad freight workers, asphalt layers, shoemakers or small-business owners, and mothers who did laundry or domestic work, ran the home, or insisted that the children stay in school. Tellers often describe a father as a model of discipline and self-education, and sometimes as absent, brutal or lost early to death or divorce. Some stories turn to the household that results, with grandparents, aunts and uncles, stepfathers and foster homes raising the children, and siblings sharing chores. The cluster is set in many places (Texas, Chicago, New Orleans, New York, Arizona) and includes immigrant and refugee backgrounds, such as Morgenstern's Vienna boyhood and LaBarbera's Sicilian grandfather. The tellers agree on poverty, hard work and the weight of a parent's example, and differ on whether home was warm and stable or broken. Several samples drift into adjacent topics (language loss, a family florist business, the Nazi threat), so the common thread is loose rather than tight.
threads: Fathers' jobs and characters: mechanics, laborers, county agents, preachers
Mothers' labor: laundry, domestic work, keeping boys in school
Broken homes: parental death, divorce, foster care, stepfathers
Raised by grandparents, aunts and uncles
Family businesses and chores for the parents
Immigrant and displaced family backgrounds

communities.name: Where the family came from: grandparents and ancestry
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians open their life stories by telling who their people were: grandmothers and grandfathers, great-grandparents, and the parents' home towns and marriages. Most of these accounts look back to the 1800s and early 1900s, to the Deep South and the Southwest (Mississippi, Alabama, Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Georgia, Missouri), and to the migrations that took families to Pittsburgh, Chicago, Kansas City and Los Angeles. Many tellers, including Milt Hinton, Abbey Lincoln, Milton Batiste and J. C. Higginbotham, describe grandparents born into slavery, with vivid family anecdotes such as a smallpox quarantine, a grandmother whose lips were stitched, or a plantation name that survives in the family. Others, including Charles Lloyd, Jay McShann, Gene Ramey, John Simmons and Dorothy Donegan, stress Cherokee, Choctaw, Comanche or other Native ancestry, and sometimes a land claim that was missed. A smaller group of tellers trace parents and siblings, stepfathers and mothers' second marriages, or a mother's work as a teacher. A few non-Black tellers, such as Marian McPartland, James Lincoln Collier and Avakian George, tell European, New England or Armenian lineages. The tellers share the genealogical framing and the family-story tone. They differ in how far back they can go and how much was passed down. A handful of segments drift away from family into interview mechanics or other topics, such as a re-recording, a nonprofit and a magazine's ownership.
threads: Grandparents born into slavery and what they passed down
Native American (Cherokee, Choctaw, Comanche) ancestry and land claims
Parents' origins, marriages and stepfathers
Migration from the South to Pittsburgh, Chicago, Kansas City and Los Angeles
European and immigrant lineages
Family anecdotes, nicknames and the origin of a name

communities.name: Naming parents and siblings at the interview's start
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Across 68 interviews, musicians answer the interviewer's routine biographical opening: who were your parents, and how many brothers and sisters did you have? Phil Woods, Marian McPartland, Gunther Schuller, Von Freeman, Hank Jones, Chico Hamilton, Budd Johnson, Mary Lou Williams and many others recite mothers' maiden names, fathers' names, birth order, siblings who died as infants, and sometimes aunts, uncles and cousins. Most are set in the 1910s and 1920s, with places such as Kansas City, New Orleans and St. Louis, but the geography matters less than the genealogy itself. The tellers largely agree on the format: short, factual lists, often at the start of a reel or after a break. They differ in depth. Some give only names, while others add colour, such as Higginbotham's sister listing 14 children, Dan Morgenstern's father's novels, or McPartland joking about a cousin joining the Hare Krishnas. A few edge cases drift into photo identification (Danny Barker), a printer's trombonist uncle (Sonny Williams) or a recent move to New Orleans (Babe Stovall), but these still revolve around kin. The stories come from New Orleans, Kansas City, New York and Midwest players, and from Tulane, Rutgers, Smithsonian and Hamilton collections alike. They matter as a genealogical record rather than as narratives.
threads: Parents' names and birthplaces
Sibling lists and birth order
Children who died young
Aunts, uncles, cousins and extended kin
Family photos and relatives of other musicians

communities.name: Where the family came from: names and ancestry
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians from New Orleans, the Northeast, the West Coast and beyond answer the interviewer's opening questions about family origins: who their parents and grandparents were, where the family came from, and how the surname got its shape. The stories are mostly undated and drawn from early-life or genealogy portions of the interviews. Many trace immigrant roots, such as Albanian and Sicilian (Schiro), Lebanese (Shiner), German under the French flag (the Brunies/Bruenies spellings), and French (Barbarin, Cottrell). Others describe mixed American and Caribbean ancestry: Indian, Mohawk, Coeur d'Alene, Irish, Mexican, Scottish, Ashanti and Barbadian strands (Durham, Callender, Higginbotham, Leeman, Norvo's account of his wife). Slide Hampton and Higginbotham's family bring in slavery, a slave owner's surname and a family Bible. Tellers differ in how much they know. Some, like Barbarin, know little, while Callender and Leeman have worked out family trees. A few segments are bare name-and-parents lists, with no wider story.
threads: Immigrant roots and spelling of the family name
Mixed heritage: Indian, Irish, Scottish, African strands
Slavery, surnames and family records
Naming parents and grandparents, namesakes and juniors
Family reunions and genealogy research

communities.name: Where I was born and who my people were
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: Musicians open their interviews by giving the basics of their origins: birth date and place, parents' names and jobs, siblings, and where the family came from. The stories are set mostly between about 1902 and 1932, across Chicago, New Orleans, the Carolinas, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Columbus and other places, and the tellers come from all four archives. Many describe a childhood shaped by hardship or loss. Amos White and Steve Brown were orphaned, Jimmie Crawford and Theodore Saunders were raised by grandparents or an older sister, and Howard McGhee and Jeff Riddick lost parents early. Others stress that nobody in the family was musical (Harry Edison, Monk Montgomery), while a few mention a musical parent such as Chauncey Morehouse's pianist father, Mary Lou Williams's mother or Basie's mother. The shared move is the biographical preamble that interviewers prompt for. Some tellers add migration details, such as the family's move to Chicago or the North Carolina and Savannah streams. The cluster is broad and is held together by the genre of the opening biography rather than by any one event. A few samples drift to adjacent topics: the Decca session, the Streckfus family boat business and Lillie Delk Christian's start in entertainment.
threads: Birth date, place and parents' names and jobs
Orphaned or raised by grandparents and relatives
Family migration to Chicago, the North and other cities
Ancestry, grandparents and family origins in the South
No one in the family was musical
Siblings and a household with a musical parent

communities.name: Where I was born: birth, parents and siblings
communities.parent_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth
communities.narrative: This is the opening-of-the-life-story ritual that nearly every interviewer begins with: the musician states his or her name, birth date and birthplace, then names the parents, where they came from, and the brothers and sisters. The tellers span New Orleans traditional players such as Alton Purnell, Clem Raymond and Louis Nelson, and bebop and postwar figures such as Sonny Rollins, Percy Heath, Roy Haynes, Benny Golson and Elvin Jones. Most were born between the 1880s and the 1930s, with a few later, in places from Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi to Harlem, Philadelphia, Pontiac, Council Bluffs, Surrey and Kyushu. Common details include parents' Southern or Caribbean origins (Barbados, the Virgin Islands, Vicksburg, South Carolina), twins and large families, uncertain or discrepant birthdates, changed birth names, and whether anyone in the family played music. The tellers differ mainly in whether music runs in the family: cornet-playing fathers, accordion, harmonica and fiddle on one side, and "nobody in my family was musical" on the other. Some segments drift into early moves, a father's trade, or the first teachers, but the birth-and-family frame dominates.
threads: Name, birth date and birthplace stated for the record
Parents' names, origins and occupations
Siblings, twins and family size
Migration and moves in childhood (Southern roots, relocation west or north)
Musical or non-musical family background
Disputed birthdates and birth names

communities.name: Closing thanks and sign-offs at the end of interviews
communities.parent_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview
communities.narrative: This cluster gathers the last minutes of interviews, when the interviewer wraps up and the musician says goodbye. The 55 interviews come from all four collections (Hamilton is the largest, with Tulane, Smithsonian and Rutgers also present), and most segments have no stated period. The common moves are the interviewer thanking the musician, the musician thanking the interviewer or the archive, and an invitation to add final words. Some tellers add brief personal touches: Fuller hopes the project will help listeners, Chubby Jackson pays tribute to his wife, Mead hopes to play to 95, Owens says he is lucky to be paid for what he loves, and Wilson mentions his religious faith. A few segments carry project credits, such as the NEA and Jazz Interactions, or transcription credits. Souchon's remarks on the acceptance of jazz in New Orleans and Papa Jack Laine's fire company story are the only ones with real topical content, and they are incidental to the closing. What unites the cluster is the interview mechanics of the ending, not any shared subject matter in the musicians' lives.
threads: Interviewer thanks the musician and the recording ends
Musician thanks the interviewer, archive or project
Final words of wisdom and hopes for the music
Personal tributes: family, faith and gratitude for a musical life
Project and funding credits, transcription notes
